result.synthesis:
# Gateway battery backup — recommendation

## 1. Direct answer

**Partly, and not as currently specified.**

Yes, the box can carry its own cells and ride out a mains cut. No, it does not "charge like a phone," and no, the current spec does not deliver this at the tier anyone will actually buy.

Current spec status: the UPS battery HAT (~$25) appears **only in Tier C** ($180–240). Tier B — the doc's own "pilot workhorse" — has PoE and no battery. Yet §1's comparison table advertises the Gateway generically as "on PoE, battery-backed," and the one-line pitch at the top of the doc says it "survives power cuts." **Those two statements are false for the tier we will ship most of.** They will be falsified in front of a customer. Fix the copy or fix the BOM; do not ship both as written.

Two other defects in the same table, since parts get ordered from it: Tier B's line items sum to **$93–113**, not the stated $95–120. And "$25 UPS HAT" is board-only on every candidate part — cells are not included.

## 2. "Charges like a phone" is the wrong mental model

A phone is a **cycling** device: charge to 100%, discharge to ~20%, repeat daily, ~500 cycles over its life. A wall-mounted gateway is a **float** device: it sits at or near full charge, permanently, for years, in a warm enclosure, and discharges perhaps 10–30 times in its entire service life.

The failure mode is therefore **calendar aging, not cycle life**. Cycle-life spec sheets are close to noise here — we will consume under ~100 cycles in ten years, which is inside even a mediocre Li-ion cell's rating. What kills the pack is sitting at high state-of-charge at elevated temperature. Reference data for cobalt-blend Li-ion: ~80% capacity retained after one year at 25 °C/100% charge, ~65% at 40 °C/100% charge. A sealed box above a ceiling tile runs 15–25 °C above room ambient.

**Correct behaviour: charge, then stop. Do not hold a continuous float.**

- Charge to ~3.45–3.50 V/cell (LFP), terminate, and let the pack rest.
- Re-top from coulomb count at ~70–80% SoC — **not** from open-circuit voltage. LFP's plateau spans ~3.29–3.33 V across roughly 20–80% SoC, so millivolt-level sense error maps to tens of percent of charge. An OCV-triggered recharge threshold is unusable on this chemistry.
- If a maintenance voltage is unavoidable, hold **3.30–3.35 V/cell**, not 3.65 V (that is the charge-termination voltage) and not 3.45 V.
- Specify charger hysteresis explicitly. A charger that re-tops every time the cell relaxes a few millivolts accumulates thousands of invisible micro-cycles.
- Mandatory BMS charge lockout **below 0 °C and above ~45 °C**. The enclosure is uncontrolled at both ends.

Also: do not reuse a lead-acid/AGM charge profile. Its periodic equalisation stage (14.4–15.5 V on a 4S bus = 3.60–3.875 V/cell) sits at or above LFP termination, and its negative temperature compensation raises voltage when cold — the opposite of what LFP needs.

## 3. Recommended configuration

**Chemistry: LiFePO4.** Justified on calendar-life-at-float and thermal-runaway severity, **not** on cycle life (irrelevant here) and not on runaway onset alone (LFP ~256 °C vs NMC ~198 °C measured start-of-runaway — a real margin, not a categorical difference). The decisive argument is that in nail-penetration and low-SoC thermal abuse testing, LFP cells did not enter runaway at all, and LFP decomposition releases far less heat and gas with no cathode oxygen release. For a box screwed to a wall in an occupied venue, that is the argument that matters.

Accept the density penalty honestly: small-format LFP is ~110–130 Wh/kg and ~250–300 Wh/L against ~240 Wh/kg and ~685 Wh/L for an NMC 18650 — roughly 2× by mass, 2.5× by volume.

**Cells: 4× LFP 26650, 3000 mAh, 1S4P.** Note that LFP **18650** cells are a trap — merchant parts are 1100–1500 mAh (~3.5–4.8 Wh), and "1800 mAh 18650 LFP" listings are not credible against LFP's energy density. 26650 is the honest small-format LFP part.

**Arithmetic (Tier C, dual BLE radios, no LTE):**

```
Gross pack     4 × 3.0 Ah × 3.2 V             = 38.4 Wh
Usable derate  × 0.78  (3.0 V cutoff, aging,
                        cold, BMS quiescent)  = 30.0 Wh
Boost 3.2→5 V  × 0.86                         = 25.8 Wh delivered at 5 V

Load (measure this — see §8):
  Tier B, Pi 4, shed          ~3.0 W → 8.6 h
  Tier C, CM4, dual BLE       ~5.0 W → 5.2 h
  Tier C + LTE transmitting   ~6.5 W → 4.0 h
```

**Design figure: 5 hours at Tier C, unshed.** Not "rides out a power cut" open-endedly. Cost-down option: 2× 26650 = 19.2 Wh gross → ~12.9 Wh delivered → ~2.6 h at 5 W. That is a clean-shutdown-plus-short-outage budget, not an event-length one.

**UPS board approach — this is the honest gap.** There is no off-the-shelf UPS HAT that gives us LFP, ~38 Wh, CM4/CM5 carrier compatibility, and host-readable state of charge:

- **Sequent Multichemistry Watchdog HAT** ($65) supports LiFePO4 and adds a hardware watchdog, but is 40-pin Pi header, requires both 18650 sockets populated, exposes only a raw voltage read (no fuel gauge — useless on LFP's flat curve), and has a fixed 2.8 V discharge floor.
- **LiFePO4wered/Pi+** ($51, Tindie) is architecturally right — 4 µA standby, clean I²C, smooth transfer — but ships one 1500 mAh cell (4.8 Wh, ~15–25 min on a Pi 4) and is capped at 2 A continuous. Too small.
- **Geekworm / Waveshare UPS HATs** are all Li-ion/LiPo and mostly 40-pin Pi parts; the Waveshare pogo-pin boards additionally have vendor-documented intermittent-contact behaviour ("scratch off the oxide layer of the pin header") that I would not specify for a wall-mounted appliance.
- **PiJuice is dead.** Pi Supply Ltd was dissolved 15 July 2025; Nebra Ltd is in liquidation; storefronts return HTTP 402. DigiKey still shows PIS-0212 as "Active" with zero stock — stale metadata, do not trust it.

**Therefore: integrate the charger and power path onto the Tier C CM4/CM5 carrier.** A TI BQ25798-class NVDC charger with input-current DPM (IINDPM/VINDPM) plus a real coulomb-counting fuel gauge (BQ27441 / MAX17048 class). DPM matters: it throttles charge current automatically so the compute load always wins over recharge, instead of hard-coding a conservative fixed charge rate. Budget the carrier respin as NRE, not a BOM line.

Board-level requirement, non-negotiable: **the UPS must report to the OS.** Pack voltage, signed current, and coulomb-counted SoC over I²C, plus a mains-present GPIO. A pass-through UPS with only LEDs makes the entire shutdown design in §5 impossible.

## 4. The PoE-switch problem — and what battery-backing actually buys

This is the most important thing in this document and it is currently unaddressed in the spec.

**Tier B and Tier C both take power *and* network from the same PoE cable.** In a venue mains failure the PoE switch dies. A battery-backed gateway therefore keeps its SoC alive but loses its Ethernet link — and with it every mTLS console session (§5 step 4, §6 Layer 1). A mains-powered control-room desktop is dark anyway.

So battery-backing the gateway *alone* delivers:

- ✅ BLE mesh relay continues (the gateway is still the best-placed, highest-gain node)
- ✅ SQLite site database keeps recording — incidents, muster confirmations, the hash-chained audit log
- ✅ LTE uplink survives if the dongle is fitted (it runs off the gateway's own 5 V rail), so HQ gets a positive "site on battery" event instead of inferring an outage from silence
- ❌ **No console.** Command cannot attach over a dead LAN.

That last line is the honest limit. **Battery-backing the gateway alone is worth doing — the local record and the mesh are the point — but it does not deliver a working control room.**

Three consequences for the spec:

1. **State the scope explicitly in customer-facing copy.** "Keeps the mesh and the site record alive through a power cut; consoles reconnect when the network returns." Not "control-room backbone that survives power cuts."
2. **Add a documented console path.** Two options, in order of cost: (a) **USB-C gadget mode** — a tethered laptop reaches `loc8-sited` directly and recovers the full console including stored site state, at zero BOM cost. This requires redesignating the USB-C port as **data-only** (Pi 4/CM4 OTG only works when USB-C is not powering the board — move alt-power to the GPIO header) and confirming D+/D− are routed on the carrier. On CM4 specifically, enabling device mode **disables the USB-A host port**, i.e. the LTE dongle — that trade must be documented or a PCIe USB host added. (b) Gateway soft-AP: cheaper operationally, but adds an RF attack surface behind a Layer 2 payload-encryption story that is currently unbuilt. Ship gadget mode first.
3. **Put "PoE switch on a UPS" on the site-survey sheet** as an install condition. It is the venue's purchase, it protects their cameras and access control too, and it is the only thing that keeps the LAN and consoles up. Sell it; do not depend on it.

Note also: the existing **guard-phone bridge** fallback (§8) does not rescue this case. It is a WebSocket over IP and cannot cross a dead LAN — it needs a laptop hotspot stood up first — and it carries live mesh frames only, not the Gateway's stored site state.

## 5. Load-shedding on battery, and the shutdown sequence

Justify shedding on **graceful degradation and card wear**, not as a runtime multiplier. On Pi/CM-class hardware, shedding buys roughly **1.2–1.4×**, not 2× — the static floor (SoC leakage, LPDDR4 self-refresh, PMIC and boost quiescent) dominates, and a Pi 4's entire idle-to-full-load span is only 2.37×. On a CM4 it is 1.46×.

**On mains loss (immediately):**
- Enter BATTERY state; latch it.
- **Checkpoint now, not later** — SQLite `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` + fsync. Costs seconds and negligible energy, and is the only placement that gives a recovery point independent of the shutdown succeeding.
- Emit one high-priority `SITE ON BATTERY` event over LTE if fitted.
- **Block OTA and USB-stick updates via hard interlock**, gated on the mains-present GPIO. The risk is not a corrupt inactive slot (A/B absorbs that) — it is the slot-switch metadata commit and the first unconfirmed boot, where automatic rollback itself needs charge to complete a second reboot.
- Shed `loc8-provisiond`'s **gateway-claiming path only**. Keep cert issuance and per-shift key issuance running — a guard clocking on during a blackout with no key cannot join the mesh and is invisible for the entire outage.
- Collapse position-frame persistence to a last-known-position table plus a coarse 30–60 s appended track. This is a **write-amplification** measure (~70 mW, ~2% of budget), not a power measure. Do not discard the track entirely — it is often the contractual proof-of-presence deliverable, and a power cut is a high-incident window.
- `loc8-syncd`: batch to bursts no more frequent than 1 per 15 min, retaining a low-rate heartbeat so HQ can distinguish "quiet" from "dead."
- Suspend all DB housekeeping (VACUUM, log rotation, index rebuilds) — chiefly because VACUUM holds a write lock that blocks incident and audit writes.
- Status lens: **amber**, slow breath, rate increasing as reserve drains. Do not use red — red is already "fault" in §3, and red/amber is the classic colour-vision-deficiency confusion pair, so encode the state in the **waveform**, not the hue. Do not dim: the lens draws ~2 mW, 0.04% of budget.

**Never shed:** mesh receive/relay, critical-class persistence (SOS, duress, muster, incident), the status lens, the shutdown supervisor.

**Shutdown triggers — specify in volts and coulombs, not SoC percent.** LFP's flat plateau makes percentage the least trustworthy quantity in the system, and 40% of an 8 Wh pack differs 3× from 40% of a 25 Wh pack.

| Stage | Trigger | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Warning | ~25% of usable reserve, coulomb-counted | Broadcast on mesh; raise breath rate; report a runtime **range**, not a point estimate |
| Shutdown begin | ~15% reserve | Stop accepting new writes; final WAL checkpoint; fsync; remount read-only |
| Complete by | ~10% reserve | Halt |

Pick **one** warning trigger, not two. Pairing "25%" with "~15 min estimated" is inconsistent by 1.5× — as an OR, the time arm fires at ~17%, leaving under two minutes before shutdown begins and collapsing the warning stage.

**Budget the shutdown in seconds, measured, then convert to a voltage/coulomb trigger.** Do not derive it from a 5-percentage-point band in the region the spec itself calls untrustworthy.

**Reserve an explicit energy floor for the supervisor.** Without it, tier-1 loads run the pack to hard cutoff and the hash-chained audit log is lost to a dirty unmount — the exact failure the battery exists to prevent. The hardware watchdog must be extended or disarmed on entering orderly shutdown, or undervoltage produces reset loops and repeated dirty mounts.

**Boot hold-off after a depletion shutdown:** require mains-present stable 60–120 s before boot. Two constraints: charging must be autonomous PMIC hardware that runs with the SoC powered off (otherwise you deadlock — won't boot until charged, won't charge until booted), and provide a physical long-press force-boot override that boots degraded/read-only. This device backs muster during evacuation; it must never be unavailable during the incident it exists to record.

**Structural mitigations matter more than thresholds.** Read-only root via overlayfs, one persistent writable partition (`/var/lib/loc8`) plus tmpfs for `/run`, `/tmp`, `/var/log`, machine-id, DHCP leases and SSH host keys, and split the database: audit/incident/muster at `synchronous=FULL`, position at `synchronous=NORMAL`. This is ~$0 of BOM and removes most of the corruption exposure. Note that the split buys tunable durability, **not** corruption isolation — both files share one FTL. And a hash chain does not self-report loss: tail truncation is its known undetectable failure mode, so periodically export the signed chain head and entry count off-box so a missing tail is detectable by comparison.

Finally, correct one common item: **do not put "drop the Ethernet PHY" on the shed list unconditionally.** On a PoE install the switch is already dead, so the PHY has auto-entered energy-detect and the marginal saving is tens of mW; if the switch *is* on a UPS, dropping the PHY severs the console and sync path precisely when you most want to report the outage.

## 6. Cost delta and tier placement

| Line | Tier B (proposed option) | Tier C (standard) |
|---|---|---|
| LFP cells | 2× 26650 ≈ $12–16 | 4× 26650 ≈ $24–32 |
| Charger/power path | Sequent HAT $65, or carrier-integrated | Carrier-integrated (NRE) |
| Fuel gauge | included above | included above |
| **Added BOM** | **~$30–45** | **~$35–50** |
| Runtime at load | ~2.6 h @ 5 W | ~5.2 h @ 5 W |

Plus one-time NRE for the Tier C carrier respin (schematic, layout, at least one spin, EMC retest inside the metal enclosure) and the compliance work in §7.

**Placement recommendation:**

- **Tier C: battery standard.** Already the case; increase the line from ~$25 to ~$50 and specify LFP + fuel gauge + carrier-integrated charger. Tier C's stated $180–240 absorbs this.
- **Tier B: battery as a priced option, not standard.** Adding it to Tier B's base takes the BOM from $93–113 to ~$125–160, which breaks the "~$100 BOM → sell at $299–399" economics in §2. Sell it as "Tier B + backup."
- **Correct the §1 table and the one-line pitch now**, regardless. Change "on PoE, battery-backed" to "on PoE; battery-backed at Tier C or from a UPS-backed switch," and change "survives power cuts" to "rides out power cuts when specified with the UPS option."

There is a real argument that **every** tier should carry a small supercapacitor hold-up (~60 J, ~10–15 s at load, ~$8–15 in parts) purely for clean-shutdown-on-power-loss — Tiers A and B run from microSD and are the tiers actually exposed to filesystem corruption, while Tier C's soldered eMMC is already the most resilient. But the read-only-root + WAL work above is cheaper and removes more of that risk, so **do that first** and treat hold-up capacitance as a second-order addition, not a headline BOM change. Note also that supercaps do not remove maintenance — EDLC life halves per +10 °C and they fade silently, so any hold-up design needs voltage derating and a periodic self-test that measures actual hold-up energy.

## 7. Compliance consequences — stated proportionately

Adding a lithium cell is a real but bounded increment. It is **not** the dominant compliance cost; the radio is.

**Genuinely mandatory, and new:**

- **UN 38.3** transport testing. Not optional, applies to all modes (not just air). Buy cells that already hold a UN 38.3 test summary and IEC 62133-2 certification from the cell manufacturer — you generally *cannot* commission cell-level testing on someone else's cell, since it requires construction data they withhold. **The assembled pack still needs its own UN 38.3 (T.1–T.5) and pack-level IEC 62133-2 evaluation.** Budget ~£1,500–5,000 per pack configuration, 3–6 weeks. Note also the Special Provision 310 / 49 CFR 173.185(e) exception: annual runs of ≤100 cells/batteries and prototypes for testing are excepted from the testing requirement, so pilot units can ship legally before certification completes.
- **IEC 62368-1 Annex M.** Ed. 4 (2023) expanded M.4 to cover **non-portable** equipment, so a permanently-installed wall unit is now in scope where it previously was not. Coin cells >3 Ω are exempt. Confirm subclause numbering against the edition in force — the EU harmonised standard is still EN IEC 62368-1:2020+A11:2020, with Ed. 4 not expected mandatory until ~2026–27.
- **Regulation (EU) 2023/1542.** The battery is itself a CE-marked product with its own Annex VIII technical file. CE marking obligations have applied since 18 Aug 2024. The CE mark goes **on the battery** — or, if not possible, on the packaging *and* accompanying documents. Never on the host device. The DoC must be a **single** consolidated declaration covering RED and the Battery Regulation together, not a separate one. Conformity assessment is Module A (self-declaration); no notified body for a pack this size. **Art. 11 removability/replaceability applies from 18 February 2027** — a design constraint, not a test-lab one. Derogations exist (Art. 11(2)/(3)) but relying on one requires documented justification, and the data-integrity derogation will likely fail for a device with non-volatile memory. **Assume user-replaceable unless and until a derogation is documented**, and budget the Art. 11(7) five-year spares obligation running from the last unit of the model shipped.
- **EPR registration:** WEEE + battery EPR, per member state, recurring. Real recurring cost, often underbudgeted.

**Explicitly not triggered:** NFPA 855 / IFC §1207 energy-storage fire code (applicability floor is 1 kWh; a 38 Wh pack is ~26× below it), UL 9540/9540A, UL 1973, IEC 62619. Anyone budgeting an ESS compliance programme for this has misread the scale.

**UK fire/building regulation:** no regulation names lithium cells or prohibits them in occupied venues, and Approved Document B is silent. But the RRO 2005 requires the venue's responsible person to review their fire risk assessment on any significant change, and installing a permanent cell is one. **Practical consequence: ship a one-page fire-safety statement** (chemistry, Wh rating, UN 38.3 test summary reference, IEC 62133-2 certificate number, protection-circuit description, enclosure fire-rating basis, operating temperature limits, end-of-life removal instructions). This is not merely commercial good practice — it substantially discharges duties you already owe under HSWA 1974 s.6(1)(c) and GPSR reg. 7(1). Caveat: naming specific certificates on a shipped document locks the BOM to that exact cell, so gate second-sourcing behind a document update.

**Insurer sensitivity:** rising and real (QBE recorded 1,760 UK lithium-ion fires in 2025, up 147% in three years, 23% in commercial premises), but the published insurer guidance corpus addresses EV charging, BESS and bulk storage — not small installed devices. Treat this as a plausible near-term procurement gate to hold evidence against, **not** a confirmed requirement.

**Proportionate budget:** battery-specific compliance work is roughly **£4,000–9,000** and **6–10 weeks** on top of the base first-product programme (which is realistically £15,000–39,000 with a pre-certified radio module, dominated by safety/EN 62368-1 and RED cybersecurity assessment under EN 18031, not by the battery). LFP buys **zero** regulatory relief over NMC — it is a lithium-ion chemistry and every standard applies identically. Choose it for float life and runaway severity, and say so.

## 8. Open questions — bench measurement, not more research

These cannot be resolved by reading. Nothing in §3's arithmetic is trustworthy until item 1 is done.

1. **Actual gateway power draw at the 5 V rail**, measured with an INA260 (not an INA219 — its external shunt sized for fine resolution inserts ~100 mV of drop at 1 A and manufactures the sag you are measuring). Log at 10–100 Hz for a full hour under the real production workload: real BlueZ scan/advertise parameters, real SQLite write rate, real client count, in a genuinely dense RF environment. Measure separately: Tier B idle, Tier B under mesh load, Tier C dual-radio, Tier C + LTE transmitting. **Every runtime figure above is an estimate against this number.**

2. **Transient droop under LTE transmit.** Separate instrument required — an INA2xx tops out around 1–1.8 kHz, so Nyquist hides anything shorter than ~2 ms and a sampled reading will alias straight past the true minimum. Use a scope in peak-detect with a current probe, tens of kHz minimum, probing at the DUT connector (100–300 mΩ of cable and connector resistance alone gives 100–300 mV at 1 A). Size bulk capacitance from the measured burst current and duration, and confirm the rail holds above the SoC's brownout trip.

3. **BLE increment.** No controlled Pi-4 measurement of continuous scan+advertise exists in the published literature that I could find. The commonly cited 13 mA figure is an nRF51822 number and does not apply — the Pi 4 uses a CYW43455 combo part with materially higher BT RX current. **Reserve +0.6 W and measure it.** This is the weakest number in the budget. Note the baseline convention matters: measure against a Pi idling with Bluetooth enabled-but-idle, not against `dtoverlay=disable-bt`.

4. **Measured LFP discharge curve** at the chosen pack and load, at 0 °C, 25 °C and 45 °C, to fixed the voltage/coulomb shutdown triggers in §5. Do not use SoC percentages until this exists.

5. **In-enclosure cell temperature over a full summer**, logged at 5-minute intervals with a 1%-tolerance NTC or PT1000 Class A bonded to a cell can and electrically isolated from it (cans sit at a terminal potential; a grounded-junction thermocouple creates a galvanic path into the logger). Type-K Class 2 at ±2.2 °C implies ±15% error in predicted degradation rate — unusable for an argument premised on 10 °C mattering. **The output that matters is the Arrhenius rate-weighted effective temperature, not the 95th percentile** — on a representative plant-room profile P95 overstates the degradation rate by ~1.9× while the simple mean is only ~1.14× low.

6. **Boost-converter efficiency at the actual operating point**, including at the shed operating point (which is *lower* than unshed, and therefore erodes the shed benefit).

7. **Mechanical:** does the chosen charger/power-path arrangement physically coexist with the PoE+ HAT? Both contend for the same header and stack height. Confirm before ordering anything.

8. **Verify the USB-C OTG path** on the exact Tier C module (Pi 4 yes via dwc2; CM4 requires the carrier to route OTG; Pi 5 USB-C is reported power-only). The §4 console fallback depends on it.

**Prices in this document are July 2026 snapshots and must be re-quoted at order time.** Geekworm runs continuous sale pricing; Waveshare and Pi Supply pages were partly unreachable during research; the Pi 4 2GB has moved to ~$45 on DRAM pricing, which already puts §2's "$35–45" at its ceiling.

corrected.why:
The narrow, SKU-level part of the claim checks out, but two load-bearing parts fail — and the failure mode is exactly the kind that causes an engineer to order the wrong part (or to wrongly rule out the right one).

WHAT SURVIVED. Each of the five enumerated SKUs is genuinely Pi 5 only. wiki.geekworm.com/X1202 states it is "designed specifically for the Raspberry Pi 5" and its compatibility table lists only Raspberry Pi 5. wiki.geekworm.com/X1206 is blunter: "For use with Raspberry Pi 5 Only," with no mention of Pi 4B anywhere. geekworm.com/products/x1200 likewise says "designed specifically for the Raspberry Pi 5." The collection-page groupings and prices in the DETAIL also match what I fetched (X1200 $45, X1201 $46, X1202 $49, X1203 $45, X1205 $46 2x21700, X1206 V2.0 $48 4x21700). The mechanical reason is real: these boards feed the Pi 5 through pogo pins onto power pads that simply do not exist on a Pi 4.

FAILURE 1 — the Pi 4 inventory is wrong. The DETAIL asserts "The Pi 4 group contains only X728 ($44.00) and X703 ($22.00)." Geekworm's own Pi 4 tagged view (geekworm.com/collections/ups-hat/raspberry-pi-4) returns five products, not two: X728 $44.00, X-UPS1 12V/5V dual output $45.00, X703 $22.00, X1209 5.1V 6A UPS HAT $45.00, and X12-A1 stackable 4-slot 18650 holder $2.00. The word "only" is false as written.

FAILURE 2 — the generalization inverts the sourcing conclusion. The headline says the X12xx "family" is "NOT a Pi 4 option." But the X1209 is an X12xx-series UPS HAT, currently sold at $45.00, and geekworm.com/products/x1209 states support for "Raspberry Pi 5 / Raspberry Pi 4 Model B / Raspberry Pi 3B/3B+" — corroborated by wiki.geekworm.com/X1209 ("Raspberry Pi 5 Model B / 4 Model B / 3 Model B") and by Amazon listings marketing it for "Pi 5/4B/3B+/3B." So the X12xx family IS a Pi 4 option; the claim generalizes from five hand-picked SKUs to a family that contains a direct counterexample. An engineer reading the spec as written would eliminate Geekworm's X12xx line for a Pi 4 build and thereby skip the one X12xx part that actually fits.

The trailing rhetorical flourish — "which invalidates a common assumption in this product category" — is unsupportable and should be deleted rather than corrected. It presents a five-SKU observation as a category-level finding, and in the direction that matters for procurement it is backwards.

ONE SPEC CAVEAT worth carrying forward: the X1209 is not a drop-in substitute for the holder-based boards. It has no onboard 18650/21700 holders — it exposes two XH2.54 connectors for user-supplied cells (hence the companion X12-A1 holder at $2.00), and takes 6-18Vdc via DC jack or 5Vdc 5A via USB-C. Anyone swapping an X1202 for an X1209 is changing the mechanical and wiring proposition, not just the host compatibility.

Price hygiene: the DETAIL's snapshot framing is appropriate and I would keep it. Note the X1200 product page shows $45.00 as a sale price against a $46.00 regular price, which reinforces that these are volatile snapshots, not quotable BOM figures.

The Geekworm X728 is one of several mainstream Geekworm UPS boards compatible with the Raspberry Pi 4, not the only one. Geekworm's own Raspberry Pi 4 UPS collection lists the X728 ($44.00, sale from $45.99), the X-UPS1 12V/5V dual-output stackable shield ($45.00), the X1209 5.1V 6A UPS HAT ($45.00) and the X703 18650 UPS shield ($22.00); the X708 and X729 also support Pi 4B per their wiki pages.

X728 confirmed specifics (geekworm.com/products/x728, accessed July 2026): exact storefront name "Geekworm Raspberry Pi X728 (Max 5.1V 5A) 18650 UPS & Power Management Board with Auto On & Safe Shutdown Function"; $44.00 USD, in stock; 1-2x 18650 Li-ion, batteries NOT included; vendor requires UNPROTECTED cells — "Do not use the 18650 battery with built-in protection circuit because it will limit the discharge current", i.e. the stated rationale is discharge-current headroom, not safety, which means cell-level over-discharge and short-circuit protection must be provided by the design; integrated Maxim fuel gauge reporting voltage and percentage over I2C; software safe shutdown and full power-off; "Advanced system power-path management" with an IN-to-SYS pass-through path; onboard RTC and buzzer; supports Pi 4B/3B+/3B/3A+/2B/B+ and, per the wiki, Pi 5 Model B.

CAUTION before ordering: the vendor's own documentation is inconsistent on the headline rating. The storefront title and spec table state Max 5.1V 5A, while wiki.geekworm.com/X728-hardware states "UPS power output: 5.1Vdc 8A", and a separately marketed "X728 (Max 5.1V 8A)" variant is sold bundled with the X708-A1 8-cell holder. Six hardware revisions are documented (V1.2, V1.3, V2.0, V2.1, V2.3, V2.5). Confirm the rating against a specific revision with the vendor before committing to parts.

The X728 is also NOT the strongest spec match on paper among Geekworm's Pi 4 options. The X1209 ($45.00) supports Pi 5B/4B/3B/3B+ and matches or exceeds the X728 on every headline spec: 5.1V 6000mA vs 5A, the same Maxim I2C fuel gauge, the same advanced power-path management, programmable low-battery safe shutdown, AC power-loss detection via GPIO, auto power-on, a top-mount pass-through 40-pin extended GPIO header, and broader cell support (18650/21700/4680). The X728's only substantiated advantages are its onboard RTC and buzzer. Select the X728 over the X1209 only if the RTC, buzzer, or the specific 40-pin mounting arrangement is a stated requirement; otherwise the X1209 is the better on-paper match, and the X708 (up to 5.1V 8A with an off-board 8-cell holder) is the option to evaluate if sustained current is the binding constraint.

All figures above are vendor marketing specifications, not independently measured values; no regulatory certification (UL/CE/UN38.3) is claimed by the vendor for the board or for user-supplied unprotected cells, which is a material gap for a commercial appliance.
corrected.why:
The DETAIL block is almost entirely accurate — I confirmed against geekworm.com/products/x728 and wiki.geekworm.com/X728: title "Geekworm Raspberry Pi X728 (Max 5.1V 5A) 18650 UPS & Power Management Board with Auto On & Safe Shutdown Function", $44.00 (compare-at $45.99), in stock (176 units), 1-2x 18650, batteries not included, "Do not use 18650 battery with built-in protection circuit", Maxim fuel gauge over I2C, safe shutdown, and "Advanced system power-path management". Price is current, not stale, and the product is not discontinued.

But the CLAIM's two load-bearing assertions both fail.

(1) "Only mainstream Geekworm UPS for Pi 4" is flatly false. Geekworm's own /collections/raspberry-pi-4-ups landing page lists five products, not one: X728 ($44), X-UPS1 12V/5V dual-output stackable ($45), X1209 5.1V 6A UPS HAT ($45), X703 18650 UPS shield ($22), plus the X12-A1 battery holder. Beyond that collection, the X708 (5.1V 8A backup, Pi 4B, separate 8-cell X708-A1 holder) and X729 (5.1V 6A, 2x 18650, Pi 4B) both support Pi 4B per their wiki pages. That is at minimum four to six mainstream Geekworm Pi 4 UPS options.

(2) "Strongest spec match on paper" is unsupportable, because the X1209 dominates the X728 on nearly every axis the DETAIL itself uses as evidence, at a $1 higher price. Per wiki.geekworm.com/X1209: supports RPi 5B/4B/3B/3B+; 5.1V 6000mA vs X728's 5A; the identical "Integrated Maxim's fuel-gauge systems for reading battery voltage and percentage over i2c"; the identical "Advanced system power-path management"; programmable low-battery safe shutdown; AC power loss detection via GPIO; auto power-on; top-mount with a pass-through 40-pin extended GPIO header; and broader cell support (18650/21700/4680 rather than 18650 only). The only X728 differentiators I could substantiate are the buzzer and onboard RTC, which the X1209 docs do not mention. Unless the unstated requirements specifically demand a buzzer or RTC, X728 is not the strongest match — it is mid-pack on current capacity.

Two further defects an engineer would order against. First, the vendor contradicts itself on the headline current rating: the storefront title and spec table say "Max 5.1V 5A" and "UPS output 5.1V ±5% Max 5A", while wiki.geekworm.com/X728-hardware states "UPS power output: 5.1Vdc 8A", and a separately marketed "X728 (Max 5.1V 8A)" variant exists on Amazon bundled with the X708-A1 holder. The 5A/8A figure must be pinned to a specific hardware revision (the wiki documents V1.2, V1.3, V2.0, V2.1, V2.3, V2.5) before parts are ordered. Second, the supported-model list is incomplete: the wiki lists Pi 5 Model B as supported, which the DETAIL omits.

One nuance in the claim's favor that is worth stating correctly: the vendor's stated reason for requiring unprotected cells is throughput, not safety — "Do not use the 18650 battery with built-in protection circuit because it will limit the discharge current." The DETAIL is right to flag this as a commercial-appliance constraint, and arguably understates it, since unprotected cells push over-discharge and short-circuit protection entirely onto the board and enclosure design.

corrected.original: The X728 has a substantial and officially-documented reliability complaint record that should disqualify it from an unattended always-on commercial deployment without mitigation.
corrected.corrected:
The X728's public complaint record is thin and largely attaches to discontinued board revisions, but there is one well-documented latent failure mode on the current revision that must be mitigated before unattended always-on deployment.

What the sources actually support:

- Current shipping revision is X728 V2.5 (released 2023-07-27); V1.2 and V1.3 are marked "Product Discontinued" on Geekworm's wiki. Spec charging current is 2.3-3.2A.
- CURRENT-REVISION DEFECT (the one that matters): on V2.5 paired with a Raspberry Pi 5, battery charging is gated by GPIO16. The Pi 5 drives GPIO16 low on shutdown (the Pi 4 held it high), so the UPS stops charging while the Pi is powered off. A node that auto-shuts-down on low battery will not recharge unattended. Source: Raspberry Pi forums t=392008, 19 Sept 2025. Mitigation required: hold GPIO16 high across shutdown (gpio config / dtoverlay set at firmware level), or qualify on Pi 4B, or verify by test on the exact Pi model being deployed.
- Software SoC reporting is unreliable: x728bat.py reported 2% while the pack measured 4.12V immediately after a full charge (github.com/geekworm-com/x728/issues/3). Treat the bundled script's percentage as unfit for fleet telemetry; derive SoC from the raw INA219 voltage reading with a validated curve.
- Power-button behaviour has been reported as unpredictable, but only on discontinued revisions: v1.2 (RPi forums t=289613, which also contains a single user's oscilloscope-based diagnosis of a brownout during SSD boot) and v2.1 (t=330294, where the reporter had fitted a latching switch against the documented "momentary switch only" requirement). Both are single unreplicated reports on superseded hardware; neither is vendor-confirmed.

What is NOT supportable and should be removed from the spec:
- Batteries requiring physical removal/reseating after ~3 months of powered-off storage: no primary source found in any cited URL.
- Charging stalling at 100% and not resuming until the charger is unplugged/replugged: no primary source found; not in the wiki FAQ.
- "Very slow charging, ~0.15A at 5.01V": no source, and dimensionally implausible (0.75W cannot describe a system charging while running a Pi).
- "Officially-documented": the vendor documents none of these as defects. The record consists of user-submitted GitHub issues (11 total across ~2021-2025, most of them documentation/licensing/feature tickets) and unresolved third-party forum posts.

Net for the spec: the X728 is not disqualified by a substantial documented reliability record — that record does not exist at the claimed scale. It should be qualified conditionally, with the GPIO16 charge-gating behaviour treated as a blocking item to verify on the target Pi model, the bundled SoC script replaced, and a burn-in that includes at least one full discharge-to-shutdown-and-recover cycle per unit.
corrected.why:
Checked all four cited URLs plus the Geekworm wiki spec/FAQ. The directional caution may be defensible, but nearly every load-bearing specific is wrong, mis-sourced, or attached to discontinued hardware. An engineer ordering parts against this text would be misled.

(1) Item 4 is INVERTED. github.com/geekworm-com/x728/issues/3 reports the script showing 2% while the pack read 4.12V immediately after a full recharge — i.e. a gross UNDER-report on a nearly-FULL battery. The claim's "2% shown when actually depleted" describes a CORRECT reading. It is also a Python lookup-table/reporting bug, not a hardware reliability failure.

(2) Items 1, 2 and 3 are NOT in any cited source. The three-month-storage battery-reseat, the charge-stall-until-replug, and the 0.15A/5.01V slow charge appear in none of the four URLs. The Geekworm wiki FAQ runs Q1–Q12 and contains no such entry; its only battery-seating item (Q6) states batteries are not hot-swappable — a design statement, not a complaint. The Geekworm charging forum thread (topic 21154) is a "which port do I use" question answered by staff, not a defect report. Web search appeared to corroborate item 1, but the summarizer was paraphrasing my own query back; no primary source exists. These three items are currently unsupportable.

(3) Items 5 and 6 are the SAME thread, not independent reports. t=289613 is the source for both the unpredictable power button and the oscilloscope-diagnosed SSD-boot power drain. That thread is against X728 **v1.2**, which Geekworm's own wiki marks "Product Discontinued." t=330294 is a genuinely separate power-button report but is against **v2.1**, also superseded — and that user states they fitted a **latching switch contrary to the explicit "use momentary switch only" instruction**, a user-error confound the claim omits. Current shipping revision is **V2.5** (July 2023). Complaints against two discontinued revisions cannot support a purchasing decision on V2.5.

(4) "Substantial ... complaint record" overstates the tracker. The vendor GitHub repo has **11 issues total across ~2021–2025**, and most are not reliability: "Please add a software license" (#5), "$HOME instead of /home/pi" (#4), "fix documentation" (#6), "I2C with arduino" (#2), "Lame" (#10), plus a feature request (#11). That is a thin software/docs backlog on a script repo, not a hardware reliability record.

(5) "Officially-documented" is false. GitHub issues and forum posts are user-submitted, mostly unanswered by the vendor. The only genuinely vendor-authored source cited (the wiki) documents none of the six items.

(6) The 0.15A figure has a units/context defect. 0.15A x 5.01V = 0.75W. The wiki specs UPS charging current at 2.3–3.2A, and a Pi 4 alone idles near 2.7W. A 0.75W input cannot describe a system simultaneously charging and running a Pi — the number is either a terminated-charge/full-battery measurement or a different node entirely. Presented as "very slow charging" it is dimensionally suspect as well as unsourced.

(7) The claim MISSES the one well-sourced, current-revision latent failure. Raspberry Pi forum t=392008 (19 Sept 2025) documents that on **V2.5 with a Pi 5**, charging is gated by GPIO16; the Pi 5 drives GPIO16 low at shutdown (the Pi 4 held it high), so **the UPS stops charging whenever the Pi is powered down**. For an unattended always-on fleet that is the real trap: a node that auto-shuts-down on low battery never recovers. This is against current hardware and is materially more relevant than the discontinued-board anecdotes the claim leans on.

corrected.original: The Sixfab Power Management & UPS HAT is RETIRED and cannot be designed in.
corrected.corrected:
The Sixfab Power Management & UPS HAT (v2) is RETIRED and must not be designed in.

Status evidence: the Sixfab product page states verbatim "This product is retired because of supply problems with power components," lists the board as "Currently unavailable" (EUR 69.00, notify-me only) and categorizes it as Obsolete. Sixfab staff confirmed on the community forum (2022-11-10) that discontinuation is a component-supply issue, not a design fault, and that "We are not working on another version of the HAT"; a further batch would require a bulk order of 250+ units. The forum files it under "legacy-products." No live distributor stock was found: Chicago Electronic Distributors has stopped accepting orders, and Pondesk lists it quote-only with no stock or price. Note the retirement statement lives on the PRODUCT PAGE (sixfab.com/product/raspberry-pi-power-management-ups-hat/), not in the docs; the cited FAQ page contains no retirement notice at all, which is precisely why the docs read as live.

Second, independent EOL - the real trap: Sixfab Power cloud software and the cloud API "will not be accessible and supported after December 31, 2022" (docs.sixfab.com/page/power-software-end-of-life-notification). Any cloud-dependent capability described in the still-online documentation is already dead. Only the local Python API remains, in a repository with 7 commits and no published releases - treat as unmaintained.

For the record, what the board offered (all verbatim-supported by docs.sixfab.com/docs/raspberry-pi-power-management-ups-hat-technical-details and .../introduction):
- I2C at TWO addresses: 0x41 (HAT MCU, ATSAMD21G18) and 0x48 (battery sensor). If replicating, budget both; 0x48 collides with the default addresses of ADS1115, LM75, and TMP102.
- Single-cell 3.7V Li-ion/Li-Po via JST (J5, Battery Cable JST-SFH) or J9 for external packs, or an onboard protected-18650 holder (battery not included). Default design capacity 2500 mAh.
- Power: USB-C input (J3) 5V/3A max; terminal-block input (J4) 5V-21V/4A max; output (J7) 5V rated, 2.6A max. Recommended input 5V at >=2A, or 12V at >=1.5A.
- "Dynamic power management boosts the system output from the battery if the needed power is more than the input supply provides" (TI bq25703A supplement mode; bq27441-G1 fuel gauge, INA219 current monitor).
- Hardware watchdog timer - ships DISABLED by default (WATCHDOG_PASSIVE, 4-minute interval); must be armed in firmware configuration.
- "Battery protection circuit enhanced with integrated temperature sensors"; battery cutoff at 65 degrees C.

On the watchdog: it is useful but NOT rare. Before building a bespoke replacement, evaluate the PiJuice HAT, which is currently purchasable and provides a hardware watchdog with a configurable timeout (1 to 65535 minutes; zero disables) that power-cycles the Pi on a missed heartbeat, independent of the Pi's OS. Sourcing that feature off the shelf is likely cheaper than replicating it.
corrected.why:
The headline verdict (RETIRED, do not design in) is CORRECT and well-supported, but the claim is imprecise in three ways that matter for a hardware spec an engineer will order against, plus one unsupportable editorial assertion.

CONFIRMED: sixfab.com product page states verbatim "This product is retired because of supply problems with power components," shows "Currently unavailable" at EUR 69.00 with only a notify-me option, and is in the Obsolete category. Sixfab staff on the community forum (2022-11-10) confirmed discontinuation: "The current version doesn't have any issues, it's just the component supply issue" and "We are not working on another version of the HAT," with a new batch contingent on a 250-unit minimum bulk order. The forum category is literally "legacy-products." No live channel stock: Chicago Electronic Distributors has "stopped accepting orders," Pondesk is quote-only with no stock/price shown. Feature descriptions quoted are verbatim-accurate against docs: "Dynamic power management boosts the system output from the battery if the needed power is more than the input supply provides"; "Watchdog Timer keeps the system alive when the Raspberry Pi freezes up"; "Battery protection circuit enhanced with integrated temperature sensors"; single-cell 3.7V Li-ion/Li-Po via JST (J5, Battery Cable JST-SFH) or J9, plus protected-18650 holder.

ERROR 1 - source attribution is scrambled. The retirement sentence appears on the PRODUCT PAGE, not the documentation. I fetched the cited FAQ page (docs.sixfab.com/docs/raspberry-pi-power-management-ups-hat-faq) and it contains NO retirement or discontinuation notice at all. The docs page that does carry EOL language is a different URL (docs.sixfab.com/page/power-software-end-of-life-notification) and it is primarily about the cloud software. The claim's two facts are swapped between its two cited URLs.

ERROR 2 - I2C address incomplete; the most design-relevant defect. The board presents TWO I2C addresses: 0x41 (HAT MCU) and 0x48 (battery sensor). Allocating only 0x41 risks a bus collision at 0x48, which is the default address for ADS1115, LM75, and TMP102 - a common conflict.

ERROR 3 - omits a second, separate EOL. Sixfab Power cloud software and cloud API "will not be accessible and supported after December 31, 2022." Only the local Python API survives, in a repo with 7 commits and no published releases (effectively unmaintained). The claim warns that live-looking docs are the hazard but omits the specific functionality that is already dead - the sharper trap.

ERROR 4 - "genuinely rare" is unsupportable. The PiJuice HAT, a currently purchasable product, ships a hardware watchdog with configurable timeout (1 to 65535 minutes, zero disables) that resets the Pi on missed heartbeat. Recommending the feature be "replicated elsewhere in the design" is misleading when an off-the-shelf live alternative provides it. Also, the Sixfab watchdog ships DISABLED (default WATCHDOG_PASSIVE, 4-minute interval) and must be armed in firmware config.

MINOR: the documentation describes the v2 board ("Power Management & UPS HAT v2"); the claim does not state the revision.

corrected.original: PiJuice is effectively not procurable at commercial volume and should be treated as end-of-life risk, not a live option.
corrected.corrected:
PiJuice HAT (PIS-0212) is END-OF-LIFE and must not be designed into this hardware. Do not order against it.

Vendor status (verified at Companies House, July 2026): PI SUPPLY LTD (company no. 08518826) was DISSOLVED on 15 July 2025. The parent/successor trading entity NEBRA LTD (company no. 06732600, formerly RAAMAUDIO UK LTD), under which the PiJuice brand traded, is IN LIQUIDATION. There is no solvent counterparty for supply, warranty, RMA, errata, or firmware maintenance.

Storefronts are dead, not merely unreachable: uk.pi-supply.com and nebra.com both return HTTP 402 with Shopify's "Store unavailable" page; pi-supply.com and learn.pi-supply.com return HTTP 523 (origin unreachable). Any PiJuice product still "listed" on these domains — including PiJuice Zero — is non-transactable.

Channel status: SparkFun — "retired from our catalog and is no longer for sale". Rapid Online — "Discontinued". Core Electronics — retired, "Replaced by: WS-27966" (Waveshare UPS HAT (E)). PiShop.ca — out of stock. Only finite new-old-stock remains; e.g. kjdelectronics lists 124 units at $79.95. Small quantities are therefore still physically obtainable, but there is no restock path and no second source.

WARNING — stale distributor metadata: DigiKey still shows PIS-0212 (manufacturer listed as "Maker Emporium Ltd") with Part Status "Active". This is stale. The same page shows In-Stock 0 and states DigiKey "is unable to accept backorders at this time", with only a 50-unit bulk line at $91.75/unit. Do not treat DigiKey's "Active" flag as evidence of availability.

PRICE: no current authoritative price exists. Figures in circulation ($73.95 SparkFun legacy, $79.95 residual NOS, $91.75 DigiKey bulk line, CAD $119.95 PiShop.ca) are legacy or residual-stock and must not be used for costing.

ACTION: select an actively manufactured alternative and re-qualify. Candidates seen displacing it in distributor catalogs include the Waveshare UPS HAT (E) (WS-27966) and UUGear Witty Pi series; neither has been evaluated here for RTC behaviour, true-UPS cutover, deep-sleep current, or I2C API parity with PiJuice, so any substitution requires its own electrical and firmware review.
corrected.why:
The claim's bottom line (treat PiJuice as EOL, not a live option) is correct and in fact understated, but it is refuted as written because a load-bearing supporting detail is factually wrong and two others are misread — errors that matter in a document an engineer orders parts against.

(1) MATERIAL ERROR: "Pi Supply itself appears to still be trading" is false. Companies House shows PI SUPPLY LTD (08518826) "Dissolved on 15 July 2025". The parent/successor trading entity NEBRA LTD (06732600, formerly RAAMAUDIO UK LTD) has company status "Liquidation". There is no solvent vendor behind the product — no warranty, RMA, errata, or firmware-support counterparty. The claim implies a live vendor exists, which would wrongly encourage an engineer to "just email sales".

(2) MISREAD EVIDENCE: the claim treats the HTTP 402 as merely "could not verify price". Inspecting the response shows `HTTP/2 402`, `powered-by: Shopify`, body `<title>Store unavailable</title>` — Shopify's frozen/deactivated-store response. Both uk.pi-supply.com AND nebra.com return it; pi-supply.com and learn.pi-supply.com return 523 (origin unreachable). The 402 is affirmative proof the storefront is dead, i.e. stronger support for the claim's own conclusion. Consequently "PiJuice Zero remains listed" is meaningless — the listing sits on a deactivated store and cannot be transacted.

(3) IMPRECISE DATING: "became unavailable roughly two years prior" is an unanchored relative statement. Discussion #1093 runs Sept 2024 to Sept 2025; the 2,000-unit run was promised for end of Sept 2024 and never cured the shortage; dissolution was July 2025. As of July 2026 the correct anchor is: manufacturer dissolved ~12 months ago, supply degraded ~2 years ago.

(4) TOO ABSOLUTE IN ONE DIRECTION: "effectively not procurable" overstates. Residual new-old-stock is genuinely buyable now — kjdelectronics lists 124 units at $79.95. The accurate statement is that only finite NOS remains with no restock path, which is what makes it unsuitable for a production BOM.

(5) A TRAP THE CLAIM MISSES: DigiKey still shows PIS-0212 (mfr "Maker Emporium Ltd") with Part Status "Active" — stale lifecycle metadata — while showing In-Stock 0, refusing backorders ("Due to temporary constrained supply, DigiKey is unable to accept backorders at this time"), and quoting only a 50-unit bulk line at $91.75/unit. An engineer spot-checking DigiKey would see "Active" and wrongly conclude the part is live. The spec should pre-empt this.

Corroborating retirements verified: SparkFun "This product has been retired from our catalog and is no longer for sale" (legacy $73.95); Rapid Online "Discontinued"; Core Electronics retired and "Replaced by: WS-27966" (Waveshare UPS HAT (E)); PiShop.ca out of stock (CAD $119.95). The claim's caution on price is correct and should be kept: no current authoritative price exists; $73.95/$79.95/$91.75/CAD$119.95 are legacy or residual-stock figures, not a quotable procurement price.

corrected.original: Waveshare UPS HAT (E) is the highest-capacity Waveshare option and supports Pi 4B, but takes 21700 cells rather than 18650.
corrected.corrected:
Waveshare UPS HAT (E) is the highest-capacity UPS in Waveshare's Raspberry Pi line and supports Pi 5 / 4B / 3B+, but takes 21700 cells rather than 18650.

Cells: 4x 21700 Li-ion in SERIES (4S1P), NOT included. Pack is ~14.8 V nominal / 16.8 V fully charged. Because the cells are in series, usable amp-hours equal a SINGLE cell, not four: roughly 62-74 Wh total depending on cell capacity (4200-5000 mAh). Order flat-top, unprotected, length-compliant cells as a capacity- and IR-matched set; protected cells with an integral PCB are commonly too long for the holder and interfere with balance charging. Cells must be installed in the documented V1-V2-V3-V4 order or the board's warning indicator trips.

Power: onboard high-power buck rated 5V 6A (manufacturer rating, not measured; Waveshare notes the module can source up to ~10 A but recommends limiting to 6 A for thermal reasons, and pogo-pin contact resistance is the practical limit at high current). Type-C with bi-directional fast charging, PD3.0, up to 40W (manufacturer spec). Charger IC is IP2368 (Injoinic bi-directional 4S buck-boost). Pi 5 self-limits to 3 A unless PSU_MAX_CURRENT=5000 is set in EEPROM; this does not apply to Pi 4B.

Telemetry: BQ4050 fuel gauge reporting pack voltage, current, power, remaining capacity and per-cell voltages, plus real-time Type-C port state. The host does NOT address the BQ4050 directly - an onboard MCU aggregates all telemetry at I2C address 0x2D (default; remappable 0x08-0x77 via register 0x41), with per-cell voltages at registers 0x30-0x37.

Mechanical: pogo-pin power delivery, no GPIO consumed; board 88 x 56 mm.

Note: the CNX Software article commonly cited for this part incorrectly credits an "INA219 IC" with the 40 W bi-directional charging. INA219 is a current-shunt monitor, not a charger; that reference belongs to the UPS HAT (D) (INA219 at 0x43) and does not apply to the (E).
corrected.why:
The claim is directionally correct but imprecise in ways that matter for a parts order.

CONFIRMED: 4x 21700 not included; 5V 6A rated output; Type-C bi-directional PD3.0 up to 40W; fuel-gauge telemetry plus Type-C port state over I2C; pogo-pin connector; Pi 5/4B/3B+ compatibility. "Highest-capacity Waveshare Pi UPS" also holds (UPS HAT (D) = 1x 21700; UPS Module 3S = 3x 18650; UPS HAT (B) = 2x 18650).

DEFECT 1 - series topology omitted, causing a 4x runtime overestimate. Waveshare's product page states "21700 Li battery x 4 (in series)"; the wiki exposes four per-cell voltage registers (0x30-0x37) and requires V1->V2->V3->V4 install order or a warning indicator trips. Pack is ~14.8V nominal / 16.8V full. Pack Ah therefore equals ONE cell, not four: ~72 Wh with 5000 mAh cells, ~62 Wh with the 4200 mAh cells The Pi Hut references. Reading "4x 21700" as 4x the Ah budget overestimates runtime fourfold. Series operation also constrains the purchase to flat-top, unprotected, length-compliant, capacity/IR-matched cells (protected cells with integral PCBs are commonly too long for these holders and interfere with balance charging) - none of which the claim states.

DEFECT 2 - false negative on the fuel gauge. The claim says the part number and I2C address could not be confirmed; both are documented on the "UPS HAT (E) Register" wiki page. Fuel gauge is BQ4050 (TI 1-4S), charger is IP2368 (Injoinic bi-directional 4S buck-boost, PD3.0). The Pi does not address the BQ4050 directly - an onboard MCU aggregates telemetry at I2C address 0x2D (default, remappable 0x08-0x77 via register 0x41). 0x2D is the address firmware needs.

DEFECT 3 - the stated source carries a hardware error. The cited CNX Software article attributes bi-directional 40W fast charging to an "INA219 IC." INA219 is a current-shunt monitor and cannot charge; the line appears copy-pasted from the UPS HAT (D) page, where an INA219 genuinely sits at 0x43. Specifying from that source risks ordering/《writing drivers for》the wrong part.

DEFECT 4 - 6A is a rated buck figure presented without qualification. Waveshare's wiki notes the module can source up to ~10A but recommends limiting to 6A thermally; the practical constraint is pogo-pin contact resistance, which commenters on the cited article question at 3-4A. Separately, a Pi 5 self-limits to 3A unless PSU_MAX_CURRENT=5000 is set in EEPROM (Pi 5 only, not a Pi 4B issue). 40W PD is likewise a manufacturer spec, not a measured figure.

MINOR: "highest-capacity Waveshare option" should be scoped to the Raspberry Pi UPS line; Waveshare also ships a UPS Power Module (C) for Jetson Orin that takes 21700s.

Wiki and product pages return HTTP 403 to direct fetch, as the claim notes; content was recovered via a text-extraction proxy and corroborated across CNX Software, The Pi Hut, Electronics-Lab, and search-indexed wiki text.

Vendor volume tiers: $31.99 @ qty 2, $31.49 @ qty 3, $31.29 @ qty 4+. AliExpress is approximately $37-38 including shipping (not confirmed precisely). Amazon should not be quoted as a price source right now: ASIN B0DBLMFX57 shows "No featured offers available" (no buybox price), and the alternate listing B0DCB6D1F8 shows "Currently unavailable" — the previously cited $44.99 has no live offer behind it.

CRITICAL for BOM purposes: this price is for the board only. Package contents are UPS HAT (E) x1, acrylic protection panel x1, screws pack x1. The 4x 21700 Li-ion cells the board requires are explicitly NOT included and must be line-itemed separately (budget roughly $30-60 for four cells depending on source and capacity). Budget ~$41 landed for the board direct from Waveshare, and ~$70-100 for a functioning UPS including cells.

Note that the vendor page is directly fetchable with a normal browser user-agent; a 403 from an automated fetcher is a tooling artifact, not a vendor restriction. Re-verify at order time — these are time-sensitive.
corrected.why:
The claim is right to counsel caution but wrong on its load-bearing specifics, and it omits the one fact that will actually cause a bad parts order.

1. "Could not verify from the vendor directly" is false. The 403 was a WebFetch user-agent limitation, not a vendor block. A plain curl with a browser UA returned HTTP 200 (210 KB). The page carries schema.org structured data reading "price": 32.99, "priceCurrency": "USD", "availability": "https://schema.org/InStock", SKU 27966. Vendor pricing is directly verifiable and the $32.99 figure is confirmed exactly — it should be stated as vendor-confirmed, not as an unverified snippet.

2. The $44.99 Amazon figure is not supportable. ASIN B0DBLMFX57 (fetched successfully, HTTP 200, no captcha) currently renders "No featured offers available" — no buybox, no Add-to-Cart price, no live price at all. The parallel UPS HAT (E) listing B0DCB6D1F8 shows "Currently unavailable." So the top of the claimed "$33-45 band" is a stale snippet with no purchasable offer behind it. Presenting $44.99 as a current channel price is wrong.

3. The claim omits vendor volume tiers that matter for a parts order: $32.99 @ qty 1, $31.99 @ qty 2, $31.49 @ qty 3, $31.29 @ qty 4+.

4. The $37.47 AliExpress figure remains unconfirmed; current search indicates roughly $38 with free shipping. Directionally fine, not confirmed to the cent.

5. Most material for a hardware spec: the price band is board-only and materially understates the cost of a working UPS. Vendor package content is "UPS HAT (E) x1, Acrylic protection panel x1, Screws pack x1", with the explicit note "The 21700 batteries are NOT included." The product needs 4x 21700 Li cells, which are a separate purchase (realistically another ~$30-60). An engineer ordering against a "$33-45" line gets a board with no energy storage.

6. Corroborating the claim's own caution: search-engine summaries were demonstrably unreliable here — one returned "$67.95-$69.99" and "$7.81-$8.49" for this same SKU. That is an argument for fetching the vendor directly (which works), not for publishing snippet values.

Prices verified 2026-07-20 and are time-sensitive.

corrected.original: The Waveshare pogo-pin mounting scheme is a mechanical liability for a wall-mounted appliance.
corrected.corrected:
The Waveshare pogo-pin mounting scheme is a contact-reliability risk for an appliance exposed to vibration or shock, and should not be specified without mitigation.

SUPPORTED BY VENDOR DOCS: Waveshare's own UPS HAT (B) user guide instructs that "If the Pogo pins are not conducting, you can press the pin to loosen it or use a knife to scratch off the oxide layer of the pin header" — the vendor documenting an expected intermittent-contact failure mode. Separately, the UPS HAT (C)/(D)/(E) wikis recommend locking/tightening the screws and soldering the pin headers for better contact when the board is not recognized. (Note: that screws-and-solder recommendation is on the (C)/(D)/(E) pages, NOT the HAT (B) page.) UPS HAT (E) uses the same pogo-pin connector — Waveshare rates the pins to 5V 10A but recommends staying under 6A for thermal reasons — so the concern carries forward to the current part.

FIELD EVIDENCE, STATED ACCURATELY: Raspberry Pi forum thread t=337826 reports a UPS HAT (B) rebooting on minor physical disturbance. A commenter suspected a cracked header solder joint, but the reporter resolved it by undoing and redoing all mounting screws, aligning from the pogo-pin side first. Treat this as one anecdote demonstrating assembly/alignment sensitivity — not as a confirmed inherent defect.

CORRECTED BOOT-BUTTON POSITION: The wiki states the board "may not work when you mount the batteries for the first time, you need to press the Boot button to activate the circuit." This is a one-time step at battery installation, when the unit is necessarily open, so it is not by itself incompatible with sealed field units. The open risk — which the cited source neither confirms nor rules out — is whether a deep-discharge or protection-latch event in the field requires the same physical press on a sealed unit. Confirm with Waveshare before committing to a sealed enclosure.

DESIGN IMPLICATION: If specifying pogo-pin mounting, require the pin headers soldered, the standoff screws torqued and thread-locked, assembly alignment started from the pogo-pin side, and either external access to the Boot button or a documented non-physical recovery path. Note also that an intermittent pogo contact here carries main 5V power, so the failure mode is an uncommanded hard reboot rather than degraded signal.
corrected.why:
The claim's core thrust survives, but the DETAIL contains a source misattribution and an overstated inference, so it must not go into a parts-ordering spec as written.

VERIFIED:
1. The pogo-pin troubleshooting text is real and verbatim. Waveshare's UPS HAT (B) guide (confirmed via the spotpear.com/index/study/detail/id/713.html mirror of the Waveshare user guide, and independently via search of the wiki): "If the Pogo pins are not conducting, you can press the pin to loosen it or use a knife to scratch off the oxide layer of the pin header." This is vendor documentation of an expected intermittent-contact failure mode — strong support for the claim.
2. The Boot-button text is real and verbatim: "The board may not work when you mount the batteries for the first time, you need to press the Boot button to activate the circuit."
3. UPS HAT (E) does use the same scheme. Waveshare and resellers market it as "Pogo Pins Connector," pins rated to 5V 10A with 6A recommended for thermal reasons, powering the Pi "without using any GPIO resource." The extrapolation to (E) holds.
4. The forum thread exists and is titled around the unit being extremely sensitive to minor shocks, with a commenter suspecting a cracked header solder joint.

REFUTATION POINTS:
A. MISATTRIBUTED QUOTE. The claim states that "Waveshare's own wiki for UPS HAT (B)" recommends locking the screws and soldering the pin headers. That recommendation is genuine Waveshare text but appears in the UPS HAT (C), (D), and (E) wikis — not on the HAT (B) page cited. The HAT (B) user guide mirror contains the pogo-pin/knife text but no screws-and-solder recommendation. The STATED SOURCE does not support that half of the sentence.

B. FORUM THREAD REPORTED SELECTIVELY. The claim cites the thread as documenting inherent fragility with "solder joints suspected," but omits the resolution: the OP fixed it by undoing and redoing all the mounting screws, starting alignment from the pogo-pin side. The cracked-solder-joint theory was a guess that the outcome did not confirm. It is a single anecdote, root-caused to assembly/alignment, and resolved — evidence of mounting sensitivity, not of an unfixable design defect. Presenting it as documentation of a design liability overstates it.

C. BOOT-BUTTON INFERENCE OVERSTATED — the most significant error. The wiki scopes the press to when batteries are mounted "for the first time," i.e. during assembly, when the enclosure is by definition open. Calling that "a manual intervention step incompatible with sealed field units" does not follow from the cited text. The defensible concern is different: a deep-discharge or protection-latch event in the field could require the same physical press on an already-sealed unit. The source neither confirms nor excludes that, so it must be stated as an open question to verify with the vendor, not as an established incompatibility.

Net: the headline claim is directionally correct and vendor-documented, but as written it attributes a quote to the wrong page, launders one resolved anecdote into a design verdict, and states the sealed-unit conclusion more confidently than the source supports. Per instructions, substantially right but imprecise = refuted with correction.

corrected.original: LiFePO4wered/Pi+ is the direct answer to the LiFePO4 question and is architecturally the best fit for always-on service, but its 2A continuous limit is a hard constraint.
corrected.corrected:
LiFePO4wered/Pi+ (Silicognition LLC) is the direct answer to the LiFePO4 question and is architecturally the best fit for always-on service. Confirmed specs: 2 A continuous load, 8 A boost converter, 5 V-20 V input including solar with an MPPT controller, 4 uA typical standby with the Pi off, I2C to the Pi with CLI tools plus Python and Node.js bindings, and smooth transfer between external and battery power. ~$51 direct from Silicognition (Tindie); SparkFun has retired its listing, so order direct.

The hard constraint is the energy budget, not the 2 A rating. The included standard 18650 is 1500 mAh at 3.2 V = 4.8 Wh nominal. At the board's full 2 A / 10 W rating that yields roughly 26 minutes (4.8 Wh x ~0.90 boost efficiency / 10 W); a Pi 4 under real load measures 15-25 minutes. Treat this as a ride-through UPS for clean shutdown, not as a device that runs a Pi untethered.

The vendor's "1 to 9 hours" is a range across cell sizes and Pi models, not across load on the shipped configuration: the 9-hour end implies ~0.5 W (below Pi Zero idle) and is only approachable with the 2000 mAh / 6.4 Wh cell, which is currently out of stock; the 1-hour end corresponds to a Pi 4 at idle (~4 W). Order the cell variant explicitly — a "battery compartment removed" SKU exists.

Pi 5 support carries a real derate, not just a footnote. Pi 5 expects a 5 V/5 A (25 W) USB-PD profile; fed from this board it will not see one, and firmware clamps total USB port current to a nominal 600 mA instead of 1.6 A. Budget for that, or plan on a Pi 4 or lower-power model.

Clean shutdown is reliable but software-dependent: it requires the open-source lifepo4wered daemon installed and running on the Pi. The hardware fallback is a programmable timeout that cuts power whether or not the OS has quiesced, so validate the daemon as part of commissioning.

LiFePO4 cycle life is genuinely far better than Li-ion (order 2000+ cycles vs ~300-500 to 80% for quality Li-ion); the vendor's "only a couple hundred cycles" characterization of Li-ion is marketing and should not be cited as a specification.
corrected.why:
The product identification and most individual specs check out against the vendor page (2A continuous, 8A boost, 5-20V input with MPPT, 4 uA standby, I2C with CLI/Python/Node.js, cell included, live at $51 on Tindie with 34 standard 18650 in stock). But the claim is materially imprecise in ways that would misdirect a parts order, so it fails the standard for a hardware spec.

(1) Wrong binding constraint. The claim names 2A as "the hard constraint." The included standard cell is 1500 mAh at 3.2 V = 4.8 Wh nominal. Re-deriving: 4.8 Wh x 0.90 boost efficiency / 10 W = ~26 minutes at the board's own 2A rating (~25 min at 85%). An independent report of a Pi 4 at high load gives 15-25 minutes, corroborating the arithmetic. The binding constraint for always-on service is the ~4.8 Wh energy budget, not the current rating — and the two interact, since 2A cannot be sustained for any useful duration. The claim omits cell capacity entirely, which is the single most load-bearing number for the stated use case.

(2) The "1-9 hours" vendor figure is presented without the load assumptions that make it meaningful. 9 hours implies ~0.53 W, below Pi Zero idle on the standard cell; it is only reachable with the 2000 mAh cell (6.4 Wh) on a Pi Zero at idle — and that high-capacity variant shows 0 in stock. The 1-hour floor corresponds to a Pi 4 at idle (~4 W), not under load. Marketing bracket presented as a runtime range.

(3) Pi 5 caveat misattributed and understated. The vendor's "when USB ports not fully loaded" attaches specifically to Pi 5, but the claim's DETAIL explains it via a Pi 4 with peripherals. The actual Pi 5 issue is sharper: Pi 5 expects a 5V/5A (25W) PD profile, and absent it the firmware clamps total USB current to a nominal 600 mA rather than 1.6 A. "Supports Pi 5" therefore means operating degraded, not merely un-maxed.

(4) "Always performs a clean shutdown" is stated as an unconditional hardware property but requires the open-source daemon installed and running on the Pi; the hardware fallback is a programmable timeout that removes power regardless.

(5) The LiFePO4-vs-Li-ion cycle-life comparison ("a couple hundred cycles") is vendor marketing and understates quality Li-ion (typically 300-500+ cycles to 80%). LiFePO4 does genuinely win (2000+ cycles), but the strawman figure should not enter a spec unqualified. The claim does attribute it to the vendor, which is honest, but it is repeated without correction.

(6) Sourcing detail: "ships WITH a cell" is variant-dependent — a "battery compartment removed" SKU exists and must be avoided at order time. SparkFun has retired its listing (product not discontinued; still sold direct by Silicognition on Tindie).

Substantially right on architecture and identification, wrong on which constraint is hard and silent on the capacity figure an engineer must order against.

corrected.original: LiFePO4 chemistry is the correct choice over Li-ion 18650 for a permanently-installed, permanently-charging wall appliance, on both cycle life and thermal safety grounds.
corrected.corrected:
LiFePO4 is the better of the two lithium chemistries for a permanently-floated wall appliance, but on calendar-life-at-float and runaway-severity grounds only — not on cycle life — and only once a runtime requirement is fixed.

(1) Strike cycle life from the justification. A mains-backed UPS sees only outage cycles, on the order of 100-300 over a 10-year life, which is inside a Li-ion 18650's 300-800 cycle rating (Panasonic NCR18650GA datasheet). LFP's thousands-of-cycles advantage will never be consumed in this application. Justify on calendar aging at high SoC instead.

(2) Remove the "few hundred cycles for Li-ion" figure or attribute it. It is the LiFePO4wered vendor page's own marketing wording ("consumer lithium-ion cells that only last a couple hundred cycles"), not an independent derivation, and the DETAIL's "not a vendor claim" is false for it.

(3) Correct the thermal statement. ARC data on 18650s: LFP ~195 °C, NMC ~170 °C, LCO ~150 °C — a 25 °C margin over NMC, not "markedly higher." Cite severity instead, which is where LFP genuinely wins: no cathode oxygen release, far lower heat and gas output, smoke rather than an ignitable jet flame.

(4) Specify float voltage and ambient, not just chemistry. LFP is float-tolerant, not float-immune (SEI >300 nm, >20% conductivity loss after 36 months at 55 °C / 90% SoC). Set a reduced float near 3.4 V/cell for LFP and a maximum enclosure ambient. Note that charge-voltage de-rating is the dominant lever for both chemistries — the Sequent HAT's selectable 3.5-4.4 V end-of-charge can de-rate a Li-ion pack to ~4.0 V and recover most of the calendar-life gap.

(5) Cost the density penalty explicitly. LFP 18650 ~2000 mAh at 3.2 V = 6.4 Wh vs Li-ion 18650 3500 mAh at 3.6 V = 12.6 Wh. As shipped, LiFePO4wered/Pi+ is one cell (~6.4 Wh) vs Geekworm X1200's two cells (~25 Wh) — about 4x less stored energy. The Pi+ is limited to 2 A continuous with a stated Pi 5 caveat, against the Pi 5's 5 A / 25 W ceiling, and its "9 hours" upper runtime figure implies ~0.7 W average draw (Pi Zero territory). Both LFP-capable options require sourcing cells separately.

(6) State the runtime requirement before concluding. If the requirement is graceful shutdown only, a supercapacitor UPS board beats LFP on both criteria named — >500k cycles, no thermal runaway mechanism, no float-aging path — and should be the baseline. LFP becomes the correct choice only if the spec requires minutes-to-hours of ride-through that supercaps cannot deliver.

(7) Date and scope the vendor survey. No Geekworm or Waveshare LFP variant was found (Waveshare UPS HAT / B / C / D / E are all Li-ion/LiPo), but record the survey date and the model list rather than asserting a universal.
corrected.why:
The conclusion (prefer LiFePO4) is probably right, but it is right for one of the two reasons given, the survey behind it has gaps, and one supporting number is vendor marketing restated as independent judgement. For a document an engineer orders parts against, that is refuted-with-corrections.

1. CYCLE LIFE IS THE WRONG METRIC AND THE CLAIM CONTRADICTS ITSELF. The DETAIL correctly identifies calendar aging at float as the dominant stressor, then cites cycle life as one of its two grounds. A mains-backed UPS only cycles on outages — order 100-300 cycles over a 10-year service life at 10-30 outages/year. That is inside the rating of even mediocre Li-ion 18650s. Panasonic NCR18650GA is commonly cited at 500-800 cycles at mild discharge, 300-500 under load (https://www.omnitron.cz/_dokumenty/792019123600416/ncr-18650ga.pdf, https://endless-sphere.com/sphere/threads/panasonic-ncr18650ga-disclosed-specs-and-30q-samsung-cells.92205/). LFP's thousands-of-cycles advantage is real and irrelevant here — it will never be consumed.

2. PROVENANCE DEFECT. The DETAIL asserts "not a vendor claim," but the "few hundred" Li-ion figure is near-verbatim from the page cited as its own source: lifepo4wered.com says "consumer lithium-ion cells that only last a couple hundred cycles." That is a vendor comparison reused as an independent premise.

3. "MARKEDLY HIGHER THERMAL RUNAWAY ONSET" OVERSTATES THE ONSET DELTA. ARC data on 18650s gives LFP ~195 °C, NMC ~170 °C, LCO ~150 °C (https://www.mdpi.com/2313-0105/3/2/14). 25 °C over NMC is a margin, not "marked." LFP's genuine safety advantage is severity, not onset: no cathode oxygen release, far lower heat/gas output, and predominantly smoke rather than an ignitable jet flame. The spec should cite severity.

4. FLOAT TOLERANCE IS NOT FLOAT IMMUNITY, AND THE LEVER IS CHARGE MANAGEMENT, NOT CHEMISTRY ALONE. LFP at high SoC and elevated temperature still degrades measurably — SEI >300 nm and >20% conductivity loss after 36 months at 55 °C / 90% SoC (https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2025/ta/d5ta03813h). Recommended practice is a chemistry-specific reduced float (~3.4 V/cell for LFP). The identical lever exists for Li-ion: charging to 3.9-4.0 V instead of 4.2 V transforms its calendar life. Critically, the Sequent Multichemistry Watchdog HAT the claim names has software-selectable end-of-charge from 3.5 V to 4.4 V (https://sequentmicrosystems.com/products/multichemistry-watchdog-hat-ups-battery-backup-for-raspberry-pi), so it can de-rate a Li-ion pack too. A de-rated Li-ion HAT can plausibly outlast an LFP pack floated hard at 3.65 V. The spec must set a float voltage and an enclosure ambient limit; without those, the chemistry choice does not carry the argument.

5. THE ENERGY-DENSITY COST IS OMITTED AND IT IS AN ORDERING CONSTRAINT. LFP 18650 ~2000 mAh at 3.2 V = 6.4 Wh vs Li-ion 18650 3500 mAh at 3.6 V = 12.6 Wh — roughly 2x per cell. As shipped it is worse: LiFePO4wered/Pi+ carries one cell (~6.4 Wh; the 2000 mAh OSN cell is the 2024-onward default) against Geekworm X1200's two 18650s (~25 Wh) — about 4x less stored energy. The Pi+ is also 2 A continuous with an explicit Pi 5 caveat ("when not fully loaded on the USB ports"), against the Pi 5's 5 A / 25 W ceiling. Its "1 to 9 hours" runtime implies ~0.7 W average draw at the top end — a Pi Zero figure, not a Pi 4/5 appliance. If the appliance needs ride-through rather than shutdown-only, this is a hard blocker on the only single-source LFP product named.

6. THE BINARY FRAMING EXCLUDES THE OPTION THAT WINS ON BOTH STATED CRITERIA. If the requirement is graceful shutdown (10-60 s), supercapacitor UPS boards beat LFP on both cycle life and thermal safety outright — no runaway mechanism at all, no float-aging path, >500k cycles, decade-plus maintenance-free (e.g. AQEX qUPS-P-SC, https://lectronz.com/products/aqex-qups-p-sc-13-supercap-ups-hat-raspberry-pi; see also https://www.smbaker.com/supercapacitor-uninterruptable-power-supply-ups-for-raspberry-pi). "LiFePO4 is the correct choice" only follows once the spec commits to a runtime requirement supercaps cannot meet — and that requirement is absent from the claim.

7. VENDOR SURVEY: I found no LiFePO4 variant from Geekworm or Waveshare, so that part holds as far as I could check — Waveshare's UPS HAT / B / C / D / E are all Li-ion/LiPo 18650/21700. But it is stated as a universal from an undated survey and should be scoped and dated. Also, Sequent is a multichemistry charger (Li-ion, LiPo, LiFePO4, sodium-ion), not an LFP product; both named LFP-capable options require sourcing cells separately, which the claim does not flag.

No repository files were relevant to this review; all checks were external.

corrected.original: No vendor in this survey offers a Compute Module 4 UPS solution — every option is a 40-pin GPIO HAT.
corrected.corrected:
Geekworm's UPS collection contains no Compute Module 4 product — its UPS line (X728, X1200) is 40-pin HAT hardware for Pi 3B/4B/5, and its CM4 catalogue covers IO boards, NAS, PiKVM and cooling only. PiJuice, Sequent and LiFePO4wered are likewise 40-pin HAT form factor. Waveshare, however, is NOT: it sells at least two CM4 carrier boards with integrated UPS.

- **Waveshare CM4-POE-UPS-BASE** (SKU 22116): standard CM4 socket (Lite/eMMC), onboard UPS with 3× 18650 in PARALLEL (1S3P — capacity adds, voltage does not), simultaneous charge-and-supply with automatic switchover on input loss. Inputs 7–36 V DC / USB-C 5 V / 802.3af PoE (5 V, 2.5 A). Battery voltage, current, power and remaining capacity readable over I2C, with documented low-voltage graceful shutdown. Also exposes a 40-pin GPIO header and an M.2 M-key slot.
- **Waveshare CM4-IO-WIRELESS-BASE-B**: industrial CM4 carrier with UPS module, M.2 B-key for 4G/5G (SIM7600G-H-M.2 / SIM8202G-M2 / SIM8200EA-M2), RS485, CAN, RTC, DIN-rail enclosure available. This is the product previously and incorrectly attributed to "ThinkRobotics" — ThinkRobotics is a reseller, not the manufacturer.

Ordering notes: prices vary widely and the low figures in circulation are stale — Pi Hut £58.60 inc. VAT, PiShop.us $94.95, Core Electronics A$94.20 inc. GST (lead time, not in stock), Tinytronics €89, RareComponents out of stock. Budget ~$95 USD, not ~£27.
