Batteries and the RTC CR2032 are NOT included; 18650 cells must be under 67 mm, which excludes many protected cells. If using PoE, the 802.3af path caps at ~12.5 W (5 V/2.5 A) — a CM4 with NVMe plus a 5G modem can approach or exceed that on transmit peaks, so power from the 7–36 V DC input for those configurations rather than treating 2.5 A as headroom.

Conclusion: a carrier-plus-stacked-HAT mechanical workaround, or moving backup off-board to a DIN-rail DC-UPS, is NOT required for CM4. Single-board CM4 carriers with integrated UPS and I2C battery telemetry are stocked catalogue parts. Those remain valid alternatives if the specific I/O mix of the Waveshare boards does not fit, but they are choices, not necessities.
corrected.why:
REFUTED — and refuted by the very vendor the claim names as an example of the opposite.

**1. The load-bearing negative is false.** Waveshare sells the **CM4-POE-UPS-BASE** (Waveshare SKU 22116): a Compute Module 4 carrier board with a **standard CM4 socket** (Lite and eMMC variants) and an **integrated UPS**. It charges and supplies simultaneously from external power, and auto-switches to battery when input drops. Inputs: 7–36 V DC, USB-C 5 V, or 802.3af PoE (5 V/2.5 A). Batteries: 3× 18650, **not included**. This is a CM4 carrier with onboard UPS, not a 40-pin HAT — it happens to also *expose* a 40-pin header, which is exactly the distinction the claim collapses. The claim's sentence "Waveshare, PiJuice, Sequent and LiFePO4wered all assume the 40-pin Pi header form factor" is directly wrong on Waveshare.

**2. The claim's own hedge misattributes the vendor.** The "ThinkRobotics industrial 5G expansion module with onboard UPS and rail-mount enclosure" is not a third-party product — it is Waveshare's **CM4-IO-WIRELESS-BASE-B**, resold by ThinkRobotics (also carried by PiShop.us and RobotShop). So the one exception the survey flagged as unverified third-party is in fact a second product from a vendor already inside the survey. That means the survey did not merely miss an obscure part; it fetched Waveshare's pages and drew the opposite conclusion from them.

**3. The "unverified host signalling" caveat is unnecessary and understates what's documented.** The CM4-POE-UPS-BASE monitors **battery voltage, current, power, and remaining capacity over I2C**, with documented low-voltage graceful-shutdown. That is at minimum the same class of signalling the survey credits the HAT options with.

**4. Pricing in the survey's orbit is stale/inconsistent — flag before ordering.** Search snippets surface £27 for the Pi Hut listing, but the live Pi Hut page reads **£58.60 inc. VAT** (15 units left). PiShop.us: **$94.95**. Core Electronics: **A$94.20 inc. GST**, dispatch lead time, not immediate stock. Tinytronics: €89. RareComponents: out of stock. Anyone ordering against a ~£27 figure will be short by roughly 2×.

**5. Two spec traps an engineer must not inherit.** (a) The 3× 18650 are in **parallel (1S3P, ~3.7 V nominal, boosted to 5 V)**, not series — one distributor's page can be read as "3S," which would triple the assumed pack voltage and wreck any runtime/energy arithmetic. Capacity adds, voltage does not. (b) Cells must be **<67 mm long**; many protected 18650s exceed this and will not fit. (c) Batteries and the RTC CR2032 are **not in the box** — a real BOM gap.

**6. Only the Geekworm sub-claim survives.** Geekworm's UPS line (X728, X1200, etc.) is indeed 40-pin HAT product for Pi 3B/4B/5; its CM4 catalogue is IO boards, NAS, PiKVM and cooling, with no CM4 UPS. That narrow statement is fine. The error is generalizing it to "no vendor in this survey."

Net effect on the spec: the claim would push an engineer toward an unnecessary architectural detour — a carrier-plus-stacked-HAT mechanical stackup, or moving backup off-board to a DIN-rail DC-UPS — when a single-board CM4 carrier with integrated UPS and I2C telemetry is a stocked, catalogue part.

One genuine constraint worth carrying forward that the claim does not mention: if powering via PoE, the 802.3af path is rated **5 V/2.5 A (~12.5 W)**, which a CM4 plus NVMe plus a 5G M.2 modem can approach or exceed on transmit peaks — size the DC input (7–36 V) rather than PoE for that load, and do not treat the 2.5 A figure as headroom.

corrected.original: For a commercial wall-mounted appliance, the PULS UC10.241 supercapacitor DC-UPS is the strongest reliability play — but its 9-second hold-up only solves ride-through, not outage survival.
corrected.corrected:
For a commercial wall-mounted appliance, the PULS UC10.241 supercapacitor DC-UPS is a strong maintenance-free ride-through option — but it does not solve outage survival, and its headline reliability numbers do not hold at enclosure temperatures.

Model UC10.241 (verify lifecycle status with PULS before design-in: DigiKey lists it Active, other distributors describe it as discontinued/stock-only, PULS states "lead time on request", datasheet is Rev 2.4 dated Aug 2021).

Storage: electrochemical double layer capacitors (EDLC), 6 kWs, no batteries. The EDLCs contain acetonitrile and tetraethylammonium tetrafluoroborate; PULS declares them non-dangerous for shipment and provides an SDS on request.

This is a DC-UPS control unit, NOT a power supply — budget a separate 24V DC PSU upstream.

Input: DC 24V nominal, 22.5-30Vdc continuous. Transfer to buffer mode at 22.45-22.88V input. Output is NOT a regulated 24V: in normal mode it follows the input minus 0.3V (at 10A) to 0.45V (at 15A); in buffer mode it is regulated to 22.45V no-load, 22.25V at 10A, 22.12V at 15A. Rated 15A / 360W.

Buffer time — use the datasheet table, not proportional extrapolation (the curve is not inverse-linear and is bounded at zero load): 9s at 15A, 16.5s at 10A, 39s at 5A, 68s at 3A, 200s at 1A, 340s at 0.5A, 1650s at 0A. At the ~1-2A a Pi draws, expect roughly 100-200s. These are new-unit figures; buffer time scales linearly with remaining capacitance, so at 75% end-of-life capacity derate accordingly (~150s at 1A). Seconds to a few minutes — not hours.

Lifetime expectancy is strongly temperature-dependent and the ">10 years" marketing figure only holds near 25C. Datasheet, at 85% remaining capacity: 186,000h (21 yr) at 10A/25C; 55,000h (6.3 yr) at 15A/40C; 19,000h (2.2 yr) at 15A/55C. Size the enclosure thermals against the actual internal ambient, not room temperature.

MTBF is standard-dependent by roughly 10x — always cite the standard. SN 29500/IEC 61709: 899,000h at 10A/40C, 854,000h at 15A/40C (the PULS web page's unqualified 954,000h at 40C is not corroborated by the datasheet table). MIL-HDBK-217F Ground Benign: 385,000h at 10A/40C. MIL-HDBK-217F Ground Fixed: 95,000h at 10A/40C — Ground Fixed is the appropriate profile for a wall-mounted commercial appliance.

PC-Mode is supported for host shutdown coordination, with an important behavioral caveat: it forces the output off for at least 5 seconds after any buffer event lasting longer than 1s, so a brownout just over 1s will hard-cycle the load rather than ride through it.

Output is decoupled from the input (shared negative rail, not galvanic isolation), allowing buffered and non-buffered load circuits to be split.

Warranty 36 months. Advantage over VRLA: no ventilated cabinet required, as it generates no hydrogen.

Price: publicly listed by distributors at roughly $870-1,125 in North America (DigiKey $1,012.50, TSI $866.66, Affiliated Control $1,125; RS UK GBP 389.51 ex-VAT). Confirm current pricing and lead time with PULS or a distributor, but note this is a roughly $1,000 device plus a separate PSU — weigh that against the load it is protecting.
corrected.why:
The claim's core thesis (supercap DC-UPS, 9s = ride-through not outage survival) is sound, and several specs check out (EDLC/no batteries, 24V/15A/360W, 9s typ at 15A, PC-Mode, 36-month warranty, no-hydrogen advantage over VRLA). But six factual errors survive verification against the Rev 2.4 datasheet and distributor data, several of which would cause an engineer to order or spec wrongly.

(1) MTBF "954,000h at 40C" is unqualified and not corroborated. The datasheet gives SN 29500/IEC 61709 = 899,000h at 10A/40C and 854,000h at 15A/40C. The same table gives MIL-HDBK-217F Ground Fixed at 40C = 95,000h — a 10x swing by standard. Ground Fixed is the applicable profile for a wall-mounted commercial appliance, so the bare 954,000h is a marketing-tier figure presented as a reliability measurement.

(2) ">10 years operational lifetime" carries no temperature qualifier in the claim and is false at realistic enclosure temperatures. Datasheet: 186,000h (21 yr) at 24V/10A/25C, but 55,000h (6.3 yr) at 15A/40C and 19,000h (2.2 yr) at 15A/55C at 85% remaining capacity. Most consequential error for a wall-mounted appliance, which runs well above 25C ambient.

(3) "24V out (22.5V minimum)" mislabels an input parameter as an output spec. 22.5V is the bottom of the INPUT continuous range (transfer threshold 22.45-22.88V input). Regulated buffer-mode OUTPUT is 22.45V no-load / 22.25V at 10A / 22.12V at 15A. In normal mode the output is not regulated — it follows input minus 0.3V (10A) to 0.45V (15A).

(4) "Proportionally longer" is the wrong scaling model. Datasheet publishes an actual table: 200s at 1A, 340s at 0.5A, 1650s at 0A. Inverse-proportional scaling from 9s/15A predicts 135s at 1A (actual 200s) and infinity at 0A (actual 1650s, bounded by internal quiescent draw). Table values are for a new unit; buffer time tracks capacitance linearly, so at 75% end-of-life capacity 1A falls to ~150s.

(5) "Price NOT listed, do not quote" is over-cautious to the point of concealing the decision-relevant fact. Distributor pricing is public: DigiKey $1,012.50 (52 in stock), TSI $866.66, Affiliated $1,125, RS UK GBP 389.51. ~$1,000 to protect a 1-2A Raspberry Pi, and it is a DC-UPS control unit, not a PSU — a separate 24V supply is still required. This materially undercuts "strongest reliability play."

(6) Lifecycle unresolved: DigiKey shows Active, several distributors describe it as discontinued/stock-only, PULS states "lead time on request" against an Aug 2021 Rev 2.4 datasheet. Must be confirmed before design-in.

Additional gotchas: PC-Mode forces the output OFF for at least 5s after any buffer event longer than 1s, so a 1.5s brownout hard-cycles the load — this cuts against citing PC-Mode as a ride-through benefit. And the EDLCs contain acetonitrile and tetraethylammonium tetrafluoroborate (declared non-dangerous for shipment, SDS on request), so the no-hydrogen point is correct but does not mean zero hazmat considerations.

corrected.original: If you need hours rather than seconds of backup in an industrial form factor, Phoenix Contact QUINT-UPS/24DC with IQ technology is the reference-class option, but I could not verify pricing.
corrected.corrected:
For hours rather than seconds of backup in an industrial form factor, the Phoenix Contact QUINT UPS family is the reference-class option — but specify the generation deliberately and budget the battery as a separate line item.

Two generations exist. The IFS-interface QUINT-UPS/24DC with IQ technology comes in 5A/10A/20A/40A (item numbers 2320212 / 2320225 / 2320238 / 2320241), DIN rail with mounted universal adapter UTA 107/30. The newer QUINT4-UPS generation replaces IFS with fieldbus integration (PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, EtherCAT, USB) — e.g. 2907069 (10A, EtherNet/IP), 2907072 (20A, USB), 2907073 (20A, PROFINET). For a new fleet design, default to QUINT4 unless something in the existing plant specifically requires IFS. Do not mix numbers across the two families.

Features that matter for a fleet, per manufacturer copy (marketing claims, not independently measured): automatic battery detection, tool-free battery replacement during operation for hot-swap service visits, preventive energy-storage monitoring, and IQ reporting of state of charge, remaining runtime, and battery service life.

Critical for the BOM: the UPS module contains no battery. Energy storage is ordered separately — UPS-BAT/VRLA/24DC/7.2AH (2320319), 12AH (2320322), or 38AH. Size it from actual load, not from the module rating. At 24V nominal: 38Ah = 912Wh, giving roughly 7.6h at a 120W load or about 1.9h at 480W before efficiency and Peukert derating, so treat those as optimistic ceilings and derate 20-30%. The integrated-storage variant QUINT-UPS/24DC/24DC/5/1.3AH is a minutes-class device, not an hours-class one: 1.3Ah x 24V = 31.2Wh, about 10-15 minutes at its own 5A rating. Do not select it if the requirement is hours.

Ordering note: 2320225 and 2320238 are Phoenix Contact item numbers, not distributor order codes — Newark uses 73T9490 (10A) and 73T9491 (20A). Newark also lists MPN 1597619 against the 20A unit, which conflicts with Phoenix Contact's own 2320238; confirm with the distributor which physical part that resolves to before ordering.

Pricing: one reseller listed the 10A (2320225) at $631.67 list / $526.39 sale, normally in stock, as an order-of-magnitude anchor only. Batteries are additional. Get a live quote from your distributor rather than budgeting off a single reseller listing.
corrected.why:
The feature set is accurate but the part numbers conflate two product generations, and the "hours of backup" framing omits the battery, which is a separate purchase.

CONFIRMED: QUINT-UPS/24DC with IQ technology exists in 5A/10A/20A/40A (Phoenix Contact item numbers 2320212 / 2320225 / 2320238 / 2320241), DIN rail with mounted universal adapter UTA 107/30. Automatic battery detection, tool-free battery replacement during operation, preventive energy-storage monitoring, and IFS-interface communication are all confirmed in Phoenix Contact and distributor copy. POWER BOOST (1.5x nominal continuous) and SFB are also real. Note these are marketing-copy features, not independently measured figures.

REFUTED 1 — generation conflation (would cause a wrong order). The Mouser numbers 2907069 / 2907072 / 2907073 are NOT the IFS-based QUINT-UPS described. They are QUINT4-UPS, the newer generation, whose differentiator is fieldbus integration (PROFINET, EtherNet/IP, EtherCAT, USB) instead of IFS. Ratings are also mismatched against the claim's 5/10/20/40 framing: 2907069 = 10A/EtherNet-IP, 2907072 = 20A/USB, 2907073 = 20A/PROFINET. None is 40A and none speaks IFS. An engineer ordering 2907073 expecting the IFS device described gets a PROFINET device. Relatedly, presenting the IFS-generation QUINT-UPS as "the reference-class option" is stale for a new design when QUINT4-UPS is the current generation (a QUINT4-UPS/24DC/24DC/40 datasheet is published).

REFUTED 2 — "Newark part references" are manufacturer item numbers, not Newark order codes. 2320225 is Phoenix Contact's own item number; Newark's order code for the 10A is 73T9490 and for the 20A is 73T9491. Separately, Newark lists MPN 1597619 against QUINT-UPS/24DC/24DC/20 while Phoenix Contact's own item number for that same 20A unit is 2320238 — two different manufacturer numbers for a nominally identical part, which I could not reconcile and which needs distributor confirmation before ordering.

REFUTED 3 — the backup-time framing is misleading (most material defect). The UPS module ships WITHOUT energy storage; batteries are separate orderable line items (UPS-BAT/VRLA/24DC/7.2AH = 2320319, 12AH = 2320322, plus a 38AH). An engineer ordering only 2320241 gets zero runtime. The claim promises "hours rather than seconds" while citing the integrated-storage variant, but that arithmetic fails: 1.3Ah x 24V = 31.2Wh, and at the unit's own 5A rating (120W) that is ~15.6 min at ideal 100% efficiency and full depletion — realistically ~10 min after conversion losses and lead-acid Peukert derating at that C-rate. That is minutes, not hours. Hours require the large external modules at modest load: 38Ah x 24V = 912Wh gives ~7.6h at 5A/120W ideal, but only ~1.9h ideal at 20A/480W and well under that in practice. Runtime is a function of battery Ah and actual load, not of the module.

REFUTED 4 — pricing. The claim's "no current price appeared in any search result" reflects not fetching distributor pages (which it admits) rather than genuine unavailability. One distributor fetch returned a live price for 2320225 (10A): $631.67 list / $526.39 sale, "normally in stock." A budgetary anchor is obtainable; the honest caveat should be that this is one reseller's price and not authoritative, not that pricing could not be found. I could not verify the stated Phoenix Contact source URL directly — it returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch — so product confirmation here rests on search snippets and third-party distributor listings.

corrected.original: A supercapacitor HAT eliminates the single worst failure mode of this product class — scheduled battery replacement across a deployed fleet.
corrected.corrected:
Supercapacitor hold-up is a defensible architecture for an appliance whose only requirement is to die cleanly rather than ride through an outage, but it does not eliminate scheduled maintenance — it trades a visible, scheduled battery swap for a silent capacitance-fade failure, which must be budgeted for explicitly.

Sourcing: Geekworm's site shows a "100F Supercapacitor UPS HAT Module for Raspberry Pi 5" at $46.90, but only in the "You may also like" cross-sell module on /collections/ups-hat and /collections/raspberry-pi-5-ups — NOT in the Pi 5 group, whose main grid is entirely battery-based X-series parts (X1200–X1209, X-UPS1). The item carries no Geekworm X-series model number and I could not locate a product page. There is no orderable model number; do not put this line in a BOM until a part number, datasheet, and bank topology (cell count, per-cell F and V, balancing method) are obtained from the vendor. The "5V 5A" rating is unverified — comparable supercap HATs in this class are 5V/3A — and in any case describes converter peak output, not hold-up.

Hold-up: size against measured load at end-of-life capacitance, not nameplate. For a favorable 2×100F/2.7V series bank (50F @ 5.4V, 2.0V boost cutoff, 85% efficiency, 535 J usable): ~107 s at 5W, ~53 s at 10W, ~36 s at 15W, ~21 s at the 25W nameplate — and after a −30% aged-capacitance derate, ~75/37/25/15 s respectively. Since a Pi 5 clean shutdown commonly takes 10–20+ seconds, a 15W appliance on an aged bank has single-digit seconds of margin. "Seconds to low minutes" holds only near idle on a fresh bank.

Aging: supercapacitors do NOT remove calendar aging. EDLCs fade in capacitance and rise in ESR under temperature and float voltage — end-of-life conventionally −20% to −30% C and/or 2× ESR, with lifetime roughly halving per +10°C and typical datasheet endurance of 1,000–2,000 h at rated voltage and 65–70°C. A UPS HAT floats its caps continuously, the worst-case aging condition. Because hold-up scales linearly with C, this silently erodes shutdown margin with no symptom until an outage finds it. Mitigate by derating float voltage, controlling enclosure temperature, sizing for ≥2× the worst-case shutdown time at end-of-life C, and — critically — periodically self-testing and telemetering actual hold-up rather than assuming it.

Regulatory: supercaps are not outside dangerous-goods rules. UN3499 (Capacitor, electric double layer; Special Provision 361, A186, PI 971) classifies EDLCs above 0.3 Wh as Class 9. A 100F/2.7V cell (0.101 Wh) or a 50F @ 5.4V bank (0.203 Wh) falls under the threshold and is exempt, but a 100F bank at 5.4V (0.405 Wh) does not — so the exemption depends on the undisclosed topology and disappears on any scale-up for longer hold-up. The correct statement is that the DG burden is substantially lighter than UN3480/3481 lithium, not that it is removed. Likewise, thermal-runaway/fire risk is much lower than Li-ion, but temperature sensitivity is higher, so enclosure thermals remain a reliability constraint.

Finally, hold-up capacitance is necessary but not sufficient: the power-loss detection, switchover behavior, and shutdown-signalling path (I2C or GPIO) are what actually convert stored energy into a clean unmount, and none of that is verified for this part. Qualify those on real hardware before committing the fleet.
corrected.why:
The claim is directionally reasonable (supercap hold-up is a legitimate architecture for a "die cleanly" appliance) but fails on several load-bearing specifics, and fails in the direction that would cause an engineer to under-spec margin.

1. SOURCING / PART IDENTITY — fatal for a purchase spec. The 100F Supercapacitor UPS HAT is NOT "in the Pi 5 group." On both https://geekworm.com/collections/ups-hat and https://geekworm.com/collections/raspberry-pi-5-ups it appears only in the "You may also like" cross-sell module, never in the main grid. Both main grids are 100% battery-based Geekworm X-series parts (X1200, X1201, X1202, X1203, X1205, X1206 V2.0, X1207, X1208, X1209, X-UPS1). The item also carries no X-series model number — every other Geekworm UPS product does — and my guessed product URL 404'd. There is no orderable model number here. An engineer cannot order against this line as written.

2. "5V 5A" IS UNVERIFIED AND CONFLATES PEAK WITH HOLD-UP. Comparable supercapacitor HATs in this class are 5V/3A with 25F banks. I could not confirm 5A for this part. More importantly, 5V/5A is a converter output rating (peak deliverable current), not a hold-up budget — hold-up scales inversely with load, so quoting 5A alongside a runtime figure is precisely the peak/average conflation to avoid.

3. "REMOVES CALENDAR AGING" IS FLATLY FALSE — the biggest error. Supercapacitors have well-documented calendar aging: capacitance fade plus ESR rise, driven by temperature and float voltage. Conventional EDLC end-of-life is −20% to −30% capacitance and/or 2× ESR; lifetime roughly halves per +10°C and is strongly voltage-dependent (typical datasheet endurance 1,000–2,000 h at rated voltage, 65–70°C). A UPS HAT holds its caps at float voltage continuously, and potentiostatic float is the worst-case aging condition — exactly this duty cycle. Because hold-up time scales linearly with C, aging directly consumes the shutdown margin, and it does so SILENTLY: no user-visible symptom until an outage arrives and the shutdown does not complete, producing the exact SD/eMMC corruption the design was meant to prevent. That is arguably a worse fleet failure mode than scheduled battery replacement, which is at least a known, planned, budgeted cost. The claim inverts the risk it is arguing about.

4. "REMOVES SHIPPING REGULATIONS" IS OVERSTATED. UN3499 "Capacitor, electric double layer" is a real Class 9 dangerous-goods entry for EDLCs with energy storage capacity greater than 0.3 Wh (Special Provision 361; A186 ICAO/IATA; PI 971). Supercaps are not categorically outside DG regulation — they have their own entry with a threshold. Whether this part clears it depends on an undisclosed bank topology. My arithmetic: a single 100F/2.7V cell = 364.5 J = 0.101 Wh (exempt); 2× in series (50F @ 5.4V) = 729 J = 0.203 Wh (exempt); but 100F at the 5.4V bank level = 1458 J = 0.405 Wh, which is over threshold and IS Class 9. So exemption is plausible but unestablished, and narrow — any scale-up for longer hold-up crosses into UN3499. The DG burden is genuinely much lighter than UN3480/3481 lithium, but "removed" is wrong.

5. "REMOVES THERMAL RISK" IS OVERSTATED. Fire/thermal-runaway risk is genuinely much lower than Li-ion. But the EDLC is the most temperature-sensitive component in the design (lifetime halving per +10°C), so a hot enclosure remains a direct reliability problem — just not a fire one.

6. "SECONDS TO LOW MINUTES" IS OPTIMISTIC AT THE TOP END. Measured comparables: a Waveshare-class 25F supercap HAT holds 5V for only 5–6 s at 3A, reaching "several minutes" only at very low current; smbaker's 5V supercap build sagged 4.25V→3.4V in ~10 s and browned out a Pi 4. My own re-derivation for a favorable 2×100F/2.7V series bank (50F @ 5.4V, boost cutoff 2.0V, 85% efficiency, usable 535 J): 107 s at 5W, 53 s at 10W, 36 s at 15W, 21 s at the 25W nameplate. After a −30% aged-capacitance derate: 75 s / 37 s / 25 s / 15 s. So "low minutes" materializes only at near-idle draw on a fresh bank. Since a Pi 5 clean shutdown commonly takes 10–20+ seconds, a 15W appliance with an aged bank is into single-digit seconds of margin.

7. PREMISE. The battery alternatives cited (X1200–X1209) use user-replaceable 18650/21700 cells in holders — a cell swap, not a board RMA — which weakens "single worst failure mode." And the claim concedes that I2C reporting, switchover behavior and reliability record are unverified; those determine whether the clean shutdown is ever triggered at all. A hold-up circuit that does not reliably signal power loss provides zero protection regardless of capacitance.

Verdict: refuted. Substantially right in architectural direction, wrong on part identity, wrong on calendar aging, overstated on regulatory and thermal elimination, and optimistic on hold-up.

corrected.original: Vendor 'seamless switchover' claims in this category are marketing text and none were independently verified with instrumentation.
corrected.corrected:
Switchover behavior in this category is specified in marketing prose, not in measurable terms: none of Geekworm (X728, X1200), Waveshare (UPS HAT C/D), or LiFePO4wered publishes a switchover time, hold-up time, or transition waveform, and none of these claims was verified with instrumentation for this spec.

Exact vendor wording differs and should not be conflated. Geekworm X1200 states it "seamlessly switches to backup power in the event of a power outage or power adapter failure." LiFePO4wered/Pi+ states it "will smoothly switch from external to battery power and back without hiccups." The X728 page does not use "seamless" — it describes an "integrated IN-to-SYS pass-through path" with "advanced system power-path management." Power-path topology plausibly shortens the transition, but with no published transition spec it must be treated as unverified, not as an architecture that guarantees no dropout.

Waveshare documents a related but distinct limit — steady-state battery discharge capability, not transition glitch. UPS HAT (C) states discharge current is about 1.8 A when fully charged and decreases as battery voltage falls, and that if the Pi's required working current is too big it may cause over-current and low-voltage problems with the Pi rebooting repeatedly. UPS HAT (D) describes a high-power load causing insufficient current and unstable boosting, leading to continuous restarts. The remedy for this is sizing the converter and cells, which is separate from adding bulk capacitance to survive the transition.

Screen candidates on steady-state current before evaluating switchover. For a Pi 5-class appliance (5.1 V/5 A target; USB current capped at a nominal 600 mA without 5 A supply detection), LiFePO4wered/Pi+ at 2 A continuous max and UPS HAT (C) at ~1.8 A are out of class on their own datasheets; the vendor itself caveats Pi 5 support "when not fully loaded on USB ports." X1200 (5.1 V ±5%, 5 A max) is the only cited part rated for the load.

Before committing, scope the 5 V rail across a mains-drop event at worst-case load (boot surge, peripherals, display) and record the actual undershoot depth and duration against the SoC's minimum rail spec. Do not cite wiki.geekworm.com/X728-Software for electrical specs; it carries a deprecation banner.
corrected.why:
Substantially right in thrust but imprecise in ways that matter for a procurement spec.

Verified as correct: (a) Waveshare UPS HAT (C) wiki does state discharge current is ~1.8 A fully charged, decreasing as battery voltage drops, and that if the Pi's required working current is too big it "may cause over-current and low-voltage problems and the Pi may keep rebooting"; UPS HAT (D) states a high-power load can cause insufficient current and unstable boosting leading to continuous restarts. (b) Geekworm X1200 states it "seamlessly switches to backup power in the event of a power outage or power adapter failure." (c) LiFePO4wered/Pi+ states it "will smoothly switch from external to battery power and back without hiccups." (d) No vendor publishes a switchover time, hold-up time, or transition waveform.

Defects:
1. Self-contradiction. The claim asserts nothing was instrumented, then endorses X728's power-path/IN-to-SYS architecture as "the architecture that genuinely produces no dropout." That is itself an unverified engineering assertion of the type the claim exists to flag. Power-path management shortens the transition but does not guarantee zero dropout, and Geekworm publishes no transition spec.
2. Misattribution. The X728 product page does not use "seamless" — it says "Uninterruptible Power Supply," "advanced system power-path management," "integrated IN-to-SYS pass-through path." X1200 is the part that says "seamlessly." Treating them as one marketing category misstates the wording.
3. Mechanism misread. The Waveshare caveat describes steady-state battery/boost-converter current capability, not a switchover transition glitch. The engineering remedies differ (size converter and cells vs. add bulk capacitance across the transition). The quoted wording is also from UPS HAT (C), a Raspberry Pi Zero-class board, not (D) as the source list implies.
4. Buried lede. Two of the four cited parts are disqualified for a Pi 5-class appliance on steady-state current before switchover is even considered: LiFePO4wered/Pi+ is 2 A continuous max (vendor caveats Pi 5 "when not fully loaded on USB ports"); UPS HAT (C) is ~1.8 A and falling. Pi 5 targets 5.1 V/5 A, and absent 5 A supply detection USB current is capped at a nominal 600 mA. X1200 (5.1 V ±5%, 5 A max) is the only cited part in the correct class.
5. Overstated as a fact about the world. "None were independently verified with instrumentation" should be scoped to what is checkable: no vendor publishes a switchover time or waveform, and the author did not measure. LiFePO4wered does claim the +2 A rating is "fully tested and characterized on a statistically relevant sample size" — vendor data, not independent, but not nothing.

Sourcing hygiene: wiki.geekworm.com/X728-Software carries a deprecation banner ("This page is outdated and may contain inaccurate information") and should not be cited for electrical specs.

corrected.original: Data freshness caveat: prices were fetched live on 2026-07-20 but this category re-prices constantly and two key vendor sites blocked verification.
corrected.corrected:
Data freshness caveat: prices were fetched live on 2026-07-20, but this category re-prices constantly, Geekworm publishes simultaneous list and sale prices (so its numbers are volatile by design), and two key vendor sites blocked verification. Treat all figures as indicative, not as order-ready quotes; re-confirm at PO time.

Verified by direct vendor fetch on 2026-07-20 (Geekworm product pages unless noted): X728 $44.00 sale / $45.99 list; X1200 $45.00 sale / $46.00 list; X1201 $46.00 sale / $49.00 list; X1202 $49.00; X1203 $45.00 sale / $46.00 list; X1205 $46.00; X1206 V2.0 $50.00 (product page; note the /collections/ups-hat listing still shows $48.00 — the collection page is stale, and Geekworm records V1.1 as discontinued 2026-04-07, so budget against $50.00); X703 $22.00 sale / $25.00 list; Sequent Microsystems Multichemistry Watchdog HAT $65.00.

LiFePO4wered/Pi+: no price on the manufacturer page, which directs buyers to Mouser Electronics and Tindie (not Crowd Supply). Tindie lists $51.00, in stock. A European retailer listing at 59.00 EUR was seen but not confirmed and sits materially above the direct-channel price.

NOT verified: all Waveshare pricing (HTTP 403); PiJuice pricing (HTTP 402); PULS UC10.241 (quote only); Phoenix Contact QUINT-UPS (no price surfaced). The "100F Supercapacitor HAT $46.90" figure carries no identified vendor and could not be reproduced — do not order against it until a source is attached.

Where a vendor's collection page and product page disagree, the product page governs; collection-page prices in this category are demonstrably stale.
corrected.why:
The claim's overall posture is sound and its blocked-fetch disclosures are honest — I independently reproduced Waveshare HTTP 403 and PiJuice HTTP 402, and confirmed 8 of the 10 stated prices exactly (X728 $44.00 sale/$45.99 list, X1200 $45.00, X1201 $46.00, X1202 $49.00, X1203 $45.00, X1205 $46.00, X703 $22.00, Sequent $65.00). The observation that Geekworm shows simultaneous list and sale prices is correct.

However, two specifics are wrong, and since this is destined for a spec an engineer orders parts against, they must be corrected.

(1) X1206 V2.0 price is wrong. The claim states $48.00 as "confirmed by direct vendor fetch." The Geekworm collection page (/collections/ups-hat) does show $48.00, but the product page (geekworm.com/products/x1206) shows regular $50.00 / sale $50.00 for V2.0, with $48.00 appearing nowhere. Two separate fetches of the product page returned $50.00. This is a $2 error on the orderable page. It is compounded by a misplaced caveat: the claim labels X1202 as "(collection page)" — where collection and product page in fact agree at $49.00 — while omitting that caveat for X1206, the single item where the two Geekworm pages disagree. The product page also documents that X1206 V1.1 was discontinued on 2026-04-07 in favor of V2.0, making $48.00 plausibly a stale V1.1-era figure persisting on the collection listing. This is exactly the stale-price failure mode the review was asked to hunt for.

(2) LiFePO4wered/Pi+ retail channels are misstated and the "not verified" status is overstated. The vendor page (lifepo4wered.com/lifepo4wered-pi+.html) links to Mouser Electronics and Tindie — not "Crowd Supply and Mouser" as claimed. Crowd Supply hosted the original campaign but is not a current linked channel. Tindie lists the LiFePO4wered/Pi+ at $51.00, in stock, one hop from the vendor page the claim states it already fetched. Filing the price as unverified while citing an unconfirmed 59.00 EUR European retailer listing understates what was readily obtainable, and 59 EUR is materially above the $51.00 USD direct-channel price.

Additional traceability gap (not itself a refutation): the "100F Supercapacitor HAT $46.90" line names no vendor and I could not reproduce it from any source. An unattributed price is not actionable in a procurement spec.

One thing I checked and dismissed: Geekworm product pages render contradictory boilerplate ("Only N items in stock! Out of stock!"). This initially read as several parts being sold out, but the collection page confirms all listed parts are in stock. It is a theme rendering artifact, not an availability issue, and should not be reported as one.

corrected.original: Recommended shortlist by architecture, given the always-on commercial wall-mount constraint.
corrected.corrected:
Recommended shortlist by architecture, given the always-on commercial wall-mount constraint.

Pi 4, clean-shutdown-only (ride-through of seconds to a few minutes): LiFePO4wered/Pi+ is the strongest HAT-form option — LiFePO4 chemistry is the right choice for permanent float service at elevated in-enclosure temperature, the cell is included, it manages a clean shutdown, and it reports over I2C. Order the 18650 variant specifically: it is rated 2 A continuous, whereas the 14500 (600 mAh) variant of the same product is rated only 0.75 A, which a Pi 4 exceeds at idle. Confirm cell-option stock before release; the 2000 mAh high-capacity cell has been intermittently unavailable. Note this is a battery part, not a maintenance-free one — budget a cell-replacement interval.

Pi 4, hours of runtime: do NOT specify a HAT. Re-derive before ordering: the LiFePO4wered/Pi+ included 1500 mAh 18650 holds 4.80 Wh (2000 mAh option = 6.40 Wh); after boost efficiency and usable depth-of-discharge roughly 3.8 Wh reaches the load. Against a measured Pi 4B draw of 2.85 W idle and 3.5-6.5 W under typical load, that is ~79 min idle, ~45 min at 5 W, and ~23 min at the part's own 2 A ceiling. Best case with the high-capacity cell at bare idle is ~1.75 h. The vendor's "1 to 9 hours" spans all Pi models and cell sizes; a Pi 4 sits at the bottom of it. For genuine hours-class runtime, use the DIN-rail path below sized from an energy budget in Wh, not from a current limit.

Pi 4, zero-battery-maintenance clean shutdown: a supercapacitor HAT removes battery service entirely, but this category has thin commercial supply — the main off-the-shelf option is the AQEX qUPS-P-SC-1.3 (Lectronz), with the remainder being open-source/DIY designs. Qualify supply before committing, and hold it to the same procurability standard applied to PiJuice.

CM4: HATs are not categorically unavailable — the official CM4 IO Board carries a standard 40-pin GPIO header and Raspberry Pi documents building with off-the-shelf HATs; fitment is a per-part mechanical-clearance check. For industrial ride-through, a 24 V DIN-rail DC-UPS remains the better architecture: PULS UC10.241 for seconds-class (EDLC capacitor storage, >10-year lifetime expectancy, typ. 9 s at its full 15 A rating — far longer at Pi-scale loads; note it is a 15 A unit despite the "10" in the name), or Phoenix Contact QUINT-UPS/24DC/24DC for hours-class (tool-free battery replacement during operation, IQ Technology SOC/SOH reporting). Size the Phoenix battery module from a Wh budget. Power topology: on the official CM4IO, feed the 24 V bus in directly at the barrel jack — that board accepts 12 V nominal and up to 26 V when PCIe is unused — so no 24 V-to-5 V converter is required. Specify a converter only for a custom 5 V carrier board. For shutdown signalling, verify the UPS output type first: the PULS UC10.241 provides volt-free Ready and Buffering relay contacts that may be wired switch-to-ground against a GPIO pull-up (consider an external stiffer pull-up to meet contact wetting current over a multi-year deployment), but many DIN-rail UPS units expose 24 V logic outputs, and Pi GPIO is 3.3 V and not tolerant of higher voltages — opto-isolate anything that is not a dry contact.

Avoid: Sixfab Power Management & UPS HAT (officially retired; unsourceable components, cloud API dead since end-2022). Waveshare pogo-pin boards (documented shock sensitivity and a documented BOOT-button manual activation step on first battery install).

Qualify with caution rather than avoid outright: PiJuice is not discontinued and remains listed by Pi Supply, but availability is intermittent and some resellers have dropped it — verify stock at order time. Geekworm X728 has real documented issues — battery-holder solder reliability (holder type changed from SMD to pin-type in Aug 2022), latching-switch behavior cutting power instead of shutting down cleanly, and ACFail assertion on powered USB-C — but there is no evidence for any "3-month" latent failure mode; that figure should not appear in a specification.
corrected.why:
The shortlist's structure is sound and several specifics check out, but the headline recommendation is wrong by roughly an order of magnitude for its own stated use case, and it contains one false existence claim and one fabricated failure statistic.

WHAT SURVIVED VERIFICATION:
- PULS UC10.241: correct part number and correct characterization. It is genuinely capacitor-based (EDLC), rated >10 year lifetime expectancy, typ. 9 s buffering at 15 A — legitimately seconds-class. (Note: it is a 15 A unit despite the "10" in the name; its signalling is two dry relay contacts, Ready and Buffering.)
- Phoenix QUINT-UPS: hot-swap claim confirmed — tool-free battery replacement during operation, IQ Technology reporting SOC/SOH and remaining runtime.
- Sixfab retired: confirmed by Sixfab's own EOL notice (chip shortage / unsourceable critical components; cloud API dead after 2022-12-31).
- Waveshare pogo-pin boards: both criticisms substantiated — a Raspberry Pi forum thread documents UPS HAT (B) being "extremely sensitive to even minor shocks," and Waveshare's own wiki documents the BOOT-button first-activation requirement and pogo-pin oxide/contact remedies.

REFUTATION 1 — "hours of runtime" is unsupported arithmetic (the binding error). The included cell is a 1500 mAh 18650 LiFePO4 = 4.80 Wh (2000 mAh option = 6.40 Wh, and showed 0 in stock). After boost-converter efficiency (~87%) and usable DoD (~90%), ~3.76 Wh reaches the load. Measured Pi 4B draw is 575 mA @ 5 V = 2.85 W idle and 3.5–6.5 W under typical server load. That yields ~79 min at idle, ~45 min at 5 W, ~35 min at 6.4 W. Best case (2000 mAh cell, bare idle) is ~1.75 h. The vendor's "1 to 9 hours" figure is a range across ALL Pi models and cell sizes — the Pi 4 sits at the bottom of it, and quoting the top of a marketing range for the highest-power board is exactly the marketing-as-measured error. An engineer specifying this part for a wall-mount Pi 4 needing "hours" of ride-through gets tens of minutes.

REFUTATION 2 — internal contradiction / peak-vs-average conflation. The claim names 2 A as "the binding constraint. Verify that first" for a use case defined by needing hours of runtime. But at 2 A (10 W) runtime is ~23 minutes. The 2 A number is a thermal/converter ceiling, not a sustainable operating point for an hours-class requirement. For that requirement the binding constraint is energy (Wh), not current — the two halves of the recommendation are mutually exclusive.

REFUTATION 3 — "CM4: no HAT exists" is false. The official Compute Module 4 IO Board carries a standard 40-pin GPIO header, and Raspberry Pi's own documentation describes building systems from off-the-shelf HATs on it. UPS HATs attach subject to mechanical clearance, which is a per-part check, not a categorical absence. Relatedly, the prescribed "24V-to-5V converter" is the wrong topology for an official CM4IO build: that board takes 12 V at the barrel jack and tolerates up to 26 V when PCIe is unused, so a 24 V DC-UPS can feed it directly with no converter at all. The 24→5 V part is only correct for a custom 5 V carrier board, which the claim does not state.

REFUTATION 4 — X728 "documented latent failures at the 3-month mark" is unsupported. No source establishes any 3-month failure characteristic. The actually-documented issues are different in kind: battery-holder solder-joint reliability (Geekworm changed SMD to pin-type holders in Aug 2022), latching-switch cutting power instead of clean shutdown, ACFail LED asserting on powered USB-C. Fabricated numeric specificity is more dangerous in an ordering document than honest vagueness.

REFUTATION 5 — "PiJuice (unprocurable)" overstates and applies an inconsistent standard. PiJuice is not officially discontinued; Pi Supply still lists it and Pi Supply auto-delists out-of-stock items (a known source of false discontinuation reports). Some resellers (SparkFun) retired it; availability is intermittent. Meanwhile the claim recommends "a supercapacitor HAT" with no manufacturer or part number — the procurable options there are thinner than PiJuice's (chiefly AQEX qUPS-P-SC-1.3 via Lectronz, otherwise DIY/open-source designs). Rejecting one part for procurability while recommending an unnamed part with worse supply is not a defensible ordering instruction.

ADDITIONAL ORDERING HAZARD — the 2 A rating applies to the 18650 variants only. The 14500 (600 mAh) variant of the same product is rated 0.75 A continuous, which a Pi 4 exceeds at idle. Ordering the wrong SKU silently violates the claim's own stated constraint.

SIGNALLING CAUTION — "wire the UPS signalling contact to a CM4 GPIO" is safe for the PULS UC10.241 because its outputs are volt-free relay contacts (switch to ground against a pull-up), though low-current dry contacts may not meet minimum wetting current from a ~50 uA GPIO pull-up over a multi-year float deployment. It is NOT safe as a general instruction: DIN-rail UPS units commonly expose 24 V logic outputs, and Pi GPIO is 3.3 V and not tolerant of higher voltages. The output type must be verified per unit and opto-isolated if it is not a dry contact.

corrected.original: A headless Raspberry Pi 4B idles at 2.2-2.85 W depending on configuration and firmware, with 2.7 W the most defensible single reference point.
corrected.corrected:
A headless Raspberry Pi 4B idles at approximately 2.2-2.4 W measured on the DC side (5 V input, ~0.43-0.48 A), rising to roughly 2.7-3.0 W measured at the AC wall, where PSU conversion losses are included. State which measurement plane a figure refers to; the two are not interchangeable.

If a single DC-side reference point is required, use 2.4 W with a stated tolerance of +/-0.3 W rather than a bare 2.7 W. Geerling's 2.7 W (540 mA @ 5 V, SATECHI USB-C meter, Pi Dramble) is a single undated reading with no stated OS, firmware, EEPROM version, or board revision, and its test condition is "nothing plugged into USB" with HDMI state unspecified - the page carries an unfinished TODO for "HDMI off, LEDs off" - so it is not a verified headless figure and should not be treated as the most defensible number.

Source detail, corrected: ChipWired (36 measurements, Raspberry Pi OS Bullseye 32-bit, two USB meters plus one household watt meter) reported idle of 2.2 W / 2.3 W / 3.0 W and headless baseline of 2.4 W / 2.3 W / 2.7 W across its three meters - the wall-meter readings must not be dropped. Notably, ChipWired's peripheral-loaded configuration did not draw more than its headless one, so attaching HDMI and USB peripherals does not explain the inter-source spread; meter accuracy, board revision, and firmware version are the better explanations.

Unresolved and not to be asserted without a primary source: the magnitude of idle-power reduction from bootloader/EEPROM and VL805 USB-controller firmware updates. Note also that the early-2019 Pi 4 USB-C failure was a hardware CC-resistor design flaw corrected at board revision 1.2, not a firmware issue - do not describe it as "USB-C/VLI firmware."

Specify RAM variant and board revision (1 GB/2 GB/4 GB/8 GB; rev 1.1/1.2/1.4) alongside any quoted figure, since the 8 GB board uses a different switching regulator and idle draw varies by variant.

For supply sizing, do not use idle. Budget against 5 V / 3 A (15 W), the official recommendation: Geerling measured 6.4 W (1280 mA) under 400% CPU stress with no USB load, and downstream USB ports may draw up to 1.2 A on top of that.
corrected.why:
Directionally in the right neighborhood but imprecise and misrepresents its own sources in ways that matter for a parts-ordering spec.

(1) CHERRY-PICKED RANGE. The claim credits ChipWired's "three independent meters" as evidence of rigor, then quotes a range derived from only two of them. ChipWired's household watt meter read 3.0 W at idle and 2.7 W headless. Including it, ChipWired's idle span is 2.2-3.0 W (not 2.2-2.3) and its headless span is 2.3-2.7 W (not 2.3-2.4). The suppressed meter is also the only one measuring at the wall, i.e. including PSU conversion loss - the figure most relevant to sizing an upstream supply.

(2) MIXED MEASUREMENT PLANES. The 2.2-2.85 W envelope splices DC-side USB pass-through readings with an AC wall reading. Not commensurable; the plane must be stated.

(3) CAUSAL EXPLANATION CONTRADICTED BY THE CITED SOURCES. The claim attributes the spread to whether HDMI/USB peripherals were attached. But ChipWired's peripheral-loaded "Idle" (HDMI + keyboard + mouse + WiFi) measured 2.2-2.3 W on its USB meters while its headless baseline measured 2.3-2.4 W - peripherals did not raise power. Geerling's 2.7 W is explicitly "nothing plugged into USB," the most stripped configuration, yet reads highest. The peripheral hypothesis runs backwards across the cited evidence; meter accuracy and board/firmware revision explain the spread better.

(4) THE CHOSEN REFERENCE POINT IS THE LEAST DOCUMENTED. Geerling's page states no OS, no firmware/EEPROM version, no date, no sample count, no error bars - one reading from one SATECHI USB-C meter. By the claim's own standard ("verify EEPROM firmware is current before trusting any bench measurement"), 2.7 W fails that test. Calling it "most defensible" is unsupported.

(5) "HEADLESS" OVERSTATES GEERLING. The page says "nothing plugged into USB" and carries an unfinished TODO for "HDMI off, LEDs off" - so HDMI was in default state and LEDs active. Not a headless figure.

(6) USB-C/FIRMWARE CONFLATION. The early-2019 USB-C failure was a hardware CC-resistor flaw (one resistor shared across both CC pins), fixed in silicon at board rev 1.2 - not firmware. Idle-power savings came from separate VL805/bootloader-EEPROM work. "USB-C/VLI firmware" merges two unrelated issues. The "several hundred mW" magnitude was not independently verified (web search budget exhausted) and should be treated as unsourced.

(7) BOARD REVISION CONFOUND. Pi 4B ships in 1/2/4/8 GB across revs 1.1/1.2/1.4, with a different switching regulator on the 8 GB. No cited figure is pinned to a variant, so none is reproducible.

Arithmetic verified where checkable: 540 mA x 5 V = 2.70 W; 575 mA x 4.965 V = 2.855 W; 0.43-0.44 A x 5 V = 2.15-2.20 W. The errors are in sourcing, framing, and measurement boundaries, not in the multiplication.

Separately, for a hardware spec: idle power is the wrong number to order a PSU against. Geerling's own page records 1280 mA / 6.4 W under 400% CPU stress with no USB load, and downstream USB ports can draw up to 1.2 A more. Any spec quoting idle must not let that figure propagate into supply sizing.

corrected.original: Disabling HDMI and onboard LEDs on a Pi 4 saves about 0.11 W total and is NOT worth engineering effort.
corrected.corrected:
Disabling HDMI and onboard LEDs on a Pi 4 is NOT worth engineering effort — and on current Raspberry Pi OS the HDMI portion is largely unachievable anyway.

Measured figures (RPi forum thread t=257144, Pi 4): HDMI output off saves ~20 mA (0.10 W at 5 V); ACT and PWR LEDs save <2 mA each (<0.02 W total); Ethernet LEDs (dtparam=eth_led0=4 / eth_led1=4) save a negligible additional amount. Combined best case is ~22-24 mA = 0.11-0.12 W, which is 4.1-4.4% of a 2.7 W budget (NOT "under 4%").

Two caveats that reduce the realizable saving to near zero:

1. HEADLESS SYSTEMS SAVE ALMOST NOTHING. On Pi 4, HDMI is already powered down at boot when no display is connected (t=257144), and t=248191's original poster reports "I didn't notice any difference when I tried doing this with the RaspberryPi 4" — unlike Pi 2/3 where tvservice -o did help. For a headless build, budget ~0.02 W (LEDs only, <1% of a 2.7 W budget), not 0.11 W. The 0.10 W HDMI figure applies only with a display attached and active.

2. NO WORKING COMMAND ON CURRENT RASPBERRY PI OS. tvservice does not function under vc4-kms-v3d (default since Bullseye, mandatory on Bookworm and Pi 5). Critically, `vcgencmd display_power` does NOT work under vc4-kms-v3d either — both are firmware-side tools, and under full KMS the firmware no longer owns the display. The only documented workarounds are reverting to vc4-fkms-v3d (deprecated in Bookworm, absent on Pi 5) or using KMS-native tooling (wlr-randr --output HDMI-A-1 --off, xset dpms force off, or the DRM sysfs interface). If a firmware-era system is genuinely in use, the correct display IDs per the vcgencmd man page are HDMI0 = 2 and HDMI1 = 7 (ID 3 is Composite), and both ports must be addressed separately — bare `display_power 0` only affects the current display.

Budget zero savings from HDMI disabling on Pi 4. If the power budget is genuinely tight, change the board (a Pi Zero draws substantially less) rather than pursuing these tweaks — the position taken by a Raspberry Pi engineer in t=248191: "Tweaks like that are completely pointless. You won't save enough to justify the effort."
corrected.why:
The conclusion (not worth engineering effort) is correct and well-supported, but four specifics fail verification, and one is actionably wrong for a spec an engineer orders against.

(1) ARITHMETIC: The claim says ~22 mA is "under 4% of a 2.7 W budget." Re-derived: 22 mA x 5 V = 0.110 W; 0.110/2.7 = 4.07%, which is OVER 4%. The thread's upper figure of 24 mA gives 0.120 W = 4.44%. The mA-to-W conversion is itself correct at 5 V.

(2) THE RECOMMENDED FALLBACK IS ALSO NON-FUNCTIONAL. The claim correctly states tvservice is dead under vc4-kms-v3d, then directs the engineer to "use vcgencmd display_power 0 if attempting it." But display_power is firmware-side as well, and under full KMS the firmware no longer owns the display. Multiple sources document this: "Linux KMS controls the display hardware now so you need to use the correct Linux utility to do it. The display_power option had race conditions when using KMS" and "If I switch to kms driver (vc4-kms-v3d), the command no longer works." The workaround offered in those threads is reverting to vc4-fkms-v3d, which is deprecated in Bookworm and does not exist on Pi 5. The claim substitutes one broken command for another.

(3) WRONG DISPLAY ID / INCOMPLETE COMMAND. The authoritative vcgencmd.1 man page (raspberrypi/utils, master) lists: Main LCD 0, Secondary LCD 1, HDMI 0 = 2, Composite = 3, HDMI 1 = 7. Bare "display_power 0" acts only on "the current display" and will not cover both Pi 4 HDMI ports. Separately, cited source t=248191 recommends "vcgencmd display_power 0 3" — ID 3 is Composite, not HDMI0 — so the stated source contains an error.

(4) PEAK vs REALIZABLE CONFLATION. Source t=257144 states HDMI is already "off at boot (probably without devices connected)" on Pi 4, and t=248191's OP reports "I didn't notice any difference when I tried doing this with the RaspberryPi 4." The 0.10 W HDMI figure is thus the display-attached best case. For a headless deployment — the typical shape of a 2.7 W budget — HDMI is already powered down, so the realizable saving is the LEDs alone at roughly 0.02 W (<1% of budget). The claim overstates headless savings by roughly 5x.

VERIFIED AS STATED: the ~20 mA HDMI figure, <2 mA per ACT/PWR LED, and the dtparam=eth_led0=4/eth_led1=4 parameters all match thread t=257144. A Raspberry Pi engineer in t=248191 independently supports the conclusion: "Tweaks like that are completely pointless. You won't save enough to justify the effort." Also noted: neither tvservice nor vcgencmd display_power appears anywhere in current official Raspberry Pi OS documentation (graphics-utilities.adoc), consistent with both being legacy.

Refuted on precision grounds per instructions: substantially right conclusion, but the percentage arithmetic is wrong, the recommended command does not work on current Raspberry Pi OS, the display ID is incomplete/wrong, and the savings figure is unachievable in the headless case it would actually be budgeted for.

corrected.original: Disabling onboard WiFi is the single largest available saving for this appliance at ~0.23 W, since Ethernet is the uplink.
corrected.corrected: Disabling onboard WiFi via 'dtoverlay=disable-wifi' saves roughly 40-50 mA on the 5 V rail (order 0.2 W; ~0.25 W at the wall assuming ~85% PSU efficiency) on a Raspberry Pi 4, which is acceptable here because Ethernet is the uplink. It is NOT the largest available saving: in the same source, a firmware/EEPROM update is worth ~100 mA (~0.5 W) and the CPU governor difference between 'performance' and 'ondemand' is ~48 mA (485 mA vs 437 mA), both equal to or larger than the WiFi saving. Note that Raspberry Pi OS defaults to 'ondemand', so the governor figure is a saving to preserve rather than one to claim. WiFi is roughly 1.6-1.9x the HDMI (~20 mA) plus LED (<2 mA per LED, an upper bound, not a measurement) savings combined — not "more than double." Removing the vc4 DRM overlay is worth ~10 mA; disabling Bluetooth, CPU cores, and onboard audio produced no measurable change. Because Bluetooth must remain enabled and shares the CYW43455 combo module with WiFi, the WiFi-only saving must be re-verified on the actual shipping configuration. All figures are single-unit, single-observer forum measurements on 2019/2020-era Pi 4 firmware with no stated accuracy, and are firmware- and model-dependent; treat them as ±20% planning estimates for Pi 4 only and do not apply them to Pi 5, CM4, or Zero 2 W.
corrected.why:
The component figures are faithful to the source, but the headline assertion is wrong and is contradicted by the claim's own detail block.

1. NOT THE LARGEST — self-contradiction. The claim states WiFi (~45 mA / 0.225 W) is "the single largest available saving," then in the same detail reports the governor change at ~50 mA (0.25 W). 50 > 45. The source measures performance=485 mA vs ondemand=437 mA, a 48 mA / 0.24 W delta. WiFi is at best second.

2. NOT THE LARGEST — the thread's own biggest item is omitted. soundcheck's first measurement is a firmware/EEPROM update worth ~100 mA (~0.5 W, ~20% of idle) — more than twice the WiFi saving, and cited in the same thread the claim points at.

3. "More than double the HDMI+LED savings combined" is false. Source: HDMI ~20 mA, mainboard LEDs "<2 mA potential savings per LED." Pi 4 has 2 mainboard LEDs (+2 Ethernet port LEDs the thread also disables). 20 + ~4 = ~24 mA → 45/24 = 1.9x, not "more than double." Counting the Ethernet LEDs (~28 mA) it drops to ~1.6x. If the 20 mA is per-HDMI-port and both are disabled, WiFi is barely larger at all.

4. The governor saving is not "available" from a stock baseline. Raspberry Pi OS ships with ondemand as the default governor. The 50 mA only exists if someone has deliberately set performance — so it is a saving you can forfeit, not one you can bank, and it is bought with DVFS ramp latency. This cuts both ways: it weakens the governor line item, but it does not restore WiFi to first place because of item 2.

5. Precision overstated for a hardware spec. These are one hobbyist's single-unit bench readings on 2019/2020-era Pi 4 firmware, with no instrument accuracy, no repeat count, no error bars. The thread itself demonstrates the deltas are firmware-dependent (a firmware update alone moved idle 100 mA), so quoting 0.225 W to three significant figures is unsupportable. Cite as "~40-50 mA, order 0.2 W, single-source." The "<2 mA per LED" figure is explicitly an upper bound labelled "potential," not a measurement, and must not be summed as if measured.

6. Rail vs wall ambiguity. 45 mA x 5 V = 0.225 W is arithmetically correct but is the saving on the 5 V input rail, downstream of the PSU. At ~85% PSU efficiency the wall-side saving is ~0.26 W. The spec must state which side of the supply it means; the two differ by ~15%.

7. BT reasoning is not a safe inference. Pi 4 uses the CYW43455 combo WiFi/BT module. "disable-bt showed no measurable impact" means the overlay does not gate the module's idle draw — it does not license the conclusion that BT idle is negligible. Since BT must stay powered in this appliance, the module remains energized, and the 45 mA represents only the WLAN/SDIO portion. Plausible that it still holds with BT on, but it must be re-measured in the actual shipping config rather than assumed.

8. Model scope. All figures are Pi 4 only. They do not transfer to Pi 5 (different power architecture, RP1 southbridge), CM4, or Zero 2 W. The spec must name the target board.

corrected.original: Forcing Ethernet to 100 Mbit saves roughly 0.25 W per Pi, a larger saving than HDMI and LEDs combined.
corrected.corrected:
Forcing Ethernet to 100 Mbit saves roughly 0.2 W per Pi 4 at the board (0.25 W measured at the wall, less PSU losses) — modestly more than disabling HDMI and the board LEDs, which together account for about 0.12 W on the same hardware.

Provenance: a single uncontrolled measurement — one operator reported 2 W saved across eight Pi 4s running Rosetta@Home at 100% CPU, divided by 8. That 2 W delta is only 4-5% of the cluster's 36-51 W draw, i.e. near the resolution limit of a wall meter on a fluctuating compute load, and it was measured AC-side through a PSU whose efficiency and power factor were disputed in the same thread. Treat 0.2 W as an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a budget figure; verify on your own board before it drives sizing.

The HDMI comparison rests on one unreplicated 20 mA reading — another user in the same thread measured no drop at all — and `tvservice -o` no longer exists on current Pi OS with the KMS driver, so that baseline is not reproducible as written.

Applicability: Pi 4 with real wired gigabit only. The saving is zero on Pi Zero 2 W (no Ethernet), Pi 3B+ (gigabit over USB 2.0), or any Wi-Fi-connected gateway. For a BLE mesh gateway relaying WebSockets, 100 Mbit is far more bandwidth than needed, so the throughput tradeoff is genuinely free — but confirm the deployment is actually wired before claiming the saving.

Implementation: `ethtool -s eth0 speed 100 duplex full autoneg on` is runtime-only and is lost on reboot and on link renegotiation. It must be made persistent via a systemd unit or a NetworkManager/dhcpcd dispatcher hook, or the link silently returns to gigabit in the field.
corrected.why:
The source substantiates the raw figure and the claim quotes it honestly, but it is imprecise in four ways that matter for a hardware spec.

VERIFIED: The thread does contain "saved 2 watts across 8 pis (approximately .25w per pi)" via ethtool on Pi 4s. 2/8 = 0.25 W, arithmetic correct. The claim's own caveat about cluster-level-divided-by-8 is appropriate and already stated.

THE COMPARISON HOLDS, NARROWLY: The same thread quantifies Pi 4 HDMI at 20 mA (0.10 W @ 5 V) and board LEDs at <2 mA each (<0.02 W for both). Combined ~0.12 W vs 0.25 W = 2.1x. So "larger than HDMI and LEDs combined" is directionally supported — but the claim's stated source page (start=25) does NOT quantify HDMI or LEDs; those figures come from other pages of the thread. The comparative half was unsourced as presented.

DEFECTS:
1. AC vs DC conflation. The measurement is wall-side through a PSU whose efficiency was actively disputed in that same thread — the poster challenged Anker's 85% claim, and Trejan corrected that the SMPS has poor power factor so real watts don't match apparent VA. At 80-85% efficiency the board-level DC saving is ~0.20-0.21 W, not 0.25 W. If the meter read VA, lower still.
2. Below the noise floor. 8 Pi 4s under Rosetta@Home draw 36-51 W total (the poster's own best was 4.516 W/Pi). A 2 W delta is 3.9-5.5% of a continuously fluctuating BOINC load — not resolvable on a wall meter. The 4.516 W best case also had MULTIPLE tweaks applied simultaneously, so ethernet was never isolated.
3. Load/idle mismatch. Measured at 100% CPU; the stated use case (BLE gateway relaying WebSockets to a handful of clients) is essentially idle. PHY power is largely load-independent so it likely transfers, but it is an untested extrapolation.
4. Command is non-persistent. `ethtool -s` is runtime-only, lost on reboot and typically on link renegotiation. Shipped in a spec without a systemd unit or NetworkManager/dhcpcd hook, the link silently reverts to gigabit in the field.

CONTESTED BASELINE: Another user in the same thread found disabling HDMI/audio/USB produced "no measurable drop in power, or possibly even a .01 watt increase" — so the 20 mA HDMI figure the 2x margin depends on is unreplicated. Also, `tvservice -o` was removed once the KMS driver became default, so the 2019 HDMI comparison is not reproducible as written on current Pi OS.

SCOPE: Pi 4-specific and requires real wired gigabit. Zero on Pi Zero 2 W (no Ethernet), Pi 3B+ (gigabit over USB 2.0), or any Wi-Fi-connected gateway. The thread's own data shows disabling Wi-Fi saves ~45 mA (0.225 W) — comparable magnitude, opposite tradeoff.

corrected.original: No published measurement exists for continuous BLE scan+advertise power on a Raspberry Pi 4; the increment must be derived, and I estimate +0.1 to +0.4 W.
corrected.corrected:
Continuous BLE scan+advertise power on a Raspberry Pi 4: UNMEASURED — reserve +0.6 W, do not treat as derived.

No controlled Pi-4 BLE scan measurement was located, but this is a search limitation, not an established absence, and it should not be stated as fact. The vendor BT current table for the Pi 4's actual radio IS published and must be consulted before this line is trusted.

Radio term: the Pi 4's Bluetooth is a Cypress/Infineon CYW43455 Wi-Fi 5 + BT 5.0 combo, not a single-mode BLE SoC. The 13 mA / 43 mW figure previously used here is an nRF51822 number and does not apply; combo silicon draws materially more BT RX current. Take the RX figure from the CYW43455 datasheet BT current table at the VBAT rail, then divide by ~0.85-0.90 for the PMIC. Pending that, assume the radio term is 2-3x the naive single-mode estimate, i.e. roughly 0.10-0.15 W at the 5 V input rather than 0.05 W. Advertising TX bursts at 100-1000 ms intervals remain negligible on average.

Host CPU term: with all four Pi 4 cores on one cpufreq policy and an idle floor of 600 MHz, a continuous HCI advertising-report stream over the PL011 holds the policy ramped. The cost is therefore governed by the DVFS step, not by a linear percentage of the 0.925 W/core figure derived from stress --cpu 4 (which is an average over four saturated cores and an upper bound being misused as a marginal rate). Budget 0.1-0.4 W for the host regardless of device density; density shifts the number within that band rather than scaling it from near-zero.

Total: budget +0.2 to +0.6 W, reserve 0.6 W in the power envelope. Do not quote a range tighter than 0.1 W — the reference data (Satechi inline USB meter, tabulated at 10 mA / 0.1 W) cannot support finer resolution, and independent sources disagree on the Pi 4 idle/load span by ~13% (2.7/6.4 W vs 3.0/6.25 W).

Baseline convention: this increment is measured against a Pi 4 idling with Bluetooth enabled and idle (Raspberry Pi OS default), NOT against dtoverlay=disable-bt.

Status: unvalidated engineering reserve, not a derived figure. This is the weakest number in the budget and must be bench-measured before parts are ordered against it.
corrected.why:
REFUTED. The framing ("no published measurement, must derive") is defensible and the closing advice ("measure this first") is correct, but the derivation has one wrong-part substitution, one internal arithmetic inconsistency, a headline range that does not reconcile with its own body, and precision below the resolution of its own source. An engineer sizing a PSU against +0.1 to +0.4 W would be working from a number the derivation does not actually produce.

WHAT SURVIVED
- pidramble figures quoted correctly. Fetched the page: Pi 4 B, "Idle | 540 mA (2.7 W)" and "400% CPU load (stress --cpu 4) | 1280 mA (6.4 W)". Accurate.
- (6.4 - 2.7) / 4 = 0.925 W. Arithmetic correct.
- CPU sub-terms compute correctly: 1-5% x 0.925 = 9.3-46.3 mW ("0.01-0.05"); 10-25% x 0.925 = 92.5-231.2 mW ("0.09-0.23").
- 13 mA x 3.3 V = 42.9 mW. Correct.
- BT HCI on the Pi 4 is on the PL011 (UART0), not the mini-UART. Correct.

FAILURE 1 — WRONG DEVICE CLASS FOR THE RADIO TERM (the substantive one)
I fetched the claim's own cited Nordic thread. The 13 mA figure there is explicitly the nRF51822: "the typical current draw when in RX is then 13 mA," discussing a single-mode, coin-cell-targeted BLE SoC. The Pi 4 does not contain an nRF51. It uses a Cypress/Infineon CYW43455 Wi-Fi 5 + Bluetooth 5.0 combo. The Pi 4 reduced schematic (pip-assets.raspberrypi.com, RP-008345-DS-1) redacts the wireless section but exposes the rail label WLBT_VBAT, confirming a discrete combo-radio supply rather than a generic 3.3 V tap. Combo silicon carries Wi-Fi-sized regulators, PLLs and always-on analog that a single-mode BLE part does not; its BT RX current is materially higher, and the error is directional (understates). The claim's own supporting data point argues the same way: pidramble measures onboard Wi-Fi on a Pi 3 B+ at +50 mA / +0.25 W (350 mA -> 400 mA) for a *DTIM-sleeping, heavily duty-cycled* link. A 100%-duty-cycle receiver on comparable combo silicon costing 1/5 of that (50 mW) is not credible. The right primary source — the CYW43455 BT current table — is published and was not consulted, which also undercuts the "no published measurement exists" framing.

FAILURE 2 — INTERNAL ARITHMETIC INCONSISTENCY
42.9 mW / 0.90 = 47.7 mW; / 0.85 = 50.5 mW. The stated 85-90% regulator efficiency yields 48-51 mW, not the claimed "~50-75 mW". Reaching 75 mW requires 57.2% efficiency. The upper bound is unsupported by the assumption printed next to it.

FAILURE 3 — HEADLINE DOES NOT MATCH THE DERIVATION
Running the claim's own numbers end to end: sparse = 56.9-96.7 mW (0.06-0.10 W); dense = 140.2-281.7 mW (0.14-0.28 W). Full span 0.06-0.28 W. The headline says "+0.1 to +0.4 W". The low end of the headline is the *top* of the sparse case, and the high end exceeds the derived maximum by 43% with no shown work. "Up to ~0.45 W pathological" has no derivation at all. Three different ranges appear in one claim.

FAILURE 4 — THE LOAD-BEARING TERM IS AN UNSOURCED GUESS
"1-5% of a core" and "10-25% of a core" carry ~82% of the dense-case total (231 of 282 mW) and are pure assertion — no measurement, no packets/sec, no per-report cost, no duplicate-filtering assumption. This is presented as derivation but is assumption wearing a derivation's clothes. Note also that advertisement *report rate*, not device count, drives host cost, and BlueZ duplicate filtering changes it by an order of magnitude either way.

FAILURE 5 — DVFS NONLINEARITY MAKES THE SPARSE END OPTIMISTIC
0.925 W/core is an average over four cores saturated at 1.5 GHz. Applied as a *marginal* rate to a 1-5% load it understates cost: the Pi 4 idles at 600 MHz, all four cores share one cpufreq policy, and a persistent UART wakeup stream holds the whole policy at high frequency and voltage. The first fraction of load pays the entire frequency/voltage step. "+0.01 W CPU sparse" is the least defensible figure in the estimate.

FAILURE 6 — PRECISION BELOW THE SOURCE'S RESOLUTION
pidramble measured with a "SATECHI USB-C Power Meter" — an inline USB meter, not lab instrumentation — and tabulates at 10 mA / 0.1 W granularity. Its own Pi 3 B row shows 230 mA and 250 mA both rounding to "1.2 W". The claimed increment (0.1 W = 20 mA at 5 V) sits at or below the quantization of the data it is derived from; distinctions like "0.15-0.3 W" are false precision. The page's Pi 4 entries for every other state (HDMI off, Wi-Fi off, single-core) are marked TODO, so no cross-check exists.

FAILURE 7 — PER-CORE CONSTANT IS NOT STABLE ACROSS SOURCES
Wikipedia lists Pi 4 idle at 3.0 W and 6.25 W under stress, giving 0.81 W/core against pidramble's 0.925 — ~13% disagreement. Also, attributing the entire 3.7 W delta to CPU cores ignores uncore, memory controller and PMIC loss rising under stress, so 0.925 is an upper bound being used as a marginal rate.

FAILURE 8 — UNSTATED BASELINE
The claim never says whether the 2.7 W baseline has Bluetooth enabled-but-idle (Raspberry Pi OS default) or disabled via dtoverlay=disable-bt. The increment means entirely different things in the two cases, and a spec built against it will be measured against whichever the technician happens to have.

ON "NO PUBLISHED MEASUREMENT EXISTS": the WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted (200/200) before I could test this negative, so I cannot confirm or falsify it. That is itself a reason not to assert it as fact in a hardware spec — and it is misleading regardless, since the vendor BT current table for the actual part is published.

Sources checked: [pidramble power consumption](https://pidramble.com/wiki/benchmarks/power-consumption) (fetched, figures and test conditions confirmed), [Nordic DevZone thread](https://devzone.nordicsemi.com/f/nordic-q-a/2305/receive-current-power-consumption-and-continuous-scanning) (fetched; 13 mA confirmed as nRF51822), [Pi 4 reduced schematics](https://pip-assets.raspberrypi.com/categories/545-raspberry-pi-4-model-b/documents/RP-008345-DS-1-raspberry-pi-4-reduced-schematics.pdf) (fetched; wireless section redacted, WLBT_VBAT rail present), [Wikipedia Raspberry Pi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raspberry_Pi) (Pi 4 3.0 W idle / 6.25 W stress). The [Argenox page](https://argenox.com/library/bluetooth-live-energy/using-raspberry-pi-ble) returned HTTP 403 and could not be verified at all — a cited source that cannot be retrieved should not appear in a spec.

corrected.original: BlueZ under high BLE device density is a documented reliability risk on Pi 4, independent of power.
corrected.corrected:
BlueZ/bluetoothd scaling under high BLE advertiser density is an UNQUANTIFIED risk for the Pi 4 gateway — treat it as a design hedge, not as a documented failure mode, because neither cited source establishes it.

What the sources actually support:
- bluetoothd is documented to spin one core at 100% CPU in an endless loop when a paired device enters standby, requiring a service restart. Source: raspberrypi.com forum t=215660 (June 2018). Note this is Raspbian Stretch, predates the Pi 4, and involves a Bluetooth Classic HID keyboard, not BLE scanning or device density. A Raspberry Pi engineer on the thread stated it is a general Bluetooth-stack issue, not Pi-specific. Whether it still reproduces on current BlueZ on a Pi 4 is UNVERIFIED.
- bleak issue #1433 does NOT support any density claim. It is a passive-scanning capability-check error on BlueZ 5.55, resolved by upgrading to 5.56. Remove this citation, or re-cite it accurately as evidence that BlueZ patch-level matters for passive scanning (pin BlueZ >= 5.56).
- The "300-400 devices causes silent scan stall on Pi 4" scenario has no located source. Either drop it or replace it with a citation that actually documents it.

Power figure: ~0.93 W per fully-loaded core is a reasonable UPPER BOUND, derived as (6.4 W at 400% CPU - 2.7 W idle) / 4 cores from pidramble's measured Pi 4B figures. A bluetoothd spin loop will draw less than a stress-ng core. Also note that one pinned core out of four does not itself starve the gateway; the gateway fails because bluetoothd is wedged.

Recommended spec language: budget a scan-stall watchdog that restarts bluetoothd (justified by the documented standby-loop hang and by general prudence, not by a density-specific report), pin BlueZ >= 5.56, and BENCH the actual density limit on target hardware before committing to a raw-HCI-socket architecture. The D-Bus object-per-device overhead is a real and plausible scaling concern, but its threshold is untested here and must be measured, not assumed at 300-400 devices.
corrected.why:
Both citations were checked directly and neither supports the claim as written.

(1) bleak issue #1433 (verified via GitHub API, title "Passive scanning on Raspberry Pi 4 model B", opened 2023-10-04, closed, 4 comments) is about a BleakError capability check — "passive scanning on Linux requires BlueZ >= 5.55 with --experimental enabled and Linux kernel >= 5.10" — failing despite an apparently valid config. It was resolved by the reporter upgrading BlueZ 5.55 -> 5.56 ("In 5.56 it fixes the advertisement monitor issue from passive scanning"). The issue contains NO mention of 300-400 devices, high device density, continuous scanning, silent scan stall, or connection failure. The claim's detail that "bluetoothd remains in an 'active' state" appears to be a misreading of a routine `systemctl status bluetooth.service` paste in comment 2, which shows "Active: active (running)" and "CPU: 56ms" — i.e. an idle daemon, the opposite of a spin. The density scenario is unsourced.

(2) forums.raspberrypi.com t=215660 is a real report of bluetoothd pinning one core at 100%, triggered by a paired device entering standby, with a restart-based workaround. But: it is dated June 2018 on Raspbian Stretch, roughly a year BEFORE the Raspberry Pi 4 launched (June 2019), so it cannot document Pi 4 behavior; the device is a Bluetooth Classic HID keyboard, not BLE, and nothing to do with advertiser density; and RPi engineer jamesh explicitly stated it is "presumably a problem with the bluetooth software stack somewhere, and not specific to the Pi."

(3) The power arithmetic does check out. pidramble measures Pi 4B at 540 mA (2.7 W) idle and 1280 mA (6.4 W) at 400% CPU; (6.4-2.7)/4 = 0.925 W per core, so ~0.93 W is a fair figure. Two caveats: it is a stress-ng upper bound (a D-Bus spin loop draws less than a vectorized stress load), and it presumes linear per-core scaling. Separately, "a 100%-pinned core would kill the gateway function" conflates two things — on a 4-core SoC one pinned core does not starve the system; the gateway dies because bluetoothd is wedged, which is the same root cause but a different mechanism than CPU saturation.

I could not locate any bleak issue matching the described symptom (searched the repo's issues; the nearest hit, #1424 "Missing telegrams and scanning stops randomly", is Windows 10 and not density-related). WebSearch budget was exhausted, so an exhaustive search of the broader BlueZ bug record was not possible — but the burden is on the claim, and its two stated sources demonstrably do not carry it.

The underlying engineering concern is plausible and the mitigations (scan-stall watchdog, raw HCI socket to bypass per-device D-Bus objects) are sound defensive design. But as written this is a documentation claim, and the documentation does not exist at the cited locations. Putting a fabricated citation into a spec an engineer orders parts against is the specific failure mode to avoid here.

corrected.original: Defensible total design figure for the described workload: 3.0 W typical, with a defensible range of 2.6 W (best case) to 3.5 W (dense/busy, hot enclosure).
corrected.corrected:
Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (all three cited sources are Pi 4; none contains Pi 5 data — do not apply this budget to a Pi 5).

ENERGY BUDGET (average, measured at the 5 V DC input, excluding PSU losses):
- Sourced optimized headless floor, WiFi disabled, Ethernet up: ~2.4 W. Built from Geerling's 2.7 W Pi 4B idle, minus a measured 45 mA (0.23 W) WiFi-off delta and a measured ~14 mA (0.07 W) for LEDs + vc4 overlay, both from the Pi 4 forum thread. No cited source measures an HDMI-off delta for the Pi 4 — Geerling's row is marked TODO — so no HDMI saving is claimed.
- Workload adders are unmeasured engineering estimates, not sourced figures: BLE scan+advertise +0.1 to +0.4 W, SQLite small writes +0.1 to +0.3 W, WebSocket relay +0.1 to +0.2 W.
- Typical average: 2.7-3.3 W DC. Quote 3.3 W for energy/thermal planning.
- Note: the WiFi-off saving and continuous BLE cannot both be fully banked — the CYW43455 is a WiFi/BT combo part — so the low end is optimistic.

AT THE WALL / BATTERY: add PSU and conversion losses. ChipWired's AC-side readings run roughly 25-30% above its DC readings on the same test. Size solar, battery, or PoE budgets on ~4.0-4.3 W AC-equivalent, not 3.0 W.

PSU / FUSE / WIRE SIZING — DO NOT USE THE AVERAGE. Instantaneous draw is far higher: Geerling measures the same Pi 4 at 5.1 W serving web requests and 6.4 W at full CPU load, before USB peripherals (up to 1.2 A more). Specify the Raspberry Pi 4 official supply rating: 5 V / 3 A (15 W). Fuses, wire gauge, and any battery BMS must be sized to that, not to any figure in the energy budget.

THERMAL: no cited source supports a percent-per-degree power/temperature coefficient; the temperature adder should be dropped from the budget. The actual risk in a sealed outdoor enclosure running 20-30 C above ambient is CPU throttling at 80-85 C, which lowers power while degrading service. Treat enclosure venting/heatsinking as an open thermal-design item requiring in-enclosure validation, not as a wattage line item.
