CONFIDENCE: the 2.4 W floor is the only well-sourced number, and even it carries roughly +/-0.3 W of instrument uncertainty — ChipWired's three meters disagree by 0.4-0.5 W on a single test. All workload adders are unvalidated. Measure the actual build before committing to any power-limited design.
corrected.why:
Arithmetic is internally consistent and the 0.23 W WiFi delta is correctly sourced (forum: ~45 mA x 5 V = 0.225 W). Everything else has defects that matter for a parts order.

(1) No board is named. All three sources are Raspberry Pi 4. Geerling/pidramble contains no Pi 5 data whatsoever, and its Pi 4B "HDMI/LEDs disabled" row is explicitly TODO. A spec with no model on it can be ordered against the wrong board, where PSU requirements differ (Pi 5 needs 5V/5A vs Pi 4's 3A).

(2) The 0.17 W subtraction is mostly unsourced. The forum gives LEDs <2 mA each and vc4 ~10 mA = ~14 mA = 0.07 W. No cited source measures HDMI-off for the Pi 4 (Geerling = TODO). The ~0.10 W HDMI portion is fabricated. Sourced floor is 2.40 W, not 2.30 W. Additionally, on a headless unit with no display attached, HDMI output is already largely quiescent, so subtracting it from an idle measurement risks double-counting.

(3) Baseline/delta rig mismatch. The 2.7 W start is Geerling's 540 mA; the forum's own default idle is 437-465 mA (2.19-2.33 W). Deltas measured against a ~450 mA baseline are subtracted from a 540 mA baseline. The forum's untouched baseline is already below the claim's "optimized floor," which undercuts the buildup.

(4) Measurement plane never stated and the corroboration mixes planes. ChipWired's 2.2-2.4 W are USB inline (DC) meters; its 2.7 W on the same test is an AC watt meter including PSU losses; on its idle test the spread is 2.2 W DC vs 3.0 W AC (~30%). Three meters disagree by 0.4-0.5 W on a single test — wider than several of the claim's line items — and this is never acknowledged. ChipWired's baseline is also WiFi-up/no-Ethernet vs the claim's WiFi-off/Ethernet-up, so it is not the same configuration being corroborated.

(5) WiFi-off + BLE-on double-discount. The Pi 4's CYW43455 is a combined WiFi/Bluetooth part. The claim banks the full disable-wifi saving while requiring continuous BLE scan+advertise on the same silicon; shared front-end/PLL remains powered. This inflates the optimistic end.

(6) Thermal derating is unsupported by any cited source. I checked the forum thread directly: it does not discuss temperature, leakage, or any percent-per-degree relationship. The "~2.5% per 10 C" figure appears nowhere in the three sources but is presented as part of a sourced synthesis. The direction of concern is also wrong: in a sealed enclosure 20-30 C above ambient, the dominant effect is thermal throttling at 80-85 C, which reduces power while degrading service. The claim converts the headline thermal risk into a +0.2 W adder.

(7) Peak/average conflation — most dangerous for a parts order. The budget is entirely average. Geerling's same Pi 4 table shows 5.1 W serving web requests and 6.4 W at full CPU load; a WebSocket relay plus SQLite fsync bursts produces exactly those transients. Calling 3.5 W a "design ceiling" invites sizing a PSU, fuse, wire gauge, or battery BMS against 3.5 W. Raspberry Pi specs 3.0 A / 15 W for the Pi 4 for this reason.

(8) 3.0 W is asserted rather than derived — no step yields it; the buildup gives 2.6-3.2 W. Derating is also applied only to the ceiling, not the floor, artificially widening the apparent range.

corrected.original: Boost converter efficiency assumption: 87% average across the discharge curve, with a realistic band of 85-90%.
corrected.corrected:
Boost converter efficiency assumption: 84% average integrated across the discharge curve for a commodity non-synchronous design, with a realistic band of 80-88%. Assume 90-93% ONLY if the BOM specifies a synchronous boost (TPS61088 class) — that is a part-selection decision, not a default.

Basis and caveats:
- MT3608-class parts are asynchronous, requiring an external Schottky whose ~0.3-0.45 V forward drop sits in the 5 V output path and costs ~6-9% by itself. Datasheet "up to 93%" is a peak at favorable Vin/Vout, not an average. Efficiency degrades further below ~3.4 V/cell where input current is highest, which is precisely the end of the runtime budget.
- TP4056 is a linear battery CHARGER (~74% from 5 V into a 3.7 V cell), not a boost converter. It is irrelevant to discharge-path efficiency and must not be cited as evidence for it.
- Neither cited source substantiates the band. DFRobot product-2840 states "up to 95%" for its STEP-DOWN/charging converter, names no chips, and is an "up to" marketing peak. The zbotic.in page is unverifiable (HTTP 403) and is a blog comparison, not a datasheet or measurement. Replace both with the actual boost IC datasheet efficiency curve for the specific part ordered, or with a bench measurement.
- Apply a separate usable-capacity derate of ~0.90-0.95 alongside efficiency, covering cutoff-voltage residual, low-rate/25 C rating optimism, cell aging, and continuous board quiescent/fuel-gauge draw. Converter efficiency alone does not cover these.

Corrected runtime, stated for one explicit cell capacity (the original mixed 2600 mAh and 3000 mAh without flagging it):
4 x 2600 mAh = 38.48 Wh nominal. At 3.0 W continuous, energy-only:
  80% -> 10.3 h | 84% -> 10.8 h | 88% -> 11.3 h
With a 0.92 usable-capacity derate: 84% -> 9.9 h. This agrees with DFRobot's own "up to 10 hours" rating for a 4-cell 18650 HAT.
(If 3000 mAh cells are actually being ordered, 4 x 3000 = 44.4 Wh: 84% -> 12.4 h energy-only, 11.4 h with derate. Specify which cell before ordering.)

On sensitivity: across 80-88% the runtime spread is about +/-4.5%, genuinely smaller than the +/-20% from workload uncertainty — so measuring the actual load remains the highest-value action. But this argument bounds the SPREAD, not the BIAS. Centering on 87% when the hardware delivers ~84% is a systematic ~4% overstatement that workload averaging never removes. Pick the center from the datasheet curve of the part actually ordered; then stop refining it.
corrected.why:
Refuted on five independent grounds, two of them hard arithmetic/factual errors.

1) SENSITIVITY TABLE ARITHMETIC IS WRONG FOR THE CLAIM'S OWN CELL. Using the 2600 mAh cell the claim itself uses in its worked example: 4 x 2600 mAh x 3.7 V = 38.48 Wh; at 3.0 W that yields 10.90 h / 11.16 h / 11.80 h at 85/87/92%, NOT the stated 12.6/12.9/13.6 h. Reverse-solving the stated table (12.9 x 3.0 / 0.87 = 44.48 Wh, /4 = 11.12 Wh, /3.7 V = 3006 mAh) shows the table silently assumes 3000 mAh cells. The document mixes two cell capacities without flagging it, and the runtime table is the optimistic one — a ~15% overstatement in exactly the figure an engineer would size a pack against.

2) TP4056 IS NOT A BOOST CONVERTER. It is a linear CC/CV Li-ion charger in the charge path, roughly 74% efficient from 5 V into a 3.7 V cell (it dissipates the voltage difference as heat). Citing "MT3608/TP4056-class parts" as documentation of 85-90% boost/discharge efficiency is a category error; half the named evidence concerns the wrong direction of power flow.

3) THE CITED SOURCES DO NOT SUPPORT THE CLAIM. DFRobot product-2840 (verified by fetch) states "up to 95% efficiency" and that figure is explicitly for the integrated STEP-DOWN DC-DC converter on the 6-18 V input/charging path, not the battery-to-5V boost. It names no chips whatsoever (no MT3608, TP4056, or TPS61088). It therefore supports neither the 85-90% band nor the part family. It is also an "up to" marketing peak, not a measured average. The zbotic.in URL returned HTTP 403 and is unverifiable; a vendor blog comparison would not be an adequate source for a hardware spec in any case.

4) THE CITED HARDWARE IS LESS OPTIMISTIC THAN THE CLAIM. DFRobot rates its own 4-cell 18650 UPS HAT at "up to 10 hours" continuous, against the claim's 12.6-13.6 h table for a 4-cell config.

5) 87% IS OPTIMISTIC FOR THE NAMED SILICON, AND THE LOGIC IS SELF-CONTRADICTORY. MT3608 is asynchronous, requiring an external Schottky whose ~0.3-0.45 V drop is in the output path, costing ~6-9% alone before switching, inductor DCR, and quiescent losses. Its "up to 93%" is a peak at favorable Vin/Vout ratios. The claim concedes efficiency sags at end of discharge, then places its point estimate near the midpoint of a band whose ceiling is the peak — the stated reasoning and the chosen number contradict each other. An integrated-over-discharge average of 83-85% is defensible for commodity non-synchronous designs; 90%+ requires a synchronous part (TPS61088 class), which is a BOM decision, not an assumption.

6) METHODOLOGICAL: the "second-order, don't agonize" conclusion conflates spread with bias. Narrowing the band makes the sensitivity look small, but a wrong center is a one-directional offset that workload noise does not average out. The framework also applies efficiency to nameplate Wh with no usable-capacity term, so the converter figure is being asked to absorb cutoff-voltage residual, temperature/age derate, and board quiescent draw that it does not cover.

The one part that survives: the worked example 2600 x 3.7 / 5.0 x 0.88 = 1693 mAh (claim says ~1695, acceptable rounding), and the directional point that workload measurement dominates uncertainty. Corrected estimate (4 x 2600 mAh, 84%, 0.92 usable derate) = 9.9 h, converging on DFRobot's own ~10 h rating.

corrected.original: Usable cell capacity should be derated to 88% of rated for Li-ion and 90% for LiFePO4, and 3500 mAh 18650 cells are really 3300-3450 mAh rated.
corrected.corrected:
Base all derating on an explicitly named figure — the NCR18650GA datasheet TYPICAL of 3450 mAh for nominal sizing, or the guaranteed minimum (3300-3350 mAh; the two cited sources disagree, verify against the Panasonic datasheet directly) for worst-case sizing. Do not derate from the 3500 mAh label.

Replace the single 88% with an explicit multiplicative stack, so each allowance is visible and auditable:
  - cutoff at 3.0 V (vs the datasheet's 2.5 V @ 0.2C basis): x0.96; at 3.2 V: x0.92
  - end-of-season aging: x0.90 (use x0.80 if the spec must hold to standard end-of-life)
  - cold-weather discharge near 0degC: x0.88
  Net for a Li-ion field appliance: ~0.75 (0.73 at a 3.2 V cutoff). Use 75%, not 88%.

LiFePO4: the flatter curve genuinely improves cutoff retention (~0.98 vs 0.96), but LFP low-temperature discharge is WORSE than NCA/NMC and charging below 0degC is prohibited. Net LFP derate is comparable to or worse than Li-ion — use ~0.75, not a more generous 0.90.

Average discharge voltage: 3.6 V is the NCR18650GA's datasheet NOMINAL, not a conservative derate from 3.7 V (that baseline applies to older generic LCO cells). For energy budgeting under a real 2-3 A load to a 3.0 V cutoff, use 3.5 V mean.

Resulting per-cell budget: 3.5 V x 0.75 x 3.45 Ah = 9.1 Wh, not the ~10.9 Wh the original figures imply. Order cells against the 9.1 Wh number.

Drop the "3500 mAh is a marketing number" framing — independent bench tests meet or exceed 3500 mAh at 1 A, so the label is not inflated; the reason to derate is cutoff, aging, and temperature, not label dishonesty. Also drop the specific 3507-3569 mAh range unless a source that actually publishes those numeric values is cited: the referenced Lygte review discharges to 2.8 V and reports capacity only in chart images.
corrected.why:
The claim is directionally sensible (derating is right; the 3500 label is optimistic) but fails on several independent grounds that matter for a parts order.

(1) DERATE STACK — the fatal one. The detail says 88% "accounts for" three effects: raised cutoff, aging, and cold. These multiply. 0.96 (3.0V cutoff vs the datasheet's 2.5V @ 0.2C basis) x 0.90 (end-of-season aging, itself generous — standard EOL is 0.80) x 0.88 (~0degC) = 76%, and 73% at a 3.2V cutoff. 88% is one factor's margin covering three. Sizing against 88% under-provisions by ~14%.

(2) SELF-CONTRADICTION. The detail calls 3500 mAh "a lab-conditions marketing number" then concedes independent bench tests reached 3507-3569 mAh. If measurement meets or exceeds the label, the label is not marketing inflation.

(3) SOURCE CONFLICT ON THE CORE FIGURE. The cited Lygte page lists rated 3300 / minimum 3350 / typical 3450. The cited Alibaba page says "3300 mAh minimum, 3450 mAh typical." The claim's "guaranteed MINIMUM of 3300" follows the Alibaba page, which that page's own framing identifies as a vendor commerce page (ElectronicsHub/Alibaba), not manufacturer documentation. A marketing source is being used for the figure that indicts marketing. I could not resolve 3300 vs 3350 against the primary Panasonic datasheet — the Orbtronic PDF returned 404 and my web-search budget was exhausted — so the minimum should be stated as a source-dependent 3300-3350, not asserted as 3300.

(4) UNDEFINED BASE. "88% of rated" never specifies the base. 88% of 3500 = 3080 mAh; of 3450 = 3036; of 3300 = 2904. A 6.1% spread with no stated referent, in a document parts are ordered against.

(5) THE 3.6V MARGIN IS ILLUSORY. 3.6V is the NCR18650GA's datasheet nominal (confirmed by the cited Alibaba page: "nominal voltage of 3.6 V"), not a conservative substitute for 3.7V — the 3.7V baseline belongs to older generic LCO cells. Truncating the discharge at 3.0V does raise the mean of the retained portion, so 3.6V is defensible at low current, but it carries no safety margin. Under real 2-3A load the mean sags to ~3.5V.

(6) LiFePO4 AT 90% INVERTS THE COLD ARGUMENT. The flat-curve reasoning for cutoff retention is correct in isolation, but LFP has worse low-temperature discharge performance than NCA/NMC (higher internal resistance at low temp) and charging below 0degC is prohibited. Assigning LFP the MORE generous factor while naming cold-weather loss as a derate driver is backwards. LFP's flatness also produces a sharper knee — less graceful-shutdown warning, not more.

(7) UNSUBSTANTIABLE PRECISION. The 3507-3569 mAh at 1A cannot be verified from the cited Lygte page: it cut discharge at 2.8V (the reviewer states he therefore does not get full capacity) and its numeric values are embedded in chart images rather than text.

Energy impact: claimed 3.6V x 88% x 3.45Ah = 10.93 Wh/cell vs realistic 3.5V x 76% x 3.45Ah = 9.18 Wh/cell — 19% optimistic.

corrected.original: (a) 2x 18650 Li-ion 3500 mAh delivers 19.3 Wh at 5V, giving 6.4 h typical and a 5.5-7.4 h range.
corrected.corrected:
2x 18650 Li-ion 3500 mAh (2 x ~12.6 Wh datasheet = 25.2 Wh gross, fresh cells at 0.2C to the rated ~2.5-2.65 V cutoff).

Derating, stated as separable terms:
- 3.0 V cutoff instead of rated cutoff: x0.94 -> 23.7 Wh
- Aging to 80% EOL: x0.80 -> 19.0 Wh at end of life (23.7 Wh at beginning of life)
- Load-weighted boost efficiency: x0.85 (range 0.80-0.90 depending on idle fraction and light-load mode)

Delivered at 5 V: approximately 20 Wh beginning-of-life, approximately 16 Wh end-of-life. Quote as ~16-20 Wh, not 19.3 Wh.

Runtime at room temperature:
- 3.0 W design figure: ~6.7 h BOL, ~5.4 h EOL
- 2.6 W best case, BOL: ~7.7 h
- 3.5 W ceiling, EOL: ~4.6 h
Overall range ~4.5-7.5 h. Use ~5.5 h (3.0 W, EOL, room temperature) as the design figure rather than 6.4 h. Subtract a further 10-20% for 0-10 C outdoor/overnight operation. Unaccounted: BMS quiescent draw and cable/connector IR drop, both small and both negative.

Topology: 2S (7.4 V, buck) and 2P (3.7 V, boost) store identical energy. A synchronous buck at 7.4->5 V / 0.6 A runs ~92-95% vs ~88-91% for a good boost - a 3-5 point advantage worth roughly 12-20 minutes over a ~6 h run, not a decisive margin. That advantage is partly offset because an unbalanced 2S pack terminates when the first cell reaches 3.0 V, whereas paralleled cells in 2P self-equalize. Boost input current here is only ~0.9 A, so converter sag is not a real constraint at this power level. 2S additionally requires a balancing BMS and a 2S charger (boost charger if charging from USB 5 V), against commodity 1S charge ICs for 2P. Choose 2S for efficiency and headroom if the BOM and charging complexity are acceptable; runtime alone does not justify it.

All figures are engineering estimates from datasheet-class inputs, not measured. Confirm against the specific cell and converter datasheets, and validate with a bench run at the actual duty cycle before committing to a parts order.
corrected.why:
Arithmetic re-derives exactly (25.2 -> 22.18 -> 19.29 Wh; 6.43/7.42/5.51 h), so there is no computational error. The claim is refuted on assumptions, precision, and the topology recommendation.

(1) The x0.88 derating cannot cover both the 3.0 V cutoff and aging. These are separable: 3.0 V cutoff vs the ~2.5-2.65 V rating cutoff costs ~4-7% (x~0.94); aging to the industry-standard 80% EOL is a separate x0.80. Combined EOL is ~0.75, not 0.88. 0.88 describes a fresh pack with essentially no aging allowance - the wrong basis for a spec an engineer orders parts against.

(2) Chain-construction error: 3.6 V nominal is the average over a FULL discharge to deep cutoff, so applying a cutoff derating on top double-books the low-voltage tail (remaining average is ~3.65-3.7 V). Cleaner to use the datasheet Wh/cell directly.

(3) Cold temperature is absent - an outdoor/overnight festival device loses a further 10-20% at 0-10 C.

(4) 87% is a peak-of-curve boost efficiency applied to a load profile including idle. Boost efficiency collapses at light load (50-75% at tens of mW). Applying a flat 87% to a flat 3.0 W average conflates peak-load with load-weighted efficiency.

(5) The topology recommendation is the weakest part and partly self-contradicting. "Store identical energy" is true but "deliver" is not: a 2S pack terminates when the FIRST cell hits 3.0 V, and mismatch (1-3% new, widening with cycling) costs usable energy, while 2P self-equalizes. So the buck's edge is partly given back as imbalance loss. "Avoids the high input currents that make boost converters sag" is overstated by roughly an order of magnitude - at 3.0 W out from 3.7 V, input current is only ~0.9 A, trivial for any modern boost IC; sag is a 10-15 W / 3-5 A power-bank concern. No buck efficiency is quoted; honest numbers (92-95% buck vs 88-91% boost) give a 3-5 point delta worth 12-20 min on a 6.4 h budget, which does not support "meaningfully more efficient." The recommendation also silently imports a balancing BMS and a 2S (boost) charger vs commodity 1S charge ICs - real BOM cost for a parts order.

(6) False precision: 19.3 Wh / 6.4 h are 3 and 2 sig figs built from two estimated multipliers; +/-5 points on each spans ~17-21 Wh.

(7) Structural tell: every omission (cold, light-load efficiency, BMS quiescent, cable IR drop, EOL aging, 2S imbalance) points the same direction. A derating chain with no conservative term is a ceiling presented as a typical.

Verification limitation: this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before I could pull the cell datasheets or converter efficiency curves. The arithmetic was re-derived independently; the per-cell Wh figures, cutoff loss, 80% EOL convention, and efficiency ranges rest on domain knowledge and should be confirmed against the actual chosen parts.

corrected.original: (b) 2x 18650 LiFePO4 1800 mAh delivers 9.0 Wh at 5V, giving only 3.0 h typical and a 2.6-3.5 h range - less than half of config (a).
corrected.corrected:
(b) 2x 18650 LiFePO4 delivers approximately 5.5-7.5 Wh at 5 V, giving roughly 1.8-2.5 h typical (range ~1.6-2.9 h) — NOT 9.0 Wh / 3.0 h.

The 1800 mAh input is not orderable. Merchant-market LFP 18650 cells are 1100-1500 mAh; the qualified part (A123 / Lithium Werks APR18650M1-class) is ~1100 mAh, and specialist cell retailers largely do not stock LFP in 18650 at all — LFP volume has moved to prismatic. 1800 mAh in an 18650 steel can implies 348 Wh/L, near the ceiling of LFP's 227-396 Wh/L band, a ceiling set by prismatic cells with better packaging efficiency. Fix a specific manufacturer part number and its datasheet rated capacity before ordering.

Arithmetic at a realistic 1500 mAh: 2 x 1.5 Ah x 3.2 V = 9.6 Wh gross; x0.90 usable = 8.6 Wh; x0.87 converter = 7.5 Wh. At 3.0 W = 2.5 h; at 2.6 W = 2.9 h; at 3.5 W = 2.1 h. At 1100 mAh: 5.5 Wh, 1.8 h typical.

Specify the pack topology, which the original omits and which changes the converter line: 2S (6.4 V nominal, 5.0-7.2 V) requires buck-boost, not buck, because the discharged pack voltage equals the 5 V rail and a plain buck strands capacity; 2P (3.2 V nominal) requires a boost whose real efficiency at a 3 W load is nearer 80-88% than a flat 87%.

Drop the "less than half of config (a)" comparison unless (a)'s usable Wh is stated in the same document under the same derating chain. It holds only if (a) exceeds 18 Wh, which needs 3400+ mAh Li-ion cells; with 3000 mAh cells the ratio is ~56%, i.e. more than half. Also apply the 0.90 usable factor consistently to both configs or justify it per-chemistry — the original justifies 0.90 by LFP's flat discharge curve, which is an argument for a HIGHER factor for LFP, not the same one.

The qualitative tradeoff stands: LFP buys materially longer cycle life and a higher thermal-runaway onset with no oxygen release, which matters for an appliance in a hot enclosure. But no standard — UL 2054, UL 1642, IEC 62133, UN 38.3 — mandates LFP or exempts it from testing, so fire-safety certification cannot be cited as a forcing function; LFP merely tends to pass more easily. Note also that LFP's prohibition on charging below 0 C is stricter than Li-ion's, relevant for a gateway recharged overnight. For runtime parity with a 2-cell Li-ion config at realistic LFP capacity, budget 5-8 cells, not 4-6.
corrected.why:
The arithmetic is internally correct — I re-derived every step and all six figures reproduce exactly (11.52 -> 10.368 -> 9.02 Wh; 3.01 h / 3.47 h / 2.58 h). The claim fails on its inputs and on an unsupportable comparison.

(1) THE 1800 mAh INPUT IS NOT A PROCURABLE SPEC — this is the load-bearing error, since an engineer orders parts against it. Merchant-market LFP 18650 cells are 1100-1500 mAh (the actually-qualified part, A123/Lithium Werks APR18650M1-class, is ~1100 mAh). Two specialist US cell retailers I checked (IMR Batteries, 18650BatteryStore) stock no LFP 18650 cells at all — their LFP lines are prismatic (EVE LF304, BYD 302Ah). Density cross-check: 1.8 Ah x 3.2 V = 5.76 Wh in a 0.0165 L can = 348 Wh/L, i.e. 88% of the top of LFP's published 227-396 Wh/L band (Wikipedia), and that band's ceiling is set by prismatic/pouch cells with far better packaging efficiency than a steel can with header, vent, mandrel and can wall. Real LFP 18650s land at 213 Wh/L (1100 mAh) to 290 Wh/L (1500 mAh). So 1800 mAh is a marketing/AliExpress-tier rating. Realistic outcome: 7.5 Wh and 2.5 h at 1500 mAh, or 5.5 Wh and 1.8 h at 1100 mAh — the spec over-promises runtime by 17% to 40%.

(2) "LESS THAN HALF OF CONFIG (a)" IS NOT DERIVABLE from anything stated. Config (a)'s Wh does not appear in the claim. The assertion only holds if (a) exceeds 18.0 Wh, which for a 2-cell Li-ion pack requires ~3400-3500 mAh cells AND the identical 0.90/0.87 derating chain. With 3000 mAh cells the ratio is ~56% — MORE than half. A knife-edge conclusion resting on an unstated input is presented as flat fact.

(3) THE 0.90 FACTOR'S JUSTIFICATION CONTRADICTS ITS USE. Rated Ah x nominal (mean-discharge) V already is the energy delivered to the manufacturer's cutoff. Applying a further 0.90 haircut while justifying it as "LFP's flat curve keeps more capacity above cutoff" conflates two things. Either 0.90 is a generic system derating (aging, temperature, BMS margin), in which case the flat-curve rationale is irrelevant and it applies equally to config (a); or it is chemistry-specific, in which case the reasoning runs backwards and LFP should get a higher factor than Li-ion — which would narrow the gap the claim is asserting.

(4) CONVERTER TOPOLOGY UNSPECIFIED, AND 0.87 IS NOT TOPOLOGY-NEUTRAL. "2x" never says series or parallel. 2S LFP is 6.4 V nominal over a 5.0-7.2 V range — the pack's bottom equals the 5 V output, so a plain buck browns out with usable capacity stranded; you need buck-boost, and the 0.90 does not cover that. 2P LFP is 3.2 V nominal needing a boost, where 87% is optimistic at a 3 W load (light-load boost from 3.2 V is commonly 80-88%, and quiescent draw is non-trivial at this power). The answer moves materially depending on which the engineer builds.

(5) REGULATORY OVERSTATEMENT. No safety standard — UL 2054, UL 1642, IEC 62133, UN 38.3 — mandates LFP or exempts it from testing. LFP typically passes more easily; it confers no certification. Saying "fire-safety certification is what is driving the decision, in which case it is the right call" implies a regulatory forcing function no standard provides. Relatedly, the hot-tent framing omits that LFP's charge-below-0C prohibition is stricter than Li-ion's, which matters for a gateway recharged overnight in shoulder-season ambient.

(6) The "4-6 cells" remedy only works at the fictional 1800 mAh; at 1100-1500 mAh you need 5-8 cells for parity.

Directionally sound: LFP nominal 3.2 V (confirmed), the cycle-life advantage (Wikipedia cites 2,500-9,000 for LFP; the claim's conservative 2000-3000 vs 300-500 Li-ion is fair), and the higher thermal-runaway onset.

Sources: [Wikipedia — LiFePO4 battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithium_iron_phosphate_battery), [Wikipedia — 18650 battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18650_battery), [IMR Batteries LiFePO4 catalog](https://www.imrbatteries.com/collections/lifepo4-batteries), [18650BatteryStore LiFePO4 catalog](https://www.18650batterystore.com/collections/lifepo4-batteries)

corrected.original: (c) 4x 18650 Li-ion 3500 mAh delivers 38.6 Wh at 5V, giving 12.9 h typical and an 11.0-14.8 h range - the only config that covers a full festival day.
corrected.corrected:
(c) 4x 18650 Li-ion delivers 36.9 Wh at 5V when computed on minimum rated cell capacity (~3350 mAh, not the 3500 mAh typical figure): gross = 4 x 3.35 Ah x 3.6 V = 48.2 Wh; usable x0.88 = 42.5 Wh; converter x0.87 = 36.9 Wh. Fresh-cell runtime is 12.3 h at 3.0 W, with a 10.6-14.2 h range across the 2.6-3.5 W draw band. At 80% state-of-health (conventional Li-ion end-of-life, reached within normal reuse across seasons) the same pack delivers ~29.5 Wh: 9.8 h typical, 8.4 h worst case.

This does NOT reliably cover a 12-14 h gates-open-to-close festival day. It covers a 12 h day only with fresh cells at or below ~3.0 W average draw, and fails a 14 h day in every case. Plan on a mid-day swap or hot-swappable pack, budget a 5th or 6th cell, or reduce average draw below ~2.6 W if single-charge all-day operation is a hard requirement.

Converter sensitivity is -2.3%/+5.7% (12.6 h at 85%, 13.6 h at 92%, against a 12.9 h base at typical capacity), not +/-4%.

Topology: 2S2P (7.4V nominal, 6.0-8.4V range) into a buck converter is a reasonable choice and keeps input current near 0.5 A, but it requires a 2S BMS with cell balancing, and neither BMS nor converter quiescent draw is included in the figures above. The 87% converter efficiency is a mid-load point estimate and will be lower at light load and at the top of the voltage range. Before ordering, confirm minimum rated capacity against the specific part's datasheet, and confirm whether the 3.0 W figure is a true average including transmit and display peaks or a steady-state figure that excludes them.
corrected.why:
Every number in the DETAIL reproduces exactly (50.4 → 44.352 → 38.586 Wh; 14.84 / 12.86 / 11.02 h). The arithmetic is not the problem. The claim fails on four other grounds, the first of which is fatal and needs no external source.

1. SELF-CONTRADICTION — the headline conclusion is refuted by the claim's own numbers. It states a festival day is "typically 12-14 h" and then asserts this config "covers a full festival day." It does not. Typical runtime 12.9 h is below the 14 h upper bound, and the 11.0 h worst case is below even the 12 h lower bound. By its own stated requirement the config fails the high end typically and fails the entire window at worst case. "The only config that covers a full festival day" is therefore false as written, independent of any other objection — and it is doubly unsupportable as an exclusivity claim, since nothing shown rules out, say, 5 cells or a lower-draw duty cycle. An engineer ordering parts against "covers a full festival day" would be buying a pack that misses its own spec.

2. TYPICAL CAPACITY PRESENTED AS DESIGN CAPACITY. 3500 mAh is the *typical* rating for cells in this class (Samsung INR18650-35E, LG MJ1, Panasonic NCR18650GA at 3450), measured at ~0.2C, 25 °C, fresh, to a 2.5 V cutoff. The datasheet *minimum/rated* capacity is ~3350-3400 mAh — the number a pack should be spec'd against, since typical is a distribution centre, not a floor. At 3.35 Ah minimum: 48.2 Wh gross → 36.9 Wh delivered → 12.3 h typical, 10.6 h worst case. (Note: I could not fetch the datasheets to confirm — the session's web search budget was exhausted and four datasheet URLs 404'd — so the 3350-3400 mAh minimums rest on general knowledge of these cells and should be confirmed against the specific part before ordering. The point that typical ≠ minimum stands regardless of the exact figure.)

3. THE 0.88 "USABLE" FACTOR CARRIES NO AGEING OR TEMPERATURE ALLOWANCE. It appears to cover cutoff headroom only. Li-ion end-of-life is conventionally 80% retention, and a festival device is reused across seasons. At 80% SOH the same pack delivers 29.5-30.9 Wh → 9.8-10.3 h typical and 8.4-8.8 h worst case, i.e. it loses a third of the claimed margin and misses a 12 h day badly. Cold overnight/early-morning operation derates further, and charging above 45 °C is not permitted — relevant if the stated "overnight recharge" happens in a hot tent. None of this is priced in.

4. THE SENSITIVITY FIGURE IS ARITHMETICALLY WRONG. 12.57 h at 85% and 13.60 h at 92%, against a 12.86 h base, is -2.3% / +5.7% — not the stated "only ±4%." Minor in magnitude, but it is an error in the one part of the claim whose whole authority is that the arithmetic is shown.

Lesser flags, not load-bearing but worth passing to the engineer: 87% is a plausible mid-load buck efficiency but is a point estimate presented without load dependence, and a 2S2P pack spans 6.0-8.4 V where light-load efficiency is typically worse; converter and BMS quiescent draw are absent from the model entirely. The 2S2P "most efficient, wiring losses negligible" framing is not a real differentiator — the 1S4P+boost alternative draws only ~1 A at 3 W, so wiring losses are negligible either way — and 2S silently adds a balancing BMS to the BOM. "38.6 Wh at 5V" invites misreading as pack energy; pack energy is 50.4 Wh nominal. If the 3.0 W typical figure excludes radio-transmit or display-on peaks, average draw will exceed it and every runtime above is optimistic. No regulatory overreach: 50.4 Wh is under the 100 Wh air-transport threshold, though UN38.3 testing is still required and is not mentioned.

corrected.original: (d) A 10000 mAh 3.7V LiPo pack delivers 27.6 Wh at 5V, giving 9.2 h typical and a 7.9-10.6 h range.
corrected.corrected:
(d) A 10 Ah single-cell LiPo pack stores ~36 Wh (10 Ah x 3.6 V average discharge voltage; 37 Wh if quoted against the 3.7 V nominal marketing figure). After a usable-capacity derate (x0.88, covering cutoff margin plus cell tolerance) and boost-converter loss (x0.87 typical at this load), it presents ~27.6 Wh at the 5 V rail — equivalently ~5.5 Ah at 5 V, NOT 10 Ah. At 3.0 W average draw that is ~9.2 h nominal.

The runtime spread must vary energy as well as load, not load alone:
- Best case: 37 Wh x 0.95 usable x 0.92 converter = 32.3 Wh; at 2.6 W → ~12.4 h.
- Nominal: 27.6 Wh; at 3.0 W → ~9.2 h.
- Realistic worst case (cell at 90% of rating, x0.88 usable, x0.82 converter at cold/aged/low-load conditions) = 23.4 Wh; at 3.5 W → ~6.7 h.

Specify the range as ~6.5-12.5 h, treat 9.2 h as nominal-only, and size all design margin against ~6.5 h. Do not order parts against the 7.9 h figure: it is a load-only lower bound that an ordinary in-tolerance unit can miss by ~15%. The 27.6 Wh number is an output-rail figure — do not re-apply a converter derate to it. The conclusion stands and strengthens: this configuration does not reliably cover a full festival day.
corrected.why:
The arithmetic is internally correct (36 → 31.68 → 27.56 Wh; 9.19 / 10.60 / 7.87 h all reproduce exactly), and the headline conclusion — "does not reliably cover a full festival day" — survives. But four defects make the claim unsafe as written for a document an engineer orders parts against.

(1) MISLABELED SUBJECT. "A 10000 mAh 3.7V LiPo pack delivers 27.6 Wh" states a post-conversion, post-derate derived figure as a property of the pack. The pack stores 36 Wh (3.6 V avg) / 37 Wh (3.7 V nominal). A downstream reader who takes "27.6 Wh" as the pack energy and applies their own converter derate will double-count and under-spec the battery. The 5 V rail figure must be labeled "at the 5 V output, after conversion."

(2) INCONSISTENT / DOUBLE-COUNTED DERATE. The 10000 mAh rating is defined by convention at ~0.2C down to a 3.0 V cutoff, and 3.6 V is the average discharge voltage over exactly that window. So 10 Ah × 3.6 V = 36 Wh ALREADY presumes discharge to ~3.0 V. The extra ×0.88 therefore cannot be the cutoff allowance the DETAIL says it is ("I assume a conservative 3.0-3.2 V cutoff"). If you genuinely stop at 3.2 V, the charge you do take out averages ~3.7 V, so the correct product is 8.8 Ah × 3.7 V = 32.6 Wh, not 31.7 Wh. Either the 0.88 double-counts the cutoff or it is an unlabeled aging/tolerance margin — the spec does not say which, so an engineer cannot audit or adjust it.

(3) THE RANGE IS ONE-DIMENSIONAL AND SO IS NOT A TOLERANCE. 7.9-10.6 h varies only the load (3.5 / 2.6 W) against a point-estimate energy. It excludes every energy-side uncertainty: cell capacity tolerance and the routine shortfall of low-cost "10000 mAh" cells against rating; boost efficiency spread (~80-93%, and materially below 87% at the ~600 mA this 3 W load draws, worse still near the 3.0 V end where input current peaks); converter quiescent draw integrated over a 9 h run; outdoor temperature rather than 25 C lab; and cycle aging (cells are specified to 80% of rating at end of rated cycle life). Stack realistic-bad but non-pathological values — 36 Wh × 0.90 cell × 0.88 usable × 0.82 converter = 23.4 Wh — and 3.5 W gives 6.7 h, ~15% BELOW the stated floor. A floor an ordinary unit can miss is not a floor.

(4) THE CROSS-CHECK IS NON-INDEPENDENT AND ANCHORED OPTIMISTIC. 6000-6500 mAh at 5 V is 30-32.5 Wh, i.e. 81-88% end-to-end from a 37 Wh pack. That is quality-brand, best-in-class territory, not a universal "well-known observation"; commodity banks routinely land 60-75%. The DETAIL invokes it as reassurance that 27.6 Wh is conservative, but it is reassurance drawn from the good end of the distribution. The comparison also propagates the exact unit conflation a hardware spec must avoid — "mAh at 5 V" against "mAh at 3.7 V." Quote 27.6 Wh, or 5.5 Ah at 5 V, never bare mAh without a rail.

Minor: a "10000 mAh single-cell LiPo" is usually 2x5000 mAh in parallel, adding small interconnect/imbalance loss. The "~3.7 h short of config (c)" comparison could not be checked — config (c) was not supplied.

corrected.original: If config (d) is an off-the-shelf USB power bank rather than a bare LiPo pack, three failure modes apply that the energy arithmetic does not capture.
corrected.corrected:
If config (d) is an off-the-shelf USB power bank rather than a bare LiPo pack, three failure modes apply that the energy arithmetic does not capture. These are vendor-discretionary behaviors, not specified parameters — every threshold below MUST be measured on the specific candidate bank, not designed against as a bound.

(1) Low-current auto-shutoff. Most banks disable output after a dwell period (typically 10-30 s) below a vendor-set threshold, commonly cited as ~50-100 mA but undocumented and varying from ~30 mA to "never" on always-on models. At 5 V a 3 W Pi draws 600 mA, so normal operation is clear of the band — but only at 5 V; if the bank supplies 9 V or 12 V via USB-C PD into a buck converter, the same 3 W is ~330 mA or ~250 mA at the port, materially closer to cutoff. A software reboot is NOT a risk: the 5 V rail is never dropped and the current dip is shorter than any dwell timer. The real trigger is the post-shutdown halt state (~70-80 mA on a Pi 4, ~15-25 mA on a Zero 2 W, and ~3 mA if POWER_OFF_ON_HALT is set in EEPROM, which makes cutoff certain). Consequence: after any halt, the appliance cannot be brought back by RTC/scheduled wake — it stays dead until someone physically presses the button. Specify a bank with a documented low-current or "always-on" mode, or add a fixed dummy load above the measured threshold, and account for that load in the energy budget.

(2) No pass-through, so the pack is not a UPS. Inexpensive banks fail one of two ways: output is disabled whenever input is present, so the Pi hard-cuts on mains RESTORE (not on a glitch); or output continues while charging is inhibited, so the pack silently drains to empty while nominally "on mains" — a failure the energy arithmetic cannot see. Banks that do advertise pass-through commonly still glitch 10-100 ms on source switchover, so documented pass-through is necessary but not sufficient: require a specified switchover dropout under the Pi's hold-up time, or hold-up capacitance sized to cover it.

(3) Output current ratings are per-port maxima in isolation, with a separate and lower aggregate rating across all ports — two ports cannot both deliver their labels. But the dominant cause of sag under an LTE dongle's transmit bursts (~2 A peaks for 1-2 ms against a few hundred mA average) is usually cable and connector IR drop, not the port rating: 2 A through 0.3 ohm of typical cheap cable is 0.6 V, taking a 5.0 V output to 4.4 V, below the Pi's 4.63 V undervoltage threshold. Budget cable resistance and local bulk capacitance at the load, not just port amperage.

If UPS function is genuinely required, use a purpose-built UPS HAT with documented pass-through AND an early-warning GPIO/I2C power-fail signal that triggers a clean shutdown before the rail collapses. Separately, do not buy a UPS to prevent SD corruption: mount root read-only or use an overlay filesystem first — that removes most of the corruption risk at zero hardware cost, and the UPS then only buys graceful shutdown and ride-through.
corrected.why:
Substantially right in direction (a consumer bank is not a UPS) but materially imprecise in all three mechanisms, and the stated source is unverifiable.

SOURCING: https://zbotic.in/... returns HTTP 403 and cannot be checked; "general power bank design behavior" is not a citable source. Critically, the ~50-100 mA cutoff is a widely-repeated hobbyist figure, NOT a specification — no standard governs low-current shutoff on USB-A banks; it is entirely vendor-discretionary and usually undocumented. A hardware spec must not present it as a bound to design against.

ARITHMETIC: 3 W / 5 V = 600 mA is correct, but only at 5 V. Via USB-C PD at 9 V or 12 V into a buck converter, the same 3 W is ~330 mA / ~250 mA at the bank's port — much nearer the cut band. The "normal operation is safe" conclusion is stated unconditionally but is voltage-dependent.

(1) WRONG TRIGGER. A software reboot does not drop the 5 V rail — the SoC stays powered, and the dip is far shorter than banks' multi-second dwell timers and never nears 100 mA (~400-600 mA in bootloader). The "reboot gap" hazard is essentially fictional. The real trigger is the post-shutdown HALT state (~70-80 mA Pi 4; ~15-25 mA Zero 2 W), and it is guaranteed if POWER_OFF_ON_HALT is set in EEPROM (~3 mA). Right consequence, wrong cause.

(2) WRONG MECHANISM. Non-pass-through banks fail two ways: (a) output disabled while input present → Pi dies on mains RESTORE, not on a glitch; (b) output continues but charging inhibited → pack silently drains to zero while nominally "on mains" (invisible to energy arithmetic). Banks that DO advertise pass-through still commonly glitch 10-100 ms on switchover, so "documented pass-through" is necessary but not sufficient.

(3) SELF-CONTRADICTORY AND MISATTRIBUTED. "Per-port and shared" is garbled: the per-port rating is a max in isolation; a separate, LOWER aggregate rating applies across ports. And sag under LTE TX bursts is dominated by cable/connector IR drop, not port rating — 2 A through 0.3 ohm of cheap cable is 0.6 V, dropping 5.0 V to 4.4 V, under the Pi's 4.63 V undervoltage threshold. A bigger port rating does not fix this; local bulk capacitance does. Also a peak-vs-average trap: cat-4 TX bursts are ~2 A for 1-2 ms against a few hundred mA average.

REMEDY ERROR: prescribing a UPS HAT to solve SD corruption buys hardware to fix a filesystem-configuration problem; read-only root / overlayfs is the correct primary mitigation.

corrected.original: An LTE dongle adds +1.5 W typical and up to +2.5 W in poor signal, raising the total budget from 3.0 W to ~4.5 W typical and 5.5-6.0 W worst case.
corrected.corrected:
An LTE dongle's power adder cannot be pinned to a single figure from the cited sources, and the sources do not support the stated numbers. Corrected sizing guidance:

TYPICAL AVERAGE (for thermal and battery-life estimates): +0.5-1.5 W (100-300 mA at 5 V) for a gateway sending small, frequent WebSocket updates. This is the range actually measured on real dongles in the cited source (100 mA idle, ~200 mA connecting, 400 mA transmitting). Idle/DRX floor is roughly +0.1-0.25 W. Total system: ~3.5-4.5 W typical.

SUSTAINED WORST CASE (max TX, poor signal): +5.0-5.5 W (~1.0-1.1 A at 5 V), derived from the ModalAI datasheet's band rows after subtracting its 1180 mA two-peripheral baseline per the datasheet's own footer rule. Total system: ~8.0-8.5 W. Note this is ~3x the "typical" adder, not 1.7x as claimed.

RAIL AND PSU SPECIFICATION (the number to order against): specify the 5 V rail for at least 2.5 A, which is what ofmodemsandmen explicitly recommends for LTE dongles; ModalAI provisions 4 A on its dongle connector. Do NOT size to average power. LTE modems draw large inrush transients at power-up and at TX ramp: 1.5 A on the Sierra EM7455 (explicitly labeled inrush in the source) and 2000-3000 mA spikes on the Huawei E3276. These last tens of milliseconds and will not show in an average-power measurement, but they will brown out an undersized supply. Provide bulk capacitance local to the dongle.

LTE vs 3G: the only cited source measuring both on one host shows LTE drawing ~1.3x a 3G modem (LTE 970-1085 mA vs HSDPA 750-830 mA incremental), not the 3-5x step-change asserted. Do not budget on the assumption that LTE is categorically worse than 3G.

CONFIDENCE AND CAVEATS: These figures are modem-, band-, and network-specific and none of the three cited sources measure the specific dongle being specified. The RRC/DRX inactivity-timer mechanism is directionally real but is not documented in any cited source and its power penalty here is an estimate, not a measurement. Before ordering, obtain the power table from the actual modem module's manufacturer datasheet (e.g. Quectel, Sierra Wireless, Telit) for the specific bands in use, and bench-measure the chosen dongle under the real traffic pattern with an instrument capable of capturing millisecond transients — not a multimeter averaging reading.
corrected.why:
REFUTED on five independent grounds, three of which would cause an engineer to order the wrong part.

1. THE HEADLINE LTE NUMBERS APPEAR IN NONE OF THE THREE SOURCES. The claim asserts "published LTE modem figures show 500-900 mA typical operation and 600-700 mA sustained." No such figures exist in any cited source. atx.name tested exactly one device (Huawei E3131) and has ZERO LTE measurements — every figure is 2G/3G, max 192 mA. ofmodemsandmen's measured figures are 100-400 mA (E3276: "about 200ma during most of the connection process," "100ma after connection at idle"; Sierra 320U: "100ma or less at idle"; ZTE MF668: "400ma when data was transmitted"). ModalAI gives band-specific system rows, not a 500-900 mA typical. The "600-700 mA sustained" figure is unsourced entirely.

2. THE CLAIM'S OWN LTE SOURCE SHOWS LTE IS ~1.3x 3G, NOT "SUBSTANTIALLY WORSE." ModalAI is the only source containing both 3G and LTE for the same host board. Applying the datasheet's own footer rule (subtract 500mA + ~30mA logic per removed peripheral) against the 1180 mA two-peripheral baseline: LTE increments are 970/1060/1085 mA (Bands 7/1/25); HSDPA increments are 750/830 mA (Bands 8/1). Ratio ≈ 1.3x. The claim's central thesis — that LTE is a categorical step-change over 3G — is contradicted by the one source able to test it.

3. PEAK/INRUSH PRESENTED AS SUSTAINED DRAW. ofmodemsandmen explicitly labels the EM7455's 1.5 A as "Inrush Current," defined on the page as "the momentary amount of power needed when the modem is first powered up," and the E3276's 2000-3000 mA as a "spike... at one point." ModalAI's table is a rail-provisioning table (connector rated "5.0 VDC (@4A max)") with two 500 mA-max USB peripherals baked into every row — sizing figures, not averages. The claim converts provisioning/transient data into "typical operation."

4. THE WORST-CASE BUDGET IS BELOW WHAT THE CITED SOURCE RECOMMENDS. This is the parts-ordering failure. The claim's 5.5-6.0 W worst case = 1.1-1.2 A at 5 V. ofmodemsandmen recommends a "2500ma (2.5 amp)" supply for LTE dongles, and notes 5G needs "12v5amp" in poor signal. ModalAI provisions 4 A. An engineer sizing a PSU to the claim's number would specify roughly half the current its own source says to provision, and would brown out on modem inrush.

5. INTERNAL CONTRADICTION. The detail asserts LTE draws "2.5-4.5 W at 5V" and then budgets an adder of only "+1.5 W typical." If the cited evidence were true, the adder would have to be 2.5-4.5 W. The claim cites evidence for a 2.5-4.5 W device and budgets 1.5 W for it. Separately, the headline says "up to +2.5 W" but states a 6.0 W worst case against a 3.0 W base, which requires +3.0 W; the detail's own poor-signal band is "+2.0-3.0 W." The headline understates its own detail.

ARITHMETIC that does check out: 3.0+1.5=4.5; 3.0+2.5=5.5; 0.5A x 5V=2.5W; 0.9A x 5V=4.5W. The multiplication is fine; the inputs are unsourced.

SECONDARY DEFECTS: (a) The RRC/DRX mechanism section — inactivity timers, "~10 s to DRX, another ~10 s to idle," and the +1.0-2.0 W periodic-traffic adder — is discussed in NONE of the three sources. It is plausible in shape (RRC inactivity timers are operator-configured, commonly 5-20 s) but the specific power penalty is asserted, not cited. It also overstates the effect: with C-DRX configured, a connected-but-mostly-idle modem is not at "full connected-state power," and the claim's own DRX figure (+0.15-0.25 W) sits 4-13x below its periodic-traffic figure with no bridging evidence. (b) "It is documented that poor signal requires more power" upgrades a hedged source statement — "Poorer quality signal SEEMS to require more power than a good signal FOR SOME MODEMS" — into documented fact. (c) "Signal quality drives this harder than traffic volume" is a comparative ranking no source supports. (d) The E3131 upload figures are misreported: 192 mA is a heavy DOWNLOAD figure ("192mA @ 1.7MB/s"); 3G uploads are 174-188 mA. (e) atx.name's caveat that measurements were "taken with somewhat crude instruments, beware" is dropped when the data is presented as "measured reference data."

WHAT SURVIVES: the "3G stick is ~0.5-1.0 W" characterization is a fair reading of atx.name (120-192 mA x 5 V = 0.6-0.96 W), and the directional point that poor signal raises TX power is weakly supported.

corrected.original: At a festival specifically, assume the poor-signal LTE case, not the typical case.
corrected.corrected:
At a festival, assume the modem's PA sits at or near its maximum output whenever it transmits — but budget peak and average separately, and treat the festival penalty as a duty-cycle multiplier, not a higher instantaneous power.

Peak (sizes the supply rail, regulator, and thermal path): a Power Class 3 LTE UE is capped at +23 dBm (200 mW) conducted by 3GPP; poor signal drives the PA to that cap and no further. Whole-module draw at max-power transmit is typically ~1.8-2.7 W total for a Cat-1/Cat-4 module (roughly 500-700 mA at 3.8 V) — this is a total, not an adder on top of an already-counted idle baseline. Size the rail for ~2.5 W and provide 2-3 A of transient headroom with local bulk capacitance, since the module draws in sub-millisecond slot bursts. Confirm all three numbers against the datasheet of the specific module before ordering.

Average (sizes the battery/energy budget): average = idle + (peak − idle) x uplink duty cycle. The festival adjustment is (a) assume no good-signal discount — the PA is at P_CMAX every time it keys up, so the good-signal power saving of a bench test does not apply, and (b) inflate uplink duty cycle by roughly 2-3x over the bench figure to cover HARQ retransmissions and RLC retries. For a low-rate telemetry gateway this lands in the few-hundred-milliwatt range, not 2.0-2.5 W; only a near-continuous uplink stream approaches peak as an average. State the assumed uplink duty cycle explicitly in the spec — without it the average power figure is not derivable and the reviewer cannot check it.

Note on mechanism: cell congestion mainly costs time-on-air, not instantaneous power. Under load the scheduler grants fewer resource blocks, which lowers per-transmission power (P scales with 10·log10(M_RB)), and lower-order modulation carries a lower Δ_TF offset, not a higher one. Time spent queueing is time with the PA off.

Antenna: a moderate-gain (roughly 6-9 dBi) external antenna, mounted high and clear of metal structures, is worth specifying — but scope the claim honestly. Its saving is capped by the PA's available DC headroom (on the order of 0.5-0.7 W at full transmit, less in practice), and it helps only when path loss rather than scheduler congestion is the binding constraint. Prefer a wide-beam panel over a narrow yagi unless the serving cell's bearing is confirmed on site: festival cells-on-wheels placement is usually unpublished, can be relocated mid-event, and the modem may reselect to a surrounding macro site. Antenna gain must stay within the gain listed in the module's FCC/CE modular approval — exceeding it voids the grant and forces re-certification.

Do not cite ofmodemsandmen.com/power.html as quantitative grounding. It is a community router-firmware wiki with anecdotal USB-dongle ammeter readings on 3G-era sticks, and its signal/power statement is explicitly hedged ("seems to require more power... for some modems"). It supports the qualitative direction only. Its 2000-3000 mA figure is a USB enumeration inrush spike and must not be carried into a sustained thermal or battery budget.
corrected.why:
VERDICT: directionally sound advice, but the numbers are unsupported by the cited source, the physical mechanism is partly backwards, and peak is presented as average. Not safe to order parts against as written.

1. THE SOURCE DOES NOT SUPPORT THE NUMBERS. https://www.ofmodemsandmen.com/power.html is real — it is the ROOter community router-firmware wiki. But it is anecdotal USB-dongle ammeter readings ("E3276... about 200ma... but has a spike of 2000-3000ma"; "ZTE MF668... 300ma... 400ma when data was transmitted"), and its signal-quality statement is explicitly hedged: poorer signal "seems to require more power... for some modems." That is a qualitative observation about a handful of 3G/early-LTE USB sticks. It contains no festival data, no LTE uplink power-control analysis, and nothing that yields +2.0-2.5 W vs +1.0-1.5 W. Citing it as "the documented signal-quality/power relationship" grounding a specific wattage budget is over-citation. Worse, the page's headline 2000-3000 mA figure is a USB enumeration/inrush spike, not a signal-related steady draw — carrying that regime into a sustained thermal or battery budget is a category error.

2. PEAK/AVERAGE CONFLATION — the core defect. 3GPP Power Class 3 caps UE conducted output at +23 dBm (200 mW). Bad signal drives the PA to that cap; it cannot go past it. At a realistic 30-40% PA efficiency, max-TX PA DC draw is ~0.5-0.7 W. That is the entire physically available good-signal-to-max-signal delta for the PA itself. A claimed +1.0 W swing (from +1.0-1.5 to +2.0-2.5) exceeds the PA headroom that exists. Separately, ~2.0-2.5 W is approximately the TOTAL module draw of a Cat-1/Cat-4 module at full-power transmit (roughly 500-700 mA at 3.8 V), not an adder on top of a baseline that already counts baseband and RF idle. Stating it as "+" double-counts.

3. THE CONGESTION MECHANISM IS PARTLY BACKWARDS. LTE open-loop uplink power control (TS 36.213) is P = min(P_CMAX, P_O + 10·log10(M_RB) + α·PL + Δ_TF + f). Under heavy cell load the scheduler grants FEWER resource blocks, which LOWERS per-transmission power while extending time-on-air. Lower-order modulation likewise carries a lower Δ_TF offset, not a higher one. Contention costs queueing and throughput, and during queueing the PA is off. The honest festival penalty is a multiplier on uplink DUTY CYCLE (HARQ retransmissions, RLC retries — the claim's own "another full PA transmit cycle" line is a duty-cycle argument), not on instantaneous power. The claim asserts the latter.

4. NO DUTY CYCLE IS STATED, SO THE AVERAGE IS UNDERIVABLE. Average = idle + (peak − idle) × uplink duty cycle. A gateway pushing low-rate telemetry cannot average 2.0-2.5 W under any RF condition; only a near-continuous uplink stream approaches peak as an average. The claim's number is only correct if the device transmits at P_CMAX essentially continuously, which it never states.

5. INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT REMEDY. The claim blames the excess mostly on contention/retransmissions, then proposes antenna gain — which addresses path loss, not contention. Antenna gain saves nothing once the binding constraint is scheduler congestion. Its maximum possible saving is also capped by the same ~0.5-0.7 W of PA headroom, so "cut PA output requirements substantially" is bounded well below the 1 W the claim implies.

6. OMITTED REGULATORY CAVEAT, STATED TOO CONFIDENTLY. Bolting a high-gain antenna onto a certified radio module is only compliant within the antenna gain listed in the module's FCC Part 22/24/27 or CE modular approval; exceeding it voids the grant and requires re-certification. The claim presents the antenna as unambiguously "the single highest-leverage power fix available" with no such qualification.

7. "AIMED AT THE KNOWN CELL SITE" ASSUMES FACTS NOT IN EVIDENCE. Festival COW placement and sector bearing are typically not published, can be relocated mid-event, and the modem may reselect between the COW and surrounding macro sites. A narrow-beam yagi can perform worse than a moderate-gain panel when the serving cell moves or changes.

8. "FAR CHEAPER THAN ADDING CELLS" IS A NON-COMPARISON. The party ordering this hardware cannot add cells — that is the carrier's or event RF vendor's decision. It is not a tradeoff available to the engineer reading this spec.

VERIFICATION LIMIT (disclose to the reader): the web search budget for this session was exhausted after the source fetch, so the module current figures in point 2 are from my own knowledge, not freshly confirmed datasheets. Before ordering, confirm peak TX current, supply transient requirement, and P_CMAX against the datasheet of the specific module chosen.

Sources: [ROOter power page (the cited source)](https://www.ofmodemsandmen.com/power.html)

corrected.original: With LTE at 4.5 W typical, all four battery configs lose roughly one third of their runtime; at 6.0 W worst case they lose nearly half.
corrected.corrected:
With LTE, system draw rises from a 3.0 W baseline to 4.5 W typical and 6.0 W worst case (poor signal, dense BLE) — a runtime loss of exactly 33% and exactly 50% respectively, identical for every config since it is a pure power ratio.

Runtimes must be computed from USABLE, not gross, pack energy. Applying an 85% cell-to-5V conversion and usable-DoD factor (fresh cells, 25 °C):

At 4.5 W typical: (a) 19.3 Wh gross -> 3.6 h; (b) 9.0 -> 1.7 h; (c) 38.6 -> 7.3 h; (d) 27.6 -> 5.2 h.
At 6.0 W worst case: (a) 2.7 h; (b) 1.3 h; (c) 5.5 h; (d) 3.9 h.
With an additional 80% end-of-life derate, config (c) falls to 5.8 h typical / 4.4 h worst case.

Practical consequence: with LTE, no listed configuration covers a 12-14 h festival day, and the gap is larger than a gross-Wh calculation suggests — the best config (c) delivers roughly 7 h typical, not 8.6 h.

Sizing, if LTE is a hard requirement: 8 cells (77 Wh gross) is NOT sufficient. It yields ~14.5 h at 4.5 W (no margin) and only ~10.9 h at the 6.0 W worst case. Size to the worst case: 99 Wh usable-basis (~11 cells at 9.6 Wh/cell) for 14 h with fresh cells, or ~124 Wh (~13 cells) to hold 14 h at 80% end-of-life. Below that, plan hot-swappable packs, a mid-day swap, or mains/solar top-up.

Before ordering: reconcile the pack ladder — 77 Wh / 8 cells implies 9.6 Wh/cell, which makes (a) and (c) exactly 2 and 4 cells but leaves (b) at 0.94 and (d) at 2.87 cells; confirm the actual cell and pack for those two configs. Also specify a cold-weather capacity derate (~10-20% for outdoor/overnight use, the dominant thermal risk — heat derates capacity and accelerates aging rather than raising load power), and specify pack and converter discharge ratings against LTE transmit current peaks, which are well above the 6.0 W average used for runtime.
corrected.why:
The divisions are all arithmetically correct (19.3/4.5=4.29, 9.0/4.5=2.0, 38.6/4.5=8.58, 27.6/4.5=6.13; 3.22/1.5/6.43/4.60 at 6.0 W; 77/4.5=17.1). The claim fails on method and on its own recommendation, which is the part an engineer would order parts against.

1) GROSS Wh DIVIDED BY LOAD W. Every runtime is nameplate pack energy / system power, with no DC-DC conversion loss, no usable-depth-of-discharge limit, and no aging derate. The claim says this out loud — "77 Wh gross, ~17 h at 4.5 W" — gross cell energy is not energy delivered to a 5 V load. A cell-to-5V boost stage (UPS HAT / power-bank IC) is ~85-92%, and cutoff above ~3.0 V/cell strands more. At a conservative-standard 0.85 end-to-end factor every figure drops ~15%: (a) 3.6 h, (b) 1.7 h, (c) 7.3 h, (d) 5.2 h at 4.5 W; (c) 5.5 h at 6.0 W. At 0.85 x 0.8 (EOL cells) config (c) is 5.8 h, not 8.6 h.

2) THE 8-CELL RECOMMENDATION FAILS THE CLAIM'S OWN WORST CASE. 77 Wh gross x 0.85 = 65 Wh usable = 14.5 h at 4.5 W (zero margin on a 14 h day) and 10.9 h at the 6.0 W worst case the same paragraph defines. It is self-inconsistent even before efficiency: 77/6.0 = 12.8 h already misses the top of the stated 12-14 h range. An engineer ordering 8 cells on this line ships a pack that misses a festival day in exactly the conditions (poor signal, dense BLE, hot enclosure) the spec names. Correct sizing for 14 h at 6.0 W: 99 Wh (11 cells) fresh at 85% conversion; 124 Wh (13 cells) with an 80% EOL derate.

3) THE PERCENTAGES ARE IMPRECISE IN THE WRONG DIRECTION AND FALSELY IMPLY PER-CONFIG ANALYSIS. The only baseline consistent with these numbers is exactly 3.0 W (giving 6.4/3.0/12.9/9.2 h without LTE). Runtime loss is then a pure power ratio: exactly 33.3% at 4.5 W and exactly 50.0% at 6.0 W, identical for all four configs by construction. "Nearly half" reads as under 50%; it is precisely half. "All four battery configs lose roughly one third" implies four independent results when it is one ratio restated four times.

4) INPUT LADDER INCONSISTENCY. 77 Wh / 8 cells = 9.625 Wh/cell. At that cell energy (a) = 2.01 cells and (c) = 4.01 cells, but (d) 27.6 Wh = 2.87 cells and (b) 9.0 Wh = 0.94 cells — not integer counts. Either (d)/(b) use a different cell or pack, or a figure is stale. Reconcile before issuing a BOM.

5) WRONG MECHANISM FOR THE THERMAL TERM. "Hot enclosure" is listed as a driver of the 6.0 W load. Heat does not materially raise SoC/modem draw (a Pi throttles rather than drawing more); it reduces deliverable capacity and accelerates aging — a derate on the Wh side, not an adder on the W side. Conversely cold ambient (night sets, exterior mounting) costs roughly 10-20% of Li-ion capacity and is not modeled at all.

6) NOT CHECKED HERE. The 4.5 W / 6.0 W inputs are cited to other findings and could not be verified against modem datasheets in this session; they are plausible for a Pi-4-class board plus USB LTE dongle but remain unconfirmed. Separately, runtime uses average power correctly, but the pack and converter must additionally be rated for LTE TX current bursts (peak far above average) — that is a discharge-rating spec line, absent from the claim.

corrected.original: LTE transmit current spikes of 2-3 A are a separate hardware problem from the energy problem, and are the most common cause of random reboots in battery-powered Pi + LTE builds.
corrected.corrected:
Peak current capability and energy capacity are independent design axes: a pack correctly sized in watt-hours can still fail on transients. Budget for both.

MEASURED EVIDENCE (weak, single-source, not LTE-transmit):
- Huawei E3276: ~200 mA through most of the connection process, with a reported 2000-3000 mA spike "at one point" during CONNECTION (ofmodemsandmen.com/power.html). This is an uninstrumented anecdotal figure, not a scope capture, and its DURATION is not stated.
- Huawei E3131 (HSPA+, not LTE): scope-measured maximum 258 mA RMS at heavy 2G upload, 188 mA at heavy 3G upload; 30-45 mA idle. The author notes inrush at connect that "probably" breaks USB specs (blog.atx.name/modem-power-consumption/).
- Do not describe these as "LTE transmit spikes." LTE UE Power Class 3 is capped at +23 dBm (200 mW) with continuous SC-FDMA; multi-amp bursty transmit is a GSM/2G TDMA signature. Treat the 2-3 A event as a connection/PA-startup/inrush transient of unknown duration.
- No source ranks causes of Raspberry Pi reboots. Drop any "most common cause" language. In practice, power-bank low-current auto-shutoff and cable/connector IR drop are at least as common in battery Pi builds.

DESIGN GUIDANCE:
1) Converter: specify >=3 A continuous at 5 V with documented transient headroom, and verify the CURRENT-LIMIT behavior (hiccup vs foldback vs latch), not just the nameplate. Justify this as margin and derating, not from "15 W instantaneous" — a transient rating and a continuous rating are different specs. Verify the MT3608 switch-current limit against the actual datasheet before rejecting it; the widely quoted "2 A" is a module-vendor figure and the silicon limit appears higher. Confirm TPS61088 lifecycle status before designing it in.
2) Bulk capacitance: cannot be specified without the transient's duration, which no source provides. C = I*dt/dV. At 3 A holding 5 V within 0.25 V: 1000 uF covers 83 us, 4700 uF covers 392 us, and a 10 ms event needs ~0.12 F. Electrolytic bulk therefore only helps for sub-millisecond events. Scope the actual transient first. Critically, do NOT place 2200-4700 uF at a USB port: USB 2.0 §7.2.4.1 limits device VBUS bypass capacitance to 10 uF to bound hot-plug inrush. Put bulk on a permanently-wired upstream rail, or add inrush limiting.
3) Input current: 3 A at 5 V is 15 W; from a 3.2 V pack at a realistic 85-90% boost efficiency that is 5.2-5.9 A, not ~5 A. Specify the chemistry — 3.2 V is ~5% SoC for Li-ion but mid-pack nominal for LiFePO4. Budget cell IR, wiring, and connector drop at that current.
4) Failure modes are distinct, not a chain. The Pi's ~4.63 V undervoltage flag causes clock THROTTLING, not reboots; reboots require a lower SoC/PMIC brownout trip; SD corruption results from unclean power loss. Instrument which one you are actually seeing (vcgencmd get_throttled plus a scope on the 5 V rail) rather than assuming one syndrome.
5) Power the dongle from the pack's 5 V rail via a powered hub or dedicated regulator, not the Pi's USB port. This is sound on every model. Note that "the Pi's USB current limiter" is model-specific — B+/2/3 used a ~1.2 A total polyfuse, Pi 4 removed per-port limiting, and Pi 5 gates total USB current on PSU negotiation — so state the target Pi model in the spec.
corrected.why:
Both sources were fetched and partially substantiate the raw numbers, but the claim misattributes them, over-claims causality, and contains two quantitative errors that would mislead a parts order.

1) MISATTRIBUTION — "LTE transmit" is wrong. Ofmodemsandmen says the E3276 "requires about 200ma during most of the connection process but has a spike of 2000-3000ma at one point." The spike is located in the CONNECTION process, not in LTE transmit. Physics agrees: LTE UE Power Class 3 caps at +23 dBm (200 mW) with continuous SC-FDMA transmission; even at 30% PA efficiency that is under 1 W, nowhere near 15 W. The multi-amp bursty-transmit signature is a GSM/2G TDMA artifact (2 W peak, 1/8 duty, 577 us slots). The 2-3 A event is far more likely PA/rail startup, inrush, or 2G-fallback registration.

2) THE SECOND SOURCE CONTRADICTS THE CLAIM. blog.atx.name measured the E3131 with a Rigol scope across paralleled 1-ohm shunts and reports a MAXIMUM of 258 mA RMS (heavy 2G upload); 3G heavy upload is 188 mA. That is an order of magnitude below a 2-3 A transmit spike. It is also cited for inrush "probably breaks the USB specs" — hedged in the source, stated as fact in the claim. Additionally the E3131 is an HSPA+/3G stick, not LTE, so it is conflated into an LTE claim.

3) UNSUPPORTABLE EPIDEMIOLOGY. "The most common cause of random reboots in battery-powered Pi + LTE builds" appears in neither source. Neither page discusses Raspberry Pi reboots at all. No ranking of failure causes is offered anywhere. This is the single most confident sentence in the claim and it has zero support.

4) CAPACITOR MATH IS UNMOORED. C = I*dt/dV. At 3 A with 0.25 V droop, 1000 uF holds 83 us and 4700 uF holds 392 us. Covering even a 10 ms event needs 0.12 F. Neither source characterizes the spike's DURATION, so the capacitor value cannot be derived at all — and if the event is millisecond-scale (likely for a connection/PA-ramp transient), the recommended range is off by two-plus orders of magnitude and will not fix it.

5) THE CAPACITOR FIX CREATES A SPEC VIOLATION. USB 2.0 §7.2.4.1 limits downstream-facing device VBUS bypass capacitance to 10 uF max, specifically to bound hot-plug inrush. Recommending 2200-4700 uF "physically close to the USB port" violates the very specification the claim elsewhere complains the modem violates. (Bulk on a permanently-wired upstream rail is fine; on a pluggable port it is not.)

6) OPTIMISTIC EFFICIENCY. 15 W / 3.2 V = 4.69 A at 100% efficiency; "~5 A" implies 93.75%, unrealistic for a 3.2 V->5 V boost at 5 A. Realistic 85-90% gives 5.2-5.9 A. Also "2P pack at 3.2 V/cell" is chemistry-ambiguous: 3.2 V is ~5% SoC for Li-ion but the nominal mid-pack resting voltage for LiFePO4 — opposite meanings for a worst-case spec.

7) PEAK/AVERAGE CONFLATION IN THE SIZING RATIONALE. "15 W instantaneous" is arithmetically right (5 x 3) but is then used to justify ">=3 A CONTINUOUS." Surviving a transient and sourcing 3 A continuously are different requirements. Continuous headroom is defensible conservative engineering, but the stated justification does not support it.

8) THREE FAILURE MODES CHAINED AS ONE. Pi undervoltage detection (the ~4.63 V flag) triggers CLOCK THROTTLING and does not reboot. Reboots require the SoC/PMIC brownout trip, which is lower. SD corruption results from unclean power loss, not from throttling. "Throttling and eventually SD card corruption... presents as unexplained random reboots" fuses three distinct mechanisms into a false syndrome.

9) UNVERIFIED COMPONENT RATINGS (search budget exhausted; flagged, not asserted). The "MT3608 = 2 A switch rating" figure is suspect — my recollection is the datasheet specifies a ~4 A switch current limit, with 2 A being a module-vendor marketing number; this needs a datasheet check before anyone orders. TPS61088 lifecycle status also unverified. "The Pi's USB current limiter" is model-dependent (B+/2/3 had a ~1.2 A total polyfuse; Pi 4 removed per-port limiting; Pi 5 gates total USB current on PSU negotiation) and the claim never says which Pi.

WHAT SURVIVES: The structural insight is sound and worth keeping — peak current capability and energy capacity are genuinely independent design axes, and a pack sized correctly in Wh can still fail on transient current. Recommendation (4), feeding the dongle from the pack rail rather than through the Pi's port, is good practice on every Pi model regardless of the reasoning used to reach it.

corrected.original: CM4 power data is contradictory and the carrier board, not the module, is the dominant variable - do not assume CM4 saves power.
corrected.corrected:
CM4 system power is dominated by the carrier board, not the module — do not assume CM4 saves power over a Pi 4B.

Evidence, with its limits stated. Tom's Hardware's Compute Module 4S review (note: a CM4S review, not a CM4 review) lists CM4 at 3.55 W idle / 5.2 W stress, Pi 4 at 1.02 W idle / 6.2 W stress, and CM4S at 1.02 W idle / 4.08 W stress. The Pi 4 and CM4S idle figures are byte-identical, which points to a duplicated table cell rather than a real measurement; the 1.02 W Pi 4 number should be discarded, since Raspberry Pi 4B idle is generally published at roughly 2.7 W. Treat the whole comparison as unreliable rather than as evidence that CM4 is worse.

The two Raspberry Pi forum threads often cited here do not support module-level idle claims. Thread 290379 gives only datasheet load figures (1.4 A ≈ 7 W at 5 V) and an informal 1.8 A ≈ 9 W maximum estimate — no idle measurement. Thread 346595 reports 300-350 mA at low CPU load described by its author as 3.6-4 W, which resolves only at 12 V (300 mA × 12 V = 3.6 W), not 5 V. Do not convert forum current figures at 5 V without confirming the carrier's input rail; many CM4 carriers are 12 V-fed, where 400 mA is 4.8 W, not 2.0 W.

Mechanism (engineering judgment, not measured here): unused Ethernet PHYs, USB hub controllers, PCIe bridges, and PMIC quiescent draw on a general-purpose carrier plausibly add several hundred milliwatts each. A minimal purpose-built carrier — eMMC variant so no SD controller, a wireless-less CM4 SKU since the design is on Ethernet, a single Ethernet PHY, no USB hub beyond the LTE dongle's needs — should approach Pi 4B-class power, but there is no published measurement establishing it lands below Pi 4B.

CM4 remains the right choice for this appliance on mechanical and eMMC-reliability grounds. For parts ordering, budget against peak, not idle: assume roughly 5-6 W for the module under load, plus carrier overhead, plus LTE dongle transmit peaks, and size the supply and thermal solution with margin above that. Treat ~3 W as an idle expectation only. Measure the actual carrier before committing to a PSU or enclosure.
corrected.why:
The thesis is directionally sound, but two of the three citations do not say what the claim attributes to them, and the recommended power budget is unsafe to order parts against.

SOURCE 1 (Tom's Hardware) — figures confirmed, but provenance and interpretation are wrong. The table does read CM4 idle 3.55 W / stress 5.2 W and Pi 4 idle 1.02 W / stress 6.2 W. Two problems the claim misses. (a) The URL is the Compute Module 4S review, and CM4S — a different product, SODIMM form factor for CM3 sockets — idles at 1.02 W in the same table, the identical value to the Pi 4. Two independent measurements do not land on the same figure to 0.01 W. The parsimonious explanation is a duplicated cell in the comparison table, not the "methodology difference" the claim asserts. That is a stronger reason to distrust the number, and the claim reaches the right conclusion via the wrong mechanism while never disclosing that its source is a CM4S review. (b) I could not independently re-verify the "2.2-2.85 W every other published measurement" range (web search budget exhausted); it is consistent with the widely cited ~2.7 W Pi 4B idle, but it is presented with more confidence than I could confirm.

SOURCE 2 (forum t=290379) — misattributed. The claim cites it for "CM4 idle at 400 mA (2.0 W at 5V)". The thread contains no such figure. It discusses the datasheet's 1.4 A load current (1.4 × 5 = 7 W, matches the OP) and a member's "about 9W max / 1.8 amps" estimate (1.8 × 5 = 9 W, matches). Both are load/max figures, not idle. The claim has converted a nonexistent idle number.

SOURCE 3 (forum t=346595) — misattributed and contains a unit trap. The claim cites it for "CM4 is typically slightly lower than Pi 4". The thread contains no CM4-vs-Pi 4 comparison at all. Its actual measurements are 0.5 A maximum and 300-350 mA at low CPU load, which the poster calls "3.6-4 watts". Re-deriving: 300 mA × 12 V = 3.6 W and 350 mA × 12 V = 4.2 W match; at 5 V the same currents give 1.5-1.75 W, which does not. Those currents are at 12 V. This directly invalidates the claim's conversion method — it converts forum milliamp figures at 5 V, and CM4 carriers are commonly 12 V-fed. The unsourced "1.83 W" figure appears in neither thread.

UNSUPPORTED ASSERTIONS. The "1-2 W" carrier adder is uncited (VL805-class controllers and Ethernet PHYs are typically a few hundred mW each, so 1-2 W is the high end). "Should land at or slightly below Pi 4B" is asserted, not shown — the Pi 4B already carries the same Ethernet PHY and an MxL7704-class PMIC, so stripping a carrier down gets you toward Pi 4B, not below it.

THE ORDERING RISK. "Budget the same 3.0 W" is an idle-only number presented as the design budget, conflating idle with peak. The claim's own source shows CM4 at 5.2 W under stress before any carrier overhead, and the stated appliance adds an LTE dongle whose transmit peaks are worth watts on their own. An engineer sizing a PSU or thermal solution against 3.0 W would undersize it.

corrected.original: The Pi 4 has no usable low-power sleep state, so duty-cycling is not available as a runtime strategy - this caps what any battery design can achieve.
corrected.corrected:
The Pi 4 has no SoC sleep state (no suspend-to-RAM) and no wake-on-BLE path, so the Pi's own radio cannot trigger a wake. It does, however, have a documented wake-from-halt path: the Pi 4 bootloader EEPROM ships WAKE_ON_GPIO=1 by default and wakes a halted board when GPIO3 is pulled low, so an external coprocessor or RTC can duty-cycle it. Duty-cycling should be rejected on economics, not architecture.

MEASURED FIGURES, CORRECTLY QUALIFIED
- Optimized running floor: 1.7-1.8 W on the 5 V rail (chipwired, USB meter) with WiFi off, Bluetooth off, ACT LED off, CPU underclocked. Bluetooth-off makes this configuration unreachable for a BLE gateway.
- Realistic BLE-gateway idle: 2.2-2.7 W on the 5 V rail (chipwired USB-meter idle 2.2-2.3 W; pidramble 540 mA / 2.7 W). The commonly quoted 3.0 W is chipwired's AC wall-meter column and includes PSU conversion loss — do not size a DC pack against it. Under relay load expect 4.7-5.5 W. Specify a 2.2-5.5 W band, not a single ~3 W number.
- Halt current 20-24 mA is achievable ONLY with WAKE_ON_GPIO=0 and POWER_OFF_ON_HALT=1. Per the rpi-eeprom release notes, "If WAKE_ON_GPIO=1 then POWER_OFF_ON_HALT is ignored" — the low-current state and the GPIO wake path are mutually exclusive. At 20 mA the board can only be restarted by cycling the 5 V rail, which adds a high-side load switch to the BOM. With the default WAKE_ON_GPIO=1, the cited thread reports a halted board in the hundreds of mA.
- The ~700 mA halted figure is contested within the cited thread itself (attributed both to the 64-bit foundation kernel 4.19.85-v8+ and to WAKE_ON_GPIO=1). Treat as an unresolved anomaly, not a design constant.
- Use `shutdown -h now`, not `halt`: per the thread, several onboard peripherals (USB hub, Ethernet) lack a powerdown feature and keep running at full speed after `halt`. Later firmware reportedly equalized the two, so verify on the shipping EEPROM version.

WHY DUTY-CYCLING STILL FAILS (the defensible argument)
A Pi 4 cold boot is roughly 20-30 s at 3.5-5 W, on the order of 70-150 J per wake — comparable to 30-60 s of idle — plus 20-30 s of wake latency and repeated SD-card write cycles. At festival BLE event rates the Pi would never stay off long enough to amortize a wake. Continuous-on is therefore correct, but state it this way: it survives scrutiny, whereas "there is no wake path" does not. (Boot-energy figures are order-of-magnitude; measure on the target image before freezing the spec.)

COPROCESSOR OFFLOAD — nRF52 AND ESP32 ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE
nRF52 continuous BLE scanning is roughly 5-13 mA (~15-45 mW) and genuinely reaches sub-mW averages at low duty. ESP32 draws roughly 95-130 mA while its radio is active, so a single-digit-mW average demands a scan duty cycle low enough to materially degrade detection probability for a gateway. Specify the nRF52 for this role; do not present the two as equivalent "single-digit mW" parts. (Confirm both against current vendor datasheets before ordering.)

PI ZERO 2 W
The "0.7-1.2 W class" figure appears in neither cited source. Independent measurement puts Zero 2 W idle at 0.6-0.7 W on the 5 V rail, but that is idle without sustained BLE scanning; a loaded quad-A53 exceeds 1.2 W. Re-source or re-measure before ordering against it.

BOTTOM LINE (unchanged): the Pi 4 gateway is correctly framed as mains-or-large-battery fixed infrastructure, not a portable device.
corrected.why:
The conclusion (Pi 4 = fixed infrastructure, not portable) is correct, but the load-bearing mechanism is wrong and two of the quoted numbers are mutually exclusive. An engineer ordering parts against this would draw the wrong BOM.

VERIFIED AS STATED:
- chipwired's optimized floor: 1.7 W / 1.8 W with WiFi off, BT off, ACT LED off, CPU underclocked. Correct, and the claim is right that BT-off makes it unreachable for a BLE gateway.
- Forum thread: 20 mA halt achieved by "soundcheck" via `shutdown -h now`; 21 mA by "tvjon"; the halt-vs-shutdown distinction is real ("several onboard peripherals (hub/ethernet/asf) are still running... at full speed after executing 'halt'"); a ~700 mA halted figure is present.

REFUTED — "duty-cycling is not available as a runtime strategy":
The rpi-eeprom release notes document WAKE_ON_GPIO, default 1, which lets the system wake from halt via GPIO3. A halted Pi 4 CAN be woken by an external device — which is exactly the "nRF52 wakes the Pi when there is something to relay" topology the claim presents as requiring abandonment of the Pi 4. "No wake-on-BLE" (true) has been generalized into "no wake path at all" (false).

REFUTED — the 20 mA figure and the wake path are mutually exclusive:
The thread's 20 mA config is BOOT_UART=0 / WAKE_ON_GPIO=0 / POWER_OFF_ON_HALT=1 / FREEZE_VERSION=0. Release notes: "If WAKE_ON_GPIO=1 then POWER_OFF_ON_HALT is ignored." So 20 mA requires disabling GPIO wake, leaving only 5 V rail cycling — a high-side load switch that is absent from the claim's BOM. The same thread reports the default WAKE_ON_GPIO=1 halted board in the hundreds of mA.

REFUTED — ~700 mA attribution is contested in the cited source itself:
