Two passes over the thread attributed it to the 64-bit foundation kernel (4.19.85-v8+) and to WAKE_ON_GPIO=1 respectively. Unresolved anomaly, not a design constant.

REFUTED — wall/DC conflation in "~3 W, full stop":
chipwired's 3.0 W is the household watt-meter (AC) column; the USB-meter (5 V DC) reading for the same idle state is 2.2-2.3 W. pidramble independently measures Pi 4B idle at 540 mA / 2.7 W on the rail. Sizing a DC pack against the AC number oversizes it. Also 3 W is not a ceiling — normal load is 4.7-5.5 W, so a band belongs in the spec.

UNSOURCED — Pi Zero 2 W "0.7-1.2 W class" appears in neither cited source; chipwired publishes no Zero 2 W measurements. pidramble gives 100 mA (0.6 W) HDMI/LED off, 120 mA (0.7 W) with WiFi — idle only, no sustained BLE scanning, and no load figure.

CONFIDENCE CAVEAT: web search budget was exhausted, so the nRF52/ESP32 scan currents and the Pi 4 boot-energy arithmetic in my correction rest on general knowledge, not fetched sources — flagged as such in the corrected text and should be measured before the spec is frozen.

Sources: [chipwired Raspberry Pi power use](https://chipwired.com/raspberry-pi-power-use/), [Raspberry Pi forums t=257144](https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=257144), [rpi-eeprom firmware-2711 release notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/rpi-eeprom/master/firmware-2711/release-notes.md), [pidramble power consumption benchmarks](https://www.pidramble.com/wiki/benchmarks/power-consumption)

corrected.original: The BLE increment is the largest uncertainty in this budget and should be measured with an INA219/INA260 on the 5V rail, not a USB inline meter.
corrected.corrected:
Every figure in this budget is a planning estimate until measured. The measurement requires TWO instruments, not one, because no single part covers both the energy-integration and the transient-droop question.

(A) ENERGY / AVERAGE POWER - INA260 (not INA219) high-side on the 5V rail.
Specify the INA260: its 2 mOhm integrated shunt (4.5 mOhm pin-to-pin) adds negligible series drop, and its 1.25 mA LSB = 6.25 mW at 5V, ample to resolve a 100-300 mW BLE delta. Do NOT substitute an INA219: it requires an external shunt, and a value sized for fine resolution (0.1 ohm, 100 uA LSB) drops ~100 mV at 1 A and 320 mV at its 3.2 A full scale - the instrument would manufacture the rail droop you are trying to measure. If an INA219 is used anyway, specify a 0.01 ohm shunt (1 mA LSB, ~20 mV at 2 A) and accept the coarser resolution.
Log at 10-100 Hz with long conversion times and averaging - per the INA260 datasheet (Fig 24), accuracy improves with LONGER conversion times, so do not chase speed on this instrument. Log from a separate device. Run the real production workload (actual BlueZ scan+advertise parameters, real SQLite write rate, real client count) for a full hour in a genuinely dense RF environment; a quiet bench will understate advertisement report rate.

(B) TRANSIENT / DROOP - NOT an INA2xx.
An INA219 tops out near 940 Hz at 12-bit before I2C overhead (532 us shunt + 532 us bus), and an INA260 near 1.8 kHz at its noisiest setting. At 1 kHz, Nyquist means nothing shorter than 2 ms is visible - LTE TX bursts are sub-millisecond with fast edges, so a sampled INA reading will alias straight past the true minimum and report a rail that looks fine. Use an oscilloscope in peak-detect/envelope mode with a current probe (or a low-value shunt plus differential probe), or a Joulescope/Nordic PPK2-class instrument, with bandwidth into the tens of kHz minimum. Probe at the DUT input connector, not the supply end: USB cable and connector resistance of 100-300 mOhm round trip alone produces 100-300 mV of drop at 1 A. Size bulk capacitance from the measured burst current and duration, and confirm the rail holds above the board's actual undervoltage threshold (4.75 V is the USB 2.0 lower limit and a reasonable default, but use the regulator dropout and brownout spec if they are tighter).

(C) SIZING ARITHMETIC.
Size battery ENERGY from the integrated Wh (mean power x runtime) - not from the 95th percentile. P95 is the right statistic for the regulator continuous rating, wire gauge, connector rating, thermal design, and battery C-rate/BMS current limit; using it for capacity overspecs by roughly 50% at a typical 3.0 W mean / 4.5 W P95. Then divide the measured 5V-rail Wh by the DC-DC conversion efficiency (85-92% typical) and apply usable-capacity derating (80-90% of nameplate for cutoff voltage, temperature, and cycle aging). Note that power-bank "mAh" is cell-level at 3.7 V nominal: a 20000 mAh pack is ~74 Wh, NOT 100 Wh - multiplying printed mAh by 5 V overstates delivered energy by about 50%.

(D) SCOPE OF THE UNCERTAINTY CLAIM.
Do not assert that the BLE increment is the largest uncertainty, or that advertisement report rate is the dominant CPU driver - both are untested hypotheses this measurement should resolve, not premises it may assume. In the congested venue stipulated, closed-loop LTE transmit power control plausibly swings average modem power across a wider range than the entire 100-300 mW BLE delta; instrument and report BLE and LTE contributions separately before ranking them.

(E) TOOL CHOICE CAVEAT.
"USB inline meters resolve to ~10 mA / 50 mW" is true only of low-cost testers. Mid-range USB-C meters (ChargerLAB POWER-Z KM003C, FNIRSI FNB-series) spec 0.1 mA resolution and PC logging near 1 kHz - comparable to or faster than an INA219. The real case for a dedicated current-sense part is the controlled measurement point and known shunt, not raw resolution; and neither class of tool is adequate for (B).
corrected.why:
Directionally right (measure it; a cheap USB tester is inadequate for transients) but wrong in specifics that would cause an engineer to order the wrong parts.

VERIFIED AGAINST PRIMARY DATASHEETS:
- INA219 ADC table: 84us (9-bit) / 148us / 276us / 532us (12-bit), up to 68.10ms at 128 averages. Continuous shunt+bus at 12-bit = 532+532 = 1.064ms -> 940 Hz CEILING before I2C. Two 16-bit register reads at 400kHz add ~280us -> ~700-800 Hz on a dedicated MCU, 100-300 Hz realistically from Python on a Pi. The claim's own ">=1 kHz" target is UNREACHABLE with the part it recommends.
- INA260: 140us min conversion, 1.25mA current LSB, 1.25mV bus LSB, 2mOhm integrated shunt (4.5mOhm pin-to-pin). ~1.8 kHz best case, but the datasheet explicitly warns: "To achieve the highest accuracy measurement possible, use a combination of the longest allowable conversion times and highest number of averages" (Fig 24, Noise vs Conversion Time). Cannot have both the speed and the resolution the claim assumes.

SIX LOAD-BEARING ERRORS:
1. 1 kHz cannot verify a 4.75V droop limit. Nyquist = nothing shorter than 2ms visible. LTE TX bursts are sub-ms with fast edges; sampling aliases past the true minimum. Bulk-cap sizing needs dI/dt (tens of kHz to MHz). Requires scope in peak-detect/envelope mode or Joulescope/PPK2-class, not an INA2xx.
2. INA219 and INA260 are NOT interchangeable here. INA219 needs an external shunt; sized for BLE resolution (0.1 ohm -> 100uA LSB) it inserts ~100mV drop at 1A and 320mV at full-scale 3.2A - the instrument manufactures the droop it is meant to measure. INA260's 2mOhm does not. Ordering the common 0.1-ohm INA219 breakout invalidates the droop data.
3. Battery sizing from P95 is the wrong statistic. Energy capacity = integral (mean x time); P95 sizes the regulator, wiring, and C-rate. Mean 3.0W / P95 4.5W over 12h = 36Wh vs 54Wh, a 50% overspec. The claim demands both in one sentence (internally contradictory).
4. No conversion-efficiency or usable-capacity derating. 5V-rail Wh is LOAD energy; battery must supply that / boost-buck efficiency (~85-92%). Separately, power-bank "20000 mAh" is cell-level at 3.7V ~= 74Wh, not 100Wh - a ~50% unit error if multiplied by 5V.
5. "10 mA / 50 mW" mischaracterizes modern USB-C meters. POWER-Z KM003C / FNIRSI FNB-class spec 0.1mA and log at ~1kHz - comparable to or FASTER than the INA219 recommended over them. True only of $10 testers.
6. "BLE is the largest uncertainty" and "advertisement report rate is the dominant CPU driver" are asserted, not established. In the congested venue the claim itself stipulates, closed-loop TX power control drives LTE average power across a range far wider than 100-300mW. That is plausibly the larger unknown - and it is the hypothesis the measurement should test, not a premise it may assume.

Sources: TI INA219 datasheet (https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/ina219.pdf), TI INA260 datasheet (https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/ina260.pdf), both fetched and text-extracted directly.

corrected.original: Holding conventional Li-ion (cobalt-based, 4.2V/cell) at 100% SoC in a 40C environment is the single worst combination for calendar aging, costing roughly a third of capacity in one year.
corrected.corrected:
High temperature combined with high state of charge dominates calendar aging in cobalt-based Li-ion, and the two stresses compound. Battery University's BU-808 Table 3 — an ESTIMATED, unsourced table for cobalt-blend cells, footnoted "Not all Li-ion systems behave the same" — gives one-year recoverable capacity of 65% at 40C/100% SoC versus 85% at 40C/40% SoC, 80% at 25C/100%, 96% at 25C/40%, and 94% at 0C/100%. Treat the ~20-point SoC swing at 40C and the direction of both effects as the robust content; treat 65% as a rough order-of-magnitude figure, not a measured or bounding value.

Two corrections to how this is usually stated. First, 40C/100% is NOT the worst combination in the source — the same table lists 60C/40% at 75% after one year and 60C/100% at 60% after only THREE MONTHS. Size thermal limits against the real enclosure worst case, not against 40C. Second, do not assume the 65% figure is pessimistic for modern cells: contemporary consumer cells charge to 4.4-4.48V rather than 4.2V, and the higher upper cutoff pushes calendar aging up even though electrolytes have improved. Qualify any number carried into a spec with the actual cell's datasheet storage-life data at the intended voltage and temperature.

Mechanism, per Keil et al. 2016 (JES 163 A1872): calendar fade is dominated by a shift in electrode balancing from SEI growth at the graphite anode, accelerated by the low anode potentials that accompany high SoC. That paper explicitly finds cathode-side electrolyte oxidation and transition-metal dissolution play only a minor role, with some acceleration for NMC at 100% SoC — so cathode oxidation should not be cited as a co-equal mechanism.

Design-relevant caveat the raw table hides: fade is non-monotonic in SoC. Keil et al. observed plateau regions spanning 20-30% SoC intervals with similar fade, separated by steps tracking graphite staging (near ~60% SoC for some chemistries). A modest charge-limit reduction may yield little benefit while crossing a step yields most of it, so validate the chosen storage/charge-limit SoC against the specific cell rather than assuming proportional payback per percentage point.
corrected.why:
The arithmetic and table transcription are correct, but four things fail at spec-grade scrutiny.

1. "SINGLE WORST COMBINATION" IS FALSE BY THE CITED TABLE'S OWN CONTENT. BU-808 Table 3 ("Estimated recoverable capacity when storing Li-ion for one year at various temperatures") has a 60C row the claim silently drops: 60C/40% = 75% after one year, and 60C/100% = 60% after THREE MONTHS. Extrapolated to a year that is far worse than 65%. So 40C/100% is not the worst combination in the source — it is the worst of the two mid-range rows the claim chose to quote. This matters for a parts order: sealed enclosures, dashboards, and in-sun devices routinely exceed 40C, and the spec would be sized against a condition that is not the ceiling.

2. THE MECHANISM IS MISATTRIBUTED TO THE CITED PAPER. Keil et al. 2016 (JES 163 A1872) concludes the opposite of the claim's second half: fade "is mainly caused by a shift in the electrode balancing," driven by low anode potential accelerating electrolyte reduction and SEI growth, while high-voltage cathode mechanisms — "electrolyte oxidation or transition-metal dissolution — seem to play only a minor role," with only some acceleration for NMC at 100% SoC. Presenting cathode-side electrolyte oxidation as a co-equal corroborated mechanism overstates what that source supports.

3. THE PAPER CONTRADICTS THE IMPLIED SMOOTH SoC RESPONSE, AND THIS IS THE ACTIONABLE PART. Keil found fade is non-monotonic in SoC, with "plateau regions, covering SoC intervals of more than 20%-30% of the cell capacity, wherein the capacity fade is similar," and marked steps (near ~60% SoC for some chemistries) tracking graphite staging. Engineering consequence the claim omits: a 100%-to-90% charge-limit reduction may buy almost nothing, while crossing a staging step buys most of the benefit. A spec that assumes proportional payback per SoC point will mis-size the charge limit.

4. THE 65% FIGURE IS AN UNSOURCED ESTIMATE PRESENTED AS MEASURED DATA, AND THE CAVEAT LEANS THE WRONG WAY. The table is labeled "Estimated," carries no cell model, test protocol, sample size, or citation, and footnotes "Not all Li-ion systems behave the same." Separately, the claim's caveat — that modern NMC "will do meaningfully better than 65%" so 65% is a "pessimistic bound" — is an optimistic assumption stated without support and partly cuts the wrong way: 4.2V/cell is no longer "conventional" for consumer cells, which now commonly charge to 4.4-4.48V, and a higher upper cutoff raises calendar aging even as electrolytes improved. The net direction for a 4.45V cell held full at 40C is not established, so 65% cannot be treated as a floor.

What survives: the exact 40C/25C/0C values as quoted, the 20-point 65%-to-85% swing at 40C, the ~35% loss reading as "roughly a third," the sign of both the temperature and SoC effects, and the Arrhenius-SEI-at-the-anode mechanism.

Sources: [BU-808, Table 3](https://www.batteryuniversity.com/article/bu-808-how-to-prolong-lithium-based-batteries); [Keil et al. 2016, JES 163 A1872](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1149/2.0411609jes)

corrected.original: Charge/float voltage is the dominant controllable lever on Li-ion life: every 0.10 V/cell below 4.20 V roughly doubles cycle life, at proportional cost in usable energy.
corrected.corrected:
Charge-voltage limit is one of two co-dominant controllable levers on Li-ion life (the other, per BU-808 Table 3, is temperature). Per BU-808 Table 4, each ~120-140 mV reduction below 4.20 V/cell roughly doubles cycle life, at a decelerating and disproportionately small cost in usable energy.

BU-808 Table 4 verbatim (V/cell | discharge cycles | available stored energy): 4.30 | 150-250 | 110-115%; 4.25 | 200-350 | 105-110%; 4.20 | 300-500 | 100%; 4.13 | 400-700 | 90%; 4.06 | 600-1,000 | 81%; 4.00 | 850-1,500 | 73%; 3.92 | 1,200-2,000 | 65%; 3.85 | 2,400-4,000 | 60%. There is no 4.10 V row. Article guideline: every 70 mV drop in charge voltage lowers usable capacity by about 10%. The article explicitly notes these voltage references do NOT apply to LiFePO4 or lithium titanate.

The trade is favorable, not proportional: 350 mV of derate (4.20 -> 3.85) buys ~8x cycle life for ~40% of energy. Doubling interval derived from the table is ~117 mV averaged across the full span and ~140 mV across the practically useful 4.20 -> 4.06 -> 3.92 region.

Note that Table 4 measures CYCLE life against charge-voltage limit under full-DoD cycling — it is not a float/calendar-aging dataset. The "never float a Li-ion appliance at full charge" rule derives from BU-808 Table 3 (storage SoC x temperature: 100% SoC retains 80% capacity after 1 year at 25C, 65% at 40C, and 60% after just 3 months at 60C), so any float-voltage specification must be justified on Table 3 plus vendor calendar-life data, not Table 4.

Derating NMC to a 4.00 V charge limit costs 27% of nameplate capacity, which narrows but does not erase NMC's energy-density advantage: ~250 Wh/kg x 0.73 = ~182 Wh/kg, still at or above current LFP (~150-190 Wh/kg).

These are Battery University estimates for teaching purposes, not qualification data. Any voltage-vs-cycle-life figure committed to a hardware specification should be taken from the selected cell vendor's datasheet.
corrected.why:
Directionally right, but wrong in four specifics — and misapplied in a way that matters for a hardware spec.

1. FABRICATED TABLE ROW. BU-808 Table 4 has no 4.10 V row. Actual rows: 4.30/150-250/110-115%, 4.25/200-350/105-110%, 4.20/300-500/100%, 4.13/400-700/90%, 4.06/600-1,000/81%, 4.00/850-1,500/73%, 3.92/1,200-2,000/65%, 3.85/2,400-4,000/60%. The claim's "4.10 V -> 600-1,000 cycles, 90% energy" splices the cycle count of the 4.06 row onto the energy figure of the 4.13 row — the most optimistic available pairing. The claim also drops the two rows above 4.20 V, which are relevant to any spec considering 4.35/4.4 V designs.

2. DOUBLING INTERVAL OVERSTATED ~1.2-1.4x. Re-derived from the table: 4.20->4.06 (140 mV) doubles 300-500 to 600-1,000; 4.06->3.92 (another 140 mV) doubles again. Full span 4.20->3.85 = 350 mV for 8x = 2^3, i.e. ~117 mV per doubling. 100 mV therefore buys ~2^(0.10/0.117) = ~1.8x on the most generous full-span average and ~1.6x over the practically relevant top of the range, not 2x. Only the anomalous bottom row (3.92->3.85, 70 mV) doubles faster, and it contradicts the article's own "70 mV = ~10% capacity" guideline.

3. "PROPORTIONAL COST" IS WRONG AND SELF-DEFEATING. Energy loss decelerates (10, 9, 8, 8, 5 percentage points per step) while cycle life compounds. 350 mV of derate buys 8x cycle life for 40% energy — strongly favorable, not proportional.

4. CATEGORY ERROR ON FLOAT (most serious for an ordering spec). Table 4 is cycle life vs CHARGE-VOLTAGE LIMIT under full-DoD charge/discharge cycling. It is not a float/standby calendar-aging table, so it cannot be "the quantitative basis" for a float rule. The float/storage rule rests on Table 3 (storage SoC x temperature): 100% charge retains 80% after 1 yr at 25C, 65% at 40C, 60% after only 3 months at 60C. Table 3 also refutes "dominant controllable lever" — temperature at fixed SoC costs more, faster, than any Table 4 voltage derate. Voltage and temperature are co-dominant.

CORRECT AS STATED: the 4.00 V -> 73% energy / 27% loss figure, and the LiFePO4 / lithium-titanate exclusion note.

NMC-vs-LFP CONCLUSION UNSUPPORTED: 250 Wh/kg NMC x 0.73 = ~182 Wh/kg, still at or above current LFP (~150-190 Wh/kg) — narrowed, not "materially erased." It also compares derated NMC against LFP at full nameplate, and per the article's own note Table 4's voltages do not map onto LFP, so no symmetric derate exists.

PROVENANCE: BU-808 is a teaching article of estimates, not qualification data; cycle counts assume full-DoD lab cycling to end-of-life. A spec an engineer orders parts against should cite the specific cell vendor's datasheet cycle-life-vs-voltage curve.

Caveat on my own verification: the page fetch was summarized, so I hold the two rows above 4.20 V loosely; the 4.20-3.85 rows are solid and internally consistent with the article's stated 70 mV guideline. WebSearch budget for the session was exhausted, so I could not cross-check against a second mirror of the table.

corrected.original: LFP tolerates sustained high-SoC float substantially better than NMC/LCO, and the reason is electrochemical, not marketing.
corrected.corrected:
LFP tolerates sustained high-SoC float better than NMC/LCO for electrochemical reasons — better, not immune, and the margin is conditional.

MECHANISM: The LiFePO4/FePO4 two-phase plateau sits at ~3.4-3.45 V vs Li/Li+ — a genuinely flat single plateau, not a range — roughly 0.9-1.0 V below the ~4.3-4.4 V vs Li/Li+ an NMC/LCO cathode reaches at a 4.2-4.3 V CELL cutoff. Electrolyte oxidative decomposition at the cathode is strongly potential-dependent, so a fully charged LFP cell sits well inside the electrolyte's oxidative stability window while a fully charged NMC cell sits near its edge.

REFERENCE-FRAME NOTE (do not drop from the spec): 3.2 V (LFP) and 4.2 V (NMC) are full-cell nominal/cutoff values. Potentials vs Li/Li+ run ~0.1 V higher than the corresponding cell voltage because of the lithiated-graphite anode. Never compare a cell voltage against a half-cell potential.

CAVEATS THAT BELONG IN THE SPEC:
- Cathode potential is only part of it. At 100% SoC the graphite anode is at ~0.05-0.1 V vs Li/Li+ in both chemistries, so anode SEI growth and plating risk are comparable. LFP's extra margin comes from olivine structural stability and the absence of delithiated-layered-oxide O2 release, offset by its own temperature-driven Fe-dissolution pathway.
- Temperature is co-equal with voltage, not secondary. Do not carry the voltage argument without a stated cell-temperature limit.
- The flat plateau does NOT license a loose float setpoint. dQ/dV on the plateau is large, so a small voltage error is a large charge error. Specify float-rail accuracy explicitly (state it in mV, over temperature and load).
- Float below the plateau knee — ~3.35-3.40 V/cell at 25 C — or prefer charge-then-rest / periodic top-up over indefinite CV hold. Treat 3.45 V/cell as an absorption/top-of-charge setpoint, not a sustained float target, unless the cell vendor's datasheet states otherwise.

SOURCE STATUS: Khan, Maddipatla & Pecht, J. Power Sources (2026), DOI 10.1016/j.jpowsour.2026.239788 (PII S0378775326005380) is a real and topically correct review, but its full text is TDM-restricted and no repository copy exists. The sentence "exhibits superior tolerance to minor voltage excursions" and the 3.35-3.45 V/cell window were NOT independently verified. Do not cite either as a design authority until someone reads the paper. Order parts against the cell vendor's datasheet float specification — that is the contractual number regardless.
corrected.why:
DIRECTIONALLY CORRECT, BUT NOT SPEC-SAFE AS WRITTEN. Four defects, one of which is a units/reference-frame error.

1) SOURCE IS GENUINE (the claim's strongest part). Crossref/OpenAlex/Unpaywall all confirm: "A review of float charging in lithium-ion batteries: Degradation mechanisms, influencing factors, and optimization strategies," DOI 10.1016/j.jpowsour.2026.239788, alternative-id S0378775326005380 (exact PII match), J. Power Sources, online 2026-03-07, hybrid CC-BY. Authors Khan, Maddipatla, Pecht (Pecht = CALCE/UMD, credible). Abstract matches the topic. Not fabricated.

2) THE TWO SPEC-LOAD-BEARING ITEMS ARE UNVERIFIABLE. Elsevier returns 403 with `tdm-reservation=1`; Unpaywall reports has_repository_copy=false and url_for_pdf=null; IA Scholar returns 0 hits; the abstract contains no LFP mention and no voltage numbers. So the verbatim quote "exhibits superior tolerance to minor voltage excursions" and the "3.35-3.45 V/cell" window could NOT be independently confirmed. Per the default-to-refuted rule, an unread paywalled sentence cannot be laundered into a quoted design authority.

3) UNITS / REFERENCE-FRAME ERROR (the real defect). "LFP's olivine cathode sits at a flat ~3.2-3.45 V vs Li/Li+ plateau, far below the ~4.2-4.3 V of a charged NMC/LCO cathode" mixes two frames inside one sentence. The LiFePO4/FePO4 two-phase plateau vs Li/Li+ is ~3.4-3.45 V and is a single FLAT plateau — quoting a 0.25 V "range" contradicts the word "flat" in the same clause. 3.2 V is the nominal FULL-CELL voltage of an LFP/graphite cell (Wikipedia LFP battery: "Nominal cell voltage 3.2 V"), i.e. plateau minus the ~0.1 V lithiated-graphite anode potential — it is not a potential vs Li/Li+. Symmetrically, 4.2-4.3 V is the CELL cutoff for NMC/LCO-graphite; the cathode vs Li/Li+ at that cutoff is ~4.3-4.4 V. So one number in the compared pair is a cell voltage and the other a half-cell potential, both labelled "vs Li/Li+". The ~0.9-1.0 V qualitative gap survives; the numbers as written do not. The same slip repeats when the float window is given as "3.35-3.45 V/cell" (cell terminal voltage) right after reasoning in half-cell potentials. A BMS engineer setting a float rail must know which frame each number is in.

4) CAUSAL STORY OVER-NARROWED. At 100% SoC the graphite anode sits at ~0.05-0.1 V vs Li/Li+ in BOTH chemistries, so anode-side SEI growth and plating risk — which dominate calendar/float aging — are comparable, not favourable to LFP via cathode potential. LFP's real advantage is a bundle: lower cathode potential, olivine structural stability, no highly-delithiated layered-oxide surface reconstruction / Ni4+ reactivity / lattice O2 release — partly offset by LFP's own Fe-dissolution-and-migration pathway, which accelerates sharply with temperature. Pinning it on one voltage-dependent term will mislead anyone extrapolating.

5) MOST DANGEROUS SENTENCE FOR A HARDWARE SPEC: "superior tolerance to minor voltage excursions." The flat plateau argues partly the OTHER way — on the plateau dQ/dV is very large, so a small float-voltage error maps to a large charge/SoC swing. That is precisely why LFP float current is hard to regulate and why a setpoint tens of mV high near the top-of-plateau knee drives real overcharge. The oxidative-headroom argument is sound; it is not a licence to loosen float-rail tolerance, which is how an engineer will read it.

6) 3.45 V/cell as a SUSTAINED float target is at/above common stationary practice, which floats below the plateau knee (~3.35-3.40 V/cell, 13.4-13.6 V for 4S) or drops continuous float entirely for charge-then-rest / periodic top-up. 3.45 V/cell is an absorption setpoint, not a hold-forever value.

7) The claim carries the voltage half of the source and drops the temperature half, though the paper's own abstract weights float voltage and ambient temperature equally.

corrected.original: Measured LFP calendar aging is low single-digit percent per year even at elevated temperature, an order of magnitude better than the BU-808 Li-ion numbers.
corrected.corrected:
LFP calendar aging is strongly temperature- and SoC-dependent, and is NOT low single-digit percent per year at elevated temperature. The cited study (Energies 2021, 14(6), 1732) stored high-power LFP/C cells at 40 / 47.5 / 55 °C and 10 / 50 / 90 % SoC for 27-43 months and measured approximately 35% capacity loss at 47.5 °C/50% SoC and approximately 50% at 55 °C/50% SoC, with cells reaching the 20% end-of-life criterion on the shelf without any cycling. Low single-digit %/yr is a mild-temperature (roughly 25 °C or below), moderate-SoC result, not an elevated-temperature one.

The specific figures in the original claim (0.33% / 1.33% / 5.33% at 10/20/35 °C at 70% SoC over 30 months; ~8% Sony and ~12% BYD at 100% SoC/35 °C) do not appear in the cited source and should not be used. Do not spec parts against an order-of-magnitude calendar-life advantage over BU-808: BU-808's 35%/yr at 40 °C/100% is an estimate for late-1990s cobalt-oxide cells, not a measured modern baseline, and the comparison is not temperature- or SoC-matched.

Two corrections of method for anyone reusing these numbers: (1) do not annualize by dividing a multi-year total by elapsed years -- calendar fade scales roughly as sqrt(t), so first-year loss materially exceeds the linear average; (2) the ten-year recommissioning result (>=96% retention) is for benign storage near 6 °C at ~50% SoC and carries no information about 35-40 °C float, and I could not independently confirm that paper exists at the stated PII.

For a hardware specification, elevated-temperature calendar life must be taken from the specific cell vendor's datasheet for the specific part at the actual operating temperature and SoC, not from a chemistry-level generalization.
corrected.why:
The claim is refuted by its own primary source. The cited paper (Sui, Świerczyński, Teodorescu, Stroe, "The Degradation Behavior of LiFePO4/C Batteries during Long-Term Calendar Aging", Energies 2021, 14(6), 1732; confirmed via OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar) tested 15 high-power cylindrical LFP/C cells at 40 / 47.5 / 55 °C (25 °C reference) at 10 / 50 / 90 % SoC for 27-43 months. The claim's parameters -- 10/20/35 °C, 70% and 100% SoC, 30 months, "Sony" and "BYD" cells -- appear nowhere in it; the paper does not identify a manufacturer, so the Sony-vs-BYD comparison has no basis in this source.

The paper's actual results point the opposite way: approximately 35% capacity fade at 47.5 °C/50% SoC and approximately 50% at 55 °C/50% SoC over 43 months, with cells crossing the 20% end-of-life fade criterion from calendar storage alone. Linearized that is roughly 10%/yr and 14%/yr, and higher for year one under sqrt-t kinetics. This directly contradicts "low single-digit percent per year even at elevated temperature," and it destroys the "order of magnitude better than BU-808" comparison: BU-808's 35%/yr at 40 °C/100% SoC versus this paper's ~35% over 43 months at 47.5 °C/50% SoC is not a 10x gap, and the LFP figure is at higher temperature but lower SoC.

Independent arithmetic flaw even taking the claim's numbers at face value: it converts 30-month totals to %/yr by dividing by 2.5, assuming linear aging. Calendar aging follows roughly sqrt(t). The claim's own 8%/30-month figure implies ~5% loss in year one and the 12% BYD figure implies ~7.6% in year one, both above the stated "3-5%/yr" band. The pattern 0.33 / 1.33 / 5.33 is itself a tell: those equal 0.83 / 3.33 / 13.3 divided by 2.5, the signature of already-annualized numbers relabeled as 30-month totals.

Baseline problem: BU-808's 35% is an "estimated recoverable capacity" table entry (65% remaining after one year at 40 °C, 100% charge) for late-1990s cobalt-oxide cells -- an estimate for obsolete cells, not a measurement of any orderable part. Treating it as a measured like-for-like baseline inflates the apparent LFP advantage; modern NMC/NCA substantially outperforms that table.

Second source unverified: OpenAlex returned zero matches for the 2025 recommissioning paper and ScienceDirect is CAPTCHA-gated (not bypassed). Existence at the stated PII is unconfirmed. Its own stated conditions (~6 °C, ~50% SoC) make it irrelevant to an elevated-temperature specification regardless.

Evidence caveat: the ~35%/~50% fade values come from a single text-extraction pass since MDPI 403'd direct fetch. The refutation does not depend on those exact values -- the experimental matrix alone suffices, and the 27-43 month duration is independently corroborated by two API abstracts.

corrected.original: For a permanently-floated appliance, cycle life is nearly irrelevant as a selection criterion — but LFP wins there too by 2-5x if you ever do cycle it.
corrected.corrected:
For a permanently-floated appliance, cycle life is nearly irrelevant as a selection criterion -- and the reason to choose LFP is calendar aging, not cycle count.

Duty cycle: mains-connected, a handful of real discharges per year plus BMS micro-cycles. Total cycle count over ten years is plausibly under 100, so calendar aging is the governing failure mode and cycle-life spec sheets are close to noise.

Why LFP anyway (the axis that matters): an NMC cell held at 4.2V / 100% SOC suffers markedly accelerated calendar fade, while LFP floats near 3.4V with much gentler high-SOC calendar aging. Where the design allows, float at partial SOC rather than 100%, and specify float voltage and cell temperature explicitly -- these two parameters dominate ten-year outcome far more than any cycle-life number.

If cycling ever does matter, LFP leads by roughly 2-3x on like-for-like ratings (LFP ~3,000-6,000 cycles vs NMC ~800-2,000, both to an 80% retention endpoint). Treat premium "10,000 cycle" figures as unverified vendor marketing.

Do not use the Samsung INR18650-35E cycle spec as an NMC cycle-life benchmark. Its actual wording (Ver. 1.1, section 7.9) is: capacity >= 2,010 mAh after 500 cycles, which the datasheet itself labels "60% of Standard Capacity." Standard Discharge Capacity is Min 3,350 mAh (section 3.1), not the 3,500 mAh marketing nameplate -- so the figure is 40% loss, not 43%. It is also a guaranteed floor, not measured performance, taken at 100% DoD (4.2V to 2.65V) with 1C discharge and scored to a lenient 60% endpoint. It is therefore not comparable to LFP ratings quoted to 80% retention, and no valid ratio can be drawn between them.

The one cycling caveat that does matter: micro-cycling from repeated top-up charges. A charger that re-tops every time the cell relaxes a few millivolts can accumulate thousands of shallow cycles invisibly. Specify charger hysteresis / re-charge threshold explicitly in the parts spec.
corrected.why:
Thesis is sound; the load-bearing numbers are not, and this is destined for a parts order.

1) ARITHMETIC/BASIS ERROR, verified against the primary source. I extracted the cited PDF directly. §7.9: "Capacity after 500cycles. Capacity >= 2,010mAh (60% of Standard Capacity)." §3.1 Standard discharge Capacity: "Min 3,350mAh". Cross-checked by §7.10, where 3,183 mAh is "95% of Standard Discharge Capacity" -> 3183/0.95 = 3,350.5, confirming the 3,350 basis. "3,500 mAh" appears nowhere in the datasheet. 2010/3350 = 60.0% retention = 40.0% loss. The claim's "~43% loss" comes from dividing by a 3,500 mAh marketing "typical" nameplate (2010/3500 = 57.43%), substituting a marketing figure for the datasheet's own rated basis and inflating apparent degradation. The datasheet self-labels the answer, so this was avoidable.

2) INVALID COMPARISON (more serious than the rounding). The 35E cycle test is charge 1,020 mA (0.3C) -> discharge 3,400 mA (1.0C), 4.2V to 2.65V cutoff = 100% DoD at 1C, scored to a lenient 60% retention endpoint, and stated as a guaranteed minimum (">=") rather than measured performance. LFP's 2,000-6,000 figures are conventionally quoted to an 80% retention endpoint. Setting "500 cycles" beside "2,000-6,000 cycles" compares a floor-at-60% against a rating-at-80% at different DoD and C-rate. The implied ratio is not derivable in either direction: real 35E cells typically outperform the warranty floor, while a strict 80% endpoint would be reached well before 500 cycles.

3) SOURCE MISATTRIBUTION. The cited evlithium page states LFP "3,000 - 6,000+ Cycles" and NMC "800 - 2,000 Cycles" -- not the claim's 2,000-6,000 / 1,000-2,000 -- and specifies no test conditions, no DoD, and no retention threshold. The claim's "at 80-90% DoD" is precision the source does not carry. (Could not corroborate across further vendor datasheets: WebSearch budget was exhausted this session and eve-battery.com failed DNS. The decisive check was against the primary source, which is stronger.)

4) "2-5x" is loose but defensible as a central band: 2-3x from the claim's own ranges, 3-3.75x from the cited source's. The top of the stated band is not derivable from any single like-for-like pairing. "Premium cells quoted to 10,000" is adequately hedged by "quoted to," though these are unverified vendor marketing figures.

5) SURVIVES: under ~100 lifetime cycles, calendar aging governs and cycle-life spec sheets are close to noise. The micro-cycling caveat about re-topping chargers is real and a genuine design concern.

6) OMISSION AFFECTING THE CONCLUSION: the claim rests LFP's case on cycle life while simultaneously declaring cycle life irrelevant -- it argues the axis that does not matter. The decisive LFP advantage for permanent float duty is a calendar-aging one the claim never states: NMC held at 4.2V/100% SOC suffers accelerated calendar fade, whereas LFP floats near 3.4V with substantially gentler high-SOC calendar aging. For an engineer selecting parts, that is the argument that actually supports choosing LFP.

corrected.original: LFP's thermal runaway onset is ~45C higher than LCO/NMC and the event is dramatically less energetic — this is the decisive argument for a box screwed to a wall in an occupied venue.
corrected.corrected:
LFP is the correct chemistry for a wall-mounted enclosure in an occupied venue, but the supporting numbers must be restated.

Measured data — Ohneseit et al., Batteries 2023, 9(5), 237 (DOI 10.3390/batteries9050237), heat-wait-seek ARC on commercial 21700 cells, SOC 100, mean +/- SD:

  Metric (SOC 100)              NMC             LFP
  Onset of self-heating         85.5 +/- 4.9    124.4 +/- 14.4  C
  CID trigger                   91.9 +/- 1.2    163.5 +/- 5.0   C
  Venting                       121.5 +/- 5.8   168.8 +/- 1.8   C
  Start of thermal runaway      198.0 +/- 0.2   256.3 +/- 10.3  C
  Peak recorded temperature     591.6 +/- 20.9  498.6 +/- 43.9  C
  Rate at start of runaway      55 +/- 2.6      115 +/- 16.7    C/min

LFP starts thermal runaway ~58 K higher than NMC (256 C vs 198 C) and begins self-heating ~39 K higher (124 C vs 86 C). NCA cells run between the two (runaway 196-203 C). No LCO cells were tested; do not cite LCO from this source.

Do NOT claim LFP runaway is less violent once initiated. In this dataset LFP's peak was only ~93 K lower than NMC (the authors say "about 100 K"), one NCA cell peaked at 418.8 C — cooler than LFP — and LFP's self-heating rate at runaway onset was the HIGHEST measured (115 C/min vs NMC's 55 C/min). No cell of any chemistry exceeded 352 C/min; the "thousands of C/min" figure is unsupported. The 837 C figure sometimes quoted is the single global maximum across all 57 cells tested, not typical NMC behavior.

The decisive safety argument is threshold and initiation probability, not event energy: LFP cells showed NO thermal runaway under nail penetration at any tested SOC, and none under thermal abuse at SOC 0 or SOC 30. That tolerance to mechanical insult and partial charge is the design-relevant result for an accessible wall-mounted unit.

Caveats to carry into the spec: cells were sourced from five different manufacturers and the LFP anode contained no silicon while NMC/NCA anodes contained 1-1.6 mass % Si, so these deltas confound cathode chemistry with cell construction and anode formulation. The reduced-oxygen-release mechanism of the olivine phosphate lattice is established materials science but is not evidenced by this study, which attributes severity to hydrocarbon generation from the lithiated anode. Eaton's marketing statement is vendor copy, not measurement — cite it as a design rationale from a supplier, if at all, and never alongside calorimetry as equivalent evidence. Finally, LFP at SOC 100 did enter thermal runaway and reached ~500 C: the enclosure, venting path, and separation from occupants must be designed for a real runaway event, not for vent-and-smoke only.
corrected.why:
I obtained the primary source (Ohneseit et al., Batteries 2023, 9(5), 237, DOI 10.3390/batteries9050237, KIT mirror https://publikationen.bibliothek.kit.edu/1000160506/151002866) and read Tables 10 and 11 directly. The claim's direction is right but its numbers are misattributed, cherry-picked, or inverted.

1. MISLABELED METRIC — the headline numbers are not thermal runaway. Claim: "LFP entered thermal runaway at 195 +/- 8 C; LCO/NMC at 149 +/- 2 C." Those are Table 11 values for the temperature at which a 1 C/min self-heating rate is reached — an intermediate kinetic milestone, not runaway. Table 11 (SOC 100): LFP 194.1 +/- 3.5, NCA-HE I 149.2 +/- 0.1, NCA-HP 148.7 +/- 0.2, NMC 142.7 +/- 0.2. Actual START OF THERMAL RUNAWAY (Table 10, SOC 100) is LFP 256.3 +/- 10.3 C and NMC 198.0 +/- 0.2 C. The "149" is an NCA cell, not NMC (NMC is 142.7), and "+/- 8" inflates a +/- 3.5 SD.

2. WRONG CHEMISTRY — LCO was never tested. The study covers NMC, NCA and LFP only. "LCO/NMC" is a conflation; no LCO 21700 data exists here, and the 149 C figure actually belongs to NCA.

3. THE ~45 C GAP IS AN ARTIFACT. 194.1 - 148.7 = 45.4 K, i.e. the ~45 C comes from comparing the 1 C/min milestone of LFP against NCA-HP. On the correct metric the gap is LARGER (58.3 K, LFP 256.3 vs NMC 198.0); on self-heating onset it is SMALLER (38.9 K, 124.4 vs 85.5). The claim understates the real runaway gap while citing the wrong quantity.

4. PEAK TEMPERATURES ARE WRONG AND THE GAP IS ~HALF WHAT IS CLAIMED. Claim: NMC ~800 C vs LFP ~620 C (180 K gap). Measured (Table 10, SOC 100): NMC 591.6 +/- 20.9, LFP 498.6 +/- 43.9 — a 93 K gap. The paper states LFP maxima were lower "by about 100 K." The 800 C figure appears to be the single global maximum (837 C) observed across all 57 thermal-abuse cells of any chemistry, re-presented as typical NMC behavior. Worse for the claim: NCA-HE II peaked at 418.8 C, ~80 K COLDER than LFP's 498.6 C, so "dramatically less energetic" does not hold across all layered-oxide cells.

5. THE SELF-HEATING RATE CLAIM IS INVERTED. Claim: NMC "in the thousands of C/min versus orders of magnitude lower for LFP." Measured rate at start of runaway (Table 11, SOC 100): LFP 115 +/- 16.7 C/min, NCA-HE I 89 +/- 29.6, NCA-HE II 67 +/- 34.4, NMC 55 +/- 2.6, NCA-HP 38 +/- 11.6. LFP was the HIGHEST, ~2.1x NMC. Across all SOCs and chemistries the average was 79 C/min, minimum 1.6, maximum 352 C/min — nothing approaching "thousands," and not one order of magnitude in LFP's favour, let alone several. The paper explicitly notes LFP maximum rates were higher than NCA at high SOC. This single sentence is flatly contradicted by the cited source.

6. MECHANISM NOT SUPPORTED BY THE CITED PAPER. The oxygen-release / olivine-lattice argument is real materials science in general, but this paper does not test or advance it; it mentions oxygen only as a CGHE elemental measurement. The paper attributes severity to hydrocarbon formation from a lithiated anode and concludes runaway requires a lithiated anode. Note also that these LFP cells DID enter thermal runaway at SOC 100 and reached ~500 C — "vent-and-smoke, not runaway" is not what was measured at full charge.

7. CONFOUND THE SPEC SHOULD STATE. All five cell types came from different manufacturers, and the LFP anode contained no silicon while NMC/NCA anodes contained 1-1.6 mass % Si. Cathode chemistry is confounded with cell construction and anode formulation; the authors themselves raise the construction-influence question. These are not chemistry-controlled deltas.

8. EATON QUOTE UNVERIFIED. The Eaton page was unreachable from this environment (connection failed on repeated attempts). Regardless, it is vendor marketing copy, not measurement, and should not be cited alongside calorimetry as if it were evidence.

9. THE STRONGEST REAL ARGUMENT IS OMITTED. The paper's genuinely decisive pro-LFP finding is qualitative, not the onset delta: NO thermal runaway occurred in LFP cells under nail penetration at ANY tested SOC, and none under thermal abuse at SOC 0 or SOC 30. The authors call this outstanding behavior making LFP significantly safer. For a wall-mounted box in an occupied venue that is a far better argument than a 45 K onset margin — and it is the one the claim leaves out.

Verdict: the recommendation (specify LFP) is sound and defensible, but as written the paragraph would put fabricated peak temperatures, an inverted self-heating rate, a non-existent LCO dataset, and a mislabeled onset metric into a document an engineer orders parts against. It must be rewritten.

corrected.original: Published operating and storage temperature ranges are similar between the chemistries; the meaningful difference is in what temperature does to life, not in the placarded limits.
corrected.corrected:
Charge and discharge placards are close between the two chemistries; long-term storage placards are not, and the decisive difference is what temperature does to calendar life rather than what triggers a fault.

Verified from the cited datasheets:
- LFP (BatterySpace LP12-12, a 12V 12Ah pack, not a bare cell): charge 0 to 45C, discharge -20 to 60C, storage 0 to 40C.
- NMC (Samsung INR18650-35E): charge 0 to 45C, discharge -10 to 60C. Storage is duration-tiered: 1 year -20 to 25C, 3 months -20 to 45C, 1 month -20 to 60C.

Both prohibit charging below 0C (lithium plating). Both therefore accept a 40C plant room as a valid charging condition: nothing will fault or alarm. That is the real trap — the box appears to work perfectly while consuming calendar life at an accelerated rate.

Two corrections to the original framing. First, storage placards are not similar: the NMC one-year storage ceiling is 25C versus the LFP pack's 40C, so NMC is the stricter of the two on sustained warm storage. Second, the "15-35C best life" and "-10 to 35C storage" figures come from a vendor blog, not from either datasheet, and should not be specified as datasheet limits.

Do not cite the Eaton 18-28C warranted-life band. It could not be verified against the referenced FAQ, it is close enough to the ASHRAE recommended data-center envelope (18-27C) to suggest a facilities guideline has been mistaken for a warranty term, and Eaton's public Li-ion messaging generally cites ~20-25C as a reference condition while promoting high-temperature tolerance as a Li-ion advantage. If a life-versus-temperature warranty limit is going to drive the thermal design, pull the actual warranty document for the specific part number and quote its clause, rather than paraphrasing a marketing FAQ.

Design consequence, which is unchanged: size cooling to the life target, not to the placard. Specify the intended sustained cell temperature (roughly 20-25C for both chemistries) as a design requirement in its own right, and treat the 0-45C charge window purely as an alarm boundary, not as an acceptable steady-state operating point.
corrected.why: The central engineering point survives, but three specifics fail, and one of them contradicts the claim's own cited source. VERIFIED: Samsung INR18650-35E §3.12 reads exactly "Charge : 0 to 45°C / Discharge : -10 to 60°C"; the BatterySpace LFP PDF reads "Charge Temperature 0℃ to 45℃ / Discharge Temperature -20℃ to 60℃". Both impose a 0°C charge floor, so a 40°C plant room is genuinely inside the charge window for both and nothing faults. That core insight — the placard passes while calendar life is consumed — is sound and worth keeping. FAILURES: (1) The LFP storage figure contradicts its own source. The claim says "recommended long-term storage roughly -10 to 35C"; the cited BatterySpace datasheet says "Storage Temperature 0℃ to 40℃". The "15-35C best life" number appears only in the acebattery.com vendor blog, not any datasheet — marketing copy presented as a specification. (2) The "storage ranges are similar" premise is undercut by the Samsung datasheet, which the claim never quotes on storage. §3.13 is duration-tiered: 1 year -20~25°C, 3 months -20~45°C, 1 month -20~60°C. The NMC one-year ceiling of 25°C is materially tighter than the LFP pack's 40°C placard, so on the storage axis the placards are NOT similar — and they differ in the direction that matters for a warm plant room. (3) The Eaton warranty claim is unsubstantiated: the cited FAQ URL timed out on repeated fetches and could not be read. The "18-28C" band is unverifiable and sits suspiciously close to the ASHRAE recommended data-center envelope (18-27°C), suggesting a facilities guideline has been conflated with a battery warranty term; the "10-12 year warranted life" phrasing is likewise a paraphrase of a marketing FAQ, not a warranty document. Eaton's public Li-ion positioning generally cites ~20-25°C as the reference condition and sells higher temperature tolerance as a Li-ion advantage over VRLA, which is closer to the opposite of the rhetorical use here. (4) Minor: the cited "LFP typical cell datasheet" is a 12V 12Ah pack (LP12-12), not a bare cell. Because this is destined for a hardware spec an engineer will order parts against, an unverifiable vendor warranty band and a storage range that disagrees with its own footnote must not ship as stated.

corrected.original: LFP's energy-density penalty is roughly 2-2.5x by volume and ~2x by mass at the cell level, but most of that penalty disappears once you derate NMC's float SoC to make it survive.
corrected.corrected:
At the cell level LFP's energy-density penalty is about 2.5x by volume and 2.0x by mass. Recomputed from the cited datasheets on a consistent max-dimension/max-mass convention: JGNE 26650 LFP, 3.2 V x 3.0 Ah = 9.6 Wh in 35.4 cm3 (26.2 x 65.6 mm) and 81.5 g -> 271 Wh/L, 118 Wh/kg. Samsung 35E 18650, 3.6 V x 3.35 Ah min = 12.1 Wh in 17.6 cm3 (18.55 x 65.25 mm max) and <=50 g -> 685 Wh/L, 241 Wh/kg. Note the JGNE cell is a 30 A high-rate part and is currently sold out at the cited vendor; specify an orderable energy-grade LFP cell instead.

Restricting the comparison to the small cylindrical format actually being specified, energy-optimised LFP is ~110-130 Wh/kg and ~250-300 Wh/L against ~240-260 Wh/kg and ~680-730 Wh/L for NMC/NCA — so ~2x by mass and ~2.4-2.7x by volume. The commonly quoted 1.6x figure requires large prismatic LFP (~160-180 Wh/kg) and is not available in 18650/26650 cans.

Derating NMC narrows but does not erase this. Per Battery University BU-808 Table 4 (verified: 4.00 V/cell -> 73% of stored energy, 3.92 V -> 65%), a floated NMC 18650 delivers ~500 Wh/L and ~176 Wh/kg at 4.00 V, or ~445 Wh/L and ~157 Wh/kg at 3.92 V — still ~1.6-1.8x the volumetric and ~1.3-1.5x the gravimetric density of LFP, not 1.1-1.4x. Caveat: Table 4 characterises cycle life versus peak charge voltage; it is not a calendar/float-life dataset, and it does not establish that a 4.00 V float gives NMC UPS-grade longevity in a warm enclosure. LFP's case for float-duty UPS rests mainly on calendar stability at elevated temperature and a higher thermal-runaway onset (~270 C vs ~150-210 C), which no amount of NMC derating buys back.

The absolute-size conclusion still holds. For a 40 Wh appliance UPS: ~5 LFP 26650s (~177 cm3 raw cell volume; 4S = 38.4 Wh at 12.8 V nominal if 40 Wh is a soft target) versus ~5 NMC 18650s derated to 73% (~80-90 cm3). The difference is roughly 70-100 cm3 of raw cell volume, well under a fist, in an enclosure already sized around a PSU, terminals and creepage clearances. Series strings must be integral, and the two chemistries land on different pack voltages (LFP 4S ~13.6 V float vs NMC 3S ~11.8 V at 3.92 V/cell), which affects converter design.
corrected.why:
Headline ratio is roughly right but the numbers behind it contain errors that all flatter NMC, and the "1.1-1.4x" bottom line is unsupportable and self-contradictory.

1. VOLUME ERROR. 16.5 cm3 for an 18650 implies an 18.0 mm diameter. The 35E datasheet says 18.55 mm max x 65.25 mm max = 17.6 cm3. Correct figure is ~685 Wh/L, not 730.

2. MASS ERROR. The cited JGNE page states 81.5 g, not "85-90 g". LFP is therefore 118 Wh/kg, not 110. Errors 1 and 2 run in opposite directions on the two cells but both widen NMC's apparent lead.

3. Recomputed consistently (datasheet max dims/mass): LFP 271 Wh/L, 118 Wh/kg; 35E 685 Wh/L, 241 Wh/kg = 2.5x volume, 2.0x mass. "2-2.5x volume, ~2x mass" survives but sits at the top of its stated band, not the middle.

4. DISCONTINUED PART. The JGNE 26650 is listed sold out on the cited page. An engineer cannot order the cell the sizing example is built on, and the claim itself concedes it is unrepresentative (30 A high-rate).

5. THE 1.6-2x "FAIR" BASELINE IS FORM-FACTOR SWITCHED. LFP at 160 Wh/kg exists only in large prismatic cells (EVE/CATL class). In the 26650/18650 cylindrical format the example actually specs, energy-optimised LFP is ~110-130 Wh/kg against 240-260 Wh/kg for NMC/NCA — the ratio stays ~2x by mass, ~2.4-2.7x by volume. The 1.1-1.4x conclusion depends entirely on importing prismatic-grade LFP density into a cylindrical-cell comparison.

6. INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT. The same paragraph states 1.1-1.4x and then gives 150 cm3 vs 80 cm3, which is 1.9x. An engineer sizing against the worked example gets a different answer than the stated ratio.

7. SOURCE OVERREACH. BU-808 Table 4 verified exactly (4.00 V -> 73%, 3.92 V -> 65%), so that citation is sound. But Table 4 measures cycle life vs peak charge voltage, not float/calendar life. The claim uses it to support "float NMC at 4.00 V to protect it," which the source does not establish. No evidence is offered that 4.00 V float delivers UPS-grade calendar life at the elevated temperature of a wall box sharing space with a PSU — and LFP's real UPS advantages (calendar fade at 40-50 C, ~270 C thermal-runaway onset vs ~150-210 C, non-oxygen-releasing decomposition) are not energy-density tradeables at all.

8. Derating does close the gap, but less than claimed: NMC at 73% = 500 Wh/L / 176 Wh/kg (1.8x / 1.5x vs LFP); at 65% = 445 Wh/L / 157 Wh/kg (1.6x / 1.3x). "Most of that penalty disappears" overstates it.

9. The absolute-terms conclusion does survive. 40 Wh: LFP 4.2 cells = 148 cm3 (5 cells = 177 cm3 for a practical 4S build); NMC at 73% = 4.5 cells = 80 cm3, at 65% = 5.1 cells = 90 cm3. Delta 68-97 cm3 of raw cell volume, genuinely small next to a fist (~400-500 cm3). Note series strings must be integral, which the "4-5 cells" fractional framing glosses over.

corrected.original: Cost per cell is close enough to be a non-factor at appliance scale; LFP is modestly more expensive per Wh in small cylindrical formats despite being cheaper per kWh at pack/EV scale.
corrected.corrected:
Cell cost is not the deciding factor at appliance scale, but the supporting figures need correcting and one part is unavailable.

Retail single-cell pricing (18650batterystore, checked July 2026): JGNE 26650 LFP 3000 mAh, $6.99, 3.2 V nominal → 9.6 Wh → ~$0.73/Wh — but this SKU is currently SOLD OUT and must not be specified without an in-stock second source. Samsung 35E 18650 NMC 3500 mAh, $5.99 sale / $7.99 list, 3.6 V nominal → 12.6 Wh nameplate (12.1 Wh if using Samsung's 3350 mAh minimum rating) → $0.48-0.63/Wh. On a consistent nameplate basis LFP is therefore roughly 15-53% dearer per Wh in this comparison, not 10-45%.

Note this compares a 26650 against an 18650, not like-for-like. The 26650 carries ~2.1x the cell volume for ~0.76x the energy, so LFP's volumetric penalty (~2.7x) is a packaging cost that $/Wh alone does not capture — often more consequential for an appliance enclosure than the cell price itself.

At pack/EV scale the ranking inverts, as LFP avoids cobalt and nickel. Do not cite specific LFP-vs-NMC pack $/kWh splits: BloombergNEF's published survey gives only blended averages ($115/kWh global pack in 2024; $97/kWh BEV packs; China $94, US $123, Europe $139) and does not break out chemistry at pack level. The previously cited $81 vs $128/kWh figures do not appear in the stated source, which asserts only an unsourced ~20% NMC premium with no cell/pack distinction.

For a 4-6 cell appliance the cell BOM delta is roughly $4-12 depending on whether cell count or delivered energy is held constant — negligible against a field failure, a truck roll, or a fire in a venue. Chemistry should be selected on thermal-runaway behavior, cycle life, and enclosure volume, not cost. Retail single-cell pricing is used here only as an order-of-magnitude sanity check; production BOM must be re-costed against OEM tray pricing, where the chemistry economics differ.
corrected.why:
The claim's conclusion is directionally right but the supporting numbers do not survive checking, and one of the two headline figures is not in its cited source.

CONFIRMED: JGNE 26650 LFP listed at $6.99, 3.2 V nominal, 3000 mAh → 9.6 Wh → $0.728/Wh. Samsung 35E listed at $5.99 sale / $7.99 regular, 3.6 V nominal, in stock. The qualitative shape (LFP dearer per Wh in small cylindrical retail, cheaper per kWh at pack/EV scale) is correct.

DEFECT 1 — DISCONTINUED/UNAVAILABLE PART. The JGNE 26650 product page shows "Sold out." For a hardware spec an engineer orders parts against, the entire LFP price anchor is an unpurchasable SKU.

DEFECT 2 — INCONSISTENT Wh BASIS. The 12.1 Wh figure for the 35E is derived from Samsung's MINIMUM rated capacity (3350 mAh x 3.6 V = 12.06 Wh), while the LFP's 9.6 Wh uses NAMEPLATE 3000 mAh. Mixing min-spec for one cell with nameplate for the other flatters LFP. Like-for-like nameplate: 3.5 Ah x 3.6 V = 12.6 Wh → $0.475/Wh sale, $0.634/Wh list.

DEFECT 3 — ARITHMETIC. "10-45% dearer" is wrong even on the claim's own 12.1 Wh figure: 0.728/0.660 = +10%, 0.728/0.495 = +47%. On a consistent nameplate basis the range is +15% to +53%. The claim understates the LFP premium at both ends.

DEFECT 4 — FABRICATED/UNSUPPORTED PACK FIGURES. The cited evlithium page contains no $/kWh figures whatsoever. Its only cost statement is an unsourced "NMC about 20% more expensive than LFP," with no cell-vs-pack distinction and no year. The quoted "$81/kWh LFP vs $128/kWh NMC at pack level" implies a 58% premium — nearly triple what the cited page actually asserts — and is traceable to nothing. BNEF's public 2024 survey reports $115/kWh global average pack ($97 BEV packs; China $94, US $123, Europe $139) and explicitly does not break out LFP vs NMC pack pricing. The $81 figure is also below BNEF's China pack average, making it implausible as a pack-level number; it more likely reflects a cell-level or China-domestic figure presented as pack-level.

DEFECT 5 — FORM-FACTOR CONFLATION. The claim frames this as "small cylindrical formats" but compares a 26650 to an 18650. The 26650 has ~2.09x the cross-sectional area (13/9 squared) for 0.76x the energy, i.e. roughly 2.7x worse volumetric energy density. For an appliance this is a real packaging and enclosure cost that the $/Wh framing conceals. A like-for-like 18650-vs-18650 comparison would show a substantially worse LFP penalty.

DEFECT 6 — COST DELTA HOLDS ONLY AT EQUAL CELL COUNT. "Single-digit dollars" is true at equal cell count (4 cells: $27.96 vs $23.96 = $4 delta) but not at equal energy. Energy-matched, 6 LFP cells (57.6 Wh, $41.94) vs 5 NMC cells (63 Wh, $29.95 sale) is a ~$12 delta. Separately, retail single-cell pricing from a hobbyist reseller is not a valid BOM basis for an appliance program — OEM tray/reel pricing is a different market with different chemistry economics, so the retail comparison cannot support a BOM conclusion regardless of the arithmetic.

The final judgment (cell cost is not the deciding factor at 4-6 cells; safety and field-failure cost dominate) is sound and survives. But the numbers as written are wrong enough to mislead in a document parts are ordered against, and the pack-level figures must not ship with that citation attached.

corrected.original: The correct float target for LFP is 3.35-3.40 V/cell, not the 3.65 V/cell charge-termination voltage — and definitely not the 3.45 V/cell that a legacy AGM UPS charger applies.
corrected.corrected:
Float target for LFP: specify 3.35-3.40 V/cell (13.4-13.6 V for a 4S/12 V string), with 3.375 V/cell (13.5 V) a good default — this matches Victron's published LFP profile (14.2 V absorption / 13.5 V float). If the pack will sit on float for months at a time, 3.30-3.35 V/cell (13.2-13.4 V) is the longer-life setting and is what the cited practitioner source (evlithium) actually recommends. Do not confuse float with the 3.65 V/cell (14.6 V) charge-termination voltage.

Correct the rationale. The dominant float-aging mechanism is calendar aging — SEI growth and lithium-inventory loss at high SoC, strongly temperature-accelerated — not lithium plating or cathode-side electrolyte oxidation. At 3.4-3.45 V/cell the cathode sits near ~3.4 V vs Li/Li+, far below the ~4.3 V electrolyte-oxidation onset, and float currents are milliamp-scale, far below the rate needed to drive the anode into plating. Keep float low mainly to reduce time-at-100%-SoC and to leave headroom for charger tolerance and temperature drift.

Correct the SoC reasoning. LFP's flat OCV plateau (~3.0-3.3 V) spans roughly 20-90% SoC, but float operates ABOVE it on the steep upper knee. Consequently any float between 3.35 and 3.45 V/cell holds the cell at essentially 100% SoC and the difference between 3.40 and 3.45 V is small in SoC terms — the opposite of the claim. Real SoC relief requires floating down into the plateau (3.30-3.35 V/cell).

Correct the retrofit hazard. 13.8 V / 4S = 3.45 V/cell is arithmetically right and is higher than ideal, but it is a second-order concern and within range of several LFP drop-in specs. The first-order dangers when reusing an AGM/lead-acid UPS charger, which the spec must address, are: (1) periodic equalization/boost stages at 14.4-15.5 V = 3.60-3.875 V/cell, at or above LFP termination — these must be disabled, not merely trimmed; (2) lead-acid negative temperature compensation (~-3 to -5 mV/C/cell), which must be disabled because it raises voltage in the cold; (3) absence of a low-temperature charge lockout — LFP must not be charged below 0 C (Victron specifies +5 to +50 C), and this is where lithium plating genuinely occurs. Require a BMS with low-temperature charge cutoff and confirm the charger exposes a true lithium/custom profile rather than a trimmed AGM curve.
corrected.why:
Directionally sensible (float well below the 3.65 V/cell termination) but unsupportable as written, on six counts.

1. PRIMARY SOURCE UNVERIFIABLE. ScienceDirect S0378775326005380 returns HTTP 403; the existence, title, and content of the alleged "2026 float-charging review" could not be confirmed. Per the default-to-refuted rule this alone blocks the claim from a parts-ordering spec.

2. CORROBORATING SOURCE CONTRADICTS THE HEADLINE. The evlithium page recommends 3.30-3.35 V/cell as its float recommendation and never endorses 3.40 V/cell as ideal. The claim mischaracterizes that recommendation as a merely "conservative" setting subordinate to a 3.40 V ideal the source does not support. The one checkable citation does not say what it is cited for.

3. INTERNAL CONTRADICTION. Headline asserts 3.35-3.40 V/cell and "definitely not 3.45"; the DETAIL states the window is 3.35-3.45 V/cell. The claim simultaneously includes 3.45 V in the acceptable window and calls sustained operation there actively harmful.

4. MECHANISMS MISATTRIBUTED. Lithium plating requires the anode potential driven below 0 V vs Li/Li+, which occurs at high charge current, low temperature, or fast charge — not during a milliamp-level trickle float at full charge. Cathode-side oxidative electrolyte decomposition has an onset around 4.3+ V vs Li/Li+, while LFP's redox plateau is ~3.4 V vs Li/Li+, so a cell held at 3.45 V is far from oxidation onset; the mechanism does not operate in this range. The actual degradation pathway for high-SoC float is calendar aging via SEI growth and lithium-inventory loss, temperature-accelerated. Battery University confirms high-SoC dwell as the dominant stressor (100% SoC at 25C retains ~80% after one year vs ~96% at 40% SoC) and invokes neither plating nor oxidation. The claim imports NMC/LCO high-voltage failure language into a regime where it is not physical.

5. OCV-FLATNESS ARGUMENT INVERTED AND MISAPPLIED. LFP's flat plateau is ~3.0-3.3 V (Wikipedia: working voltage 3.0-3.3 V). The entire 3.35-3.45 V float window sits ABOVE the plateau on the steep upper knee, so float never operates in the flat region the argument invokes. Because the knee is steep, every float voltage in 3.35-3.45 V parks the cell at essentially 100% SoC and the SoC difference between 3.40 and 3.45 V is negligible, not "large." The claim's own "~95-100% SoC" figure concedes this and then contradicts it. The correct inference is the reverse: only lowering float into the top of the plateau (3.30-3.35 V) produces a meaningful SoC reduction — which is exactly why the practitioner source recommends that range.

6. HAZARD MISIDENTIFIED; ARITHMETIC CORRECT BUT CONCLUSION OVERSTATED. Re-derived: 13.8 V / 4S = 3.450 V/cell exactly, and 3.65 V/cell x 4 = 14.6 V, so the stated conversions check out. But 13.8 V float is not "definitely" harmful: Victron specifies 14.2 V absorption / 13.5 V float for its 12.8 V LFP (3.550 / 3.375 V/cell) and many LFP drop-ins list 13.6-13.8 V float, so 13.8 V is modestly high, not out of bounds. Meanwhile the claim omits the mechanisms that actually destroy LFP on a legacy AGM charger: (a) periodic equalization/boost at 14.4-15.5 V = 3.600-3.875 V/cell, at or beyond the 3.65 V termination — far more damaging than a 13.8 V float; (b) negative temperature compensation (~-3 to -5 mV/C/cell) raising voltage in cold; (c) AGM chargers will charge below 0 C, whereas Victron restricts LFP charging to +5 to +50 C — sub-freezing charging is the dominant LFP retrofit failure mode and is where lithium plating genuinely occurs. The claim names plating but attaches it to the wrong cause, and by fixating on float voltage it directs the engineer away from the equalization and cold-charge lockout requirements that actually belong in the spec.

corrected.original: Deliberately floating below 100% SoC is well-established engineering practice in general, but I could NOT confirm that major commercial UPS vendors do it — they appear to prioritise guaranteed runtime and instead manage the problem via chemistry choice and temperature control.
corrected.corrected:
Holding lithium cells below full charge is well established in two regimes that are NOT UPS float: charge caps on daily-cycling devices (EV charge limits, Apple/Dell ~80% settings) and dormant-storage SoC (storage mode; IATA's <=30% limit, which applies to specific UN numbers and packing instructions — UN3480 under PI 965, with recent DGR editions extending toward UN3481 packed-with-equipment — and is a thermal-runaway safety rule, not an aging rule). Neither is continuous standby float.

For lithium UPS specifically I found no primary vendor document stating a sub-100% SoC float setpoint — but this is an untested result, not a negative one: the two most relevant sources were unreachable (Schneider/APC FA362721 returned HTTP 403; Eaton's lithium FAQ timed out), and vendors specify float *voltage*, not float *SoC*, so a search for a stated SoC setpoint can return a false negative on a practice that is real. An LFP float on the flat plateau (~3.375-3.40 V/cell) is already well under 100% SoC without any document saying so. Claims that "90% SoC float is established data-centre practice" do trace to SEO content, not vendor documentation — that part holds.

On the physics: dwelling at 100% SoC at elevated temperature is clearly the worst case (Battery University BU-808 Table 3, Li-cobalt: 96% retained after 1 year at 40% charge/25C vs 80% at 100% charge/25C). But that table has no intermediate SoC points and does not establish a knee near 80%, and it is not LFP data. LFP calendar aging shows weaker and possibly non-monotonic SoC dependence, with temperature the dominant term. For an LFP appliance UPS, temperature control is the higher-value lever and the SoC benefit is smaller than NMC/LCO figures suggest.

Before specifying a sub-100% float setpoint, resolve the open question in the right units: obtain the BMS/charger float *voltage* from the candidate vendor and convert to SoC, rather than asking whether a vendor publishes an SoC number.
corrected.why:
The bottom-line negative finding survives — I independently searched for a UPS vendor documenting a deliberate sub-100% SoC hold and found only SEO content plus Eaton datasheets that mention the BMS reporting SoC without stating a setpoint. But the claim is imprecise in five ways that would mislead an engineer ordering parts.

(a) Methodology: the two most load-bearing primary sources were unreachable, not read-and-found-silent. Schneider/APC FA362721 returned HTTP 403 on both apc.com and se.com; Eaton's lithium FAQ timed out. "Absence of confirming primary source is itself the finding" is not sound when the source was blocked rather than checked. That is untested, not negative evidence.

(b) Wrong unit — likely false negative. Vendors specify float *voltage*, not float *SoC*. An LFP standby float on the flat plateau (~3.375-3.40 V/cell) already sits well below 100% SoC without any document using the phrase "state of charge." The only search hits on this topic were about float voltage settings. Searching for a stated SoC setpoint can therefore miss a practice that is in fact routine, expressed in different units.

(c) Conflation of three regimes. EV/laptop charge caps are duty-cycle management for daily-cycling devices; IATA 30% and "storage mode" are dormant-storage rules; UPS float is continuous standby readiness. Only the third is what the spec concerns, and it is the one with no support. The cited precedents do not transfer.

(d) The "~80% knee" is not supported by the source relied on. Battery University BU-808 Table 3, which I did verify (96% retained after 1 yr at 40% charge/25C vs 80% at 100% charge/25C), compares only 40% and 100% — no intermediate points, so it cannot establish a knee at 80%, and it is Li-cobalt data. For LFP, the chemistry the detail contemplates, calendar-aging SoC dependence is weaker and reported in the literature as potentially non-monotonic (tied to graphite staging plateaus), with temperature dominating. "The physics case is uncontroversial" overstates it for the specific chemistry and the specific ~80% threshold.

(e) The IATA claim is a regulatory overstatement and a motive mismatch. The 30% limit attaches to specific UN numbers and packing instructions (UN3480 under PI 965, with recent DGR editions extending toward UN3481 packed-with-equipment), not to "air freight" generally; lithium-metal UN3090/3091 is a separate regime. It is also a thermal-runaway-propagation safety rule, not a calendar-aging rule, so it is not evidence for a longevity setpoint.

Also: Eaton ABM addresses lead-acid grid corrosion, a different failure mechanism from lithium SEI growth, so it does not support the lithium argument even as analogy.

corrected.original: RECOMMENDATION: use LFP, floated at ~3.35-3.40 V/cell, sized with derating headroom. For this duty cycle the decision is not close.
corrected.corrected:
RECOMMENDATION: use LFP, charged to a reduced ceiling with no sustained float, sized with derating headroom. The conclusion is sound; the supporting numbers below replace the original ones, several of which were wrong.

(1) Calendar aging dominates this duty cycle and favors LFP. Generic Li-ion reference data (Battery University BU-808 Table 3) shows ~35% capacity loss in one year at 40C/100% SoC versus ~15% at 40C/40% SoC. This table is uncited and undated — treat it as directional, not as an NMC measurement, and obtain calendar-aging data from the actual cell vendor's datasheet before committing.

(2) The environment is uncontrolled and reaches 40C, where aging compounds via Arrhenius with no thermal management available.

(3) LFP is the safer cathode for a wall-mounted enclosure in an occupied venue. Per Battery University BU-205, thermal runaway onset is ~270C for LFP versus ~210C for NMC (LCO and NCA are ~150C — do NOT group NMC with LCO). LFP also shows lower peak temperature and heating rate, and its phosphate cathode is markedly more thermally stable, with far less oxygen release than layered oxides — it is not literally non-oxygen-releasing. Onset temperature alone does not determine whether a pack propagates; propagation depends on cell format, spacing, SoC, venting, and enclosure design, so do not represent this as a guaranteed smoke-vs-fire outcome in any insurance or liability filing.

(4) Cost favors LFP outright — LFP is cheaper per kWh than NMC (~6% by one published comparison, typically more in cell markets) with roughly 67% greater cycle life. There is no cost penalty to offset. Energy density is a genuine LFP disadvantage that does NOT disappear: LFP is 95-172 Wh/kg (up to ~205 latest gen) versus 300+ Wh/kg for the best NMC. Derating applies to both chemistries, so it does not close the gap; accept the volume/mass penalty on its merits, justified by aging and safety.

Design specifics: charge to ~3.45-3.50 V/cell, then stop — do not hold a continuous float; never terminate at 3.65 V and sit there. If a maintenance voltage is unavoidable, keep it at 3.30-3.35 V/cell (13.2-13.4 V on 4S), not 3.40. Do NOT gate recharge hysteresis on OCV: LFP's plateau spans ~3.29-3.33 V across roughly 20-80% SoC, so millivolt-level sense error maps to tens of percent of charge. Use coulomb counting and re-top at roughly 70-80% SoC so the pack retains usable backup runtime at all times; a 3.20 V/cell trip point is ~10-20% SoC and would leave the unit effectively empty when mains fails. Derate pack capacity 30-40% at design time so end-of-life still meets runtime. Mandatory: BMS charge lockout below 0C (lithium plating) and above ~45C — the environment is uncontrolled at both ends, not just the high end. Place cells on the coolest side of the enclosure, thermally isolated from the PSU.

Not orderable as written: this specifies no load, runtime target, pack voltage, capacity, cell count, or cell format. Those must be fixed before any parts order, since the derating and BOM-delta claims are meaningless without them.
corrected.why:
The top-line recommendation (LFP, floated low, derated) is almost certainly correct for this duty cycle, but nearly every quantitative support is wrong, backwards, or internally inconsistent, and two design specifics are outright defects. Per the instruction to refute when substantially right but imprecise, this fails.

(1) Thermal runaway numbers are wrong. Battery University BU-205 gives LFP 270C, NMC 210C, LCO 150C, NCA 150C. The claim states LFP ~195C and groups "LCO/NMC" at ~149C. This understates LFP by 75C and, materially, assigns NMC a figure 60C below the standard reference by conflating it with cobalt oxide. 149C = 300F, suggesting a Fahrenheit round-trip of the 150C/302F LCO value rather than a datasheet source. Directionally LFP still wins (270 vs 210), so the conclusion survives, but the cited pair would not withstand a safety or insurance review — the exact use proposed for it.

(2) Cost is backwards. The claim concedes cell cost as an anti-LFP argument that "largely evaporates." LFP is cheaper per kWh than NMC (Wikipedia LFP article: ~6% lower per kWh plus ~67% more cycles; cell-market spreads are typically wider). There is no cost penalty to evaporate. Also, "cell BOM delta is a few dollars" is unverifiable because pack size, cell count, load, and runtime target are never specified.

(3) The energy-density argument double-counts derating. LFP is 95-172 Wh/kg (up to ~205 latest gen) vs NMC 300+ Wh/kg best variants. The claim closes this by derating NMC 27-35%, then the design specifics separately derate the LFP pack 30-40%. Applying the same derating to both leaves NMC's density advantage essentially intact. The argument works only by charging the penalty to one chemistry.

(4) Design defect: "re-top only below ~3.20 V/cell OCV" is roughly 10-20% SoC on LFP. A standby backup pack that waits until it is 80-90% depleted before recharging defeats the product's purpose. Compounding this, LFP's plateau is ~3.29-3.33 V across roughly 20-80% SoC, so +/-10 mV of sense error spans tens of percent of charge; OCV is the worst possible basis for a hysteresis trip point on this chemistry. Requires coulomb counting.

(5) Design defect: no low-temperature charge lockout. The spec calls the environment uncontrolled but bounds only the high side (40C). Charging LFP below 0C plates lithium — a mandatory BMS requirement for an uncontrolled wall-mounted enclosure, absent from a document engineers will order parts against.

(6) Minor overclaims: "non-oxygen-releasing cathode" overstates the source (LFP has higher decomposition temperatures; layered oxides release oxygen on heating — LFP is far more stable, not inert). "The difference between a smoke event and a propagating fire" is a categorical outcome claim an onset-temperature delta cannot support; propagation depends on cell format, spacing, SoC, venting, and enclosure design. Presented as a liability/insurance argument, this is stated more confidently than sources allow.

(7) Internal inconsistency: the claim specifies a float band (3.35-3.40 V/cell) while also saying the charger should stop and let the pack rest rather than float. 3.40 V/cell held continuously is near the top of the LFP curve — high SoC, which argument (1) says to avoid. Common long-life standby guidance is lower (~3.30-3.35 V/cell, i.e. 13.2-13.4 V on a 4S 12 V pack).

Argument (1)'s calendar-aging figure is the one item that checks out: BU-808 Table 3 gives 65% capacity remaining after 1 year at 40C/100% charge (=35% loss/yr), supporting "tens of %/yr." However that table is uncited, undated, and carries the caveat "Not all Li-ion systems behave the same" — it is generic reference material, not a measured NMC result, and should not be presented as one.

corrected.original: WHAT TO MEASURE — thermal: log actual cell-surface temperature in the worst real installation across a full summer, not enclosure ambient and not a spot check.
corrected.corrected:
WHAT TO MEASURE — thermal: log actual cell-can surface temperature in the worst real installation, not enclosure ambient and not a spot check.

Sensor: 1%-tolerance NTC or PT1000 Class A (±0.3–0.5C over 0–60C), bonded to a cell can and electrically isolated from it — cans typically sit at a terminal potential, so a grounded-junction thermocouple creates a galvanic path into the logger. Do not use type-K: Class 2 (±2.2C) implies ±15% error in predicted degradation rate at 45C, which is untenable for an argument premised on 10C mattering ~2x. Log at 5-minute intervals.

Primary output: the Arrhenius rate-weighted effective temperature, T_eff, defined by exp(-Ea/(R·T_eff)) = time-average of exp(-Ea/(R·T(t))). This — not the 95th percentile — is the number that sets life. On a representative plant-room profile, P95 overstates the degradation rate by ~1.9x while the simple mean is only ~1.14x low; P95 is the worse of the two errors. Record peak separately, but use it only to check safety and datasheet limits, never to predict life.

Temperature sensitivity: state the assumed activation energy explicitly and cite it, because the functional form alone determines nothing. At Ea = 55 kJ/mol the 40C→50C rate ratio is 1.92x; the plausible calendar-aging range gives 1.27x (20 kJ/mol) to 2.59x (80 kJ/mol). Because SEI-limited calendar fade goes as k(T)·sqrt(t), a 2x rate constant quarters the time to a given fade threshold — quote life impact and rate impact separately and never interchangeably.

Delta-T transfer: characterize the external-ambient-to-cell rise as a function of PSU/charger dissipation state (float versus post-outage recharge differ substantially), ventilation condition, and solar gain — not as a single constant. Report it as a distribution with design margin. This characterization takes weeks, not a season; convolve it with TMY/ASHRAE data for the target sites to synthesize annual cell-temperature profiles, then use a full hot season of logging to validate that model rather than as the sole source. This removes a months-long gate on the go/no-go decision.

Scope: cell temperature is a first-order driver of viability, but it is not the only one. Float SOC / charge-termination voltage exerts a comparable influence on calendar aging and, unlike plant-room ambient, is under design control — specify and measure it alongside temperature.
corrected.why:
The core directive (log cell-can temperature in the worst real installation, not enclosure ambient, not a spot check) is sound. But four specifics are wrong or unsupportable at spec grade.

(1) WRONG SUMMARY STATISTIC. Arrhenius damage is an integral of rate over time, so the life-determining number is the rate-weighted effective temperature, not P95. On a plausible plant-room annual profile (2400h@25C, 2000h@30C, 1800h@35C, 1400h@40C, 800h@45C, 300h@50C, 60h@55C; Ea=55 kJ/mol): mean 33.5C, P95 45.0C, peak 55C, Arrhenius-effective 35.3C.
