P95 overstates the degradation rate by 1.92x — an error the same size as the entire 40-vs-50C effect the section exists to capture — while the explicitly-rejected mean is only 1.14x off. The prescription moves the estimate further from the truth than the practice it condemns. Peak is relevant only to safety/datasheet limits, not to life.

(2) THE "2x" IS AN UNSTATED INPUT PRESENTED AS A DERIVATION. Re-deriving exp((Ea/R)(1/313.15 - 1/323.15)): the ratio is 1.268 at Ea=20 kJ/mol, 1.609 at 40, 1.812 at 50, 2.040 at 60, 2.588 at 80. Exactly 2x requires Ea = 58.3 kJ/mol. "Because degradation is Arrhenius" gives the functional form only; the factor depends wholly on an activation energy the claim never states. (Caveat: WebSearch budget was exhausted this session, so the 20-80 kJ/mol literature range is background knowledge, not verified here — the spec should cite Ea from its own referenced sources.)

(3) RATE vs LIFE CONFLATION. Calendar fade is SEI-limited, fade = k(T)*sqrt(t). A 2x k does not mean 2x worse life — time to a fixed fade threshold falls 4x. "2x worse" is undefined and, read as life, understates by 2x.

(4) SENSOR UNFIT AND UNSPECIFIED. Type-K Class 2 (±2.2C) implies ±15% error in predicted rate at 45C with Ea=55 kJ/mol; Class 1 (±1.5C) implies ±10%. An argument premised on 10C mattering 2x cannot be instrumented with a ±2C sensor. Also, a grounded-junction thermocouple bonded to a can that sits at a terminal potential creates a galvanic path into the logger — isolation is mandatory and unmentioned.

Additional overreach: delta-T is treated as a site-transferable constant, but natural-convection rise scales roughly with dissipated power (float vs post-outage recharge differ greatly) plus ventilation, mounting and solar gain, so it transfers only if characterized per dissipation state. "This single number determines whether the design is viable at all" ignores float SOC/voltage, a comparable calendar-aging lever that, unlike plant-room ambient, is under design control. Finally, gating go/no-go on a full hot season imposes a months-long schedule hit that is avoidable: delta-T versus dissipation is a property of the box measurable in weeks, which can be convolved with TMY/ASHRAE data to synthesize the annual profile, with the summer log validating the model rather than being the sole source.

corrected.original: WHAT TO MEASURE — electrical: verify the actual voltage at the cell terminals under production firmware across temperature, and log residual float current as a direct proxy for parasitic side reactions.
corrected.corrected:
WHAT TO MEASURE — electrical: verify the actual voltage at the cell terminals under production firmware across temperature, using 4-wire/Kelvin sensing at the cell tabs rather than at the charger output. Measure at 0 C, 25 C, and 45 C (JEITA zone boundaries), at the pack's real charge-termination state.

Rationale (corrected): the voltage the charger regulates to is not necessarily the voltage at the cell. The dominant overvoltage mechanisms are (a) charger reference and regulation tolerance — a typical +/-0.5% spec on a 4.20 V target is +/-21 mV, and +/-1% is +/-42 mV, so "tens of millivolts above target" is real and comes from tolerance stack-up, not IR drop; (b) sense-point placement, if the feedback node sits across a drop; and (c) misapplied temperature compensation. Note that IR drop biases the cell BELOW the setpoint while current flows and is negligible (nanovolts) at float, so it is not an overvoltage mechanism. Confirm the charger implements JEITA-style compensation (charge voltage REDUCED in cold and hot zones, e.g. ~4.10 V below 10 C to avoid lithium plating) and explicitly verify that no lead-acid-style negative tempco — which would RAISE voltage when cold — has been inherited from a multi-chemistry charger part. Treat that as a part-selection check to confirm, not an assumed default.

On float current: do NOT specify it as production telemetry or as a direct proxy for side reactions. Two independent reasons.

(1) Precision. Measured steady-state float currents are 2-25 uA on 1.1-3.2 Ah cells (C/86,000 to C/137,500) — 20-250 nV across a 10 mOhm shunt, roughly 1e2-1e4 below the ~10-20 uV input offset of standard production fuel-gauge front ends. Resolving this requires lab-grade instrumentation (the source used an Arbin LBTa2030 with a dedicated +/-1 mA range in a temperature chamber) or a purpose-built high-precision coulometry path. Budget that hardware explicitly if the measurement is wanted; a stock coulomb counter cannot do it.

(2) Interpretation. Float current is an indirect, chemistry- and SOC-dependent indicator, not a direct measure of irreversible side-reaction rate. Azzam et al. (Batteries 2024, 10(1), 3) derive I_float/I_SEI = |k_anode|/(|k_anode|+|k_cathode|), which spans 2% to 98% depending on electrode voltage slopes, and report empirically "only a part correlation ... and for some test cases strong deviations," with float current systematically under-reading the capacity loss rate. Above roughly 4.0-4.2 V the voltage-slippery explanation weakens further, with shuttle reactions or cathode lithiation suspected — a shuttle raises float current with no proportional capacity loss. Any use of float current therefore requires per-chemistry calibration against dU/dQ electrode slopes plus correlation to conventional check-ups; it does not replace capacity testing. Also allow a ~60-day settling period, since reversible anode-overhang effects dominate early data.

Scope caveat on the source: it is a lab study of three 18650 types (LFP/NCA/NMC) with n=1 per test condition, run entirely at 30 C — it contains no temperature-dependent float-current data (that section was deferred to a separate publication), so it cannot be cited in support of the across-temperature requirement. Separately, float/potentiostatic hold is an accelerated aging TEST method, not a recommended Li-ion operating mode; the same paper shows higher float voltage yields greater capacity loss and resistance rise. If the product continuously floats the cell, treat that as a design defect to fix rather than a signal to trend. Safety note: the authors observed a continuous 10-20 mA soft short on reaching 60 C, so bound any elevated-temperature float testing accordingly.
corrected.why:
The DOI is genuine and correctly cited (Azzam, Endisch & Lewerenz, "Evaluating the Aging-Induced Voltage Slippery as Cause for Float Currents of Lithium-ion Cells," Batteries 2024, 10(1), 3; published 21 Dec 2023). Verified via Crossref and Semantic Scholar, full text retrieved from the MDPI CDN (pages 1-10 of 27, including abstract, methods, model derivation, and the correlation results). But the claim misrepresents it and contains independent physics and feasibility errors.

1. SOURCE CONTRADICTS "DIRECT PROXY." The paper's purpose is to test, not assert, that float current reports side reactions. Its Eq. (1), I_recharge/I_SEI_growth = |k_anode|/(|k_anode|+|k_cathode|), was re-derived against its own Figure 3: for an identical 0.200 A SEI growth rate the float current is 0.100 A (equal slopes), 0.196 A (steep anode), or 0.004 A (steep cathode) — i.e. 2% to 98% of the true side-reaction rate, set by electrode slope ratio, which varies with chemistry and SOC. The paper states the float current "is not equal to the capacity loss rate due to SEI growth in all cases." Section 3.2 concludes "only a part correlation between steady-state float current and capacity loss rate and for some test cases strong deviations," and "all capacity loss rates are equal or higher than the measured float currents" — float current systematically UNDER-reads degradation. The abstract further says the theory's "explanatory power begins to diminish at higher voltage ranges," with a shuttle reaction or cathode lithiation as unidentified additional contributors — a shuttle current raises float current with no proportional capacity loss, breaking the proxy in the opposite direction.

2. MEASUREMENT INFEASIBLE AS SPECIFIED. Figure 7 gives real float currents of 2-25 uA on 1.1-3.2 Ah cells (C/86,000 to C/137,500). On a 10 mOhm shunt that is 20-250 nV, roughly 1e2-1e4 below the ~10-20 uV input offset of standard production coulomb-counter/fuel-gauge front ends. The authors used an Arbin LBTa2030 lab cycler with a dedicated +/-1 mA low-current range in an ACS DY110 chamber. "Log residual float current" under production firmware is an order-of-magnitude hardware error.

3. WRONG MECHANISM, WRONG SIGN (IR drop). At true float, 25 uA through 100 mOhm is ~2500 nV — negligible. Under charge current, IR drop holds the cell BELOW the regulation setpoint, never above. The genuine "tens of millivolts above target" mechanism is charger reference/regulation tolerance (+/-0.5% of 4.20 V = +/-21 mV; +/-1% = +/-42 mV) plus sense-point placement and tempco error. The magnitude is right; the attributed cause is wrong.

4. TEMPCO CLAIM UNSUPPORTED AND INVERTED. Standard Li-ion charger practice is JEITA, which REDUCES charge voltage in cold zones (typically ~4.10 V below 10 C) specifically to avoid lithium plating — the opposite of a lead-acid negative tempco raising float voltage when cold. "Many chargers still carry" this is an unsourced generalization presented as fact; it is at most a specific misapplication risk in multi-chemistry designs.

5. CITATION DOES NOT COVER TEMPERATURE. All float testing was at 30 C. The paper states the temperature-variation section "is greyed out, because there were no check-ups performed, and the scope of the temperature section is to be published separately." The source therefore supports none of the 0/25/45 C requirement.

6. FLOAT IS A LAB METHOD, NOT A PRODUCT MODE. Potentiostatic hold is a deliberate accelerated calendar-aging test. The paper's Figures 4-6 show higher float voltage produces greater capacity loss and resistance rise. Continuously floating Li-ion in a product is an aging accelerant; standard design is terminate-and-rest with a recharge threshold. If a product floats, that is the defect, not the telemetry opportunity.

7. OVERSTATED EARLINESS AND WEAK STATISTICS. The paper discards the first 60 days because reversible anode-overhang effects dominate, so there is a ~60-day settling floor before interpretation — undercutting "far earlier than capacity tests." Only one cell per test condition was run; the authors twice concede results "cannot be explained as there is only one cell per test condition."

8. SAFETY ITEM OMITTED. The paper reports that on reaching 60 C a SAN cell developed a continuous 10-20 mA soft short, forcing termination — relevant if elevated-temperature float testing is specified.

The first half of the claim (measure actual voltage at the cell terminals, under production firmware, across temperature) is sound and standard practice; the justification and the entire float-current half require correction.

corrected.original: WHAT TO MEASURE — validation: run an accelerated calendar-aging test at your actual float setpoint, at three temperatures, and extrapolate with Arrhenius plus square-root-of-time.
corrected.corrected:
WHAT TO MEASURE — validation: run a multi-temperature, multi-voltage calendar-aging test under your actual float condition and fit a time law you have verified against your own data rather than assuming one.

DETAIL: Use the exact production part. Cap the hottest oven at 60 C — do not run 70 C. Both cited studies stopped at 50 C (Keil 2016) and 60 C (Werner 2021); at 60 C Werner's cells reached end-of-life within 26 weeks and a 60 C constant-voltage hold at full charge collapsed in six weeks. 70 C also exceeds the datasheet storage limit of most commercial cells, so above ~60 C you are measuring electrolyte decomposition and gassing, not the SEI-growth mechanism that governs field life, and the Arrhenius fit is corrupted rather than accelerated.

Matrix: 40 / 50 / 60 C, at a minimum four float setpoints spanning your candidate range (not two). Keil found calendar fade is stepwise in SoC — plateau regions spanning 20-30% SoC where fade is essentially identical, set by graphite staging transitions — and Werner found large sensitivity at 100% SoC but little below 80%. Two voltage points can sit inside one plateau and show a spurious null, or straddle a step and over-credit a small reduction. Budget 5+ cells per condition; with ~12-20 conditions that is 60-100 cells, not 15-20.

Sampling: log- or sqrt-spaced check-ups (roughly 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 20, 30, 44 weeks), because the curvature is concentrated in the first weeks. Bring cells to a common 25 C reference for every capacity and DCIR measurement, and record the self-discharge / OCV-to-SoC correction and anode-overhang relaxation effects — without these the data are not interpretable.

Fitting: do not assume sqrt(t). Werner et al. — the paper cited here — explicitly reject it: "Instead of the commonly applied square root of the time function, our results are in excellent agreement with an exponential function," and warn that a square-root shape "underestimates aging in the further process, especially when it is extrapolated." Their model is a saturating exponential plus a linear term, with two separate activation energies (one for the exponential coefficients, a different one for the linear term). Fit at least three candidate forms — exponential-plus-linear, free-exponent power law t^n with n fitted, and sqrt(t) — and report the spread between their 10-year projections as your real uncertainty band. That model-form spread, not cell-to-cell scatter, is the dominant error term. The sqrt(t) fit will read optimistic; treat it as a lower bound on fade, not a central estimate.

Duration: 40 C and 50 C arms need 18-24 months to be useful — Werner ran ~100 weeks at those temperatures — because a 4-6 month window sits entirely in the early curved regime and gives no read on the linear long-term term that dominates 5- and 10-year retention. Arithmetic: at Ea = 50 kJ/mol, six months at 60 C equals only ~4.2 years at 25 C (AF = 8.3x), and six months at 40 C equals ~1.3 years (AF = 2.6x). A genuine 10-year projection from a 6-month test would require AF = 20, i.e. ~77 C, which is exactly the invalid regime. So: gate the enclosure freeze on a 6-9 month interim read (which supports a defensible 3-5 year projection with wide bands), and let the low-temperature arms run to 18-24 months to confirm the 10-year number. Add procurement, formation and BoL characterization ahead of that — realistically 8-10 months to first usable interim data.

Finally, note that float (constant-voltage hold) is a harsher and different stress than the open-circuit fixed-SoC storage used in both cited papers' main matrices; Werner observed that under open circuit, self-discharge lowers SoC and thereby limits degradation. Testing under float is correct for a float product, but you must fit your own coefficients — the published constants do not transfer.

Sources: Keil, Schuster, Wilhelm, Travi, Hauser, Karl & Jossen, J. Electrochem. Soc. 163(9) A1872 (2016), https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1149/2.0411609jes ; Werner, Paarmann & Wetzel, Batteries 2021, 7(2), 28, https://www.mdpi.com/2313-0105/7/2/28
corrected.why:
The two DOIs are real and correctly identified — Keil, Schuster, Wilhelm, Travi, Hauser, Karl & Jossen, "Calendar Aging of Lithium-Ion Batteries I. Impact of the Graphite Anode on Capacity Fade," J. Electrochem. Soc. 163(9) A1872 (2016), and Werner, Paarmann & Wetzel, "Calendar Aging of Li-Ion Cells — Experimental Investigation and Empirical Correlation," Batteries 2021, 7(2), 28. But the prescription attributed to them is contradicted by both, and every error runs in the optimistic direction.

1. THE sqrt(t) LAW IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT THE SECOND SOURCE FOUND. The claim cites Werner et al. as methodology for "an approximately sqrt(t) law." That paper's headline result, verbatim from its abstract: "Instead of the commonly applied square root of the time function, our results are in excellent agreement with an exponential function." Their fitted model (Eqs. 4-5) is a saturating exponential PLUS a linear term. They state explicitly that a square-root shape "has the disadvantage of overestimating the capacity fade at the beginning of aging, intersects the actual curve and underestimates aging in the further process, especially when it is extrapolated." That is precisely the failure mode this test plan would induce: fit sqrt(t) to 4-6 months, project 10 years, and systematically under-predict end-of-life fade. In a hardware spec this is a non-conservative error.

2. THE sqrt(t) BASIS DOES NOT EXTEND TO DCIR AT ALL. The claim measures capacity and DC internal resistance and fits one law to both. Werner et al. note the parabolic SEI law traces to Peled, who offered it as a "first approximation only," and that for polarization-resistance rise "the theoretical basis is lacking."

3. NEITHER SOURCE WENT TO 70 C, AND 70 C IS WHERE ARRHENIUS BREAKS. Keil used 25/40/50 C. Werner used 40/50/60 C. At 60 C Werner had to terminate at 26 weeks because cells had already hit end-of-life, and the constant-voltage arm at 60 C / 100% SoC showed "a total collapse of the cell within only six weeks." 70 C also exceeds the datasheet storage limit of essentially every commercial cell (typically 45-60 C), so those cells are out of spec and are degrading by mechanisms (electrolyte decomposition, gassing, transition-metal dissolution) that do not share the field-temperature activation energy. That arm corrupts the Arrhenius fit rather than anchoring it.

4. THE ARITHMETIC FORCES THE BAD ARM. With Ea = 50 kJ/mol, the 60 C to 25 C acceleration factor is exp[(50000/8.314)(1/298.15 - 1/333.15)] = exp(2.12) = 8.3x, so 6 months at 60 C buys about 4.2 equivalent years — not 10. Reaching 10 years from a 6-month test needs AF = 20, which requires 1/T = 0.0033539 - 3.0/6014, i.e. T = 350 K = 77 C. So the stated 4-6 month budget is only compatible with a 10-year projection if you push into the regime where the extrapolation is invalid. Conversely the 40 C arm gives AF = 2.6x, i.e. ~1.3 equivalent years in six months — it cannot support a 10-year claim and exists only to test Arrhenius linearity, which needs far longer to be useful (Werner's 40 C and 50 C arms ran about 100 weeks).

5. FLOAT IS A DIFFERENT AND HARSHER STRESS THAN THE CITED PROTOCOL. Both papers' main matrices are open-circuit storage at fixed SoC. Werner ran CV/float as a two-cell check at one condition only, and observed that under open circuit, self-discharge drops the SoC and thereby "prevents the cell from degrading even stronger." Continuous float holds the cell pinned at the worst SoC indefinitely. Testing at float is the right choice for a float application, but the cited papers' constants and time-law do not transfer to it, and the claim presents them as if they do.

6. A TWO-POINT VOLTAGE ARM CANNOT "PRICE THE SoC-VERSUS-LIFE TRADE QUANTITATIVELY." Keil's central finding is that "calendar aging does not increase steadily with the SoC. Instead, plateau regions, covering SoC intervals of more than 20%-30% of the cell capacity, are observed wherein the capacity fade is similar," driven by graphite staging transitions. Werner found large impact at 100% SoC but "the influence is small below 80%." Two voltage points can land inside one plateau (falsely showing no benefit) or straddle a step (over-crediting a small cut). The relationship is stepwise, not a smooth curve you can interpolate.

7. STATISTICS AND SAMPLING. 15-20 cells across 3 temperatures plus a parallel reduced-voltage arm is 4-6 conditions, i.e. 3-5 cells each — that does not yield meaningful confidence intervals on a 10-year extrapolation, and in any case the dominant uncertainty is model-form uncertainty (sqrt vs exponential-plus-linear vs modified power law), which no cell count reduces. Monthly check-ups are also mis-spaced: curvature is concentrated in the first weeks, so sampling should be log- or sqrt-spaced. The plan also omits the self-discharge and OCV-to-SoC correction and the anode-overhang relaxation effects that Werner had to handle to make the data interpretable, and omits that each check-up is itself a cycle plus a thermal excursion.

8. MINOR TERMINOLOGY: "Arrhenius temperature prefactor" is inverted. Arrhenius describes the exponential temperature dependence of the rate constant; the prefactor A is the temperature-independent term. Werner also required TWO activation energies (Ea,alphabeta for the exponential term, a different Ea,gamma for the linear term), so "Arrhenius plus sqrt(t)" is under-specified as a fitting recipe.

The strategic advice — run a multi-temperature, multi-SoC accelerated calendar test on the exact production part, include a reduced-voltage arm, start before freezing the enclosure — is sound and worth keeping. The specific parameters are not orderable as written.

corrected.original: WHAT TO MEASURE — product-level: define the actual Wh holdup requirement and build in self-test, because a silently dead standby battery is the real field failure mode.
corrected.corrected:
WHAT TO MEASURE — product-level: define the Wh holdup requirement and build in self-test, because a silently dead standby battery is the real field failure mode.

(1) Nail the runtime requirement in watt-hours before arguing chemistry. At ~15 Wh the LFP volumetric penalty is a rounding error and the density debate is moot. Note that 15 Wh at LFP's 3.2 V nominal is ~4.7 Ah, and small-format LFP cells are less widely available than LCO/NMC in coin/pouch/small-prismatic formats — confirm sourcing before committing to chemistry.

(2) Implement a periodic automated capacity self-test (controlled partial discharge, logged) and report SoH out of the box. LFP's flat mid-range OCV plateau (~3.2-3.3 V) makes resting-voltage SoC estimation unreliable between roughly 15% and 90% SoC, so coulomb counting with periodic discharge recalibration is mandatory rather than optional. The test must also exercise the load-transfer path, not just capacity — a healthy cell behind a failed transfer FET still fails in the field. Set the interval from the applicable occupancy/life-safety code rather than by default: if this function is life-safety, standby-power regimes conventionally require monthly functional plus annual full-duration testing, which is stricter than quarterly.

(3) Certification path — scale it correctly. At ~15 Wh (0.015 kWh) this is NOT an energy storage system under fire code. NFPA 855's applicability floor is 1 kWh and IFC Table 1207.1.1 exempts lithium ESS up to 20 kWh, so the device sits 65x to 1,300x below the trigger. UL 9540A large-scale fire propagation testing, UL 9540, UL 1973, and IEC 62619 all address installations orders of magnitude larger and do not apply. (IEC 62619 is also cell/battery level, not system level, and UL 1973 is the system-level standard — they are not interchangeable.) The actual path is:
  - Cell level: UL 1642 component recognition and/or IEC 62133-2 from the cell vendor. Note IEC 62133-2 is scoped to portable applications — ask for it because it is the certificate small-format cell vendors hold, not because the device is wall-mounted.
  - Product level: the end-product standard governs — UL/IEC 62368-1 for ICT/AV equipment, or whichever end-product standard matches the device's function, which is where the battery's charging, protection, and enclosure requirements actually land.
  - Shipping: UN 38.3 transport testing is mandatory for any lithium battery at any capacity. This is the one regulatory gate that certainly applies.
  - Only if the design later grows past ~1 kWh should NFPA 855, UL 9540, UL 1973, and possibly UL 9540A re-enter scope.
At this scale the certification path is chemistry-neutral and does not favor LFP. If LFP is chosen, justify it on float-life, thermal margin, and abuse tolerance — not on a fire-code constraint that does not trigger.
corrected.why:
Items (1) and (2) are sound; item (3) is materially wrong and internally contradicts item (1).

VERIFIED CORRECT:
- UL 1973 is system-level for stationary storage (confirmed scope 1.1: "battery systems... for use as energy storage for stationary applications such as for PV, wind turbine storage or for UPS").
- UL 9540A is correctly described as a test method rather than a listing standard; UL's own page confirms it applies when a design "exceed[s] the limits set by NFPA 855."
- UL 1642 is cell-level (covers primary and secondary lithium cells as component power sources).
- Item (1)'s "size the Wh before arguing chemistry" is correct methodology, and at 15 Wh the LFP volumetric penalty genuinely is negligible.
- Item (2)'s core physics is right: LFP's OCV plateau (~3.2-3.3 V across the mid-SoC range) makes resting-voltage SoC estimation unreliable, so coulomb counting with periodic full/deep-discharge recalibration is the correct approach, and a silently degraded standby battery is a genuine and common field failure mode.

REFUTED — five defects, one of them disqualifying:

1. SCALE CATEGORY ERROR (disqualifying). Item (1) posits ~15 Wh; item (3) then prescribes the certification path for grid-scale energy storage systems. IFC Table 1207.1.1 exempts lithium ESS up to 20 kWh, and NFPA 855's applicability floor is 1 kWh. A 15 Wh (0.015 kWh) holdup battery sits 65x to 1,300x below the threshold at which any of this attaches. UL 9540A is a large-scale propagation test run on modules/racks/units — it is categorically inapplicable at this scale, not a live item to "check with the venue's insurer." Presenting it as a real constraint is a regulatory claim stated far more confidently than the sources support.

2. SCOPE CONFLATION ON IEC 62133. IEC 62133-2's scope is explicitly limited to PORTABLE applications ("Safety requirements for portable sealed secondary cells, and for batteries made from them, for use in portable applications"). Invoking it because the device is wall-mounted/stationary inverts its stated scope. (In practice IEC 62133-2 is still the certificate most small-format cell vendors hold and is the right thing to demand from the cell supplier — but the claim's stated rationale is backwards.)

3. IEC 62619 MISLABELED. The claim calls it "system-level ... IEC 62619 or UL 1973," pairing them as equivalents. IEC 62619's confirmed scope is cell AND battery level for industrial applications (telecom, UPS, ESS, utility switching). UL 1973 is system-level; IEC 62619 is not. They are not interchangeable, and 62619's industrial framing targets installations orders of magnitude larger than 15 Wh.

4. THE ACTUALLY-APPLICABLE REQUIREMENT IS OMITTED. UN 38.3 transport testing is mandatory to ship any lithium cell or battery regardless of capacity, and is the one regulatory gate that certainly applies at 15 Wh. It is absent from the list. The governing product standard is also missing: a small standby battery inside a wall-mounted electronic product is certified via the END-PRODUCT standard (UL/IEC 62368-1 for ICT/AV equipment, or the applicable end-product standard for the device's function), with the cell carrying component-level certification.

5. THE LFP CONCLUSION IS UNSUPPORTED. "It will also point at LFP" derives entirely from the UL 9540A argument, which does not apply at this scale. At 15 Wh the certification path is chemistry-neutral. The practical availability pressure arguably runs the opposite way: small-format LFP cells are less available in coin/pouch/small-prismatic form factors than LCO/NMC, and LFP's 3.2 V nominal means more cells or larger cells for a given Wh at low voltage.

MINOR: item (2) slightly overstates by saying you cannot infer "or even SoC." LFP's curve retains usable slope above ~90% and below ~10-15% SoC, and hysteresis-compensated OCV models exploit those knees; the unreliability is specific to the mid-range plateau. Also, for a float-held standby cell the self-test must exercise the load-transfer path (does the device actually run off the battery?), not merely measure capacity — a battery that passes a capacity test but has a failed transfer FET still fails in the field. And if this function is life-safety in an occupied venue, quarterly is looser than the established standby-power norm (emergency lighting regimes conventionally require monthly functional plus annual full-duration testing) — worth confirming against the applicable occupancy code.

An engineer ordering parts against item (3) as written would budget an ESS compliance program that does not apply, select cells against a fire-test constraint that never triggers, and still miss UN 38.3.

corrected.original: PoE power available AT THE PD after cable loss is 12.95 W (802.3af Type 1), 25.5 W (802.3at Type 2), 51 W (802.3bt Type 3), and 71.3 W (802.3bt Type 4).
corrected.corrected:
Corrected for a hardware specification:

PER-CLASS MAXIMUM AVERAGE POWER AT THE PD PI (802.3bt Clause 145, Table 145-x / Ethernet Alliance Table 13). These are per-class ceilings for an ASSIGNED class, not guarantees implied by a PSE's Type:

Class | PD avg (PClass_PD) | PD peak (PPeak_PD) | PSE worst case (PClass) | PSE peak
1 | 3.84 W | 5.00 W | 4.00 W | 5.47 W
2 | 6.49 W | 8.36 W | 6.70 W | 8.87 W
3 | 13.00 W | 14.40 W | 14.00 W | 16.07 W
4 | 25.50 W | 28.30 W | 30.00 W | 34.12 W
5 | 40.00 W | 42.00 W | 45.00 W | 47.68 W
6 | 51.00 W | 53.50 W | 60.00 W | 63.62 W
7 | 62.00 W | 65.10 W | 75.00 W | 79.83 W
8 | 71.30 W | 74.90 W | 90.00 W | 96.36 W

PClass_PD is the maximum AVERAGE input power over a 1-second sliding window. The PD may exceed it up to PPeak_PD for at most 50 ms per 1 s window. Size the PD front end and DC-DC input for PPeak_PD; size the thermal/average budget to PClass_PD.

Legacy Clause 33 (802.3af/at) values, still widely quoted: Type 1 PSE 15.4 W -> PD 12.95 W (44 V min, 20 ohm loop, Cat3); Type 2 PSE 30 W -> PD 25.50 W (50 V min, 12.5 ohm loop, Cat5). Clause 145 restates the Class 3 pair as 14.00 W -> 13.00 W. Do not mix the two clauses in one table. Class 0 is an alias for Class 3 (Clause 33), deprecated in Clause 145.

TYPE DOES NOT GUARANTEE POWER — specify the CLASS when ordering:
- Type 1 PSE: 2-pair, 15.4 W, must support >= Class 1, may support up to Class 3.
- Type 2 PSE: 2-pair, 30 W, must support Class 4.
- Type 3 PSE, 2-pair-only variant: 30 W, Class 4 ceiling -> only 25.5 W at the PD.
- Type 3 PSE, 4-pair-capable variant: 60 W, Class 6 ceiling -> 51 W at the PD. Must support >= Class 1, MAY support up to Class 6.
- Type 4 PSE: always 4-pair, 90 W, must support >= Class 7 (62 W at PD), MAY support Class 8 (71.3 W at PD).
Classes 1-4 may be delivered over 2 pairs; Class 5 and above require 4-pair powering. Class 8 is single-signature only; dual-signature PDs allocate power per pairset and follow different limits.

CABLE LOSS IS DERIVED, NOT A FIXED ALLOWANCE:
PClass = VPSE * (VPSE - sqrt(VPSE^2 - 4*RChan*PClass_PD)) / (2*RChan)
with RCh <= 12.5 ohm per pairset (2-pair) and RCh/2 = 6.25 ohm (4-pair, both pairsets in parallel). The commonly quoted 2.45 / 4.5 / 9 / 18.7 W deltas are worst-case results at minimum PSE voltage and maximum channel resistance, not constants. Optional Autoclass lets the PSE measure actual loss and reserve less.

PSE MINIMUM OUTPUT VOLTAGE: Type 1 44 V; Type 2 and Type 3 50 V; Type 4 52 V (Type 4 is raised deliberately to cut current at high power). Verify against IEEE 802.3-2022 Tables 145-16/145-26 before release — Wikipedia's PoE table lists 52.0 V as the Type 3 PSE minimum, which does not reproduce the standard's own 60 W Class 6 figure.

PD INPUT VOLTAGE WINDOWS (design the DC-DC to these): Type 1 37.0-57.0 V; Type 2 42.5-57.0 V; Type 3/4 41.1-57.0 V.

TYPE 4 PSE UPPER BOUND: 90 W is the nominal Class 8 PClass, not a hard cap. PPeak is 96.36 W, and the LPS rule (ILPS-2P) only forbids sourcing more than 99.9 W for longer than 4 seconds. Budget upstream supply and thermals accordingly.

Verify all final numbers against the purchased copy of IEEE 802.3-2022 Clause 145 before releasing the spec; the Ethernet Alliance whitepaper is a 2018 pre-publication overview.
corrected.why:
The four headline numbers (12.95 / 25.5 / 51 / 71.3 W) are real figures from the standard, and every stated arithmetic allowance re-derives correctly. I verified against the claim's own cited Ethernet Alliance whitepaper (extracted its text locally after the PDF failed to parse via fetch) and re-ran the standard's own equation.

WHAT CHECKS OUT:
- 802.3af Clause 33: 15.4 W at 44 V into 20 ohm -> I=0.350 A, loss=2.450 W, PD=12.950 W. Exact.
- Type 2: 30 W at 50 V into 12.5 ohm -> I=0.600 A, loss=4.500 W, PD=25.500 W. Exact.
- EA Eq.(5), PClass = VPSE*(VPSE - sqrt(VPSE^2 - 4*RChan*PClass_PD))/(2*RChan), reproduces EA Table 13: Class 4 -> 30.00 W, Class 6 -> 60.00 W, Class 8 -> 90.04 W. The 9 W and 18.7 W deltas are correct.
- PD voltage windows 37.0 / 42.5 / 41.1 V min match Wikipedia, and 41.1 V re-derives from Class 8 worst case (52 V PSE, 6.25 ohm, 1.7308 A -> VPD = 41.18 V).

WHY IT IS STILL REFUTED FOR A PARTS-ORDERING SPEC:

1. PEAK/AVERAGE CONFLATION (the specific failure mode requested). PClass_PD is an AVERAGE limit over a 1-second sliding window. 802.3bt separately defines PPeak_PD, drawable up to 50 ms per 1 s: 5.00 / 8.36 / 14.40 / 28.30 / 42.00 / 53.50 / 65.10 / 74.90 W for Classes 1-8. The claim presents flat "power available" with no qualifier. A DC-DC input stage sized only to 71.3 W ignores the 74.9 W the PD is entitled to draw, and a designer budgeting average load may unknowingly exceed PClass_PD.

2. "TYPE 3 = 60 W -> 51 W" IS WRONG AS STATED. EA Table 2 defines two Type 3 PSEs: 2-pair-only Type 3 = 30 W max, Class 4 ceiling (25.5 W at PD); only 4-pair-capable Type 3 = 60 W / Class 6 / 51 W. Ordering "an 802.3bt Type 3 PSE" can legitimately yield half the assumed power. This is the most order-against-able error.

3. TYPE FIGURES ARE CEILINGS, NOT GUARANTEES. EA: "Type 3 PSEs must be able to support at least Class 1, and may support up to Class 6"; "Type 4 PSEs must be able to support at least Class 7, and may support Class 8." So a compliant Type 3 PSE guarantees only 4 W, and a compliant Type 4 PSE guarantees only Class 7 = 62 W. The claim's phrase "power available AT THE PD" reads as a floor; it is a per-class maximum.

4. CLAUSE MIXING / INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY. The claim pairs Clause 33 values (15.4 W -> 12.95 W) in the headline with Clause 145 values ("cl3 13 W") in the ladder. Under 802.3bt, Class 3 is PD 13.00 W / PSE 14.00 W (1.00 W delta), not 15.4 -> 12.95. Class 1 PSE is 4.00 W and Class 2 PSE is 6.70 W (not 7 W). Class 0 is omitted entirely (alias for Class 3 in Clause 33, deprecated in Clause 145).

5. TYPE 4 PSE IS NOT CAPPED AT 90 W. 90 W is PClass; PPeak is 96.36 W, and the LPS rule permits up to 99.9 W for as long as 4 seconds. Upstream supply and thermal budgeting off "90 W" is optimistic.

6. THE "ALLOWANCE" IS NOT A CONSTANT. Eq.(5) depends on actual VPSE and actual RChan; 2.45 / 4.5 / 9 / 18.7 W are worst-case values at minimum PSE voltage and maximum channel resistance. Optional Autoclass measures real loss and reduces the reserved allowance. Presenting them as fixed allowances overstates their determinism.

7. SIDE CAUTION ON THE CITED SOURCE. Wikipedia's table lists PSE 52.0-57.0 V for Type 3, but Eq.(5) only reproduces the standard's 60.00 W Class 6 figure at VPSE = 50 V (52 V is the Type 4 minimum, which reproduces 90 W for Class 8). If the engineer pulls PSE voltage limits from the same Wikipedia table, that entry is suspect. The claim itself does not state PSE voltages, so this is a warning about the source rather than the claim.

Given the instruction that a substantially-right-but-imprecise claim must be marked refuted, and given that items 1-3 could cause a real parts-ordering error, refuted = true.

corrected.original: The PD figures are a floor, not a meter reading: a short patch lead does not entitle the appliance to draw more than its class limit.
corrected.corrected:
P_Class is both a guaranteed minimum available at the PD and a hard maximum the PD may draw — and cable length changes neither. The per-class PD figures (Class 3 = 12.95 W, Class 4 = 25.5 W, Class 6 = 51 W, Class 8 = 71.3 W) are derived as PSE minimum output voltage minus the drop across worst-case 100 m channel resistance, at the class current: 37.0 V x 350 mA (20 ohm Cat3 loop), 42.5 V x 600 mA (12.5 ohm), 42.5 V x 1.2 A (6.25 ohm, two pairsets in parallel), 41.1 V x 1.732 A (6.29 ohm). Design the PD budget to P_Class for the class the PSE will actually grant, regardless of lead length — note these are class values, not type values, so a Type 3 PSE granting Class 5 yields 40 W and a Type 4 granting Class 7 yields 62 W.

Do not assume the PSE enforces this. IEEE 802.3 port protection is current-based (I_cut / I_Lim over T_cut), not power-based. On a 3 m lead at ~53 V, a PD drawing a non-compliant 30 W pulls only 566 mA — under the 600 mA class current, so the port does not trip; at 57 V the port tolerates up to 34.2 W before current protection engages. An over-drawing PD on a short lead therefore fails silently at the port and instead oversubscribes the switch's aggregate budget, which is allocated per advertised class. Budget compliance must be verified by design and bench measurement, not inferred from the absence of a trip.

The main benefit of a short lead is not reduced sag — the PD front end must tolerate the full 42.5-57 V range by spec anyway. It is the elimination of channel I2R heat: 4.5 W per Type 2 channel and 18.9 W per Class 8 channel at worst case (~21% of PSE output), which drives cable-bundle temperature rise and TIA bundle derating limits on how many powered runs share a pathway. A secondary PD-side gain is lower input current at the same output power, reducing conduction loss in the input bridge and FETs.
corrected.why:
The core design guidance is correct and the arithmetic checks out exactly, but three substantive errors make the claim unsafe as written for a hardware spec.

VERIFIED CORRECT: The four PD figures are exactly reproducible as PSE minimum output voltage minus worst-case channel resistance drop, at the class current. Type 1: 37.0 V x 350 mA = 12.95 W, implied loop R = 7.0/0.350 = 20 ohm (Cat3 100 m limit). Type 2: 42.5 V x 600 mA = 25.5 W, implied R = 7.5/0.6 = 12.5 ohm (Cat5 100 m limit). Type 3: 42.5 V x 1.2 A = 51 W, implied R = 7.5/1.2 = 6.25 ohm = 12.5/2 parallel pairsets. Type 4: 41.1 V x 1.732 A = 71.2 W ~ 71.3, implied R = 10.9/1.732 = 6.29 ohm. The "guaranteed minimum under worst-case 100 m channel" framing and the conclusion "budget to 25.5 W on 802.3at regardless of cable length" are both sound.

ERROR 1 (material): "the PD must still not exceed P_Class or the PSE trips it" misstates the enforcement mechanism. IEEE 802.3 PSE overload protection is defined on CURRENT (I_cut / I_Lim sustained over T_cut), not on watts. Counterexample in the claim's own scenario: a Type 2 PD on a 3 m lead sees ~53 V; drawing a non-compliant 30 W pulls only 30/53 = 566 mA, under the 600 mA class current and well under I_cut. The PSE does not trip. At 57 V the port tolerates 600 mA x 57 V = 34.2 W before current-based protection engages. The short cable is precisely the case where over-draw escapes detection. What actually fails is the switch's aggregate budget, allocated per advertised class — the port stays up while the chassis is silently oversubscribed. An engineer relying on "the PSE trips it" would design the wrong validation test and would wrongly assume compliance is self-policing.

ERROR 2: "The only real benefit of a short cable is less voltage sag at the DC-DC input" is wrong. Worst-case channel dissipation is 4.5 W on Type 2 (7.5 V x 0.6 A) and 18.9 W on Class 8 (10.9 V x 1.732 A), the latter ~21% of PSE output burned as heat inside the bundle. Eliminating that is the dominant benefit — it drives cable-bundle temperature rise and TIA bundle derating, which governs how many powered runs may share a pathway. Energy cost and data insertion-loss margin follow.

ERROR 3: Even the named benefit is described backwards. Reduced sag is not a design benefit, because the PD front end must tolerate the full 42.5-57 V range by spec regardless. The actual PD-side gain is lower input current at the same output power, reducing conduction loss in the input bridge and FETs.

ERROR 4 (precision): Type is conflated with Class. These are per-class values (Class 3/4/6/8), not per-type constants. A Type 3 PSE granting Class 5 delivers 40 W; a Type 4 granting Class 7 delivers 62 W. A parts-ordering engineer needs the class actually granted.

ERROR 5 (framing): Calling P_Class "a floor" emphasizes the less useful half. It is simultaneously a guaranteed minimum available from the PSE and a hard maximum the PD may draw; for hardware specification the ceiling is the operative constraint.

Note on sourcing: the cited Sifos PDF returned unparseable binary via fetch, so it does not independently support the claim as presented; the figures were validated by re-derivation against published PSE/PD voltage, current, and channel-resistance parameters. Web search budget was exhausted, so the I_cut threshold values were not confirmed to the exact milliamp — however the refutation does not depend on the exact threshold, since the counterexample current (566 mA) falls below even the nominal class current of 600 mA.

corrected.original: Yes, PoE+ has enough headroom to run a Pi 4 gateway and trickle-charge simultaneously — but only about 1.2 A of charge current, because the binding constraint is the HAT's 20 W output ceiling, not the 25.5 W PoE budget.
corrected.corrected:
PoE+ can run a Pi 4 gateway and trickle-charge simultaneously, but budget ~1.1 A worst-case charge current, not 1.25 A - and use an input-current-limited charger rather than a fixed setpoint.

Verified HAT specs (raspberrypi.com product page): official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT, IEEE 802.3at-2009 Class 4, 37-57 V DC in, 5 V/4 A out = 20 W ceiling, isolated SMPS, 25 mm/2.2 CFM fan, 0-50 degC. The 20 W nameplate is the binding constraint, not the 25.5 W PD budget (25.5 W x ~0.85-0.88 typical isolated-flyback efficiency = 21.7-22.4 W at 5 V). Do not attribute the 25.5->20 W gap to any specific loss breakdown; Raspberry Pi publishes none.

Loc8 Tier C 5 V load (ENGINEERING ESTIMATE - not measured; the raspi.tv article supports only 2.85 W idle and a 4.4 W desktop-load peak, and explicitly excludes multi-core stress):
- typical ~8.5 W (Pi 4 + BLE scan 4.5, LTE idle 1.5, LoRa RX 1.5, LED/OLED 0.5, fan 0.5)
- coincident worst case ~14.6 W, using a Pi 4 all-core figure of 6.4-7.6 W that needs its own citation
Count the fan exactly once.

Charge current at worst case (5.4 W headroom), sized at the 4.2 V top of the CC phase where input power peaks - NOT at 3.9 V nominal:
- synchronous buck charger @ 90%: 5.4 x 0.9 / 4.2 = 1.16 A
- linear charger (TP4056 class): 5.4 / 5.0 = 1.08 A, with ~1 W dissipated as in-enclosure heat
=> spec ~1.1 A worst case, and state which topology the number assumes.

Under typical load (11.5 W headroom) the same charger supports 2.3-2.5 A. Therefore specify a power-path charger with programmable input current limit (VINDPM/DPM, e.g. BQ2589x class) set to the 20 W rail budget, so charge current throttles automatically on TX bursts instead of being permanently derated to a transient. Derate the 20 W further for sustained operation near the 50 degC limit in a sealed enclosure.

Drop the Geekworm cross-check: 1.5 A does not confirm 1.1-1.25 A, it is a vendor headline max under different conditions, and no single Geekworm SKU combining 802.3at PoE+ PD with battery charging has been confirmed to exist.

Mechanical blocker to resolve before ordering: the official PoE+ HAT covers the 40-pin header with no pass-through. LoRa, OLED and LED cannot be attached alongside it without a stacking extender or a custom carrier board. Budget for that or select a third-party PoE+ solution that preserves GPIO access.
corrected.why:
Directionally right, but the derivation fails in six ways and would mislead an engineer ordering parts.

VERIFIED CORRECT: The PoE+ HAT product page confirms 37-57 V DC input, Class 4, "5 V DC/4 A" output, IEEE 802.3at-2009, 25 mm fan, isolated SMPS, 0-50 degC. 25.5 W is the right 802.3at Type 2 PD-side budget. The core premise also survives: 25.5 W x ~0.85-0.88 flyback efficiency = 21.7-22.4 W at 5 V, so the 20 W nameplate is indeed (marginally) the binding constraint. All stated sums add correctly (4.5+1.5+1.5+0.5+0.5=8.5; 7.6+3.0+2.0+1.0+1.0=14.6; 20-14.6=5.4).

FAILURE 1 - CITATION DOES NOT SUPPORT THE NUMBER. The cited raspi.tv page measures Pi 4B idle at 575 mA / 2.85 W (at 4.965 V) and a PEAK of 885 mA (~4.4 W) loading the LXDE desktop. It explicitly says "These simple tests do not consider multi-core CPU operation" and warns the averaging clamp meter "won't give a true picture of peak instantaneous current." There is no 7.6 W figure in it. The single largest line item in the worst-case budget is attributed to a source that does not contain it. (Commonly reported Pi 4B all-core stress figures are ~6.4 W; 7.6 W needs a real citation or must be labelled an estimate.)

FAILURE 2 - FAN DOUBLE-COUNTED. The detail explains the 25.5 -> 20 W gap as "isolated-flyback loss and the 25 mm fan," then bills the fan AGAIN as a 5 V rail load (0.5 W typ / 1.0 W worst). It is one or the other. Worse, Raspberry Pi publishes no loss breakdown at all - the 78% split and its attribution to flyback+fan is an unsourced rationalisation presented as spec.

FAILURE 3 - WRONG VOLTAGE IN THE SIZING CALCULATION. 3.9 V is a mid-charge nominal, but CC-phase input power peaks at the TOP of CC, at 4.2 V. Redo at 4.2 V: 5.4 W x 0.90 / 4.2 V = 1.16 A, not 1.25 A. An engineer replicating the arithmetic gets a different answer.

FAILURE 4 - UNEARNED EFFICIENCY. 90% presumes a synchronous buck charger (BQ2589x/BQ25171 class). A linear 1S charger - TP4056/MCP73831, the default cheap choice - has efficiency = Vbat/Vin, i.e. 84% at 4.2 V falling to 72% at 3.6 V, and dumps the difference as heat inside the same enclosure the HAT fan is already fighting. Linear case: charge current = 5.4 W / 5 V = 1.08 A. The spec must name the topology or 90% is not defensible.

FAILURE 5 - THE CROSS-CHECK IS NOT ONE. 1.5 A differs from 1.25 A by 25%; if it is evidence of anything it is disagreement, not confirmation. It is also a vendor headline max for a board with a different input source and different coincident load, i.e. a marketing figure doing the work of a measurement. I could not verify that any single Geekworm SKU combines 802.3at PoE+ PD with battery charging - their UPS line (X728/X1200/X1202) is USB/DC-fed, not PoE. Risk that this "product" is a conflation of two separate boards; must be confirmed before it appears in a BOM.

FAILURE 6 - COINCIDENT-PEAK STACKING TREATED AS A STEADY STATE. Summing Pi stress + LTE TX + LoRa TX + LED + fan-max as simultaneous is conservative (safe for the rail budget) but makes "only about 1.2 A" an artifact of the assumption rather than a real ceiling. LTE TX is a millisecond-scale burst that bulk capacitance absorbs; it is not a continuous 3.0 W rail load. The correct architecture is an input-current-limited (VINDPM/DPM) power-path charger that throttles charge current dynamically - which delivers ~2.3-2.5 A during the far more common 8.5 W typical state and folds back automatically on peaks. Hard-coding 1.2 A for a transient forfeits ~40% of achievable charge rate.

OMISSION THAT BLOCKS THE BUILD: the official PoE+ HAT occupies and covers the full 40-pin GPIO header with no stacking/pass-through. The Tier C load list includes LoRa RX/TX, an OLED and an LED - all GPIO/SPI/I2C. Those cannot coexist with this HAT without a stacking extender or custom carrier. A power-headroom answer that implies a buildable BOM must say so. (Verify against the mechanical drawing before ordering; the product page lists only fan/PSU specs.)

ALSO: 20 W is a nameplate maximum, not a guaranteed continuous rating at the top of the stated 0-50 degC range. Budgeting to nameplate in a sealed outdoor festival enclosure leaves zero thermal margin.

corrected.original: The resulting battery performance is roughly 1.6-2.1 hours of runtime and 4-5 hours of recharge — which contradicts the gateway doc's implied 'rides out a venue power cut' framing.
corrected.corrected:
The gateway doc does not specify a battery at all — docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md line 50 lists only a "UPS battery HAT (~$25)", with no chemistry, capacity, cell format, or charge current. The endurance implied by "battery-backed" (line 20) and "rides out a venue power cut" (line 51) is therefore unquantified rather than contradicted, and must be pinned down before parts are ordered.

Working the numbers for representative packs at a realistic gateway load of ~5 W (Pi 4B measures 2.7 W idle and 6.4 W at full CPU stress; a BLE-scan/SQLite/WebSocket workload plus PoE HAT conversion loss and fan lands near 4-6 W, not the 8.5 W originally assumed), and using 80% usable capacity with 90% boost efficiency:

- Single 21700 5000 mAh (~18.0-18.5 Wh): ~2.7 h runtime; recharge at 1.25 A is ~4.8-5.2 h (CC floor alone is 4.0 h, plus CV taper).
- 2x18650 1S2P (~25 Wh, ~7000 mAh): ~3.6 h runtime; recharge at 1.25 A is ~6.7-7.3 h (CC floor alone is 5.6 h).

At a 2 A charge current, typical of UPS HATs in this price class, recharge drops to roughly 3.0-3.3 h and 4.2-4.7 h respectively.

So the realistic figure is roughly 2.5-4.5 hours of runtime with a 5-7 hour recharge, and recharge takes about 1.9x as long as discharge — not 2.5x. The operational caution stands and is the part worth keeping: a single-cell or dual-18650 UPS HAT covers a short outage, not a night, and repeated generator cycling will progressively deplete the pack because recharge is slower than discharge. If "rides out a venue power cut" is meant to mean a full event, size the pack against a stated target (e.g. 8 h at 5 W needs ~55 Wh usable, roughly 3-4x the capacity of a $25 HAT) and specify cell count, chemistry, and charge current explicitly. Also confirm mechanical feasibility: Tier B already allocates the 40-pin header to a PoE+ HAT with a tall fan, so stacking a second UPS HAT needs verification before ordering.
corrected.why:
The claim's directional instinct (a ~$25 UPS HAT buys hours, not a night) is defensible, but every number in it is wrong, and two of the errors run in opposite directions.

1. BOTH RECHARGE FIGURES ARE PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE. They fall below the constant-current floor, before any CV taper is even considered. 5000 mAh / 1.25 A = 4.00 h absolute minimum, but the claim states 3.8 h. 2x18650 at 25 Wh implies ~7000 mAh, so 7000 / 1.25 A = 5.60 h minimum, but the claim states 5.1 h. You cannot move 5000 mAh into a cell at 1.25 A in under 4 hours. Neither figure is reproducible from the stated inputs under any interpretation (including 1.25 A per cell). Realistic CC-CV with a 20-30% taper: ~4.8-5.2 h and ~6.7-7.3 h.

2. THE 8.5 W "TYPICAL LOAD" EXCEEDS THE MEASURED FULL-STRESS DRAW OF THE BOARD. Pi Dramble measures a Pi 4B at 2.7 W idle and 6.4 W at 400% CPU stress. The claim's "typical" figure is 33% above the measured maximum. The stated derivation — "computed from official PoE+ HAT 20 W ceiling and measured Pi 4 draw" — conflates a supply ceiling with a load: I confirmed the PoE+ HAT outputs 5 V/4 A (20 W), but that is what the HAT can deliver to the Pi plus USB, not what the Pi consumes. The gateway workload in the doc (BLE scan/advertise, SQLite writes, WebSocket fan-out) is not CPU-saturating; realistic sustained draw including PoE conversion loss and the fan is ~4-6 W. So the runtime is UNDERSTATED, not overstated. The 1.6/2.1 h arithmetic is internally correct (13.32 Wh / 8.5 W = 1.57 h; 18.0 Wh / 8.5 W = 2.12 h) but rests on a bad load input.

3. THE ASYMMETRY RATIO IS WRONG. With corrected figures, recharge/discharge is ~1.9x, not the claimed ~2.5x. The qualitative point survives; the magnitude does not.

4. THE CLAIM ATTACKS A CONFIGURATION THE DOC DOES NOT CONTAIN. I read docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md in full. Line 50 says only "UPS battery HAT (~$25)". No chemistry, capacity, cell format, or charge current appears anywhere in the document. The 21700 5000 mAh pack, the 2x18650 1S2P pack, and the 1.25 A charge current are all the reviewer's own assumptions presented as if derived from the source. Common UPS HATs in that price class charge at up to 2 A, which would materially change the recharge number. Line 20's "battery-backed" and line 51's "rides out a venue power cut" are UNQUANTIFIED, not contradicted — the honest finding is a spec gap, not a contradiction. This distinction matters because an engineer ordering parts against this would be sizing a pack that no one has actually specified.

5. MINOR: the "80% usable capacity (3.0 V cutoff, cold derating)" justification is muddled. Li-ion cells are typically rated to a 2.5-3.0 V cutoff, so a 3.0 V cutoff alone retains ~95%+ of rated capacity. The 20% derate is essentially all cold/aging margin; the cutoff contributes little.

Defaulting to refuted: the central load figure could not be substantiated (official Raspberry Pi docs publish no consumption figures at all, only a 15 W PSU rating), and the one independent measurement I found contradicts it.

corrected.original: 802.3af is a non-starter for this appliance — Tier C worst case exceeds the af PD budget by over 5 W, and af leaves zero charging headroom even at Tier B.
corrected.corrected:
802.3af cannot carry Tier C, but 802.3at (PoE+) — not bt — is the correct procurement target.

- af PD-available power is 12.95 W (15.4 W PSE less worst-case 100 m cable loss). At 80-87% PD converter efficiency that is 10.4-11.3 W at the 5 V rail.
- Pi 4 draw under a worst-case synthetic CPU+GPU load is 6.41 W peak on current firmware; 7.28 W was the superseded launch-firmware value (raspberrypi.com thermal testing article). The 7.6 W figure appears in no cited source. Both are peaks, not sustained draw — size the rail on peak, size thermals on average.
- Tier B (6.4 W Pi peak + ~1 W fan = 7.4 W) leaves 3.0-3.9 W at 5 V on af, roughly 0.6-0.8 A of charge current. Slow, but not zero headroom.
- Tier C at 14.6 W on the 5 V rail needs 16.8-18.3 W at the PD depending on converter efficiency, exceeding af's 12.95 W by 3.8-5.3 W. af is genuinely ruled out for Tier C, and remains ruled out even at an implausible 95% efficiency — but quote the exceedance as 3.8 W at a realistic 87%, not "over 5 W".
- 802.3at Type 2 Class 4 delivers 25.5 W at the PD = 20.4-22.2 W at 5 V, covering Tier C's 14.6 W with 5.8-7.6 W spare for charging, and is the class the official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT implements. Verify the HAT's own 5 V rail current limit before ordering — the HAT, not the class budget, is usually the binding constraint.
- If bt is still specified, quote the class rather than the type: Type 3 spans Class 5 (40 W PD) and Class 6 (51 W PD), and bt-capable ports are sometimes deployed at Class 4. Applying a single consistent 80% efficiency, 14.6 W load + 10 W charge = 24.6 W at 5 V = 30.75 W at the PD, leaving 20.25 W under Class 6 — not 28.9 W and 22.1 W.
- On af overload, expect the PD's own converter input current limit to collapse the 5 V rail at or before the PSE's ICUT/TCUT disconnect; either path is an outage, but do not specify the mechanism as purely a PSE trip without bench confirmation.
corrected.why:
The directional conclusion (802.3af cannot carry Tier C) is correct and robust, but three of the supporting numbers are wrong or unsupportable, and the recommended alternative skips the option that actually fits.

1. FABRICATED/MISATTRIBUTED SOURCE FIGURE. The cited Raspberry Pi thermal-testing article contains no 7.6 W figure. It reports 7.28 W peak on launch firmware, declining across firmware revisions to 6.79 W, 6.67 W, and finally 6.41 W at load on the beta firmware. The article's thesis is that this number decreased. 7.6 W is higher than any value in the source.

2. PEAK PRESENTED AS SUSTAINED. Every figure in that article is an instantaneous peak under a worst-case synthetic CPU+GPU workload. The claim uses it as a continuous rail budget ("Pi 4 stress alone is 7.6 W measured"), conflating peak and average.

3. ASYMMETRIC EFFICIENCY ASSUMPTION. 80% is applied where it condemns af but not where it blesses bt: 14.6 + 10 = 24.6 W at 5 V is 30.75 W at the PD at 80%, not 28.9 W (28.9 implies ~85%), and the Class 6 margin is 20.25 W, not 22.1 W. 80% is also pessimistic for a 48 V-to-5 V isolated PD front end (85-90% typical), so the headline "over 5 W" exceedance is assumption-dependent: at 87% it is 3.8 W.

4. "ZERO HEADROOM AT TIER B" IS OVERSTATED. With the source's actual current-firmware figure (6.41 W) plus 1 W fan, af leaves 2.95 W at 80% or 3.9 W at 87% — roughly 0.6-0.8 A at 5 V. Slow, but not "insufficient to charge anything meaningfully."

5. MATERIAL OMISSION — 802.3at. The claim jumps from af to bt and then argues bt is impractical (no official HAT, uncommon switches), never evaluating 802.3at Type 2 Class 4 at 25.5 W PD = 20.4-22.2 W at 5 V, which covers Tier C's 14.6 W with 5.8-7.6 W spare and is the class the official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT implements. An engineer ordering parts against this spec would procure bt switches unnecessarily.

6. IMPRECISE CLASS/TYPE USAGE. "Type 3" spans Class 5 (40 W PD) and Class 6 (51 W PD), and bt-capable ports are sometimes deployed at Class 4; the 51 W implied by "28.9 + 22.1" assumes top-of-type. Specs should name the class. "The PSE will disconnect on overcurrent" is also stated more confidently than the design supports — in practice the PD converter's own input current limit typically collapses the rail before or alongside the PSE's ICUT/TCUT trip.

VERIFIED CORRECT: af PD-available power of 12.95 W; 12.95 x 0.80 = 10.36 W; 14.6/0.80 = 18.25 W; 18.25 - 12.95 = 5.3 W. The Tier C exclusion holds even at an implausible 95% efficiency (15.4 W > 12.95 W).

corrected.original: A Class 4 PD on a switch that does not do LLDP is silently demoted to 15.4 W PSE / 12.95 W PD — the appliance must survive being given af power without warning.
corrected.corrected: An 802.3at Class 4 PD is held at Type 1 power (15.4 W at the PSE, 12.95 W guaranteed at the PD) whenever the PSE presents only a SINGLE classification event — not merely when the switch lacks LLDP. 802.3at requires a Type 2 PSE to implement 2-event physical-layer classification, LLDP/data-link-layer classification, or both, while a Type 2 PD must implement both. A PSE doing 2-event grants full 30 W with no LLDP involved, and the PD may lift its self-imposed cap on the 2-event flag alone and skip LLDP entirely. The silent-failure case is therefore the opposite of as-written: a Type 2 PSE that implements ONLY LLDP-based classification, paired with an LLDP exchange that never completes (LLDP disabled on the venue switch port, no LLDP stack running on the gateway, or LLDP frames filtered in between), leaves the PD on an af-level budget indefinitely. A genuine 802.3af/Type 1 switch produces the same outcome and cannot be rescued by LLDP at all; such a PSE treats a Class 4 signature as Class 0 (not Class 3). Note also that until mutual identification completes a Type 2 PD must self-limit to 13 W, a distinct figure from the 12.95 W Type 1 PD guarantee. This failure mode is an at-era concern: 802.3bt Type 3/4 PSEs use multi-event physical classification and grant Class 4 power without LLDP. Design consequence is unchanged: the gateway must boot and run indefinitely within ~12.95 W at the PD, detect that it has not been granted Type 2 power, log it loudly rather than failing silently, and shed the charger first.
corrected.why:
The claim's causal condition is inverted, and its own stated source says so.

1. The trigger is single-event classification, not absence of LLDP. IEEE 802.3at requires a Type 2 PSE to implement 2-event physical-layer classification, data-link-layer (LLDP) classification, or both — the claim gets this part right. But it then draws the wrong conclusion. A switch that does not do LLDP and satisfies the standard must therefore be doing 2-event classification, and a 2-event PSE grants full Type 2 power with no LLDP involved at all. The Silvertel app note cited as the source states the PD may drop its self-imposed cap on the 2-event flag alone: "if no LLDP is received and at-flag is set... load limit can be removed" and skip LLDP negotiation. It also notes most PSEs deliver 30 W immediately after 2-event, and that only *some* require DLL negotiation first. So "no LLDP → demoted to 15.4 W" is refuted by the cited document.

2. The real silent-failure mode is the mirror image of what is written. The PD is stranded at Type 1 power when the PSE presents only ONE classification event. That happens in two cases: (a) a genuine 802.3af / Type 1 switch, where LLDP cannot help because the PSE has no Type 2 power to give; or (b) a Type 2 PSE that implements only DLL classification, where the escalation never arrives because LLDP failed to complete — disabled on the port, no LLDP daemon on the gateway itself, LLDP frames filtered by an intervening device, or the PD not sending the Power-via-MDI TLV. Note that case (b) is precisely a switch that DOES do LLDP; a switch doing neither mechanism is non-compliant and behaves as Type 1. Writing the spec as "the switch lacks LLDP" would send an engineer chasing the wrong switch feature on the datasheet and could lead them to spec an LLDP-capable switch as the mitigation, which does not remove the risk.

3. Wrong class label. A Type 1 PSE presented with a Class 4 signature treats it as Class 0, not Class 3. The wattage is identical (15.4 W PSE / 12.95 W PD), so the power budget is unaffected, but the label is wrong and would confuse anyone reading a classification table.

4. Two different numbers conflated. 12.95 W is the Type 1 PD minimum guaranteed power (worst-case 100 m cable loss from 15.4 W at the PSE). 13 W is the separate figure a Type 2 PD must self-limit to before mutual identification completes. The claim uses 12.95 W throughout; that is the conservative one, so the design budget is safe, but the two figures should not be treated as the same quantity.

5. Stale relative to current hardware. This is an 802.3at-era (2009) failure mode. 802.3bt Type 3/Type 4 PSEs — what an engineer ordering in 2026 will mostly encounter — use multi-event physical classification, so Class 4 power is granted at the physical layer without LLDP. The risk is real for older/cheap af-only or at-era venue gear, which is a legitimate concern for festival deployments, but the spec should scope it rather than state it as universal.

6. The engineering conclusion survives. The appliance must boot and run indefinitely inside the Type 1 budget (~12.95 W at the PD), and shedding the charger first is sound. That part is not disputed — only the stated cause, the class label, and the confidence.

The second cited source (flukenetworks.com/blog/cabling-chronicles/what-is-PoE-Negotiation) returned HTTP 403 and could not be verified; it should not be relied on in a hardware spec without a retrievable copy. WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted, so the standard's exact clause text (802.3at clauses 33.2.4 / 33.6, 79.3.2) was not independently pulled — the refutation rests on the claim's own primary source, which is decisive on the key point.

Sources: [Silvertel ANX-POE Data Link Layer Classification](https://silvertel.com/images/appsnotes/ANX-POE-Data-Link-Layer-Classification.pdf) (fetched, read in full); [Fluke Networks PoE Negotiation](https://www.flukenetworks.com/blog/cabling-chronicles/what-is-PoE-Negotiation) (403, unverifiable).

corrected.original: Drawing full Class 4 power to charge a battery can cause the venue switch to shed power from another device — installing the Loc8 gateway could knock a camera offline.
corrected.corrected:
PoE switch power budgets are shared and commonly oversubscribed, so adding a Class 4 (802.3at Type 2) device to a loaded switch can cause a power-deny or power-shed event affecting another device such as a camera.

Mechanism (corrected): most switches reserve budget by ADVERTISED CLASS at classification time, not by measured draw. A Class 4 port commits the full 30 W of PSE budget from link-up regardless of actual consumption, so the contention event occurs at INSTALLATION, not when charging begins. When the budget cannot accommodate a new device, the switch typically denies power to the newly connecting port; an already-powered camera is dropped only if the new port holds higher configured priority. Among equal-priority ports many vendors deny the highest-numbered port first, but this is vendor-specific and overridden by explicit priority configuration. On switches configured for actual-consumption allocation, a mid-session load spike can trigger shedding — treat this as the exception, not the rule.

Power accounting (corrected): Class 4 = 30 W at the PSE / 25.50 W at the PD; budget is consumed at the PSE figure of 30 W. Class 3 = 15.4 W PSE / 12.95 W PD. Class 0 = 15.4 W PSE / 12.94 W PD.

Arithmetic (corrected): a 65 W budget supports 2 ports at the full 30 W Class 4 allocation (65/30 = 2.17), leaving ~5 W. Averaged across 8 ports a 65 W budget yields only 8.1 W per port — roughly Class 2 territory (7 W PSE / 6.49 W PD). Note that 8-port PoE+ budgets vary widely (~52-125 W depending on model, with low-budget units often powering only 4 of 8 ports); verify the budget of the specific switch model rather than assuming 65 W.

Recommendation (corrected): (a) Advertise Class 3 by default and request Class 4 via LLDP only when charge current is actually needed, so the appliance reserves 15.4 W rather than 30 W of budget while idle. (b) Cap steady-state PD draw at or below 11-12 W so the unit remains within the 12.95 W 802.3af PD ceiling with headroom and continues to function when demoted to af — a 15 W steady draw would exceed that ceiling and trip overload disconnect. (c) Make charge current back off under contention. (d) Document the worst-case PSE budget reservation (30 W), not the PD figure, since that is what the installer must subtract from the cabinet's budget.
corrected.why:
Directionally sound (PoE budget contention is a real install risk) but defective in four ways that matter for a parts order.

(1) Arithmetic error: 65 W / 8 = 8.1 W per port, not "~15 W average per port across 8." A 15 W/port average across 8 ports requires ~120 W. The "2 ports at full 30 W" figure is correct (65/30 = 2.17).

(2) PSE/PD conflation: IEEE Class 4 is 30 W at the PSE and 25.50 W at the PD (verified against the IEEE 802.3 class table). Switch budget is accounted PSE-side, so the gateway consumes 30 W of budget, not the 25.5 W the claim attributes to it.

(3) Wrong causal mechanism for the default case: most switches reserve budget by advertised class at classification/link-up, not by measured draw. A Class 4 PD commits its full 30 W whether it idles at 8.5 W or spikes — so the contention event occurs at INSTALLATION, not "when charging," and the spike changes nothing. Further, an over-budget switch normally denies power to the newly connecting port rather than shedding an already-powered camera; the camera drops only if the gateway port holds higher configured priority. The spike-triggered-shed story applies only under actual-consumption allocation modes, presented here as the general case.

(4) Self-contradictory recommendation: "cap steady draw near 15 W" and "still functions when demoted to af" are mutually exclusive — 802.3af caps the PD at 12.95 W (Class 3: 15.4 W PSE / 12.95 W PD). A 15 W steady PD draw exceeds the af ceiling and trips overload disconnect.

Sourcing is also inadequate for a hardware spec: one cited source is a user forum thread; the Extreme Networks article returned HTTP 403 and could not be independently checked. "Usually higher-numbered ones" is a vendor default among equal-priority ports only and is overridden by configured priority. "Typical 65 W" is weakly supported — 8-port PoE+ budgets span roughly 52-125 W, and low-end figures often belong to units where only 4 of 8 ports are powered.

Note: web-search budget for this session was exhausted, so vendor-specific allocation-mode behavior and the 65 W "typical" figure could not be confirmed against primary vendor documentation. The class-power figures and all arithmetic were verified.

corrected.original: The official PoE+ HAT and common UPS HATs do NOT stack — they are geometrically incompatible, not merely tight. The blocker is the 4-pin PoE header, which fixes the PoE HAT at standard HAT height and cannot be raised.
corrected.corrected:
The official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT (compatible with Raspberry Pi 3B+ and 4 only — there is no official PoE HAT for Pi 5) and typical top-mounting UPS HATs will not stack as shipped, but this is a missing-interface and clearance problem, not a geometric impossibility.

The PoE+ HAT mates via both the 40-pin GPIO header and the 4-pin PoE header (J14) beside the Ethernet jack, and ships with plain closed female sockets and no pass-through, so it presents no pins to a board above it. Its 25 x 25 mm fan also occupies the z-space directly over the SoC, so any upper board must clear it.

However, Raspberry Pi's own launch material states that stacking is supported in principle — "Because the fan is controlled over I2C, none of the GPIO are used, so you can stack a second HAT on top of the connector" — and points to extended risers available from RS and element14. Stacking therefore requires non-stock pass-through/riser headers plus a mechanical fan-clearance check, which is an integration cost and a supply risk, not an impossibility.

Note also that nothing stacked above the PoE HAT consumes the 4-pin header; it is a bottom-board-only interface. The 4-pin only matters if the PoE HAT itself is raised, and a 2x2 tall header can be cut from a standard extra-tall 2x20 stacking strip.

For procurement: treat top-stacking on the PoE+ HAT as "requires custom/extended headers; verify fan clearance and total stack height," and prefer UPS boards that mount under the Pi or connect by cable, which avoid the contention entirely (confirm per part). Do not cite forums.adafruit.com/viewtopic.php?t=190145 — it is not retrievable (HTTP 403) and does not substantiate anything here.
corrected.why:
The claim is refuted by its own cited source, and its stated mechanism is wrong.

1. STATED SOURCE CONTRADICTS THE CLAIM. Fetching https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?t=221479 shows the thread's conclusion is that stacking IS possible. It quotes Raspberry Pi's own launch post: "Because the fan is controlled over I2C, none of the GPIO are used, so you can stack a second HAT on top of the connector." The thread's recurring advice is "you will need to buy some longer pass-through headers that expose the pins on the other side of the PoE HAT." The claim cites a thread that says the opposite of "geometrically incompatible."

2. "EXTRA-TALL 4-PIN PASS-THROUGH HEADERS EFFECTIVELY UNOBTAINABLE" IS CONTRADICTED BY THE VENDOR. The official announcement (raspberrypi.com/news/introducing-power-over-ethernet-poe-hat/) states "Extended risers are available from RS and element14 to enable additional stacking." The claim asserts unobtainability while the manufacturer names two distributors.

3. THE FORUM EVIDENCE IS MISREAD. The sourcing complaint quoted in the thread (hansamann, Sept 2018) is about pin cross-section — "many pin headers are 0.65x0.35 in size (the area of the pin) and they will not fit very well with regular female jumper cables" — i.e. a jumper-wire fit issue, not an inability to buy 4-pin tall headers. The "soldered jumper wires to the bottom of the board" post is one 2018 user's workaround for a display while his ordered pass-through headers "aren't here yet" (wpns, Sept 2018). Neither establishes geometric impossibility. The thread contains no documented stacking failure.

4. THE STATED BLOCKER IS THE WRONG PART. "Stacking anything above requires pass-through headers on both" is false. The 4-pin PoE header (J14) is a bottom-board-only interface — it carries the magjack centre-tap voltage to the PoE HAT. Nothing stacked above the PoE HAT consumes it, so nothing above needs it passed through. The 4-pin only matters if you raise the PoE HAT itself. And a 2x2 0.1" tall header is a cuttable segment of a standard extra-tall stacking strip (e.g. Adafruit #2223, 10 mm pins, in stock, $2.95, verified) — 0.1" headers are routinely cut to length. "Cannot be raised" is unsupportable.

5. SECOND SOURCE UNVERIFIABLE. https://forums.adafruit.com/viewtopic.php?t=190145 returns HTTP 403; I could not confirm it says anything about this. A spec should not cite it.

6. UNSTATED MODEL SCOPE — ORDERING-RELEVANT. The official PoE+ HAT product page states compatibility with "Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 3B+" only, and the Raspberry Pi product catalogue lists exactly one PoE HAT. An engineer ordering against a Pi 5 build from this claim would order a part that does not apply.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE: the HAT does mate via both the 40-pin and the 4-pin header; it ships with plain closed female sockets and no pass-through, so it presents nothing to a board above it out of the box; and the 25 x 25 mm fan (verified on the product page, "25 mm x 25 mm brushless fan delivering 2.2 CFM") does occupy the z-space over the SoC. Those are real obstacles. But they amount to "requires non-stock headers plus a fan-clearance check" — an integration cost and a sourcing risk — not the absolute geometric incompatibility asserted. The claim also fails to exclude the class of UPS boards that never contend for that z-space (under-mounting or cable-connected units), for which no conflict arises; I could not verify specific products (Waveshare returned 403), so that should be confirmed per-part rather than assumed.

corrected.original: Even if the geometry were solved, PoE HAT feeding a UPS HAT is electrically wrong: it hard-parallels two unsynchronized 5 V sources on GPIO pins 2/4 with no ORing.
corrected.corrected:
Feeding a UPS HAT from a PoE+ HAT is not a buildable topology, but the reason is connectivity, not connector current.

PRIMARY (sound): The official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT exposes no 5 V output connector — its rated "5 V DC/4 A" output reaches the Pi only through GPIO header pins 2/4 (it connects via "the two 0.1-inch headers (40 + 4)"; the 4-pin header is PoE *input* from the RJ45 magnetics, not an output). Consequently there is no way to wire it upstream into a UPS HAT's input. The only physically realizable arrangement is both regulators tied to the same 5 V node. Two independently regulated sources on one rail without an ideal-diode/ORing controller is bad practice: the converter with the higher setpoint carries the entire load while the other sits at zero current or in foldback, and the ordering can invert with tolerance, temperature, and load, producing unannounced hand-off transients. The UPS also cannot perform its function in this arrangement — sitting in parallel on the output, it has no visibility of PoE loss upstream of its own input.

CAVEAT on mechanism: whether reverse current actually flows into the PoE+ HAT depends on its secondary-side rectification (a diode-rectified flyback secondary blocks it; only synchronous rectification can conduct backwards). Raspberry Pi publishes no PoE+ HAT schematic, so treat back-feed as an unquantified risk to be excluded by inspection, not an established failure. Likewise, "the UPS HAT has no ORing" must be verified against that specific board's datasheet — many Pi UPS HATs do integrate power-path/ideal-diode charger ICs, and several are explicitly designed to both draw from and return 5 V on the GPIO rail.

WITHDRAW the connector-current objection entirely. 4 A across pins 2/4 is 2 A per contact, which is within rating, not at or beyond it: Würth WR-PHD 2.54 mm headers are rated 3 A per contact, and Samtec TSW mated with common sockets rates 4.3–6.3 A per pin. Decisively, the official PoE+ HAT is specified to deliver its full 4 A through exactly those two pins — that is Raspberry Pi's own design point. The ground return is also not a concern: the 40-pin header has eight grounds (6, 9, 14, 20, 25, 30, 34, 39), so 4 A returns at roughly 0.5 A per contact, the least-stressed part of the interface.

ORDERING NOTE: the PoE+ HAT is documented "Compatible with Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 3B+" and is not compatible with Raspberry Pi 5; a Pi 5's 5 V/5 A requirement also exceeds this HAT's 4 A rating. Confirm the host board before ordering this SKU. Note too that the HAT carries a 25 mm fan on its top face and occupies both headers, so the mechanical conflict is not resolvable with taller spacers.

If both PoE and battery backup are required, use a single unit that arbitrates them internally (a PoE splitter or PoE-input UPS with one regulated 5 V output feeding the Pi), or place a proper ORing/power-path controller between the two sources — never tie two regulator outputs directly to the 5 V rail.
corrected.why:
The core conclusion survives, but the supporting engineering is wrong in one place and overstated in three others. Since this is destined for a parts order, the errors matter.

WHAT CHECKS OUT (verified against raspberrypi.com/products/poe-plus-hat/):
- "Output power: 5 V DC/4 A" — the 4 A figure is correct and is the HAT's rated output.
- Power is delivered by connecting "to the two 0.1" headers (40 + 4) that are fitted on your Raspberry Pi." The 4-pin header carries PoE input from the RJ45 magnetics' center taps; it is not a 5 V output. No separate 5 V output connector is listed anywhere in the specs. So the premise that 5 V exits only on GPIO pins 2/4 is sound.
- Therefore the topology conclusion is directionally right: there is no legitimate way to wire the PoE+ HAT as an *upstream source* into a UPS HAT's input, because it exposes no input-feedable 5 V. The only physically available wiring is both regulators tied to the same rail node — which is the unsafe configuration.

WHAT IS FACTUALLY WRONG — the header current sub-claim:
The claim asserts 2.54 mm header contacts are "typically ~2 A/pin rated" and that 2 A/pin is "at or beyond the contact limit." Both are false.
- Würth WR-PHD 61300211121 (2.54 mm pin header) datasheet, Electrical Properties: "Rated Current IR ... 3 A."
- Samtec TSW catalog, CURRENT RATING (PER PIN), TSW mated with ESW/SSW/SLW/SSQ/SSM/BCS/SNT: 5.2 A / 5.7 A / 5.2 A / 6.3 A / 5.2 A / 4.6 A / 4.3 A.
- Harwin M20 and Molex/FCI 2.54 mm parts are likewise 3 A class.
So 2 A/pin sits at 67% of the most conservative common rating and ~35% of a good mated Samtec pair. It is comfortably inside spec, not "at or beyond the limit."
The decisive argument is self-refuting from the claim's own source: the official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT is *specified* to deliver its full 5 V/4 A through exactly pins 2 and 4. Raspberry Pi engineered 4 A across that pin pair as the nominal design point of a shipping product. You cannot cite that product's pinout as evidence that its own rated current exceeds its own connector.

WHAT IS BACKWARDS — the ground return:
"the return path sharing the ground pins" is framed as an aggravating factor. It is the opposite. The 40-pin header has eight grounds (pins 6, 9, 14, 20, 25, 30, 34, 39). 4 A / 8 = 0.5 A per contact — the ground side is the *least* stressed part of the interface, running at roughly one-sixth of a 3 A rating. Ground is not a constraint here at all.

WHAT IS STATED MORE CONFIDENTLY THAN DERIVABLE:
