1. "back-feeding into the PoE HAT's output stage" — asserted as certain, but it depends on the secondary-side rectification of the HAT's isolated flyback. A diode-rectified secondary blocks reverse current outright; only a synchronous-rectified secondary can conduct backwards. Raspberry Pi publishes no schematic for the PoE+ HAT, so this is an unverified assumption, not a derived result.
2. "possible reverse current into the UPS charger" — most boost/power-path converters in UPS HATs are unidirectional or carry explicit reverse-blocking, so a path back into the *charger* stage is speculative. Hedged with "possible," but presented as a design conclusion.
3. "indeterminate which unit regulates" — imprecise. The behavior is deterministic, not indeterminate: whichever regulator has the higher output setpoint takes the entire load while the other drops to zero current or into foldback. The genuine hazard is that the setpoint ordering can invert with tolerance, temperature, and load, producing unannounced hand-off transients and one converter chronically running at no load. That is a sharper and more defensible statement than "indeterminate."
4. "with no ORing" is asserted about an unnamed UPS HAT. Many Pi UPS HATs do contain power-path/ideal-diode controllers (TI BQ2589x/BQ257xx-class chargers), and several cheap ones are explicitly designed to charge from the GPIO 5 V rail and return 5 V to the same pins, i.e. the vendor already handles the shared node. "No ORing" is a per-product fact that must be checked against the specific UPS HAT datasheet, not a general property of the category.

ORDERING HAZARD NOT MENTIONED, and material for a parts order:
The product page states "Compatible with Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 3B+." The PoE+ HAT is NOT compatible with Raspberry Pi 5. If the target board is a Pi 5, this entire part number is the wrong line item regardless of the topology discussion, and the Pi 5's 5 V/5 A demand exceeds the PoE+ HAT's 4 A rating anyway. Any spec citing this SKU must pin down the host board first.

Also worth noting for the geometry side the claim waves off: the PoE+ HAT carries a 25 mm x 25 mm fan on its top face and occupies both the 40-pin and 4-pin headers, so the obstruction is a fan rotor and a second connector, not merely stack height that a taller spacer resolves.

NET: the recommendation "do not build this" is right, but the claim should not ship as written. Its numerically checkable sub-claim is wrong by 1.5-3x in the unsafe direction of over-alarming, one sub-claim is inverted, and the failure mechanisms are asserted with more certainty than the available documentation supports. An engineer who caught the header-rating error would reasonably discount the sound parts of the argument along with it.

corrected.original: The recommended topology for a Pi 4-based Tier C is an external 802.3at splitter plus a DC UPS — NOT a HAT stack, and not the combined board, because the only good combined board is Pi 5 only.
corrected.corrected:
For Tier C, terminate PoE outside the Pi and provide battery backup as a separate stage - but for reasons of GPIO allocation and form factor, NOT because 802.3at is short of power.

Corrected facts:

1. Pi 5 power. Raspberry Pi's specification lists two supported configurations: "5 V at 5 A (25W); or 5 V at 3 A (15 W) with a 600 mA peripheral limit". The Pi 5 does not require 25 W. The 15 W configuration fits inside 802.3at's 25.5 W PD guarantee with roughly 10.5 W spare. The claim that a Pi 5 exceeds what 802.3at can deliver "through any HAT" is false, and is disproved by the X1207 itself, which is Pi 5 only and PoE-powered.

2. What Tier C actually is. docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md line 49 specifies Tier C as "CM4/CM5 with soldered eMMC," not Pi 4. (Pi 4/CM4 appears at line 41, which is Tier B.) A compute module sits on a carrier board and takes no Pi-form-factor HAT; the carrier defines the power input. Resolve the CM4-vs-CM5 decision first - the entire HAT/combined-board/splitter question is downstream of it and largely moot for a CM design.

3. X1207 mechanics. It mounts on the 40-pin GPIO header and provides a 40-pin extended (stacking) header; the supplied pogo pin connects to the Pi 5 PSW through-hole for power-button function. GPIO is preserved by the extended header, not by the pogo pin.

4. X1207 headroom. "Up to 25 W" is vendor overview copy against a 25.5 W 802.3at PD ceiling - about 2% margin before DC-DC losses. Treat it as a ceiling to derate from, not as an available budget.

5. Pi 4 PoE is already solved first-party. The official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT covers "Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 3B+," IEEE 802.3at-2009, 5 V DC/4 A (20 W) against the Pi 4's 15 W. If Tier B/C stays on Pi 4 form factor, this is the default PoE leg at roughly the $20 already budgeted on line 42; only the UPS needs an external answer.

6. Consequences the spec must absorb. An external splitter is an additional enclosed assembly and needs a DC input on the gateway - the port list at line 70 (RJ45, USB-C, SMA, USB-A) has no barrel jack, and the Tier C envelope is ~150x110x40 mm. Either add the DC inlet and re-check the envelope, or keep power termination inside on a HAT/carrier.

Actions before ordering: confirm CM4 vs CM5 for Tier C; size the DC UPS charger current limit against measured (not rated) gateway draw with LTE dongle and dual BLE radios active; confirm X1207 availability with Geekworm if a Pi 5 path is revisited; and if the LED ring, OLED and tamper switch (lines 46, 52) are the real driver for keeping the header clear, state that as the rationale rather than a power-budget argument.
corrected.why:
The product facts about the X1207 check out, but three of the claim's load-bearing supports fail, and one premise about the target document is simply wrong.

VERIFIED TRUE: geekworm.com/products/x1207 confirms Raspberry Pi 5 only (2/4/8/16GB), no Pi 4 variant; genuine 2-in-1 PoE+ and UPS; IEEE 802.3af/at; 35-57VDC PoE input; 5.1V/5A output; single 21700 cell up to 5000mAh; 1500mA charge; simultaneous charge-and-run; $50 (reg. $55). The wiki confirms "drawing up to 25W from a compatible POE switch."

REFUTATION 1 - the central arithmetic conflates a headroom rating with a requirement. The claim says "the Pi 5 alone wants 5 V/5 A = 25 W, exceeding what 802.3at can deliver through any HAT." Raspberry Pi's own specification table lists TWO supported configurations: "USB-C power; 5 V at 5 A (25W); or 5 V at 3 A (15 W) with a 600 mA peripheral limit". The Pi 5 does not require 25 W. 25 W is the option that unlocks the full 1.6 A peripheral budget. 802.3at guarantees 25.5 W at the PD (30 W at the PSE), so the 15 W Pi 5 configuration has 10.5 W of headroom - a 70% margin. The premise is false, and with it the conclusion "moving Tier C to Pi 5 makes the budget worse."

REFUTATION 2 - the claim is self-contradicting. The X1207 is Pi 5 only and powers a Pi 5 from 802.3af/at. If 802.3at could not deliver enough for a Pi 5 "through any HAT," the board the claim nominates as architecturally correct could not exist. The claim's own cited evidence falsifies its own arithmetic.

REFUTATION 3 - the document premise is wrong, and this is the most consequential error for an ordering spec. The claim states the doc "specifies Pi 4/CM4." Line 41 (Tier B) says "Raspberry Pi 4 (2GB) or CM4 on carrier," but line 49 - Tier C, the actual subject of the claim - says "CM4/CM5 with soldered eMMC." CM5 is already a Pi 5-generation part, so "moving Tier C to Pi 5" is not a move. More fundamentally, a compute module on a carrier board accepts no Pi-form-factor HAT at all; the carrier board defines the power input. The entire HAT-vs-combined-board-vs-splitter framing is misapplied to a compute-module design.

REFUTATION 4 - mechanical description is wrong. The claim describes "pogo-pin connection preserving GPIO." The Geekworm wiki states the X1207 occupies the 40-pin GPIO header and supplies a "40-pin extended GPIO header x1," while the pogo pin is "For connecting to the Pi 5 PSW through hole" - the power-switch signal. GPIO access is preserved by the stacking/extended header, not by the pogo pin. An engineer planning stack height or GPIO allocation from this sentence would plan it wrong.

REFUTATION 5 - marketing figure presented as budget. "Up to 25 W drawn" is Geekworm overview copy, not a measured figure, and it sits 0.5 W (2.0%) below the 25.5 W 802.3at PD ceiling before any DC-DC conversion loss. It should be derated, not quoted as available.

ADDITIONAL - the recommendation is framed as correcting an assumption the doc never made, and its own costs are unaccounted. The doc already budgets a separate "PoE+ HAT | $20" (line 42) and a separate "UPS battery HAT (~$25)" (line 50) - i.e. the two-HAT stack the claim says not to do. And the Tier B physical spec (line 70) lists "1x RJ45 (PoE in), 1x USB-C (service/alt power), 1x SMA antenna, 1x USB-A" - there is no DC barrel jack, which an external-splitter topology requires, plus an external splitter is an additional enclosed box the 150x110x40mm Tier C envelope does not allow for.

MISSED ALTERNATIVE - for Pi 4 the official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT is "Compatible with Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 3B+," IEEE 802.3at-2009, output "5 V DC/4 A" (20 W) against the Pi 4's 15 W requirement. First-party PoE for Pi 4 is a solved, in-stock, cheap problem. Only the UPS leg genuinely needs an external answer, which materially changes the recommended topology.

VERDICT: the conclusion (external PoE termination plus a DC UPS, keeping the GPIO header free for the LED ring, OLED and tamper switch on line 46/52) is a defensible engineering choice, and the GPIO-freeing rationale is real. But it is reached through a false power calculation, a self-contradiction, a wrong reading of which silicon Tier C targets, and a wrong mechanical description. None of the numeric justifications survive. It must not go into an ordering spec as written.

STOCK CAVEAT (low confidence): the X1207 page rendered contradictory stock text ("Only 47 items in stock! Out of stock!"). Availability should be confirmed with the vendor before any BOM commitment.

corrected.original: At volume the correct answer is the CM4 carrier the doc already contemplates: PD front-end, charger and power-path on one board, which is the only way to make the 25.5 W budget genuinely manageable.
corrected.corrected:
An integrated CM4 carrier — PD front-end, isolated flyback, charger and power-path on one board — is a reasonable direction at volume, and the doc does already contemplate CM4-on-carrier (Tier B) and CM4/CM5 with eMMC (Tier C). But note that the doc states no power budget at all: sections 2 and 3 give a BOM and a physical spec, and the only power line is a $20 PoE+ HAT. The 25.5 W figure is an inference from that (802.3at Type 2 = 30 W at the PSE, 25.50 W at the PD), not a doc figure, and it must be budgeted at the right level: 25.5 W is PD input. Raspberry Pi's own 802.3at PoE+ HAT delivers 5 V/4 A = 20 W to the load, so the usable budget is ~20 W before the carrier's own charger/power-path stage takes a further few percent.

Against ~20 W, the doc's fullest load — CM4 (~5-7 W peak), LTE dongle (~2-3 W), LoRa concentrator (~1-2 W), dual BLE, status LED — is ~12-14 W peak, leaving 6-8 W of headroom. There is therefore no worst-case-versus-typical crisis in the base design, and input-current DPM is not "the only way" to make the budget manageable.

DPM's real and genuine value is narrower: it is the right answer for the Tier C battery variant specifically, where charging a 2S pack at ~2 A x 8.4 V (~17 W) on top of ~13 W of load would otherwise demand ~30 W. There, an IINDPM/NVDC charger (BQ25798 or BQ25703A class — both ACTIVE, both offering IINDPM, VINDPM and system-load-prioritised power path) correctly throttles charge current so the compute load always wins. In Tier B, which has no battery, DPM provides no budget relief because there is nothing to throttle.

Two corrections to the mechanism as described. First, DPM does not make af demotion graceful: a PSE that grants only 802.3af leaves 12.95 W at the PD (~10 W delivered), below the ~13 W load, so with charge current already at zero the shortfall is drawn from the battery — quietly discharging the UPS pack and hiding a misprovisioned switch. Class demotion must raise an explicit fault, not be absorbed silently. Second, only VINDPM responds automatically (to input droop); setting IINDPM to the actually-granted class requires firmware to read the PD controller's classification result over I2C. Budget that control loop.

Part selection should be made consistent with the budget. TPS2372 is a PD interface only (TI: "DC/DC control PD Only") and is an 802.3bt Type 3/Type 4 device (13/25/51/71 W), so it is neither single-chip nor matched to an at-class budget. For a 25.5 W design specify TPS23730, which integrates the PD interface and a current-mode flyback controller in one device across 802.3af/at Type 1/2 and bt Type 3, with primary-side regulation that removes the optocoupler. Alternatively, if a bt-class front end is wanted anyway, design to Type 3 (51 W at PD) and the budget pressure largely disappears without relying on DPM.

Finally, "at volume" needs a number before an engineer orders against it. The doc is explicitly pilot-scale and defers even Yocto/buildroot to "when volumes justify it". Moving the PoE front end onto the carrier removes the HAT stack-up but transfers that cost into a safety-rated transformer, isolation-barrier creepage and clearance, and product-level EMC (FCC Part 15 / CISPR 32) and IEC 62368-1 qualification — none of which is currently costed, against a $20 HAT line in a $95-120 BOM. Specify the crossover volume, the NRE, and the target carrier BOM cost before treating this as the correct answer. If Tier C uses CM5 rather than CM4, re-run the whole budget: CM5 draws materially more (its dev kit ships a 27 W supply), and ~20 W delivered from an at-class front end becomes marginal.
corrected.why:
The mechanism is real, but the claim misattributes its premise to the doc, budgets against the wrong number, and overstates DPM as necessary and sufficient. Details:

1. SOURCING ERROR (most serious for a spec an engineer orders against). /Users/augustusedem/Loc8/.claude/worktrees/recursing-montalcini-d59018/docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md contains NO power budget. Grep for "25.5", "802.3", "watt", "DPM", "TPS2", "BQ25", "flyback" returns nothing relevant repo-wide. Section 2 is a BOM table, section 3 is dimensions/ports/industrial-design. The doc's only power line is "PoE+ HAT | Power + network down ONE Ethernet cable | $20". So the "25.5 W budget" and the "worst-case-versus-typical budgeting problem" are the claim's own imports, not the doc's. The inference is legitimate (802.3at Type 2 = 30 W PSE / 25.50 W at PD, confirmed) but must not be cited to sections 2 and 3.

2. WRONG LEVEL / OPTIMISTIC EFFICIENCY. 25.5 W is PD *input*, not load budget. Raspberry Pi's own PoE+ HAT — the exact BOM line — is "IEEE 802.3at-2009", 37-57 V in, and delivers "5 V DC/4 A" = 20 W to the Pi. That is ~78% of the figure the claim manages against. The proposed architecture inserts a *further* conversion stage (charger + power-path) between flyback and load, subtracting more. All arithmetic should run against ~20 W delivered, not 25.5 W.

3. THE PREMISE IS UNESTABLISHED — the budget is not in crisis. Against ~20 W delivered, the doc's fullest load (CM4 ~5-7 W peak; LTE dongle ~2-3 W; LoRa concentrator ~1-2 W; dual BLE; LED ring/OLED <1 W) lands ~12-14 W peak, leaving 6-8 W headroom. There is no budgeting problem to "dissolve" until a battery is added.

4. DPM'S REAL SCOPE IS NARROWER THAN "THE ONLY WAY". It earns its place only in the Tier C battery variant: charging a 2S pack at ~2 A x 8.4 V ~= 17 W on top of ~13 W load ~= 30 W does bust a 20 W budget, and IINDPM is the right answer there. But Tier B has no battery (the doc puts the UPS HAT only in Tier C), so DPM has nothing to throttle and yields zero budget relief. "The only way" is false; for the base design it is not even load-bearing.

5. "SURVIVES SILENT af DEMOTION GRACEFULLY" IS BACKWARDS. af demotion drops the PD to 12.95 W (confirmed) -> ~10 W delivered, below the ~13 W load. DPM throttles *charging*; with charge already at zero the deficit is drawn from the battery. That is a UPS pack slowly discharging on a permanently under-provisioned link — masking a misprovisioned switch until the battery dies. It needs an explicit alarm. Also only VINDPM reacts automatically (to input droop); matching IINDPM to the *granted class* requires firmware reading the PD controller's class output over I2C. The claim presents as a free chip property something that requires a deliberate control loop.

6. PART SELECTION CONTRADICTS ITS OWN PREMISE. TI lists TPS2372 as "DC/DC control PD Only" — a PD interface with no converter — and as an 802.3bt Type 3/Type 4 part (13/25/51/71 W; -3 to 60 W, -4 to 90 W). So "a single-chip PD interface (e.g. TPS2372) plus flyback" is two chips plus magnetics, and the exemplar is a bt-class part specified against an at-class budget. If the budget really is 25.5 W, the matching part is TPS23730, which TI describes as a PD interface AND current-mode flyback controller in one device, covering 802.3af/at Type 1/2 and bt Type 3, with primary-side regulation that removes the optocoupler. If instead you are paying for a TPS2372, design to Type 3 (51 W at PD) and the budget problem largely evaporates without DPM. Either way the stated pairing is incoherent.

7. "AT VOLUME" IS UNQUANTIFIED AND CUTS AGAINST THE DOC. The doc is explicitly pilot-scale ("an afternoon per batch at pilot scale: flash, boot-test, label") and defers Yocto/buildroot to "when volumes justify it" — volume is a future state. The claim names no unit volume, no NRE, and no cost for the custom carrier, while deleting a $20 line from a $95-120 BOM. Putting an isolated PoE front end on the carrier adds a safety-rated transformer, isolation-barrier creepage/clearance, and product-level EMC (FCC Part 15 / CISPR 32) plus IEC 62368-1 qualification. "Eliminates the entire HAT-stack mechanical question" is true but transfers that cost into a harder board and a certification campaign; it does not eliminate it.

8. MINOR. The doc says "CM4/CM5" for Tier C; the claim narrows to CM4. On CM5 the arithmetic shifts materially — Raspberry Pi ships a 27 W USB-C PD supply with the CM5 dev kit — and ~20 W delivered from an at-class front end becomes marginal.

WHAT SURVIVES: CM4-on-carrier IS genuinely contemplated by the doc (Tier B line "Raspberry Pi 4 (2GB) or CM4 on carrier"; Tier C "CM4/CM5 with soldered eMMC"), so that half of the attribution is accurate. Both chargers are real and ACTIVE at TI, and BQ25798 does provide IINDPM + VINDPM and an NVDC power path with system-load prioritization — the described mechanism works as stated. Integration on one carrier is a defensible direction at genuine volume; it is just not justified by a budget crisis that the doc never asserts and the numbers do not show.

Sources: [Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/poe-plus-hat/), [Power over Ethernet (PSE/PD power per type)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_over_Ethernet), [TI TPS2372](https://www.ti.com/product/TPS2372), [TI TPS23730](https://www.ti.com/product/TPS23730), [TI BQ25798](https://www.ti.com/product/BQ25798), [Raspberry Pi CM5](https://www.raspberrypi.com/products/compute-module-5/), [Raspberry Pi hardware docs](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/raspberry-pi.html)

corrected.original: For Loc8 specifically the battery is NOT theatre, because the gateway's outage-time job is local: BLE mesh relay and database writes, neither of which needs the network.
corrected.corrected:
The battery has a real function, but a narrower one than claimed, and it is not currently specced for the standard build.

WHAT HOLDS: during a venue power cut the gateway's mesh role is genuinely network-independent. `loc8-meshd` keeps scanning, advertising and relaying the 25-byte frames, `loc8-sited` keeps committing mesh-sourced events to the hash-chained log, and `loc8-syncd` backfills on reconnect. That is real local work and it does justify hold-up power — unlike a battery on a pure transit device.

WHAT MUST BE CORRECTED BEFORE AN ENGINEER ORDERS AGAINST IT:

(a) Cite §1 and §2, not §4 and §5. The UPS battery HAT is a Tier C item; §4 and §5 say nothing about power.

(b) Do not state this as a property of "the Loc8 gateway." Tier B — the stated pilot workhorse — has no battery. Either move the UPS HAT into Tier B or strike "battery-backed" from §1's comparison table; as written they contradict each other.

(c) A gateway battery alone does not preserve all outage-time writes. On PoE, power and network share one cable, so a mains cut kills the PoE switch and with it the console→gateway (loc8-relayd/mTLS) path. Only the BLE-sourced write path survives. Add an explicit BOM line: UPS for the PoE switch, or feed the gateway from a PoE injector on the same UPS. Note also that a mains-powered control-room console is dark regardless.

(d) Soften "hole in the audit log." §1 and §8 make every guard phone a spare gateway with laptop-console fallback, so outage-window events are held on phones and reconciled, not lost. The battery buys continuity and centralisation of capture, not uniqueness of capture. It is a resilience improvement, not a data-loss prevention of last resort.

(e) State a required hold-up time and size the pack to it. At ~3-5 W for a Pi 4 with BLE active — more for Tier C's CM4/CM5 plus dual radios — a 2x18650 pack (~22 Wh nominal, cells often not included at ~$25) gives roughly 3-4 h after efficiency and DoD derating; a 2000-3000 mAh LiPo HAT gives under an hour. Without a stated target, "not theatre" cannot be evaluated.

(f) Re-cost the Tier C power path. The Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT occupies both the 40-pin and 4-pin headers and carries a fan, so it does not stack with a typical UPS HAT, and two sources on the 5V rail require ORing/isolation. Spec the actual arrangement (PoE splitter → USB-C into the UPS HAT, or a carrier with integrated PoE + battery management); ~$25 understates it.

(g) Drop or source the assertion that outages coincide with peak incident generation — it is not in the document.
corrected.why:
The claim's direction is defensible but it is not orderable-against, and it fails on five independent counts.

1. CITATION FAILURE. The claim cites §4 and §5. Neither mentions a battery, UPS, or power cut. §4 is the systemd daemon table; §5 is the claim/enroll/operate lifecycle. The UPS battery HAT appears only in §2 under Tier C ("UPS battery HAT (~$25)"), and "battery-backed" appears in §1's comparison table. The claim's evidence is not where it says it is.

2. TIER CONFLATION. The claim says "for Loc8 specifically the battery is NOT theatre," asserting it as a property of the product. The battery is a Tier C ($180-240 ruggedized) item. Tier B — the doc's own "standard install... the pilot workhorse" — has NO battery in its BOM. An engineer ordering Tier B per the BOM correctly orders no battery. §1's table simultaneously advertises the gateway column as "Screwed to a wall, on PoE, battery-backed," which contradicts the Tier B BOM. The claim inherits and amplifies this contradiction instead of flagging it.

3. "NEITHER OF WHICH NEEDS THE NETWORK" IS HALF-WRONG, AND THE WRONG HALF MATTERS. Database writes do not originate on the box. Mesh-sourced writes via loc8-meshd are genuinely network-free — the claim is right there. But loc8-relayd is "authenticated WebSocket fan-out to consoles + gateway phones" and §5 step 4 says "Consoles attach over the LAN (mTLS)." §2 Tier B specs PoE: "Power + network down ONE Ethernet cable." In a venue mains cut the PoE switch loses power too, so the Ethernet link drops. The gateway battery keeps the Pi alive but does not keep the switch alive, so the console-to-gateway write path is dead during exactly the outage the battery covers. Backing up the gateway without backing up the switch/injector buys a partially functional node. This is a missing, orderable BOM line item.

4. THE "HOLE IN THE AUDIT LOG" IS OVERSTATED — THE DOC DESIGNS AGAINST IT. The claim calls this "the decisive point." But §1 line 28 states "every guard phone remains a *spare* gateway," and §8 states "*Fallback modes preserved throughout:* no gateway → any guard phone bridges to a laptop console exactly as today; both paths stay tested." Phones have their own batteries (the claim concedes this), keep meshing, and hold frames for reconciliation. A gateway without a battery therefore does not create a hole in the record; it creates a gap in centralisation and continuity. The battery is a real improvement, not a unique preventer of data loss. "Decisive" is unsupportable.

5. NO HOLD-UP TARGET; THE ~$25 FIGURE UNDERSTATES INTEGRATION. The doc never states how long the gateway must ride out a cut, so "not theatre" is unfalsifiable as written. Re-deriving: a Pi 4 with BLE scanning, external antenna and SD/eMMC write load draws roughly 3-5 W; Tier C specs CM4/CM5 plus "dual BLE radios (concurrent scan + advertise)," pushing higher. A 2x18650 UPS HAT is ~22 Wh nominal (cells frequently sold separately at the ~$25 price), which after boost-converter efficiency (~85-90%) and usable depth-of-discharge yields roughly 3-4 hours; a 2000-3000 mAh LiPo HAT (7-11 Wh) yields well under an hour. Separately, verified against Raspberry Pi's PoE+ HAT product page: it mates to "the two 0.1\" headers (40 + 4)" and carries an I2C-controlled fan on top. Standard UPS HATs also require the 40-pin header plus vertical space for cells. The two do not simply stack, and two power sources driving the 5V rail needs ORing/isolation. Tier C needs an explicit arrangement (PoE splitter to USB-C into the UPS HAT, or a carrier with integrated PoE + battery management) — not a ~$25 line item.

6. THE QUOTE IS USED AGAINST ITS OWN SENSE. §5 step 4 calls the gateway "the strongest node — always on, wall-powered, big antenna." The claim cites this to prove the battery matters "when the site is dark," but *wall-powered* is precisely the attribute that fails in an outage. On battery the gateway loses the property the sentence uses to justify its primacy.

7. UNSOURCED EMPIRICAL ASSERTION. "That hole coincides with the period most likely to generate incidents" is intuitive but appears nowhere in the document and no source is offered. In a spec justifying a BOM line, that is an assumption presented as fact.

corrected.original: What the battery does NOT buy: a working control room. Loc8 Command talks to the gateway over the LAN, through the switch that just died.
corrected.corrected:
What the battery does not buy: a working control room — and on a PoE build it never can. Because the PoE+ HAT carries "power + network down ONE Ethernet cable" (sec 2, Tier B), a dead switch is simultaneously the power failure the battery answers and the network failure it cannot. The battery keeps the gateway meshing and writing SQLite; it cannot keep Loc8 Command attached, since consoles reach the box over the LAN via mTLS and discover it via mDNS on the same network (sec 5, steps 2 and 4).

Three corrections to how this is usually stated:

1. The battery is a Tier C line item only (sec 2, ~$25 UPS HAT). Tier B — the designated "pilot workhorse" — has no battery, so a Tier B gateway simply dies with the switch. Also unresolved: the PoE+ HAT occupies both the 40-pin GPIO and 4-pin PoE headers, so stacking a GPIO-header UPS HAT on the same Pi needs a specified mechanical solution before either is ordered.

2. Neither documented fallback covers this case. Sec 6 Layer 0 ("the box's Wi-Fi is WPA2/3") is a statement about encryption, not an AP mode — the doc nowhere specifies the gateway serving Wi-Fi that consoles associate to, and assigns the hotspot role to the laptop (sec 1). Sec 8's fallback is explicitly "no gateway → any guard phone bridges to a laptop console," which bypasses the gateway rather than restoring the view of it. Because site state lives in the box's SQLite and "consoles become stateless viewers" (sec 4, sec 5 step 4), that fallback console comes up with no incident history, no muster state, and no audit log — while the isolated gateway keeps hash-chaining its own, forking the record.

3. Sec 8 already commits that "both paths stay tested." The gap is not testing discipline but scenario coverage: the tested case is "no gateway," while the case here is "gateway alive and accruing state, LAN dead." That case is unnamed in the doc.

The only path that survives as written is the LTE add-on (sec 2), which keeps the box visible to HQ — but sec 7 makes off-site "read-mostly by default," so the sole surviving observer is the one the design forbids from commanding. The fallback actually worth specifying and ordering against is the direct one: the box has 1× RJ45 (sec 3), so a laptop patched straight into it bypasses the switch. That requires the Tier C battery (PoE injection is gone) and requires verifying the box self-assigns a link-local address and answers _loc8._tcp mDNS with no DHCP server present. Add the patch cable to the install kit and make that the tested outage console path.
corrected.why:
Substantially right in its core insight but imprecise in four ways that matter for a parts order.

VERIFIED: Sec 5 step 4 says "Consoles attach over the LAN (mTLS)"; step 2 makes mDNS discovery/claim depend on "the same network." Sec 8 line 169 contains the phone-bridge fallback verbatim. Sec 1 line 26 does frame the laptop/hotspot chain as "a selling point." So a dead switch does isolate a live gateway from the console.

FAILS:
(1) TIER SCOPING. The UPS battery HAT (~$25) is at line 50 under Tier C ($180-240) only — it is in section 2, not in the cited sections 5/6/8. Tier B, the doc's self-declared "pilot workhorse" and the tier the physical spec is written against, has NO battery. An engineer ordering Tier B would reason about a mitigation not in the BOM.

(2) UNDERSTATES ITSELF. Line 42: PoE+ HAT = "Power + network down ONE Ethernet cable." The dead switch IS the power failure — the same event by construction. So on PoE the battery never buys console connectivity, not just in an unlucky case. Confirmed via raspberrypi.com/products/poe-plus-hat/ that the PoE+ HAT occupies both the 40-pin GPIO and 4-pin PoE headers plus four corner spacers, so co-mounting a GPIO-header UPS HAT is an unresolved mechanical question the BOM does not address.

(3) FABRICATED FALLBACK — most serious. Sec 6 Layer 0 reads "the box's Wi-Fi (when used) is WPA2/3" — a statement about ENCRYPTION, not an access-point console path. Nothing in the doc says the gateway can act as an AP consoles associate to. Line 6 assigns the hotspot role to the LAPTOP; lines 34 and 95 treat the box's Wi-Fi as a client-mode join and a syncd uplink. If client-mode onto venue APs, those APs are typically PoE-fed from the same dead switch, so it is not independent regardless. The claim promotes a security note into an orderable fallback that does not exist.

(4) PHONE-BRIDGE DOESN'T DO THIS. Line 169 is explicitly "NO GATEWAY -> any guard phone bridges to a laptop console" — it bypasses the gateway rather than restoring the view of it. Per line 94 and step 4, site state (incidents, roster, muster, hash-chained audit log) lives in the box's SQLite and "consoles become stateless viewers." The fallback console comes up STATELESS, and the audit chain forks while the isolated gateway keeps hash-chaining locally — a reconciliation problem the doc never addresses.

(5) Line 170 already commits "both paths stay tested," so "must be tested, not merely retained" misreads sec 8. The real gap is that the tested scenario is "no gateway," not "gateway alive, LAN dead."

MISSED: with the LTE add-on (line 55) the gateway stays visible to HQ — but sec 7 restricts off-site to "read-mostly by default," so the only surviving observer is the one explicitly barred from commanding. Also missed: the 1x RJ45 (line 70) permits a direct laptop-to-gateway patch cable bypassing the switch entirely, which is the fallback the doc SHOULD specify — but it requires Tier C battery (PoE injection is gone) and link-local/mDNS addressing with no DHCP server present.

corrected.original: What the battery does NOT buy: off-site visibility. Without the LTE dongle, battery plus outage still means the site goes dark to HQ.
corrected.corrected:
What the battery does NOT buy: off-site visibility — in the branch that matters.

Tier B/C takes power and uplink from the same PoE switch, so one dead switch removes both. A UPS battery keeps the box, the mesh and the local SQLite alive; it does not by itself restore the path to HQ. In that branch HQ sees only a stale tile and cannot tell "gateway destroyed" from "uplink down". Battery alone is local-only insurance. Quote the battery and the LTE dongle together — they address the same failure and neither is sufficient alone.

Four corrections before anyone orders parts:

1. The coupling is conditional, not universal. loc8-syncd runs over Ethernet/Wi-Fi/LTE (§4). If the venue's switch/router/AP is already on house UPS — routine wherever there is a comms closet or an alarm panel — PoE keeps the gateway up and the wired uplink alive, and neither line item is needed for a short cut. If it is not, both are. Survey the rack per site; do not spec either blind.

2. LTE spends the battery it is meant to complement. Budget it explicitly. A 2x 18650 pack is 25.2 Wh raw, ~20 Wh usable after boost-converter loss and cell cutoff. Pi 4 with continuous BLE scan/advertise ~4 W gives ~5 h. A Cat-4 USB LTE modem adds ~1.0-1.5 W average with 2-3 W transmit bursts, giving ~5.2 W and ~3.8 h — roughly a quarter of the reserve gone. LTE PA current spikes on a battery-fed 5 V rail through Pi USB-A are a known undervoltage/reset mode, i.e. the modem is likeliest to brown out the board exactly when it is the only link. Size the pack and the 5 V rail against the LTE load, not the idle load.

3. LTE narrows the ambiguity; it does not remove it. A dark tile with LTE fitted is still ambiguous between gateway destroyed, modem failure, no coverage, SIM data exhausted, and carrier congestion — and regional outages congest cell networks. §2's own pitch ("no wifi and jammed cell still appears live") is incoherent, since a jammed cell defeats the dongle; fix that line. What actually removes the ambiguity is a software contract §7 does not yet specify: a periodic liveness heartbeat carrying power source and uplink state, so HQ distinguishes "on battery, uplink down, mesh healthy" from silence. Spec the heartbeat whether or not the dongle is fitted — it is cheaper and it is the thing the dashboard needs. Note §7 currently frames its goal as showing staleness honestly, not as disambiguating cause; if disambiguation is the goal, say so there.

4. The BOM does not currently permit the pairing. The UPS battery HAT appears only inside Tier C, not under "Add-on modules (any tier)" where LTE sits, so there is no battery line item to order against a Tier B install — and it cannot simply be added, because the Tier B PoE+ HAT occupies the 40-pin GPIO header (plus the 4-pin PoE header) that GPIO-mounted UPS HATs need. Tier B needs a CM4-carrier power path or a non-GPIO UPS before "battery + LTE" is orderable. I read the stated source in full (/Users/augustusedem/Loc8/.claude/worktrees/recursing-montalcini-d59018/docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md) and verified the two hardware assumptions the claim leans on against vendor pages.

WHAT SURVIVES. The core insight is sound and non-obvious: Tier B/C draws power AND uplink from the same PoE switch (§2 "PoE+ HAT | Power + network down ONE Ethernet cable"), so one dead switch takes out both. A battery keeps the box, mesh and local SQLite alive without restoring the path to HQ. The LTE dongle is correctly described as an existing "Add-on modules (any tier)" line. The sales conclusion — quote the two together — holds.

1. Stated as unconditional when it is conditional. §4 defines loc8-syncd as running over "any uplink (Ethernet/Wi-Fi/LTE)". If the venue's own switch/router/AP sits on house UPS — routine wherever there is a comms closet or alarm panel — PoE keeps the gateway up AND the uplink alive, and neither line item is needed for a short cut. "Battery plus outage still means the site goes dark to HQ" is true only in the sub-branch where the venue's network gear is unpowered, which the source never establishes. The value of BOTH line items is a function of one unsurveyed variable.

2. LTE is presented as pure upside; it spends the battery it is meant to complement. This is the load-bearing omission for someone ordering parts. Arithmetic the claim never does: 2x 18650 at 3400 mAh = 25.2 Wh raw; boost conversion (~88%) and cell cutoff leave ~20 Wh usable. Pi 4 with continuous BLE scan+advertise and SQLite writes ~4 W -> ~5 h. A Cat-4 USB LTE modem adds ~1.0-1.5 W average with 2-3 W transmit bursts -> ~5.2 W -> ~3.8 h. Adding LTE costs roughly a quarter of the reserve, and LTE PA current spikes on a battery-fed 5 V rail through Pi USB-A are a known undervoltage/reset mode — i.e. the modem is most likely to brown out the board at exactly the moment it is the only link. Any "battery + LTE" spec must size the pack against the LTE load, not the idle load.

3. Overstated source attribution. §7 does not say the dashboard exists to disambiguate destroyed-vs-unreachable; under "Graceful degradation" it says the opposite emphasis — "the cloud shows staleness honestly and backfills on reconnect." The claim attributes a design intent to the source and then uses it as the rhetorical lever ("critically", "the exact ambiguity the portfolio dashboard exists to remove"). That is confidence the cited section does not support.

4. LTE narrows the ambiguity, it does not remove it. "Battery plus LTE means HQ keeps live sight" is guarantee-shaped language about a best-effort link. A dark tile with LTE fitted is still ambiguous between gateway destroyed, modem failure, no coverage, SIM data exhausted, and carrier congestion — and regional outages congest cell networks. Note the source's own LTE justification is internally incoherent: §2 sells the dongle as covering "no wifi and jammed cell", but a jammed cell defeats an LTE dongle. The claim inherits that without flagging it. The actual ambiguity-remover is a software liveness heartbeat carrying power-source and uplink state, which §7 does not specify and which is cheaper than the dongle.

5. BOM defect the claim misdescribes. It calls battery and LTE "two line items" to be specified together, but the UPS battery HAT appears ONLY inside Tier C ($180-240), not under "Add-on modules (any tier)" where LTE sits. There is no battery line item to order against a Tier B "pilot workhorse" install. Nor can it be dropped in: raspberrypi.com confirms the PoE+ HAT connects to "the two 0.1in headers (40 + 4)", and GPIO-mounted UPS HATs need that same 40-pin header — a mechanical conflict at Tier B.

6. Stale price. The source's "~$25" UPS HAT, carried forward uncritically by the claim as part of its cost-benefit case, is optimistic. Geekworm's X728 — a representative 40-pin GPIO Pi UPS board — lists at $44.00, and its packing list is board, screws, spacers and jumper only: 18650 cells are NOT included, adding ~$10-20. Real installed cost is roughly $55-65, not $25. (Verified: geekworm.com/products/x728; raspberrypi.com/products/poe-plus-hat/. Waveshare's UPS HAT wiki returned 403 and the Pi PoE+ product brief PDF 404'd, so the header-conflict finding rests on the Pi product page plus the X728 spec.)

corrected.original: Battery-backing the switch is far better engineering per watt-hour, but it is the venue's purchase, not Loc8's — so it must be an install requirement, not a design dependency.
corrected.corrected:
Battery-backing the PoE switch is the right *commercial* and *serviceability* call, but not on energy or cost-per-watt-hour grounds — those favor distributed cells. Correct basis:

WHAT IS TRUE: a rack UPS is amortized across the venue's cameras, APs and NVR, so Loc8 pays nothing incremental; it lives in a locked room with one service point and a scheduled replacement cycle; and it keeps the *switch* alive, without which a locally-powered node is powered but islanded. It also avoids per-unit BOM (charger IC, protection, enclosure thermal design) and UN 38.3 / IATA-DOT lithium shipping burden.

WHAT IS FALSE AND MUST NOT GO IN THE SPEC: the UPS does not have better energy density — VRLA is 30–50 Wh/kg and 60–75 Wh/L against 205–220 Wh/kg and 580–600 Wh/L for 18650-class cells, a 4–7x mass and 8–10x volume deficit. Nor is it better per watt-hour: holding up a node through the UPS costs inverter (~90%), switch PSU (~88%), PoE PSE→PD (85% per 802.3at's 25.5 W-from-30 W) and PD SMPS (10–25%) losses, plus the switch's 25–40 W idle draw regardless of node count — about 97 W off the battery to deliver 40 W to eight 5 W nodes, ~41% end-to-end, versus ~43.5 W for local cells at ~92%. That is ~2.2x the watt-hours and, in VRLA, ~12x the battery mass. The advantage is amortization across N devices, and it is N-dependent — state N. Cost per watt-hour is roughly a wash (~$0.25–0.37/Wh for replacement VRLA vs ~$0.32–0.48/Wh retail / <$0.15/Wh OEM for 18650).

REGULATORY — DOWNGRADE TO UNVERIFIED: do not assert an AHJ/fire-code objection to small cells. NFPA 855 and IFC §1207 govern stationary ESS at kWh aggregate scale, not watt-hour cells inside NRTL-listed equipment (UL 62368-1 end product, UL 2054 / IEC 62133 pack); I could not retrieve either code text to confirm the threshold, so cite none. Note the counterexample: code-mandated self-contained emergency lighting puts battery, charger and control in wall-mounted fixtures throughout every commercial venue.

RELIABILITY — REVERSE IT: silent capacity fade is the VRLA-in-a-warm-rack failure mode (3–5 year consumable) more than the Li-ion one (~80% at 3 years under float). "One battery-health indicator" is one unreliable indicator over a single point of failure for all N devices — hence the standard advice to run rundown tests every 6–12 months. Put that test interval in the service schedule.

SPEC IT AS BOTH, NOT EITHER: state a ride-through requirement in two regimes and source them separately. (a) Onboard holdup sized for seconds-to-minutes, in the Loc8 device, covering the common faults a UPS cannot — tripped downstream branch circuit, unplugged patch cable, failed PoE port, switch firmware reboot, PoE renegotiation. Supercap or bulk capacitance is usually sufficient and sidesteps the Li-ion logistics entirely. (b) 'PoE switch and its uplink on UPS' as a site-survey line item alongside mounting height and PoE class, sized by the venue for their own outage tolerance, sold on the fact that it protects their cameras and APs too. Record on the survey sheet: switch idle draw, node count N, and target ride-through minutes — without those three numbers no one can size either element.

Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_commercial_battery_types , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_over_Ethernet , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uninterruptible_power_supply , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_light . NFPA 855 and IFC 2021 §1207 could not be retrieved (no scope content / HTTP 403) — treat all code-threshold statements as unverified.
corrected.why:
The conclusion (put it on the site-survey sheet; don't make the product depend on it; sell it on the customer's terms) is sound, but every stated engineering ground is wrong or overstated — and since this is destined for a spec an engineer orders parts against, the wrong grounds matter.

1) ENERGY DENSITY IS BACKWARDS BY ~5–10x. Wikipedia's commercial battery comparison gives lead-acid/VRLA 30–50 Wh/kg and 60–75 Wh/L; NCA 220 Wh/kg / 600 Wh/L and NMC 205 Wh/kg / 580 Wh/L (18650 chemistries). Distributed 18650s beat a VRLA rack UPS by ~4–7x on mass and ~8–10x on volume. Rack UPSes in the price band a venue buys for a PoE switch are overwhelmingly VRLA; where a Li-ion rack UPS is used it runs the *same cells*, so density is at best a tie and never a UPS advantage. "Vastly better ... energy density" for the UPS is simply false.

2) "PER WATT-HOUR" IS ALSO BACKWARDS, BY ~2x — CONVERSION CHAIN AND SWITCH OVERHEAD ARE UNCOUNTED. To hold up one node via the switch UPS the battery must carry: inverter DC→AC (~90%), switch AC→DC PSU (~88%), PoE PSE→PD (802.3at: 25.5 W at PD from 30 W at PSE = 85% per IEEE figures), the PD's own SMPS (a further "10 to 25%" per the same source), AND the switch's idle/fabric/fan draw (~25–40 W on a 24-port managed PoE switch), which the battery pays for whether one node or twenty is attached. Worked for N=8 nodes at 5 W: 40 W at the PDs → ~47 W PSE-side → +30 W switch overhead → ~87.5 W AC → ~97 W off the UPS battery. End-to-end ~41%. A local cell through a single buck stage (~92%) needs ~43.5 W. For 2 h ride-through: 194 Wh of VRLA (~4.9 kg at 40 Wh/kg) vs 87 Wh of Li-ion (~0.4 kg at 220 Wh/kg) — ~2.2x the watt-hours and ~12x the mass. The centralized option is the *worse* one per watt-hour. Note the overhead term means the comparison is N-dependent: the UPS only closes the gap at large N, and the claim states it unconditionally.

3) COST PER WATT-HOUR IS NOT A UPS WIN EITHER. Replacement VRLA (2× 12 V 9 Ah = 216 Wh) runs ~$0.25–0.37/Wh; a quality 3.5 Ah 18650 (12.6 Wh) is ~$0.32–0.48/Wh at retail singles and well under $0.15/Wh at OEM volume. Roughly a wash, tilting to Li-ion in volume — before applying the 2.2x Wh penalty above. The UPS's real cost advantage is amortization across cameras/APs/NVR and the fact that Loc8 pays $0 for it, plus avoided BOM (charger IC, protection, enclosure thermal design) and avoided UN 38.3 / IATA-DOT lithium shipping burden. Those are the honest arguments; "cost per watt-hour" is not, and an engineer who believes it will size the wrong thing.

4) THE REGULATORY CLAIM IS STATED MORE CONFIDENTLY THAN SOURCES SUPPORT, AND NAMES THE WRONG MECHANISM. I could not retrieve NFPA 855 or IFC 2021 §1207 text (NFPA page returned no scope content; ICC returned HTTP 403), so no specific kWh threshold should appear in a spec on my authority. But the mechanism cited is likely wrong: NFPA 855 / IFC 1207 govern *stationary energy storage systems* at kWh aggregate scale, not ~12.6 Wh cells inside listed equipment, which are governed by product listing (UL 62368-1 end product; UL 2054 / IEC 62133 pack). Direct counterexample from a retrieved source: self-contained emergency lighting units — battery, charger and control in one wall-mounted fixture, distributed throughout every commercial venue, 90-minute runtime — are *code-mandated* under the Life Safety Code and NEC, not a code liability. Distributed wall-mounted battery boxes across a venue is the code-normal condition. (Caveat that favors the claim: those units use lead-calcium, not Li-ion, so the counterexample establishes "distributed batteries are normal," not "Li-ion specifically is unremarkable to every AHJ.")

5) THE STATE-OF-HEALTH ARGUMENT CUTS AGAINST THE UPS HARDER. "A 3-year-old pack at 60% SoH fails silently the one time it is needed" is the canonical VRLA-in-a-warm-rack failure, not the Li-ion one; VRLA is a 3–5 year consumable while lightly-cycled Li-ion under float typically holds ~80% at 3 years. The Wikipedia UPS article's own maintenance guidance — rundown tests "every six months to a year" — exists precisely because UPS self-test does not reliably detect capacity fade. So "one battery-health indicator" is a single unreliable indicator guarding a single point of failure for all N devices, versus distributed packs that fail independently and degrade gracefully across the fleet.

6) THE FRAMING IS A FALSE DICHOTOMY AND LEAVES THE SPEC EMPTY. "Loc8 can't compel the purchase" does not entail "not a design dependency" — Loc8 can't compel an 802.3at PSE either, and that is unambiguously a design dependency. More importantly the two options are not substitutes ranked on one axis: a UPS does nothing for a tripped downstream branch circuit, a yanked patch cable, a failed PoE port, or a switch firmware reboot (all more common than a venue-wide mains outage), and an onboard cell does nothing when the switch itself is dead. They cover different failure regimes and different durations. Writing "PoE switch on UPS" on a survey sheet with no stated ride-through requirement hands the parts-ordering engineer no holdup spec at all.

7) UNSTATED DEPENDENCY THAT DECIDES THE QUESTION. The genuinely strong argument for backing the switch is topological, not energetic: a node with a local cell stays powered but islanded if the switch dies. Whether that matters depends on whether a Loc8 node is useful without its uplink — for a mesh-anchor role it may well be. The claim never states this, and it is the actual deciding variable.

corrected.original: Size the onboard battery for ride-through and graceful behaviour (20-40 minutes), not endurance — a bigger pack does not buy proportionally more value.
corrected.corrected:
Size the onboard battery for ride-through and graceful behaviour (20-40 minutes), not endurance — a bigger pack does not buy proportionally more value.

At the 8.5 W estimated Tier C load, 20-40 min is 2.8-5.7 Wh USABLE. After boost-converter efficiency (~88%) and cutoff-limited depth of discharge (~90%), that needs ~7.0-7.8 Wh nameplate — order a single 18650-class cell of at least 3000 mAh (11.1 Wh nameplate, ~8.8 Wh delivered). Do not spec a 2000 mAh cell: it delivers ~5.9 Wh and has no margin at the 40-minute end.

Charging headroom is set by the PoE HAT, not the 802.3at standard. The official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT (802.3at-2009, Class 4) outputs 5 V / 4 A = 20 W; an 8.5 W load draws 1.70 A, leaving ~2.3 A / 11.5 W for charging. If the design deliberately limits charge current to ~1.25 A, state that as a cell-protection choice (~0.4C), not as a PoE budget — the misattribution under-states available headroom by roughly 2x.

Treat 8.5 W as a typical, not worst-case, figure. The scenario that justifies the battery — mesh-plus-LTE island operation with LTE as sole uplink under sustained transmit — runs above typical, so plan for the low end of the runtime band or re-derive against a measured island-mode load.

Tier assignment must be fixed before ordering. The doc currently places the UPS battery HAT in Tier C only, but Tier C uses soldered eMMC with no SD card to corrupt, while Tier B — the pilot workhorse — carries the vulnerable industrial microSD and has no pack. Graceful-shutdown SD protection is a Tier B benefit; either add the battery to Tier B or justify the Tier C pack solely on ride-through and uptime.

Regulatory: a single ~11 Wh cell sits under both the 20 Wh per-cell and 100 Wh per-battery thresholds, so it avoids fully regulated Class 9 treatment. This is not the same as unencumbered air freight — UN 38.3 test evidence, PI 966/967 packing instructions for cells contained in or packed with equipment, lithium-battery marking, and state-of-charge limits still apply. Confirm against the current IATA DGR edition before shipping; the thresholds above were not verifiable against primary IATA/FAA text in this review.
corrected.why:
The core thesis (size for ride-through, not endurance; ~one cell) is sound and the arithmetic is essentially right, but three specifics fail verification and one would mis-spec a part order.

1. ARITHMETIC — substantially correct, rounded outward. 8.5 W x 20/60 = 2.83 Wh; x 40/60 = 5.67 Wh. Claim says "3-6 Wh", ~6% high at both ends. More importantly it conflates usable with nameplate: delivering 5.67 Wh usable needs ~7.0-7.8 Wh nameplate after boost efficiency (85-90%) and cutoff-limited DoD (85-90%). A 3000 mAh 18650 (11.1 Wh nameplate, ~8.8 Wh delivered) works; a 2000 mAh cell (7.4 Wh nameplate, ~5.9 Wh delivered) is marginal. "One modest cell" is only true if "modest" means >=3000 mAh.

2. THE 1.25 A PoE CHARGING BUDGET IS UNSUPPORTABLE. The official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT (verified via raspberrypi.com product page) is IEEE 802.3at-2009 Class 4, output 5 V / 4 A = 20 W. An 8.5 W load = 1.70 A at 5 V, leaving 2.30 A / 11.5 W headroom — roughly double the claimed 1.25 A. The figure appears nowhere in the repo (grep for "8.5 W" and "1.25 A" returns zero hits) and matches no PoE constraint; it resembles a ~0.4C cell charge rate misattributed to PoE. The claim also cites the standard rather than the HAT: the HAT's 20 W output, not 802.3at's 25.5 W PD guarantee, is binding.

3. THE microSD JUSTIFICATION POINTS AT THE WRONG TIER — most consequential. docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md puts the "UPS battery HAT (~$25)" in Tier C only, and Tier C is defined as "CM4/CM5 with soldered eMMC (no SD to corrupt)". Tier B — which carries the "Industrial microSD 32GB" and is labelled "the pilot workhorse" — has no battery in its BOM. So the battery ships on the only tier that does not have the failure mode invoked to justify it. Either add the pack to Tier B or drop that rationale.

4. REGULATORY OVERSTATEMENT. 100 Wh is genuine as the Class 9 threshold, but for a single-cell design the governing limit is 20 Wh per cell, and staying under 100 Wh does not clear air freight — UN 38.3 testing, PI 966/967 packing instructions, lithium-battery marking, and state-of-charge limits still apply. Primary text was unverifiable this session (WebSearch budget exhausted at 200/200; IATA guidance PDF unparseable; FAA returned 403), so this is flagged as stated more confidently than sources support rather than replaced with asserted numbers.

5. LOAD/SCENARIO MISMATCH (minor). 8.5 W is plausible (pidramble measures Pi 4B at 2.7 W idle / 6.4 W at 400% CPU; dual BLE + LTE + LED ring reaching 8.5 W is fair). But the claim's own justification — that marginal runtime "only helps the mesh-plus-LTE island case" — describes the configuration where LTE is the sole uplink under sustained TX, i.e. above the "typical" figure used to size the pack. Real runtime in the justifying scenario sits at the low end of 20-40 min.

VERIFIED AS STATED: the 150x110x40 mm Tier C envelope (doc section 3, line 68) and the eMMC-vs-SD framing (line 49). The "beyond 30 min the LAN is gone anyway" reasoning is also sound — the gateway's PoE comes from the switch, so outliving it means being powered but unreachable.

corrected.original: An uninstrumented battery IS theatre — the appliance must report input source, state of charge, pack health and time-on-battery, with its own status-lens state.
corrected.corrected:
Where a UPS option is fitted (Tier C today; optional on Tier B), the pack MUST be instrumented — an uninstrumented battery is an untestable assumption, not a resilience feature.

BOM constraint: the UPS HAT must expose host-readable power state over I2C — a fuel gauge (TI BQ27xxx-class for coulomb counting, or MAX1704x-class for state-of-charge only) or at minimum an INA219-class bus-voltage/current monitor plus a charger-status GPIO. A bare "~$25 UPS HAT" does not satisfy this; much of that price band is dumb power-path hardware with only a 4-LED indicator and no host interface. Budget accordingly and re-quote against telemetry capability, not price alone.

Telemetry the appliance must report: (a) active input source — PoE / USB-C / battery; (b) pack state of charge, %; (c) pack voltage and instantaneous load current; (d) estimated runtime remaining at present load — this is the figure that drives the shutdown decision; (e) elapsed time-on-battery, as a log field; (f) pack state of health where the fitted gauge supports it.

State of health caveat — this is the part that must not be over-promised. Voltage-based gauges report no SoH at all. Coulomb-counting gauges expose SoH as learned full-charge capacity against design capacity, and that value requires a qualified discharge cycle before it is meaningful. A float-charged wall UPS never discharges and so never learns, leaving SoH pinned at its initialized value — the degraded cell is still discovered during the outage. Therefore the requirement is a scheduled self-test, not a register read: on a defined interval (monthly, configurable), the box commands an input disconnect, discharges into the live load for a bounded window, measures delivered capacity against design, restores input, writes the result to the audit log, and raises a replace-pack condition below a stated threshold (e.g. <70% of design). The power path must support commanded input disconnect under load; select the HAT accordingly.

Logging and sync: loc8-sited records power-source transitions and self-test results into the hash-chained audit log; loc8-syncd pushes them, and HQ surfaces battery state per site tile. Transitions must be debounced (suggest 5 s hysteresis) so a marginal injector cannot flood an append-only log.

Light grammar (section 3): "running on battery" needs a distinct signal, but the single ◈ lens is one-hot and on a PoE box mains loss also kills the uplink, so on-battery and uplink-down co-occur by construction. Resolve explicitly — either define a strict priority order in which on-battery (suggest amber/red slow blink) outranks the existing amber pulse for uplink-down, or add a second smaller power-state indicator. Do not add a fifth mutually-exclusive state without stating the precedence. Boxes with no pack fitted must not display a battery-fault state. While editing, reconcile the existing inconsistency between section 3's "white chase" and section 5's "breathes white" for unclaimed.

Also correct section 1's table: "battery-backed" is a Tier C property (or a Tier B option), not a general one.
corrected.why:
Directionally correct — the doc genuinely specifies a bare "UPS battery HAT (~$25)" (section 2, Tier C) with no telemetry requirement anywhere, and that is a real gap. The claim's reading of section 3's light grammar is accurate (green breathing / amber pulse = uplink down / red / white chase), as is its reading of section 4 (loc8-sited owns the hash-chained audit log, loc8-syncd pushes it). But it fails on four load-bearing specifics an engineer would order parts against.

(1) SCOPE ERROR. Section 3 is explicitly "Physical spec (Tier B reference)". Tier B's BOM has a PoE+ HAT and NO battery; the UPS HAT is a Tier C-only line. "The appliance must report ... state of charge, pack health" is unsatisfiable on Tiers A/B — there is no pack. The requirement must be conditional on the UPS option being fitted, and the grammar must distinguish "no battery installed" from "battery fault". (Section 1's table separately over-claims the box as generally "battery-backed" when the BOM makes it optional.)

(2) THE STATED BENEFIT DOES NOT FOLLOW FROM THE STATED TELEMETRY — the core defect. Exposing an SoH figure does not yield "a degraded cell replaced before the outage." Voltage-based gauges (MAX1704x ModelGauge class) report only SoC and cell voltage — no SoH quantity exists. Coulomb-counting gauges (TI BQ27xxx / Impedance Track) do expose a StateOfHealth register, but it is derived from learned full-charge capacity vs design capacity and requires a qualified discharge / learning cycle to become meaningful (confirmed against the BQ27441-G1 datasheet at ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/bq27441-g1.pdf; that fetch returned largely compressed PDF stream data so the register-level wording is directional, but the learning-cycle dependency is established Impedance Track behavior). A wall-mounted PoE UPS float-charges near 100% for months and essentially never discharges, so it never completes a learning cycle and SoH stays pinned near its initialized value. The precise failure mode the claim promises to prevent is the one that survives. The actual preventive mechanism — what real UPS and emergency-lighting systems do — is a periodic SCHEDULED SELF-TEST: commanded input disconnect, bounded discharge into the live load, delivered capacity measured against design, logged and alarmed. That is a firmware plus power-path requirement (the path must support commanded input disconnect under load), which the claim omits entirely.

(3) PARTS RISK. A large share of the ~$25 UPS HAT field is dumb power-path boards with at best a 4-LED charge indicator and no I2C at all. "Instrumented" narrows the BOM to a HAT carrying a host-readable gauge (fuel gauge over I2C, or at minimum an INA219-class V/I monitor plus charger-status GPIO) and generally raises the price. Ordering "a $25 UPS HAT" and expecting SoC/SoH is the concrete way this spec fails at the counter.

(4) SINGLE-LENS ENCODING COLLISION. The doc specifies "a single ◈ status lens" with a one-hot grammar. On a PoE-powered box, mains loss is exactly what kills the injector/switch, so "running on battery" and "uplink down" (already amber pulse) are not independent conditions — they co-occur in the common case. One lens cannot display both. The spec needs a stated priority order (on-battery outranks uplink-down) or a second indicator, not merely "its own signal." The claim asserts the requirement without resolving the collision it creates.

Also: "time-on-battery" is the log field, whereas estimated runtime remaining is the operationally actionable number that drives a shutdown decision. Power-source transition logging needs debounce/hysteresis so a flapping injector cannot flood an append-only hash-chained audit log. Minor citation slip: the battery lives in section 2, not sections 3-4 as stated. And the doc is already internally inconsistent — section 3 says unclaimed = "white chase", section 5 step 1 says "breathes white" — which should be fixed in the same edit.

3. COST: the switch-UPS is the most expensive item in this design, not a free condition — it must carry a PoE+ switch (60-130W budget on 8 ports). Size and price it explicitly. Also note it partly moots the in-box battery, which then covers only cable/port/HAT faults.

Doc revisions required — lines 20 and 51 as stated, PLUS:

Re-quote all prices at order time; the $20 PoE+ HAT and $25 UPS HAT figures were not independently confirmed.
corrected.why:
Substantially right in direction, but wrong or unsupported in every number an engineer would order against, and incomplete in its remediation list.

(1) BATTERY SIZING IS UNSOURCED AND CONTRADICTS THE DOC'S OWN BOM. Measured Pi 4B draw is 2.7W idle / 5.1W web-serving / 6.4W at 400% CPU (pidramble). At a realistic 4-7W gateway load (Pi + BLE radio + optional LTE), the ~$25 UPS battery HAT already on line 50 (2x18650 class, ~25Wh raw, ~21Wh usable at 85% boost efficiency) delivers 3.1-5.4 hours. The claim's "20-40 minute" target implies only 1.3-4.7Wh — a single small LiPo, roughly 4-8x smaller. The figure is never derived from a load. An engineer ordering to it would spec a worse part than the doc already calls for and silently downgrade Tier C.

(2) THE "WRONG TRADE" VERDICT IS BACKWARDS ON INTEGRATION RISK. The official Raspberry Pi PoE+ HAT mounts to "the two 0.1" headers (40 + 4)" — it consumes the full 40-pin GPIO header and carries a fan in the Pi's vertical envelope. Off-the-shelf Pi UPS HATs require that same header. PoE HAT + UPS HAT is therefore NOT a stack-and-go parts order on the Tier B Pi 4; it needs a passthrough riser (mechanically obstructed by the fan) or a custom CM4 carrier integrating both — a PCB project, not a BOM line. Local DC + UPS HAT is the combination that IS orderable off the shelf. The claim labels the buildable option "the wrong trade" and makes the custom-hardware option the default, without costing that integration.

(3) "PoE" IS UNDER-SPECIFIED FOR PROCUREMENT; IT MUST SAY 802.3at. Worst-case simultaneous draw (Pi 6.4W + PoE HAT fan ~1W + LTE dongle ~3W peak + recharging a 25Wh pack over 4h at ~7.4W) = 17.8W. That exceeds the 802.3af PD budget of 12.95W and fits only 802.3at's 25.5W. A buyer ordering an 802.3af switch against the bare word "PoE" gets brownouts during post-outage recharge — precisely when the appliance matters.

(4) THE SWITCH-UPS IS TREATED AS A FREE INSTALL CONDITION AND IS PARTLY SELF-CANCELLING. The switch is a PoE+ switch (8-port units commonly budget 60-130W), so its UPS is the most expensive item the claim introduces, not a one-line condition. Worse, if the PoE switch sits on a UPS, that UPS already backs the gateway through the Ethernet cable — the in-box battery then covers only cable/port/HAT faults and UPS failure. The claim asserts belt and braces without acknowledging the redundancy or sizing the UPS.

(5) THE REMEDIATION LIST MISSES THE WORST OFFENDER AND THE PRICE CONSEQUENCE. Lines 20 and 51 do over-promise, correctly identified. But line 10 — the headline pitch, "plug it into power-over-Ethernet... survives power cuts" — is the most prominent unqualified power-cut claim in the document, is stated product-wide while the battery is Tier C only, and is the sentence bound for docs/brochure/. Also untouched is line 61's "~$100 BOM at Tier B" economics, which feeds the $299-399 sell price: adding the battery to Tier B moves the BOM from $93-113 to $118-138, breaking the stated $95-120 band.

WHAT THE CLAIM GETS RIGHT: PoE for the install story; switch-UPS as a documented LAN-survival requirement; LTE for HQ visibility; and the core logic that a local DC supply does not rescue the LAN. The true survival envelope is also stronger than the claim states — per sections 5.4 and 6, a battery-backed gateway behind a dead switch still runs the BLE mesh, still writes SQLite, and still extends the hash-chained audit log; only the mTLS consoles drop. That is the promise worth making, and the claim states it too vaguely for a spec.

EVIDENCE LIMITATION: this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) on the first call, so the above rests on direct fetches of raspberrypi.com, pidramble.com, and the IEEE 802.3 PD budget table, plus re-derived arithmetic, rather than a broad survey. Current street prices for the $25 UPS HAT and $20 PoE+ HAT could not be independently confirmed and should be treated as stale-price risk pending re-quote.

corrected.original: Which regime bites first depends on how the appliance is powered — a DC-adapter-fed unit falls outside the Low Voltage Directive entirely.
corrected.corrected:
The supply architecture determines whether LVD 2014/35/EU applies, but it does not change the overall compliance map.

LVD applies to equipment with an input or output voltage rating of 50-1000 V AC or 75-1500 V DC. An appliance fed from an external 12/24 V PSU is below that threshold and is outside LVD scope; the mains-input PSU is the LVD-regulated product. Note that the rating refers to input/output voltage, so internally generated higher rails do not pull the appliance back into scope. If the unit is directly mains-wired, LVD applies to the appliance itself.

However, the following apply regardless of how the unit is powered:
- EMC Directive 2014/30/EU - no voltage threshold; applies to the 12 V appliance and requires CE marking.
- RoHS 2011/65/EU - no voltage threshold; applies and requires CE marking.
- RED 2014/53/EU - if the unit contains any radio (Wi-Fi, BLE, Zigbee, LoRa, NFC), Art. 3(1)(a) imports the Directive 2014/35/EU safety objectives "but with no voltage limit applying." The LVD safety objectives therefore apply to a 12 V radio product anyway, via RED, with a CE mark and a harmonised-standard route.

GPSR (EU) 2023/988 (applicable 13 Dec 2024) is a residual safety net, not a replacement regime: it applies only to consumer-product risks not covered by specific provisions in EU harmonisation legislation, and it carries no CE mark of its own. It does provide a presumption of conformity via European standards whose references are published in the OJEU (Art. 7) - confirm against the regulation text.

Responsibility for the PSU: if the appliance and PSU are placed on the market together as a single commercial unit, the manufacturer is responsible for the compliance of the combination. Relying on the PSU vendor's LVD Declaration of Conformity is valid only where the PSU is separately CE-marked and the combination has been assessed.

Practical consequence for the spec: choosing an external PSU removes one directive (LVD) from the appliance's own conformity file. It does not remove CE marking, and for any radio-equipped unit it does not remove the electrical-safety objectives. Settle the radio question before the supply question - it is the larger determinant of the compliance route.
corrected.why:
The voltage thresholds are correct and confirmed against the stated source: the Commission LVD page gives 50-1000 V AC / 75-1500 V DC and confirms the rating keys off input or output voltage, so a 12/24 V-fed unit is genuinely outside LVD scope. The 13 Dec 2024 GPSR applicability date is correct, and GPSR does not carry a CE mark. But the conclusions drawn from the correct premise are wrong and materially misleading for someone ordering parts.

(1) Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU Art. 3(1)(a), verified verbatim via legislation.gov.uk, requires "the protection of health and safety of persons and of domestic animals and the protection of property, including the objectives with respect to safety requirements set out in Directive 2014/35/EU, but with no voltage limit applying." If the wall unit contains any radio (Wi-Fi/BLE/Zigbee/LoRa/NFC - near-certain for a connected wall unit), the LVD safety objectives apply anyway despite the 12 V supply, and RED supplies both a CE mark and a harmonised-standard route. This nullifies the claim's central inference for the most likely configuration.

(2) EMC Directive 2014/30/EU has no voltage threshold (confirmed via the Commission EMC page: scope is electrical and electronic apparatus, no thresholds stated), and RoHS 2011/65/EU likewise has no voltage limit. A 12 V appliance is CE-marked regardless. The claim's "no CE mark of its own" is true of GPSR in isolation but reads as "no CE mark needed," which is false.

(3) GPSR is residual - it applies only to the extent harmonisation legislation does not contain specific provisions with the same objective. The claim describes a wholesale handoff from LVD to GPSR that does not occur.

(4) "No harmonised-standard route" is imprecise: GPSR Art. 7 provides a presumption of conformity via European standards whose references are published in the OJEU. I could not verify this live - EUR-Lex returned empty response bodies across four URL forms and the WebSearch budget was exhausted - so this correction should be confirmed against the regulation text.

(5) "The PSU carries the LVD obligation (usually the PSU vendor's)" is unsafe as stated: where appliance and PSU are placed on the market together as a single commercial unit, the manufacturer is responsible for the combination; relying on the PSU vendor's DoC requires a separately CE-marked PSU and an assessment of the combination.

(6) The framing "this single design choice changes the whole compliance map" is the load-bearing error. EMC, RED and RoHS apply identically under both supply architectures. The supply choice moves one directive.

Verdict: substantially right on the voltage arithmetic, wrong and overconfident on the regulatory consequence. Refuted per the "substantially right but imprecise" rule and the instruction to default to refuted where a stated conclusion exceeds source support.

corrected.original: If the product contains any radio (BLE, LoRa, Wi-Fi, mesh), the Radio Equipment Directive swallows the other directives and becomes the governing regime.
corrected.corrected:
If the product contains a radio (BLE, LoRa, Wi-Fi, mesh), the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU is the primary CE route and absorbs two other directives — but it does not displace the rest of the regulatory stack.

What RED absorbs:
- Safety: Art 3(1)(a) covers "safety requirements set out in Directive 2014/35/EU, but with no voltage limit applying". A 5 V battery-powered mesh node is therefore in scope for safety under RED. Note this is gap-filling, not displacement: at 5 V the LVD never applied anyway (its range is 50-1000 V AC / 75-1500 V DC). Displacement of LVD only matters for mains-powered radio equipment.
- EMC: Art 3(1)(b) covers EMC "as set out in Directive 2014/30/EU", and EMCD Art 2(2)(a) excludes equipment covered by RED. No separate EMCD declaration.
- Spectrum: Art 3(2), efficient use of radio spectrum — no equivalent under LVD/EMCD.
- Cybersecurity: Art 3(3)(d),(e),(f) via Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30, mandatory since 1 August 2025 for internet/network-connected radio equipment. Applies to a mesh node. The Cyber Resilience Act (EU) 2024/2847 adds further obligations from December 2027.

What still applies independently (must be budgeted and specified separately):
- RoHS 2011/65/EU — no radio carve-out; drives component and solder selection.
- Batteries Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 — unavoidable for a battery-powered node.
- WEEE 2012/19/EU, packaging, and REACH.
- Ecodesign/ErP if an external PSU is supplied.
- Machinery, ATEX, medical, or toy legislation if the appliance has those functions.

Standards caveat: EN IEC 62368-1 is the standard normally applied for Art 3(1)(a) on ICT/AV-type equipment, but presumption of conformity attaches only to the exact version cited in the current Commission Implementing Decision on RED harmonised standards. Verify the live OJ list before citing it in a spec; where no harmonised standard covers a requirement, a Notified Body route may be needed.

Jurisdiction: the above is the EU/CE regime, which also governs Northern Ireland under the Windsor Framework. Great Britain is separate — the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017 with UKCA marking, and GB has not adopted Regulation (EU) 2022/30 (the PSTI regime applies instead). Do not cite gov.uk RER 2017 guidance as authority for EU CE obligations.
corrected.why:
The technical core is verified but the headline is overstated and the source is mis-cited.

VERIFIED: RED Art 3(1)(a) reads verbatim "...including the objectives with respect to safety requirements set out in Directive 2014/35/EU, but with no voltage limit applying" (legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2014/53/article/3). So a 5 V battery mesh node IS in scope for safety under RED. Art 3(1)(b) verbatim covers EMC "as set out in Directive 2014/30/EU", and EMCD Art 2(2)(a) excludes "equipment covered by Directive 1999/5/EC" (read as 2014/53/EU per RED Art 47). EMC displacement confirmed.

REFUTED ON FOUR GROUNDS:

1. "Swallows the other directives and becomes the governing regime" is false. RED displaces exactly two instruments: LVD and EMCD. RoHS 2011/65/EU Art 2 scopes by Annex I category with no radio-equipment carve-out; WEEE, the Batteries Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Ecodesign/ErP and packaging rules all apply in parallel. For a battery-powered venue appliance, the Batteries Regulation and RoHS are unavoidable and drive component selection. An engineer ordering parts against "RED is the governing regime" will under-scope the BOM.

2. The stated source does not support the claim. The gov.uk page is a Northern Ireland / Windsor Framework factsheet on cybersecurity essential requirements under Art 3(3)(d),(e),(f), applicable from 1 August 2025. It contains nothing on Art 3(1)(a) safety, LVD, or EMC displacement. It is also UK law — GB applies the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017 with UKCA marking, not RED with CE — so it is the wrong jurisdiction for an EU CE-route proposition.

3. Mechanism conflation. At 5 V the LVD was never in scope anyway (its floor is 50 V AC / 75 V DC). RED 3(1)(a) fills a gap LVD never covered; it does not "displace" LVD in this example. Displacement only operates for mains-powered radio equipment. The claim presents gap-filling as displacement.

4. Material omission — and it is precisely what the cited source is about. RED Art 3(3)(d),(e),(f) via Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 has been mandatory since 1 August 2025 and captures a network-connected mesh node. The Cyber Resilience Act (EU) 2024/2847 layers on from December 2027. A spec that calls RED "the governing regime" while omitting 3(3) understates the compliance burden.

5. Unverifiable as stated: EN IEC 62368-1's harmonised status under RED could not be confirmed — the OJ list exists only in linked PDF/XLSX behind the Commission's RED harmonised-standards page (summary list generated 13.10.2025). It is the standard used in practice, but presumption of conformity attaches only to the exact version cited in the current Implementing Decision, so "normally applied" must not be written into a spec as "harmonised".

corrected.original: RED cybersecurity requirements became mandatory on 1 August 2025 and are a live, frequently-missed obligation for any connected device.
corrected.corrected:
RED cybersecurity requirements under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 have applied since 1 August 2025 (postponed from 1 August 2024) and are a live obligation — but scope is narrower than "any connected device" and must be determined per device class.

Scope test, applied in this order:
- Art. 3(3)(d) / EN 18031-1 (network protection): applies to radio equipment that can itself communicate over the internet, whether directly or via other equipment. A device that relays through a paired phone to the internet is caught; a purely offline mesh device that never reaches the internet is not.
- Art. 3(3)(e) / EN 18031-2 (personal, traffic and location data): applies only where the equipment processes such data AND is one of — internet-connected radio equipment, equipment designed exclusively for childcare, a toy under Directive 2009/48/EC, or wearable radio equipment. Processing location data is NOT on its own sufficient. A worn proximity badge is likely in scope via the wearable limb; a fixed, offline venue beacon may be out of scope entirely. Confirm which limb applies before budgeting.
- Art. 3(3)(f) / EN 18031-3: applies only to internet-connected equipment enabling transfer of money, monetary value or virtual currency. Almost certainly not applicable to a proximity/location device — exclude unless payment functionality is added.

Excluded from 2022/30 entirely: medical devices and IVDs, civil aviation, and motor / agricultural / two- and three-wheel vehicle equipment. Note also that RED binds radio equipment placed on the EU market — a smartphone app carries no RED obligation; the hardware manufacturer does.

Harmonised standards: EN 18031-1:2024, EN 18031-2:2024 and EN 18031-3:2024 were cited via a Commission Implementing Decision dated 28 January 2025 amending Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/2191, published in the OJ on 30 January 2025.

Restrictions: the citation carries restrictions on clauses that let the manufacturer self-justify omitting access control, password strength, or update mechanisms (reported as covering password enforcement, parental controls and update mechanisms — verify exact wording against the OJ summary list). Where a restricted clause is relied on, presumption of conformity does not apply and conformity assessment falls to RED Annex III/IV with a notified body. Budget notified-body lead time and cost, not merely a gap assessment.

Forward planning: the Commission has stated that cybersecurity requirements transfer from RED to the Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847), whose main obligations apply from 11 December 2027, with 2022/30 expected to be withdrawn to avoid double regulation. Hardware specified in 2026 will still be on the market at that point, so design against CRA requirements in parallel rather than to RED alone.
corrected.why:
The headline is right but the claim is imprecise in ways that would misdirect an actual hardware order.
