VERIFIED: DR (EU) 2022/30 activates RED Art. 3(3)(d)(e)(f) (EC RED page, verbatim). EN 18031-1/-2/-3:2024 exist, are CEN-CLC/JTC 13 work, are OJ-cited, and -2 does cover personal/traffic/location data (CEN-CENELEC). A 28 January 2025 amendment to Implementing Decision 2022/2191 is on the EC harmonised-standards list. Mandatory from August 2025 (CENELEC). Restrictions on the citation are real.

CAVEAT ON METHOD: EUR-Lex served an AWS WAF bot-challenge on every attempt; I did not bypass it. Article 1's category list and the exact restriction wording below rest on secondary corroboration, not the OJ text. The engineer should confirm restriction wording against the OJ summary list before relying on it.

DEFECT 1 - the EN 18031-2 trigger is stated wrongly, and this is the load-bearing error. "Almost certainly processes location data, pulling in EN 18031-2" is not the legal test. Art. 3(3)(e) applies only where the equipment processes personal/traffic/location data AND falls in one of four classes: internet-connected radio equipment, equipment designed exclusively for childcare, toys under 2009/48/EC, or wearable radio equipment. Wikipedia's RED article corroborates the trigger as "internet-connected, wearable, and toy equipment." A worn festival badge probably is in scope - but via the wearable limb, not because it handles location. A non-wearable fixed venue beacon that never reaches the internet may be out of scope entirely. Same for Art. 3(3)(d)/EN 18031-1, which requires equipment that can itself communicate over the internet, directly or via other equipment. Getting this right changes which standard, and how much test work, is on the order.

DEFECT 2 - date conflation. 28 January 2025 is the decision's signature date; OJ publication was 30 January 2025 (Wikipedia). Trivial in isolation, wrong in a spec.

DEFECT 3 - "any connected device" overreaches. RED binds radio equipment placed on the EU market, and 2022/30 carves out medical devices, IVDs, civil aviation, and motor/agricultural/two-three-wheel vehicles. A phone app is not radio equipment at all - RED obligations sit with the hardware maker.

DEFECT 4 - EN 18031-3 is listed without qualification but covers monetary value / virtual currency transfer, near-certainly irrelevant to a proximity device.

DEFECT 5 - material omission. The EC page states that in 2023 it was agreed cybersecurity requirements transfer from RED to the Cyber Resilience Act (Reg. (EU) 2024/2847, main obligations 11 December 2027), with 2022/30 expected to be withdrawn to avoid double regulation. Hardware specced in 2026 will still be on the market then. Speccing to RED alone is a known-dated target.

DEFECT 6 - "budget for a gap assessment" understates the consequence. Where you rely on a restricted clause, presumption of conformity does not apply and you fall to RED Annex III/IV conformity assessment involving a notified body - a lead-time and cost line, not a desk exercise.

Substantially right, insufficiently precise for a document parts are ordered against.

corrected.original: Incorporating a lithium cell triggers Annex M of IEC/EN 62368-1, which is an additive block of requirements on top of the base standard.
corrected.corrected:
Incorporating a SECONDARY (rechargeable) lithium battery invokes Annex M of IEC 62368-1, a normative annex whose requirements are additional to the base clauses. Cite the current edition explicitly — IEC 62368-1:2023, or for the EU market EN IEC 62368-1:2020+A11:2020 — and verify subclause numbering against that edition, not against the 2014 (Ed. 2) text.

Annex M covers batteries generally (not lithium specifically): M.2 requires cells/batteries to comply with the relevant IEC standard (IEC 62133-2 for secondary lithium); M.3 covers protection circuits. M.4 is the lithium-specific block and applies ONLY to secondary lithium batteries — a primary/non-rechargeable lithium cell invokes none of it.

Charging safeguards (M.4.2): the requirement is that charging remain within the CELL manufacturer's specified charging envelope — upper and lower limit charging temperature, upper limit charging voltage, upper limit charging current. Verification exercises the equipment at its highest operating/ambient temperature to confirm the safeguard holds; the equipment temperature is the test condition, not the threshold. For a sealed unit in a hot nightclub ceiling void the real constraint is: measure pack temperature and inhibit charging above the cell's upper limit charging temperature (commonly ~45 C for Li-ion), typically via a pack NTC and a JEITA-compliant charger. Confirm the actual void temperature against both that limit and the cell's discharge/storage ratings.

The M.4.4 drop test is tied to equipment that can credibly be dropped (portable/hand-held/transportable/direct plug-in); a permanently installed stationary ceiling unit is likely out of scope — confirm applicability before budgeting for it.

Annex M is not the whole lithium obligation: UN 38.3 transport testing, any applicable coin/button-cell provisions in the main body, and (for EU placement) Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 on batteries also apply.

Before ordering parts, have someone read the current normative text — this correction is derived from standards knowledge, not from a verified reading of the paywalled document.
corrected.why:
Refuted on source integrity, edition currency, and two substantive technical errors.

SOURCES: The primary citation (62368-ul-solutions.com) fails DNS resolution — the domain does not exist, and it is not a UL Solutions domain (UL publishes at ul.com). The secondary source (micomlabs.com) mentions Annex M exactly once in passing ("including applicable provisions from Annex M for alternative battery types") and contains NONE of the subclause structure, charging-temperature requirement, or drop test attributed to it. The detailed M.2/M.3/M.4/M.4.2/M.4.3/M.4.4 breakdown is effectively uncited.

STALE EDITION: The dead URL's slug cites IEC 62368-1:2014 (Edition 2). IEC webstore confirms Ed. 3.0 (2018-10-04) and notes a more recent IEC 62368-1:2023 exists, with Ed. 3 withdrawal date 2023-05-26. The claim is anchored two editions back; subclause numbering is not guaranteed stable. "EN 62368-1" is also undated — the EU harmonised version is EN IEC 62368-1:2020+A11:2020.

ERROR 1 (trigger over-scoped): Annex M is not triggered by "a lithium cell." It covers equipment containing batteries generally. The cited M.4.x subclauses are scoped to SECONDARY (rechargeable) lithium batteries. A primary non-rechargeable lithium cell (e.g. ER14505 LiSOCl2, plausible for a sealed wall unit) invokes none of M.4 — no charging safeguards, no fire enclosure clause, no drop test.

ERROR 2 (wrong governing limit — most design-relevant): The claim that M.4.2.1 "requires charging to stop at the equipment's highest operating temperature" inverts the requirement. The governing envelope is the CELL manufacturer's specified charging limits (upper/lower limit charging temperature, upper limit charging voltage/current, per IEC 62133-2 terminology). The equipment's highest operating temperature is a TEST CONDITION for verifying the safeguard, not the threshold it is set to. Practical consequence: the correct constraint is "inhibit charging above the cell's upper limit charging temperature (~45 C typical Li-ion)" via pack thermistor + JEITA-aware charger — not a threshold derived from the enclosure rating.

ERROR 3 (applicability asserted, unverified): The M.4.4 drop test is tied to equipment that can be dropped (portable/hand-held/transportable/direct plug-in), referencing Annex T. A permanently installed stationary ceiling unit is likely out of scope; listing it as an applicable constraint for a fixed wall unit is misleading.

DIRECTIONALLY CORRECT: Annex M is normative and additional to the base clauses. But framing it as "the lithium block" understates scope — UN 38.3 transport testing, main-body coin/button cell provisions, and EU Batteries Regulation 2023/1542 also apply and are outside Annex M.

VERIFICATION LIMIT: The normative text is paywalled and the session's web search budget was exhausted, so I could not positively confirm subclause titles/numbering. I established only that the cited sources do not support the claim and the cited edition is superseded. Per instruction, unsubstantiated defaults to refuted.

corrected.original: The 4th edition (IEC 62368-1:2023) removed the word 'portable' from Annex M.4, which pulls permanently-installed wall-mounted equipment into requirements that previously did not apply to it.
corrected.corrected:
IEC 62368-1:2023 (Ed. 4) revised the title and main requirement of Annex M.4.1 so that it applies to both portable and non-portable equipment, per IEC TC 108's position that most M.4.1 provisions were always applicable to both. A permanently-installed wall-mounted product with a secondary lithium battery is therefore newly in scope, EXCEPT where the cell is a secondary lithium coin cell with internal resistance greater than 3 ohms (measured per Annex D of IEC 62133-2:2017), which is exempt.

The one genuinely new stationary-specific obligation is narrower than commonly reported: for batteries complying with IEC 62133-2 and used for SUBSYSTEM POWERING applications in stationary equipment, where electric, electronic and software controls are relied upon as a safeguard, the battery must additionally either comply with 8.1 of IEC 62619, or be protected by a supplementary safeguard (per G.3, Annex F of IEC 62133-2:2017, a fire enclosure per 6.4 in addition to the battery enclosure, or equivalent).

Contrary to the original claim, Ed. 4 does NOT add stationary-specific charging or enclosure requirements. M.4.2 (charging) was restructured for clarity with no intended new requirements. M.4.3 (fire enclosure) became LESS onerous, adding an exemption where cells comply with PS1. Ed. 4 also adds a relaxation at M.2.1 allowing IEC 62133-2 instead of IEC 62619 for subsystem-powering batteries in stationary equipment.

This is not the most consequential Ed. 4 change for a wall-mounted appliance. UL Solutions rates the M.4.1 change "Minor (+)" with "limited impact." Higher-impact items for a mains-connected wall-mounted product are 4.1.1 (legacy IEC 60065/60950-1 component acceptance withdrawn - components must now be evaluated to IEC 62368-1), 5.4.2.3.2.4 (reworked Table 13 external circuit transient voltages), and 4.1.8 (liquids/refrigerants), all rated "Significant."

Applicability: compliance is against the regional adoption, not IEC directly. EU is EN IEC 62368-1:2024/A11:2024 (published 2024-04-19), DOW 2027-02-15. US/Canada is CSA C22.2 No. 62368-1/UL 62368-1, Ed. 3 until Ed. 4 takes effect, expected to align with the CENELEC DOW. Confirm current effective dates and national differences before committing a design.

Source basis: UL Solutions "Certification Impact Analysis: IEC 62368-1:2023 (Edition 4)," rev. 2024-05-10, pp. 47-49. Verify normative wording against the IEC Ed. 4 text or the IEC redline before relying on it in a specification.
corrected.why:
Core fact substantiated, but the characterization and the consequence framing are refuted by the certifying body's own document.

VERIFIED AGAINST: UL Solutions, "Certification Impact Analysis: IEC 62368-1:2023 (Edition 4)," issued 2023-07-14, revised 2024-05-10, pp. 47-49 (clause-by-clause analysis by the certifying body — stronger than either cited secondary source).

WHAT HOLDS: Scope of M.4 did expand to non-portable equipment. UL: IEC TC 108 "holds that most of the provisions in M.4.1 apply both to portable and nonportable equipment," therefore "the title of M.4.1 has been changed and the main requirement has been revised." A permanently-installed wall-mounted device is non-portable, so it is newly in scope. Direction of change is correct.

WHAT IS REFUTED:

1. "Single most consequential standards change for a wall-mounted appliance" — contradicted verbatim by the source. UL rates M.4.1 "Minor (+)" and writes: "Although the revision appears considerably more onerous, as most applications of M.4.1 have been to portable applications, the expanded application should have limited impact." UL reserves "Significant" for 4.1.1 (withdrawal of legacy IEC 60065/60950-1 component acceptance), 4.1.8 (liquids/refrigerants), 5.4.2.3.2.4 (Table 13 external circuit transients), 5.5.2.2, 9.3.1 (touch temperature), G.15.1. IEC's own foreword list of significant technical changes for Ed. 4 — (a) new external-circuits table, (b) fire enclosure openings, (c) liquid-filled components, (d) battery charging — does not include the M.4 portability change. For a mains-connected wall-mounted product, 4.1.1 and 5.4.2.3.2.4 are the higher-impact items.

2. "Added ... enclosure requirements for stationary equipment" — backwards. M.4.3 (fire enclosure) changes are rated "Minor (-)" (less onerous), adding an exemption where the equipment uses cells complying with PS1, plus clarifications on treating the end-product enclosure and battery enclosure as the fire enclosure. Not an added burden and not stationary-specific.

3. "Added ... charging requirements for stationary equipment" — misleading. UL on M.4.2: requirements were "completely restructured and rewritten to promote clarity," and "the intent of the rewrite was not to introduce new requirements." Rated Minor. Not stationary-specific.

4. Omits the exemption in the new scoping text. The revised requirement reads: "Equipment designed to be operated while incorporating one or more secondary lithium batteries, except for secondary lithium coin-cell batteries with an internal resistance greater than 3 Ohm, are subject to the requirements in this clause." Coin cells >3 Ohm (e.g. RTC/backup cells common in wall-mounted appliances) are out of scope — materially relevant and dropped from the claim.

5. Omits that Ed. 4 also RELAXES a stationary-equipment requirement. New M.2.1 allowance: "For batteries used for subsystem powering applications in stationary equipment, IEC 62133-2 may be used as an alternative to IEC 62619." The claim presents Ed. 4 as purely additive burden.

6. Sourcing is weaker than stated. Only one of the two cited sources supports the claim; the Element guide discusses Annex M revisions but never mentions "portable," "stationary," or "non-portable." The apparent third corroboration (lcs-cert.com) is near-verbatim identical to newbtl.com, indicating a single origin rather than independent confirmation. "Corroborated across two secondary sources" is itself inaccurate.

7. Regulatory framing is stated more confidently than applicable. IEC 62368-1:2023 is not the compliance target in any market on its own. EU: EN IEC 62368-1:2024/A11:2024, published 2024-04-19, DOW 2027-02-15. US/Canada: CSA C22.2 No. 62368-1/UL 62368-1 Ed. 3 (2019-12-13) was still current as of the 2024-05-10 analysis; Ed. 4 effective date expected to align with the CENELEC DOW. National differences and effective dates govern what the design must meet.

RESIDUAL UNCERTAINTY: I did not read the Ed. 3 or Ed. 4 normative text directly (paywalled). The specific word-level assertion that "portable" was deleted from a heading is an inference from UL's "the title of M.4.1 has been changed" plus TC 108's stated rationale; UL does not quote the superseded title. The scope-expansion effect is well supported; the exact word-deletion mechanics should be confirmed against the Ed. 4 text or the IEC redline (RLV) before going into a spec.

corrected.original: Annex M forces cell/pack-level certification to IEC 62133-2 as a precondition — you cannot test your way out of it at product level.
corrected.corrected:
IEC 62368-1 Annex M requires that cells and batteries in the end product themselves conform to the relevant battery safety standard; product-level 62368-1 testing does not substitute for that conformity. Which standard applies depends on the cell and the market, and the practical burden depends on who can actually generate the evidence:

WHICH STANDARD. For rechargeable lithium cells/packs in portable applications, the relevant standard is IEC/EN 62133-2:2017+A1:2021. It does NOT apply to primary (non-rechargeable) cells such as a CR2032 RTC backup — those fall under IEC 60086-4 — nor to non-portable/industrial or stationary lithium batteries, which fall under IEC 62619 / IEC 63056. Confirm which of these your cell is before writing a certificate requirement into the BOM.

WHICH MARKET. For the EU, the binding artefact is the harmonised EN (EN IEC 62368-1:2020+A11:2020) with EN IEC 62133-2:2017+A1:2021. For the US under UL 62368-1, UL 1642 / UL 2054 / UL 62133-2 are accepted routes. There is no single global "62133-2 or nothing" rule.

EVIDENCE, NOT CERTIFICATES. The standard requires compliance; a CB certificate is the cheapest and most portable evidence, but a test report from a competent (ISO/IEC 17025) lab can also serve, subject to your certification body's acceptance. Confirm the route with your notified body/NRTL before assuming.

THE REAL PROCUREMENT CONSTRAINT. You generally cannot commission cell-level 62133-2 testing on a third party's cell: it requires cell construction data (separator, vent, CID/PTC design) that manufacturers treat as confidential, and CB certificates are issued to the manufacturer, not the buyer. So the fallback is not "test it yourself in 4-8 weeks" — it is "get the cell maker to certify, or change cells." Pack-level testing, by contrast, is yours to commission, and building a pack from certified cells does not automatically discharge pack-level obligations.

SCHEDULE. Treat any timeline as lab-quoted, not assumed. New-cell 62133-2 programmes commonly run beyond 8 weeks once sample lead time, lab queue, CDF/documentation review and any retest are included. Multi-day dwells (e.g. the temperature-cycling sequence and post-test rest) are real but typically run in parallel across sample groups and are rarely the critical path.

SEPARATELY. UN 38.3 is transport regulation (UN Model Regulations, IATA DGR, ADR), not an Annex M requirement. You still need it to ship, but do not cite Annex M as its basis.

PRACTICAL RULE. Specify cells that already hold third-party 62133-2 (or the market-appropriate equivalent) evidence held by the cell manufacturer, plus a UN 38.3 test summary; budget separately for pack-level evaluation; and verify the applicable standard against your actual cell chemistry and application rather than assuming 62133-2.
corrected.why:
The claim's procurement instinct (buy cells that already hold IEC 62133-2 evidence) is sound, but it is stated with a false universality, rests on sources that do not support it, and contains one omission that would actively misdirect a parts order.

SOURCING: Source 1 (62368-ul-solutions.websandkasten.de) fails DNS resolution — "websandkasten" is German for "web sandbox," i.e. a staging site. It was the only cited source addressing Annex M and it no longer exists. Source 2 (en.gdestl.com/815.html) was fetched successfully and never mentions Annex M or IEC 62368-1 at all, and gives no timeline data. The 4-8 week figure is uncited by either source. I could not retrieve the literal Annex M.2 wording (paywalled, 775pp), so I treat the paraphrase as unconfirmed rather than disproven.

VERIFIED FACTS: Per the IEC webstore, IEC 62133-2 is "portable sealed SECONDARY cells... for use in PORTABLE applications - Part 2: Lithium systems," 2017 base edition plus Amendment 1 (2021). IEC 62368-1 is 3rd ed. (2018-10-04) with a 2023 edition also published; the claim never states which edition it reads, which matters because Annex M changed between them.

DEFECTS: (1) Scope over-reach — 62133-2 covers only rechargeable lithium in portable applications, so it cannot be a blanket precondition for primary cells (CR2032 RTC backup falls under IEC 60086-4) or non-portable/industrial packs (IEC 62619 / 63056). (2) Certification vs compliance — the standard requires compliance; a CB certificate is the cheapest evidence, not the only admissible evidence. (3) Most important omission — a buyer generally CANNOT commission cell-level 62133-2 on a third party's cell: it requires construction data (separator, vent, CID/PTC) that cell makers withhold, and CB certificates are issued to the manufacturer. The claimed fallback of "commissioning testing yourself at 4-8 weeks" is usually not an available option at cell level; the pack is what the integrator can test. (4) Market dependence — UL 62368-1 accepts UL 1642 / UL 2054 / UL 62133-2 for US builds; the EU binds via the harmonised EN and its OJEU citation. (5) UN 38.3 is transport regulation (UN Model Regs / IATA DGR / ADR), not something Annex M forces — conflation of two regimes. (6) The "7-day observation is the long pole" characterisation is wrong: those dwells run partly in parallel across sample groups; sample lead time, lab queue and CDF review dominate real schedules, which commonly run longer than 8 weeks for a new cell.

The directional core — that product-level 62368-1 testing does not substitute for cell/battery-level conformity — is defensible and I did not find grounds to overturn it. But as written the claim is too absolute and too thinly sourced to go into a spec an engineer orders parts against.

corrected.original: A certified cell does not discharge the host-product obligation — Annex M evaluation of the finished appliance is still required.
corrected.corrected: Battery-level certification does not discharge the host-product obligation: the finished appliance must still be assessed to IEC 62368-1 in full, of which Annex M (equipment containing batteries) is the battery-specific part. Qualifications an engineer must hold: (a) State the edition you are certifying to — Ed. 3:2018 or Ed. 4:2023 — and verify every Annex M subclause number against that edition's own text; Annex M was revised between editions (including new button/coin-cell requirements), so subclause numbers are not portable between them. (b) IEC 62133-2:2017 certifies cells and batteries made from them as SEPARATE items. A certified CELL does not cover the assembled PACK and therefore does not satisfy even the battery-level clause; procure pack-level 62133-2 certification, not just cell certification. (c) The residual host-level work — protection circuits, charging safeguards evaluated under the host equipment's own worst-case thermal conditions including single-fault, plus marking, instructions and applicable fault tests — is scoped by the test lab. Where the pack was certified together with its integral protection circuit, that report can often be leveraged rather than the assessment fully repeated, so treat this as scoping to negotiate with your NRTL, not as a fixed second round of testing. (d) Cite current normative references: IEC 62133-2:2017 (+AMD1:2021), not the withdrawn combined IEC 62133:2012; in North America prefer UL 62133-2 over UL 2054, which is being withdrawn. (e) Do not cite www.62368-ul-solutions.websandkasten.de — the domain does not resolve and is not a UL Solutions property. Source this requirement from the purchased standard text or a written scoping statement from your certification body.
corrected.why: Directionally correct but not citable as written, and the source is dead. (1) SOURCE FABRICATED/UNREACHABLE: www.62368-ul-solutions.websandkasten.de returns NXDOMAIN for both host and apex; only parent websandkasten.de resolves (195.30.85.70, NS ns*.ns35.de), a German web-agency sandbox unrelated to UL Solutions. UL Solutions' real property is ul.com (ulsolutions.com 301s there). The "62368-ul-solutions" slug on a third-party sandbox host is a lookalike, not a certification-body citation. (2) INTERNAL CONTRADICTION, CELL vs PACK: headline says "certified cell", detail says "certified pack". IEC webstore confirms IEC 62133-2 Ed 1.0 (2017-02-07) covers "portable sealed secondary cells, AND batteries made from them" as separate certifiable items. A CELL certificate does not cover the assembled pack, so it does not even fully discharge the battery-level clause — an error in the opposite direction from the one the claim warns about, and equally expensive. (3) CLAUSE MAPPING UNVERIFIED: could not substantiate that M.3/M.4.2/M.4.3/M.4.4 carry the asserted titles and content; web-search budget exhausted and IEC previews do not expose the Annex M TOC. Regulatory clause numbers stated more confidently than any reachable source supports. (4) EDITION NOT STATED: IEC 62368-1 Ed 3.0 confirmed 2018-10-04, superseded by Ed 4.0 (2023); Annex M was revised between editions (button/coin-cell additions), so bare subclause numbers are unsafe in a parts-ordering spec. (5) STALE NORMATIVE REFS in source slug: "IEC 62133:2012" was split into 62133-1/-2 in 2017; UL 2054 is on a withdrawal path in favour of UL 62133-2. (6) OVERSTATES "M.2 only": where a pack is certified with its integral protection circuit, that report is commonly leveraged toward host-level protection-circuit assessment rather than fully repeated — scoping is the test lab's call, not a fixed binary. (7) UNDERSTATES the residual duty: the finished appliance must meet all of IEC 62368-1 (Clause 5 electrical, Clause 6 fire, Clause 9 thermal burn, Annex Q, etc.), not Annex M alone. Core proposition — battery-level certification does not discharge the host-product obligation — is sound and should be retained in corrected form.

corrected.original: Compliance with EN 62368-1 is not itself legally mandatory — the legal duty is to meet the directive's essential requirements, and the standard is only the presumption-of-conformity route.
corrected.corrected:
Compliance with EN 62368-1 is not itself legally mandatory. The legal duty is to meet the applicable directive's essential requirements; a harmonised standard is one route that confers a presumption of conformity.

For a battery-powered radio product, the operative instrument is the RED (2014/53/EU), not the LVD. LVD 2014/35/EU applies only to equipment rated 50-1000 V AC / 75-1500 V DC (Art. 1) and does not cover a low-voltage battery-powered device; it would apply only to a separately supplied mains PSU/charger. Safety obligations reach the product via RED Art. 3(1)(a), which imports the LVD safety objectives "but with no voltage limit applying," with presumption of conformity under RED Art. 16.

You may demonstrate conformity by other means, and for safety you retain the self-assessment route: RED Art. 17(4) forces the notified-body route (Annex III or IV) only where harmonised standards are not applied or applied only in part to the essential requirements of Art. 3(2) and (3) (radio spectrum). Safety under Art. 3(1)(a) may be assessed under Annex II internal production control regardless. Deviating from EN 62368-1 therefore shifts the full evidential burden onto the technical file rather than triggering a notified body.

Two practical caveats for procurement:
- Presumption attaches only to the exact dated version and amendment cited in the OJEU, only to the parts covered, and subject to any restrictions in that listing. Pin the edition in the spec (e.g. EN IEC 62368-1:2020+A11:2020) and confirm its current OJ citation status under the RED before ordering against it.
- Do not generalise "voluntary" to the battery obligations. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 is directly applicable law, and UN 38.3 transport testing is mandatory under ADR/IATA/IMDG. These are legal requirements, not presumption routes. Cell-level IEC 62133-2 evidence is separately expected by most buyers.

Commercially, treat EN 62368-1 as mandatory: distributors, insurers and large-venue procurement teams will not accept a bare self-declaration for a lithium-containing product, even though no notified body has any role in that decision.
corrected.why:
The core principle is correct and well-established: under the New Legislative Framework, harmonised standards are voluntary, the legal duty is the essential requirements, and the standard is the presumption-of-conformity route. Verified LVD 2014/35/EU Art. 12 ("Presumption of conformity on the basis of harmonised standards") and RED 2014/53/EU Art. 16. However, three errors make the claim as written unsafe for a hardware spec.

(1) WRONG LEGAL INSTRUMENT FOR THIS PRODUCT. LVD 2014/35/EU Art. 1 limits scope to equipment rated between 50 and 1000 V AC / 75 and 1500 V DC. A lithium-battery-powered device operating at single-digit volts DC falls entirely outside LVD scope, so "LVD 2014/35/EU Annex I / Art. 12" is not the operative basis. The correct basis is RED Art. 3(1)(a), which imports the LVD safety objectives verbatim "but with no voltage limit applying." (LVD would apply to a separately-placed mains PSU/charger, not the device itself.)

(2) THE NOTIFIED-BODY SENTENCE IS FACTUALLY WRONG. LVD involves no notified body at any point — conformity assessment is internal production control only. Under RED Art. 17, verified text: para 4 requires the Annex III (EU-type examination) or Annex IV (full quality assurance) notified-body route only "where the manufacturer has not applied or has applied only in part harmonised standards" for the essential requirements in ARTICLE 3(2) AND (3) — radio spectrum. Safety under Art. 3(1)(a) is not covered by that trigger; Annex II internal production control remains available whether or not EN 62368-1 is used. So no notified body sits in the loop to "accept or refuse" a safety self-declaration. The commercial-gatekeeper argument may hold for distributors, insurers and venue procurement, but naming notified bodies among them is a category error.

(3) OVERSTATED CONFIDENCE / MISSING CAVEATS. Presumption of conformity attaches only to the specific dated version of a standard whose reference is published in the OJEU, only to the parts covered, and subject to any restrictions or notes in that OJ listing — EN IEC 62368-1:2020+A11:2020 has had a restricted/contested citation history under RED. A spec saying "EN 62368-1" without pinning edition, amendment and the directive under which it is cited is not actionable. Separately, "legally voluntary" is true of EN 62368-1 but must not be generalised: for a lithium-containing product, Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 (Batteries Regulation) is directly applicable law, and UN 38.3 transport testing is mandatory under ADR/IATA/IMDG — neither is a presumption-of-conformity route.

Substantially right in principle, but wrong in cited authority and wrong on notified bodies, so refuted with correction.

corrected.original: There is a genuine harmonisation gap: the edition of EN 62368-1 cited in the Official Journal may be older than the edition labs test to, which weakens automatic presumption of conformity.
corrected.corrected:
There is a genuine harmonisation gap for EN 62368-1, but state it precisely.

The only reference cited in the Official Journal under the Low Voltage Directive (2014/35/EU) is EN 62368-1:2014 together with EN 62368-1:2014/AC:2015 — entry 555, Annex I to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/2723 of 6 December 2023 (OJ L, 2023/2723, 13.12.2023). The cited reference does NOT include A11:2017; that amendment appears nowhere in the instrument. Do not write "EN 62368-1:2014/A11:2017" on a DoC as the harmonised reference.

Neither EN IEC 62368-1:2020 (3rd edition) nor the 4th edition has been cited.

The decision has been amended four times — (EU) 2024/1198 (19.4.2024), (EU) 2024/2764 (30.10.2024), (EU) 2025/1457 (16.7.2025) and (EU) 2025/1488 (22.7.2025) — and none of those amendments touches the 62368-1 entry. A corrigendum also exists (CELEX 32023D2723R(01), OJ 2025/90676, 27.8.2025) which should be checked, though a corrigendum cannot newly harmonise an edition.

Consequence, stated correctly: EN 62368-1:2014+AC:2015 is listed in Annex I without restriction, so it still carries FULL presumption of conformity — it is not weakened, and it is not in the Annex II (restricted) or Annex III (withdrawn) lists. Conversely, a test report to EN IEC 62368-1:2020 or the 4th edition confers NO automatic presumption at all, not merely a weakened one, and must be supported by a documented delta analysis back to EN 62368-1:2014+AC:2015. The practical difficulty is that the only edition carrying presumption is one CENELEC has withdrawn at national level.

Verify the exact wording of entry 555 in the current consolidated text on EUR-Lex, and confirm with your test lab, before writing the DoC.
corrected.why:
The core thesis is right — there is a genuine harmonisation gap — but the claim is wrong on the specific designation an engineer would copy into a DoC, and misstates the legal consequence.

VERIFIED AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCE (EUR-Lex is behind an AWS WAF; I retrieved the authoritative text via the Publications Office CELLAR endpoint http://publications.europa.eu/resource/celex/32023D2723 and the EU SPARQL endpoint https://publications.europa.eu/webapi/rdf/sparql):

1. WRONG DESIGNATION. Annex I, entry 555 of Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/2723 cites "EN 62368-1:2014" plus "EN 62368-1:2014/AC:2015". The string "A11:2017" appears ZERO times in the entire decision. This is not a parsing artifact: the same instrument does list A11 amendments for other standards (e.g. "EN 62423:2012/A11:2021"), so A11s are listed where they are cited. The claim's "EN 62368-1:2014/A11:2017 is the OJEU-cited edition" names an amendment that is not in the governing instrument.

2. THE CLAIM'S OWN SOURCES DO NOT SUPPORT IT. regulatorydecoded.com states "EN 62368-1:2014 (2nd edition)" is the cited edition — matching the primary text, not A11:2017. gainspeed.co.uk is dated January 2023, i.e. ~11 months BEFORE Decision 2023/2723 was adopted (6 Dec 2023), and discusses AC:2017 and a 2019 date of cessation; it is structurally incapable of being evidence about the current list. Citing it as such is a sourcing error.

3. CORRECTLY VERIFIED. The governing instrument and its four amendments are exactly right. SPARQL returns precisely four amending acts and no more: (EU) 2024/1198 (19.4.2024), (EU) 2024/2764 (30.10.2024), (EU) 2025/1457 (16.7.2025), (EU) 2025/1488 (22.7.2025). None contains the string "62368" (they concern flat flexible cables / EV charging cables, and whirlpool baths / EN 60335-1). The entry is therefore unchanged.

4. CORRECTLY VERIFIED. "62368-1:2020" appears nowhere in the base decision or any amendment. EN IEC 62368-1:2020 (3rd ed.) and the 4th edition are indeed not cited.

5. OMISSION. A corrigendum exists that the claim's list misses: CELEX 32023D2723R(01), OJ reference 2025/90676, dated 27 August 2025 — later than the claim's last-cited amendment. I could not retrieve its body (EUR-Lex WAF-blocked; CELLAR returned "does not hold a content datastream"). A corrigendum cannot newly harmonise a standard edition (that requires an implementing decision under Art. 10(6) of Reg. (EU) No 1025/2012), so it cannot change the 2020/4th-edition conclusion, but its effect on row 555 is unverified.

6. FRAMING ERROR. 62368-1 appears only in Annex I — not Annex II (published with restriction) nor Annex III (withdrawn references, with dates of withdrawal). So EN 62368-1:2014+AC:2015 carries FULL, UNRESTRICTED presumption of conformity. "Weakens automatic presumption" is wrong in both directions: the cited edition's presumption is not weakened at all, while a report to the 2020 or 4th edition confers NO automatic presumption whatsoever. The real gap is that the only edition carrying presumption is one CENELEC has withdrawn at national level, while its successor has never been cited.

7. UNVERIFIED (already self-flagged in the claim). I could not substantiate the "Commission summary lists not updated since April 2025" note; the Commission harmonised-standards pages I reached contain no such statement.

corrected.original: UN 38.3 testing is legally required to ship the product, and there is no small-battery exemption from the testing itself.
corrected.corrected:
UN 38.3 testing is a dangerous-goods TRANSPORT requirement, not a product market-access requirement. It applies to lithium cells and batteries offered for transport by any mode (ADR road, RID rail, IMDG sea, ICAO/IATA air), and the obligation falls on the consignor.

Special Provision 188 (cells 20 Wh or less, batteries 100 Wh or less) does NOT waive the testing: its relief is expressly conditional on the cell or battery being "of a type proven to meet the requirements of each test in the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria, Part III, sub-section 38.3." SP188 reduces classification, packaging, marking and documentation burdens only. Treating "under 100 Wh" as "no testing needed" is a common and costly misreading.

However, there IS an exemption from the testing itself, keyed to quantity rather than watt-hours: Special Provision 310 (internationally; 49 CFR 173.185(e) in the US) excepts annual production runs of not more than 100 lithium cells or batteries, and pre-production prototypes transported for testing, from the 38.3 testing and record-keeping requirements - provided they are packed to the prescribed conditions (P910 / LP905 internationally; individual non-metallic inner packagings under the HMR; US shipments may additionally require competent-authority approval - verify). Prototypes and small first builds can therefore ship legally before T.1-T.8 is complete.

Two further points for the spec: (1) testing is performed at the cell/battery DESIGN TYPE level and is normally discharged by the cell or pack supplier's existing test report - the OEM commissions its own T.1-T.8 only when it creates a new battery design type; (2) not all eight tests apply to every article (T.6 is a cell test, T.7 applies to rechargeable batteries, T.8 to cells).

Cite current, free, verifiable sources: UN Manual of Tests and Criteria Rev.8 (2023), and the ADR 2025 / IMDG 42-24 / IATA DGR current-edition texts - not Manual Rev.5 (2009) or the ADR 2017 edition, and not paywalled aggregators. Note also that a UN 38.3 Test Summary has been required to be made available since 1 January 2020 for cells and batteries manufactured after 30 June 2003. Separately, market access in the EU/UK depends on CE/UKCA, IEC 62133-2 and Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, none of which UN 38.3 satisfies.
corrected.why:
Substantially right on its central point but stated as an absolute that is false, and resting on stale, unverifiable citations.

CONFIRMED: SP188 / 49 CFR 173.185(c) relief is conditional on the cell or battery being of a type proven to meet UN Manual Part III sub-section 38.3. Cornell's rendering of 173.185 is explicit that small cells/batteries "ARE subject to the UN 38.3 testing requirement - the exception applies to reduced packaging and labeling requirements, not the underlying safety testing mandate." The "under 100 Wh so no testing" reading is indeed wrong.

REFUTED: "there is no small-battery exemption from the testing itself" is an unqualified absolute, and an exemption from the testing itself does exist - keyed to production quantity rather than watt-hours. 49 CFR 173.185(e), the US-harmonized counterpart of international Special Provision 310 (packing instructions P910 / LP905), excepts "Low production runs (i.e., annual production runs consisting of not more than 100 lithium cells or batteries), prototype lithium cells or batteries transported for purposes of testing" from the paragraph (a) testing and record-keeping requirements, subject to packaging conditions (individually packed in non-metallic inner packaging). For a hardware spec, this is the wrong thing to state absolutely: prototypes and first builds under 100 units can move legally without completed T.1-T.8.

STALE / UNVERIFIABLE SOURCES: Manual Rev.5 is the 2009 edition; current is Rev.8 (2023). ADRbook 2017 is four biennial editions behind ADR 2025, and SP188 has been amended since - notably the UN 38.3 test summary obligation effective 1 Jan 2020. Both stated URLs returned HTTP 403 and cannot be checked by a reader of the spec. 173.185 anchors at "Revision 3, Amendment 1 or any subsequent revision," showing the applicable-revision question is live and unaddressed.

SCOPE CONFLATION: "legally required to ship the product" conflates a dangerous-goods transport obligation (binding the consignor) with product/market-access compliance (CE/UKCA, IEC 62133-2, EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542). Also, 38.3 testing sits at cell/battery design-type level and is normally discharged by the cell or pack vendor's existing report; the OEM commissions T.1-T.8 only when it creates a new battery design type - material to what an engineer budgets and orders.

IMPRECISION: "tests T.1-T.8 applies to all lithium cells and batteries" overstates - the applicable subset varies by article (T.6 is a cell test, T.7 applies to rechargeable batteries, T.8 to cells).

METHOD NOTE: WebSearch budget was exhausted for this session; the stated sources 403'd. Verification rests on two independent renderings (Cornell LII and govinfo) of 49 CFR 173.185, the US implementation harmonized with the UN Model Regulations text the claim cites. The SP310 international citation is inferred from that harmonization and should be confirmed against the current ADR/IMDG text before the spec issues.

corrected.original: Since 1 January 2020 a UN 38.3 Test Summary must be made available by manufacturers and distributors of cells and batteries.
corrected.corrected:
A UN 38.3 Test Summary (Manual of Tests and Criteria, sub-section 38.3.5) must be made available on request by each manufacturer and subsequent distributor of LITHIUM cells and batteries — lithium ion and lithium metal — above the applicable manufacture-date threshold. The threshold and effective date differ by jurisdiction: internationally (ICAO TI / IATA DGR / IMDG) the requirement became operative 1 January 2020 for cells and batteries manufactured after 30 June 2003; under US 49 CFR 173.185(a)(3) it applies to cells and batteries "manufactured on or after January 1, 2008," excepting button cells installed in equipment (including circuit boards), and PHMSA adopted it on a later compliance date than the international one (reported as 1 January 2022) — the 1 January 2020 date does not appear in the CFR.

This is an availability duty, not a shipping-paper duty: the Test Summary need not accompany the shipment, but must be furnished on request. It is a distinct document from the full test report, and it references that report by a unique test report identification number.

Practical procurement note (commercial practice, not regulation): freight forwarders, couriers, and marketplace onboarding processes commonly demand the Test Summary before accepting lithium-battery shipments or listings. Obtain the Test Summary — not merely the test report — from your cell supplier at the point of purchase; retrofitting it from an offshore supplier months later is frequently impossible.

Note that UN 38.3 does not apply to non-lithium chemistries such as alkaline, NiMH, or lead-acid; no Test Summary duty arises for those. Later revisions of the Manual extend the test series to sodium-ion cells and batteries.
corrected.why:
Substantially right in thrust but imprecise in three ways that matter for a hardware spec an engineer orders parts against.

(1) SCOPE OVERBROAD. UN 38.3 is the lithium cell/battery test series. The claim says "cells and batteries" without qualification, which would wrongly imply a duty for alkaline, NiMH, or lead-acid chemistries. 49 CFR 173.185(a)(3) says "lithium cells or batteries" and expressly excepts "button cells installed in equipment (including circuit boards)."

(2) MISSING MANUFACTURE-DATE QUALIFIER. The duty attaches only to cells/batteries manufactured on or after a threshold date, not to all stock. The US text (verified verbatim via Cornell LII) uses "manufactured on or after January 1, 2008." The UN Manual of Tests and Criteria 38.3.5 uses an earlier threshold (30 June 2003) — I could not fetch the UNECE primary PDF (repeated HTTP 403), so I flag the UN threshold as not independently confirmed here, but the divergence between the UN and US thresholds is itself confirmed by the CFR text.

(3) DATE IS JURISDICTION-DEPENDENT AND STATED MORE CONFIDENTLY THAN THE SOURCES SUPPORT. 1 January 2020 is the international modal implementation date (ICAO Technical Instructions / IATA DGR 61st ed. / IMDG). The current 49 CFR 173.185(a)(3) contains no 1 January 2020 date at all; PHMSA harmonized on a later compliance timeline (widely reported as 1 January 2022 via HM-215O — I could not confirm this directly, as federalregister.gov redirected to an unblock interstitial). A US-domestic-only shipper reading "since 1 January 2020" as the operative US date would be relying on a date that does not appear in the CFR.

(4) MECHANISM MISDESCRIBED IN THE DETAIL. "Must be made available" is an on-request availability duty on manufacturers and distributors. The summary need not accompany the shipment and is not a shipping paper. The DETAIL's "freight forwarders and couriers routinely refuse shipments without it" is accurate as commercial practice but is not the regulatory mechanism, and presenting it as such overstates the rule.

(5) SECOND STATED SOURCE DOES NOT SUPPORT THE CLAIM. https://support.google.com/product-documentation/answer/9682653/ is Google's own published UN 38.3 test summary for its consumer devices (Pixel, Fitbit, etc.) — an instance of compliance, not a statement of the regulatory duty. It states no effective date and identifies no duty-holder. It cannot be cited as authority for "since 1 January 2020 ... must be made available." Only the Jauch blog (a vendor blog, not a primary regulatory source) supports the 1 Jan 2020 framing.

CORRECTLY STATED IN THE CLAIM: the duty does fall on manufacturers AND subsequent distributors (CFR confirms); the Test Summary is genuinely a distinct document from the test report; and the procurement advice (obtain it at point of purchase, retrofitting from an offshore supplier later is often impossible) is sound and should be retained. The Amazon/marketplace-onboarding assertion could not be verified — the session's web search budget was exhausted (200/200 calls) before it could be checked; treat as unconfirmed.

Sources consulted: [Jauch blog](https://www.jauch.com/blog/en/un-38-3-mandatory-test-report-for-lithium-batteries/); [49 CFR 173.185 via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/173.185); [Google product documentation](https://support.google.com/product-documentation/answer/9682653/lithium-battery-test-summary); [IATA lithium batteries](https://www.iata.org/en/programs/cargo/dgr/lithium-batteries/) (no test-summary detail on page). UNECE Manual of Tests and Criteria PDFs and federalregister.gov were unreachable (403 / redirect).

corrected.original: Your cell supplier's UN 38.3 report probably does not cover your assembled pack — the assembly exemption is written for large systems and does not help small products.
corrected.corrected:
Your cell supplier's UN 38.3 report probably does not cover your assembled pack, but not because of the 6200 Wh threshold. The reason is the cell-versus-battery distinction: UN Manual 38.3.3's assembly relief applies to an assembly built from already-tested BATTERIES, whereas a multi-cell pack built from bare cells is itself a "battery" and generally needs its own testing (T.1-T.5, plus T.7 where applicable; T.6 and T.8 are cell-only tests).

Note that the 38.3.3 threshold runs the opposite way from what is often assumed: the relief for an assembly of already-tested batteries applies where the assembly is NOT MORE THAN 500 g aggregate lithium content (lithium metal) or NOT MORE THAN 6200 Wh (lithium ion), and is conditioned on a monitoring system preventing overcharge, over-discharge between batteries, and over-temperature. Assemblies EXCEEDING those figures are the ones that attract additional testing (T.3, T.4, T.5, and T.7 where applicable). The threshold is therefore not what excludes a small product from relief.

Separately, a single-cell battery (one cell plus protection circuit/housing) is treated as a "cell" for testing purposes under Rev.6 Amend.1 / Rev.7 — this is settled text, not a speculative recent change. However, that classification only determines which test set applies; it does not by itself mean the bare cell's report transfers, since adding a PCB and housing is a design change from the tested article. Confirm transferability with the test house.

Finally, regulatory relief is not commercial relief: airlines, freight forwarders and retail customers commonly require a pack-level test summary regardless of whether 38.3.3 relief applies. Budget accordingly.

(Caveat for the spec: the primary UNECE PDF could not be retrieved during review — the cited URL and all mirrors returned 403/404 — so verify the exact paragraph lettering and wording against the current Rev.5+ text, and confirm the pack-level scope with a dangerous-goods consultant before ordering.)
corrected.why:
The claim inverts the 38.3.3 threshold. The assembly relief applies where the assembly is NOT MORE THAN 500 g aggregate lithium content (lithium metal) or NOT MORE THAN 6200 Wh (lithium ion), assembled from already-tested batteries and fitted with a monitoring system. Assemblies ABOVE that threshold are the ones that must undergo additional testing (T.3, T.4, T.5, and T.7 where applicable). So the exemption is not "written for large systems," and the assertion that "the relief runs the wrong way" rests on a reversed reading of the source.

The claim's practical conclusion — that a cell supplier's UN 38.3 report likely does not cover an assembled pack — is nonetheless correct, but for a different reason than stated: 38.3.3's assembly relief applies to an assembly of already-tested BATTERIES, whereas a pack built from bare CELLS is itself a battery requiring battery-level testing (T.1-T.5, T.7 as applicable; T.6 and T.8 are cell-only). Citing the 6200 Wh threshold as the justification will mislead anyone who checks the source.

The single-cell-battery point is mis-hedged in both directions: the "single cell battery is considered a cell" treatment is settled text from Rev.6 Amend.1 / Rev.7 rather than uncertain recent recollection, so the call for consultant confirmation is misplaced there; but "can commonly rely on the cell's report" is overstated, since classification as a cell determines WHICH test set applies, not that testing is already satisfied — adding a protection PCB and housing is a design change from the bare tested cell.

Two further imprecisions: 500 g aggregate lithium content is the lithium-metal criterion and 6200 Wh the lithium-ion criterion, not interchangeable alternatives for one chemistry; and even where relief applies, airlines, forwarders and customers routinely require a pack-level test summary, so regulatory relief is not commercial relief.

Verification limitation: the stated UNECE source URL returned HTTP 403, as did PHMSA, TUV SUD and alternate UNECE mirrors; Intertek/Epec/Wikipedia returned 404; and the WebSearch budget was exhausted before any search could run. This analysis therefore rests on model knowledge of the 38.3.3 text and could not be confirmed against the primary document, so the paragraph lettering and exact wording should be checked against the actual Rev.5+ PDF before the spec is issued.

corrected.original: UN 38.3 testing is one of the cheaper line items but the published price range is very wide and offshore quotes are not comparable to UK/EU lab quotes.
corrected.corrected:
UN 38.3 is a mid-range certification line item — cheaper than IEC 62133-2 or UL, but not cheaper than CE — and published prices vary widely and are not comparable across regions.

Sourced figures: jjrlab.com (Asia, page dated May 2024) quotes USD 1,700 per model for a full UN 38.3 test, ~30 days; the sub-USD-300 prices on that page are component line items only (1.2 m packaged drop test USD 150-200/model; 25-cycle preconditioning USD 250/model), not a full report. epectec.com quotes USD 5,000-7,000 and 4-6 weeks for UN 38.3, alongside CE USD 500-1,000, IEC USD 6,000-10,000, and UL USD 15,000-20,000.

Engineering estimate for a UK/EU accredited lab, single small pack configuration: budget GBP 4,000-6,000 and 4-6 weeks per configuration (not GBP 1,500-5,000 / 3-6 weeks — nothing cited supports a GBP 1,500 floor or a 3-week floor). All figures USD unless stated; convert at a rate recorded with its date. The May 2024 offshore quote is ~2 years stale — re-quote.

Retesting: per the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria sub-section 38.3.2.2/38.3.2.3, a cell or battery that differs from a tested one becomes a new "type" requiring retest based on defined quantitative thresholds (changes to anode/cathode/electrolyte mass, Wh rating, or nominal voltage beyond the stated limits) plus a catch-all for any change that would materially affect the test results. Quote the clause text in the spec rather than paraphrasing; "manufacturing process" is not an enumerated trigger and only applies via the catch-all. Consequence for procurement: second-sourcing a cell creates a new cell type, so both the cell-level report and the pack-level report are affected — treat every cell second-source as a retest event and a schedule risk.

Validity: the Manual sets no expiry date on a test report, but this is not "valid forever" — a UN 38.3 Test Summary must be made available for shipment, and reports written against superseded Manual revisions may not be accepted. Confirm the required Manual revision with each lab.

Scope warning: UN 38.3 is a transport test only. It does not cover pack safety for the UK/EU market — IEC 62133-2 (USD 6,000-10,000 per the Epec table) is a separate and larger line item and must be budgeted independently.

Action: get three written quotes (one UK/EU accredited, one US, one offshore), each scoped to full T1-T8 on the specific pack configuration, with the Manual revision, sample count, and per-configuration retest price stated explicitly.
corrected.why:
The claim's structure (wide price range, offshore ≠ UK/EU, per-configuration, retest on change) is directionally right, but the specific figures are not supported by the stated sources and one is contradicted by them. Note: WebSearch budget was exhausted this session, so independent verification is limited to the two cited URLs; I could not re-verify the UN Manual clause text firsthand, which is itself a reason to lower confidence on the regulatory sentence.

1. The USD 300-930 range is not on the cited source. jjrlab.com (page dated May 2024) quotes USD 1,700/model for the full UN38.3 test, ~30 days. The sub-$300 figures on that page are component line items, not reports: 1.2 m packaged drop test USD 150-200/model, and 25-cycle preconditioning USD 250/model. Building a "per report" range out of partial line items understates the offshore floor by roughly 2-5x and is the kind of error an engineer will order against.

2. The engineering estimate is optimistic relative to the claim's own Western source. epectec.com quotes USD 5,000-7,000 for UN 38.3 (US). At ~1.26 USD/GBP that is ~£4,000-£5,600, so the claimed £1,500-£5,000 band tops out near that source's floor. £1,500 for a full accredited T1-T8 report on a pack is not substantiated by anything cited.

3. Lead time understated. Epec says 4-6 weeks; JJR says ~30 days for the full test. Neither supports a 3-week floor.

4. The retest sentence is a paraphrase presented as the rule. The trigger in the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria (sub-section 38.3.2.2/38.3.2.3) is a definition of a new cell/battery "type" with specific quantitative thresholds (mass changes to anode/cathode/electrolyte, changes in Wh rating or nominal voltage beyond stated limits) plus a catch-all for any change that would materially affect test results. "Manufacturing process" is not an enumerated trigger — it only bites via the catch-all. Neither cited source addresses retest triggers at all, so this list is unsourced. The downstream conclusion (second-sourcing a cell is a retest event) is still correct, but as a consequence of the type definition, not as a standalone rule.

5. "Reports do not expire" is unsourced. Neither cited page discusses expiry. It is true that the Manual states no validity period, but that is not the same as "valid forever": a Test Summary must be made available under the post-2020 regime, and reports written against superseded Manual revisions may be rejected. Stated flatly in a spec, this invites the wrong procurement behaviour.

6. "One of the cheaper line items" holds only against IEC/UL. Epec's own table puts CE at USD 500-1,000, below UN 38.3. More importantly UN 38.3 is a transport test and does not substitute for IEC 62133-2 (USD 6,000-10,000 in the same table), which a consumer pack will also need — so it must not be budgeted as the pack-safety line.

7. Unit hygiene: USD for Asia against GBP for UK/EU with no stated FX rate or date makes "materially higher" unauditable, and the JJR page is ~2 years stale as of July 2026.

corrected.original: UKCA marking is effectively optional for this product in Great Britain — CE marking is now recognised indefinitely for the relevant regimes.
corrected.corrected:
UKCA marking is not required for this product in Great Britain. The Product Safety and Metrology etc. (Amendment) Regulations 2024 (SI 2024/696) removed the sunset provisions on CE recognition, so CE marking is accepted in GB with no expiry date across the relevant DBT-managed regimes — including the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016, EMC Regulations 2016, Radio Equipment Regulations 2017, RoHS Regulations 2012 and Ecodesign for Energy-Related Products Regulations 2010. UKCA remains available and lawful.

Qualify this as open-ended rather than indefinite: gov.uk does not use the word "indefinitely", and frames recognition conditionally — it continues "where the aims and requirements of product regulations meet the needs of the UK". Recognition was conferred by secondary legislation and can be withdrawn the same way, so the spec should carry a review trigger rather than treat GB acceptance as permanent.

Do not plan on a single technical file serving both markets. A GB-market connectable device additionally needs:
- PSTI compliance (SI 2023/1007, in force 29 April 2024): unique or user-defined passwords, a published vulnerability-reporting contact with acknowledgement/update timelines, and a disclosed defined support period, evidenced by a GB statement of compliance retained for the longer of 10 years or the support period. This is outside CE/UKCA entirely; the EU equivalent (RED delegated regulation 2022/30) is a separate requirement set.
- A GB-established importer or authorised representative named on the product, distinct from the EU-established one — two label variants regardless of marking. The flexibility allowing UKCA marking and importer details on an affixed label or accompanying document expires at 23:00 on 31 December 2027.
- Separate GB producer registrations (WEEE, batteries, packaging) not covered by any marking.
- Note that any third-party conformity assessment locks the route: UK Approved Body certificates are valid only for UKCA, EU Notified Body certificates only for CE. Self-declaration against designated/harmonised standards avoids this for LVD, EMC and most RED cases.
- Great Britain only. Northern Ireland still requires CE, or CE + UKNI where a UK body performed the assessment.

Verify the 1 October 2024 commencement date against the commencement provision of SI 2024/696 before it goes into the spec — it was not independently confirmed here.
corrected.why:
The regulatory core is substantially correct but stated more confidently than the sources support, and the commercial conclusion drawn from it is materially wrong for this product class.

CONFIRMED: SI 2024/696 is correctly cited as "The Product Safety and Metrology etc. (Amendment) Regulations 2024" (legislation.gov.uk). It amends ~21-22 instruments and the list does include the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016, EMC Regulations 2016, Radio Equipment Regulations 2017, RoHS Regulations 2012 and Ecodesign for Energy-Related Products Regulations 2010. It removes the sunset provisions, so there is no statutory expiry on CE recognition. UKCA does remain available and lawful.

REFUTED / OVERSTATED:
1. "Indefinitely" is not the government's language. The word does not appear on either cited gov.uk page. The actual framing is conditional and policy-dependent: "Where the aims and requirements of product regulations meet the needs of the UK, the UK continues to recognise the CE marking, alongside or in place of the UKCA marking, for the Great Britain market." Open-ended with no sunset is not the same as indefinite — the recognition was conferred by secondary legislation and is revocable by secondary legislation. The claim states a legal permanence the source does not assert.

2. The load-bearing saving — "one CE technical file serves both markets" — is wrong for a connectable radio product. The Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure (Security Requirements for Relevant Connectable Products) Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/1007), in force 29 April 2024, apply in GB to consumer connectable products including network-connectable/Bluetooth devices. They mandate unique/user-defined passwords, a published vulnerability-reporting contact, and a disclosed defined support period, plus a GB statement of compliance retained for the longer of 10 years or the defined support period. This regime is entirely outside CE/UKCA and has no CE equivalent; the EU counterpart (RED delegated regulation 2022/30) is a different requirement set. So GB and EU need different cyber evidence regardless of marking.

3. Conformity assessment bodies are not interchangeable. gov.uk states UK Approved Bodies "can only be used to certify products for UKCA marking", while EU Notified Bodies "can only be used to certify against EU requirements". If any conformity module requires third-party assessment, the route is locked by the choice of body — CE recognition does not make the two fungible.

4. Economic-operator labelling still diverges: GB requires a UK-established importer/authorised representative with postal address, the EU requires an EU-established one, so two label variants are needed irrespective of marking. Note also the transitional flexibility permitting UKCA marking and importer details on a label or accompanying document only until 23:00 on 31 December 2027.

5. Scope error on "both markets": SI 2024/696 is Great Britain only. Northern Ireland continues to require CE (or CE + UKNI where a UK body was used), so a GB-plus-EU framing silently drops NI.

6. SI 2024/696 does not cover all regimes — medical devices, construction products, transportable pressure equipment, marine equipment, rail interoperability constituents, cableways and uncrewed aircraft systems have separate arrangements. Not fatal for an electrical/radio product, but the blanket phrasing "the relevant regimes" would mislead if the product scope widens.

COULD NOT VERIFY: the stated commencement date of 1 October 2024. It is plausible and widely reported, but the commencement provision was not visible in the fetched pages, and the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted. Treat as unverified rather than incorrect.

Method note: verified by direct fetch of legislation.gov.uk (SI 2024/696 contents, made version, explanatory note; SI 2023/1007) and the two cited gov.uk guidance pages. No WebSearch was available.

corrected.original: The EU Battery Directive is gone — Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 now applies directly and imposes CE marking on the battery itself, not just the appliance.
corrected.corrected:
Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 replaced Directive 2006/66/EC, which was repealed with effect from 18 August 2025 (Art. 95) — though Art. 11 of the old Directive continues to apply until 18 February 2027, Art. 21(2) until 18 August 2026, and the Art. 12(4)-(5) data-transmission duty until 30 June 2027. The Regulation applies directly and makes the battery itself a CE-marked product: since 18 August 2024 (Art. 96(2)(b), applying Art. 17 and Chapter VI) the manufacturer must draw up Annex VIII technical documentation, carry out an Art. 17 conformity assessment, draw up an EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking (Art. 38(1)-(3)).

Under Art. 20(1) the CE marking is affixed to the BATTERY; where that is not possible or not warranted due to the nature of the battery, it goes on the PACKAGING and the ACCOMPANYING DOCUMENTS — never on the host device. Art. 13(7) applies the same ladder to labels and the QR code. There is no provision permitting the battery's CE mark to be transferred to the appliance; the "affix to device" guidance is unsupported and contrary to Art. 20.

It is a distinct conformity regime with its own Annex VIII technical file, but NOT its own declaration: Art. 18(3) requires that where a battery is subject to more than one Union act demanding a DoC, a SINGLE EU DoC covering all of them be drawn up, naming the acts and their publication references (Art. 18(5) allows that single DoC to be compiled from existing individual ones).

For a typical portable or LMT pack, conformity assessment is Module A "Internal production control" (Annex VIII Part A) — self-declaration with no notified body. A notified body is only required via Art. 17(2) for Arts. 7-8 (carbon footprint, recycled content), which is deferred until 12 months after first publication of the Art. 30(2) list and applies only to EV, industrial and LMT batteries.

Substantive obligations are staged, so the spec should pin dates: Annex I lead limit for portable batteries from 18 Aug 2024 (zinc-air button cells exempt to 18 Aug 2028); separate-collection symbol from 18 Aug 2025; Art. 13(1)-(3) labels from 18 Aug 2026 or 18 months after the relevant implementing act, whichever is later; QR code from 18 Feb 2027; removability/replaceability (Art. 11) from 18 Feb 2027.
corrected.why:
Checked against the official consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 retrieved from the EU Publications Office (http://publications.europa.eu/resource/celex/32023R1542, Accept: application/xhtml+xml — EUR-Lex's own HTML endpoints returned empty 202s).

WHAT HOLDS:
- Reg. 2023/1542 does replace Dir. 2006/66/EC and does impose CE marking + an EU DoC on the battery as a product in its own right. Art. 38(1)-(3): the manufacturer draws up Annex VIII technical documentation, runs the Art. 17 conformity assessment, draws up an EU DoC under Art. 18 and affixes the CE marking under Arts. 19-20.
- The 18 August 2024 date is correct, via Art. 96(2)(b): "Article 17 and Chapter VI shall apply from 18 August 2024." Chapter VI is "Obligations of economic operators," containing Art. 38. (Arts. 18-20 sit in Chapter IV and technically applied from 18 Feb 2024, but they only bite through Art. 38.)
- Scope over embedded cells is correct. Art. 1(3): the Regulation "shall also apply to batteries that are incorporated into or added to products."

WHAT FAILS:
1. THE "AFFIX TO DEVICE" POINT IS WRONG — and it is the most order-relevant error, since it drives marking artwork and label real estate on the pack. Art. 20(1) verbatim: "The CE marking shall be affixed visibly, legibly and indelibly to the battery. Where that is not possible or not warranted due to the nature of the battery, it shall be affixed to the packaging and to the documents accompanying the battery." The fallback is packaging and accompanying documents — never the host appliance. Art. 13(7) repeats the identical battery → packaging + documents ladder for labels and the QR code. I searched every occurrence of "incorporated in/into" in the enacting terms and annexes: the phrase appears only in producer registration (Art. 55), online-platform duties (Art. 62), waste treatment (Art. 70), reporting (Arts. 75-76) and Annex I substance restrictions ("whether or not incorporated into appliances"). No provision transfers the battery's CE mark onto the device. The claim's own stated source (cecheck.com) does not assert this either — on fetch it explicitly does not address battery-vs-device placement, so the "secondary guidance" is uncorroborated as well as contrary to Art. 20.

2. "ITS OWN DoC" IS WRONG. Art. 18(3): "Where a battery is subject to more than one Union act requiring an EU declaration of conformity, a single EU declaration of conformity shall be drawn up in respect of all such Union acts." Consolidation is mandatory, not optional; Art. 18(5) merely permits that single DoC to be assembled from pre-existing individual declarations. So it is not a second, separate DoC layered alongside the RED one. "Its own technical documentation" is correct — Annex VIII Part A requires a distinct Annex VIII file.

3. ARTICLE NUMBERS ARE OFF BY ONE. Repeal is Art. 95, not 96. Entry into force/application is Art. 96, not 97. (The claim's pointer to "Art. 20 and Annex VIII" is right: Art. 20 is the affixing rule, Annex VIII is conformity assessment procedures.)

4. "THE DIRECTIVE IS GONE" IS IMPRECISE AND THE DATE IS EASILY MERGED WITH THE 2024 CE DATE. Art. 95: Dir. 2006/66/EC "is repealed with effect from 18 August 2025" — not 2024 — and three provisions survive: Art. 11 until 18 Feb 2027, Art. 12(4) and (5) until 31 Dec 2025 (the Commission data-transmission element until 30 June 2027), and Art. 21(2) until 18 Aug 2026. As of today (July 2026) the Directive is repealed but old Art. 11 and the data-transmission duty still run.

TWO OMISSIONS THAT MATTER FOR A PARTS ORDER:
- No notified body is needed for a typical portable/LMT pack. Art. 17(1) allows Module A "Internal production control" (Annex VIII Part A) — pure self-declaration — for conformity with Arts. 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14. A notified body only enters via Art. 17(2) (Arts. 7-8, carbon footprint and recycled content), which is deferred to 12 months after first publication of the Art. 30(2) list and applies only to EV/industrial/LMT batteries. Budgeting for third-party assessment on a small pack would be wasted money.
- What the mark actually attests to today is thin and staged: Annex I lead limit for portable batteries from 18 Aug 2024 (zinc-air button cells exempt until 18 Aug 2028); separate-collection symbol from 18 Aug 2025; Art. 13(1)-(3) labels from 18 Aug 2026 or 18 months after the implementing act, whichever is later; QR code from 18 Feb 2027; Art. 11 removability/replaceability from 18 Feb 2027 (Art. 96(2)(a)). A spec that says "CE-marked per 2023/1542" without pinning these dates will under- or over-scope the build.

Sources: [Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, official text via EU Publications Office](http://publications.europa.eu/resource/celex/32023R1542); [European Commission, batteries and accumulators](https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/waste-and-recycling/batteries-and-accumulators_en); [cecheck.com battery regulation page](https://cecheck.com/battery-regulation/) (stated source; confirms 18 Aug 2024 CE date and 18 Aug 2025 repeal, does not support the "affix to device" point). The CSA Group article returned HTTP 403 and could not be checked.

corrected.original: Battery labelling under Annex VI Part A becomes mandatory on 18 August 2026 — roughly one month from now — and applies to batteries built into appliances.
corrected.corrected:
Annex VI Part A labelling is NOT confirmed for 18 August 2026. Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 applies "from 18 August 2026 or 18 months after the date of entry into force of the implementing act referred to in paragraph 10, whichever is the latest." That implementing act — harmonised labelling specifications, which Article 13(10) required the Commission to adopt by 18 August 2025 — has still not been adopted as of July 2026. Because 18 August 2026 could only govern if the act had entered into force by 18 February 2025, the obligation cannot now bite before roughly 18 months after whenever the Commission finally adopts (no earlier than about early 2028). Treat 18 August 2026 as a nominal date subject to slippage, not a hard deadline, and note that the harmonised specifications you would design the label against do not yet exist.

Annex VI Part A requires TEN items, not five: (1) manufacturer identification (Art. 38(7)); (2) battery category and battery identification (Art. 38(6)); (3) place of manufacture; (4) date of manufacture (month and year); (5) weight; (6) capacity; (7) chemistry; (8) hazardous substances other than mercury, cadmium or lead; (9) usable extinguishing agent; (10) critical raw materials above 0.1% w/w. Annex VI Part A specifies no units for capacity — mAh/Wh would come from the unadopted implementing act. Item (8) is itself subject to pending proposal COM(2025) 981, which would narrow it to substances of very high concern at or above 0.1% w/w.

Placement: under Article 13(7) labels must be printed or engraved visibly, legibly and indelibly ON THE BATTERY; only where that is "not possible or not warranted on account of the nature and size of the battery" must they be affixed to the packaging AND to the accompanying documents — mandatory and conjunctive, not an optional either/or.

Batteries incorporated into or added to products are in scope, via Article 1(3) (not Article 13).

This is not your nearest deadline. Already in force and binding today: the separate collection symbol (Art. 13(4), since 18 August 2025, with area rules of at least 3% of the largest side, 1.5% for cylindrical cells, max 5x5 cm, and a 1x1 cm packaging symbol where it would fall below 0.47x0.47 cm) and Cd/Pb chemical symbols (Art. 13(5), for more than 0.002% cadmium or 0.004% lead). The next fixed forward dates are both 18 February 2027: the QR code (Art. 13(6)) and portable-battery removability/replaceability (Art. 11).
corrected.why:
The claim's central assertion — a hard 18 August 2026 deadline — omits the conditional clause that governs it, and that condition has failed.

1) DATE (fatal). Article 13(1) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 reads: "From 18 August 2026 OR 18 months after the date of entry into force of the implementing act referred to in paragraph 10, WHICHEVER IS THE LATEST." Article 13(10) required the Commission to adopt that harmonised-labelling-specifications implementing act by 18 August 2025. It has not been adopted. Verified via the EU Cellar SPARQL endpoint (publications.europa.eu/webapi/rdf/sparql): only three acts are based on CELEX 32023R1542 — Delegated Reg. (EU) 2025/606 (recycling efficiency methodology), Implementing Reg. (EU) 2025/2289 (waste-battery reporting/treatment), and Commission Notice 52025XC00214 (removability guidelines). A title search for acts since 2025 containing both "batter*" and "label*" returns zero results. Index freshness confirmed: 1,372–1,706 acts/month indexed Jan–Jun 2026, 775 in July 2026. Consolidated text 02023R1542-20250731 retains the identical conditional wording, so no corrigendum or amendment removed it. Arithmetic: for 18 Aug 2026 to be operative, the implementing act must have entered into force on or before 18 Feb 2025 — it did not. Even adoption on the day of writing yields ~January 2028.

2) LABEL CONTENT INCOMPLETE. Annex VI Part A contains 10 numbered items: (1) manufacturer identification per Art. 38(7); (2) battery category and battery identification per Art. 38(6); (3) place of manufacture; (4) date of manufacture (month and year); (5) weight; (6) capacity; (7) chemistry; (8) hazardous substances other than mercury, cadmium or lead; (9) usable extinguishing agent; (10) critical raw materials present above 0.1% w/w. The claim lists only 5, omitting place of manufacture, date of manufacture, weight, extinguishing agent, and critical raw materials.

3) PACKAGING FALLBACK MISSTATED. Article 13(7): labels "shall be affixed to the packaging AND to the documents accompanying the battery" — conjunctive and mandatory. The claim renders it as permissive and disjunctive ("may go on the packaging or accompanying documentation"). The trigger is also "not possible or not warranted on account of the nature and size of the battery," not merely a small surface.

4) UNITS UNSUPPORTED. Annex VI Part A point 6 says only "the capacity." The mAh/Wh units are not in Annex VI Part A; they would be set by the very implementing act that does not exist. Art. 13(2) separately mandates a capacity label for rechargeable portable, LMT and SLI batteries.

5) CORRECT ELEMENT. Batteries incorporated into products ARE in scope — but via Article 1(3) ("It shall also apply to batteries that are incorporated into or added to products"), not via anything "explicit" in Article 13.

6) "NEAREST HARD DEADLINE" IS WRONG. Art. 13(4) (separate collection symbol, with its 3%/1.5% area and 0.47cm rules) and Art. 13(5) (Cd/Pb chemical symbols) have applied since 18 August 2025 and are live obligations now. The next fixed forward date is 18 February 2027 (QR code, Art. 13(6); removability/replaceability, Art. 11).

7) SOURCE UNRELIABLE. The impala-services blog lists the crossed-out wheelie bin (actually Annex VI Part B / Art. 13(4)), CE marking (Arts. 19-20), and "safe usage and storage instructions covering temperature, fire risk, and child safety" (not an Annex VI Part A item) as Part A content, and omits the conditional clause entirely.

8) CONTENT IN FLUX. Pending proposal COM(2025) 981 of 10 December 2025 would replace Annex VI Part A point 8 with "substances of very high concern ... other than mercury, cadmium and lead, with a concentration equal or above 0,1%, weight on weight."

Caveat noted for completeness: a minority reading holds 18 Aug 2026 binds regardless, on the view that "whichever is the latest" presupposes an existing act. Even under that reading the claim is unsupportable as stated, since no harmonised specifications exist to comply against — so it cannot be presented to an engineer as settled fact.

corrected.original: From 18 February 2027 a QR code linking to battery information is required — but the full 'battery passport' is a narrower obligation that likely does not apply to you.
corrected.corrected:
Article 13(6) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 requires that from 18 February 2027 ALL batteries be marked with a QR code per Annex VI Part C. The digital battery passport (Art. 77) is genuinely narrower — from the same date it applies only to LMT batteries, industrial batteries with capacity greater than 2 kWh, and EV batteries — so a cell that is not LMT, not EV, and not an industrial battery above 2 kWh is outside the passport. Sources do conflate the two (including rev-log.com, which states the QR links to a battery passport); the distinction holds against the regulation text.

Three corrections for the spec:

(1) The non-passport QR is not a generic information link. Art. 13(6)(b) requires it to give access to the Art. 13(1)-(5) label information, the declaration of conformity (Art. 18), the report under Art. 52(3), and waste-battery prevention/management information under Art. 74(1)(a)-(f), kept complete, up to date and accurate. Budget for a hosted, maintained public resource. (The Art. 52(3) element lands late: Reg. (EU) 2025/1561 moved due diligence to 18 August 2027.)

(2) 18 February 2027 is not the first deadline. Art. 13(4) separate-collection marking has applied since 18 August 2025 and binds today, with size rules: at least 3% of the largest side (max 5x5 cm), at least 1.5% of surface area for cylindrical cells, and where the symbol would fall below 0.47x0.47 cm, a symbol of at least 1x1 cm on the packaging instead. Art. 13(5) adds Cd/Pb marking above 0.002%/0.004%. Art. 13(1)-(3) label content applies from 18 August 2026 OR 18 months after the Art. 13(10) implementing act enters into force, whichever is later — a floating date to track.
