(3) Record the statutory test, not "small portable cell." Art. 3(9) 'portable battery' = sealed, 5 kg or less, not designed specifically for industrial use, and not EV/LMT/SLI; Art. 3(13) makes any battery over 5 kg that is not EV/LMT/SLI an industrial battery. Confirm on the datasheet: not LMT, not EV, and either not industrial or industrial at 2 kWh or less. Art. 1(3) confirms the Regulation reaches batteries incorporated into products, and Art. 1(4) treats cells supplied for end use as batteries in their own right.

Placement: Art. 13(7) requires the QR printed or engraved visibly, legibly and indelibly on the battery; only where impossible or unwarranted given nature and size may it move to the packaging AND accompanying documents (both). Finally, settle who discharges the duty — buying cells already compliantly placed on the EU market pushes it upstream; importing cells and placing them on the market yourself makes it yours.
corrected.why:
Verified against the primary text (EUR-Lex CELEX 02023R1542-20250731, the current consolidated version; original 32023R1542 cross-checked). EUR-Lex blocks scripted fetches behind an AWS WAF challenge, so I read it through a browser.

WHAT THE CLAIM GETS RIGHT (verbatim confirmation):
- Art 13(6): "From 18 February 2027, all batteries shall be marked with a QR code as described in Part C of Annex VI." Broad application to all batteries — correct.
- Art 13(6)(a) routes only "LMT batteries, industrial batteries with a capacity greater than 2kWh and electric vehicles batteries" to the passport; Art 13(6)(b) gives other batteries a lighter payload. The split is real.
- Art 77(1): "From 18 February 2027 each LMT battery, each industrial battery with a capacity greater than 2 kWh and each electric vehicle battery placed on the market or put into service shall have an electronic record ('battery passport')." Scope exactly as claimed.
- Neither article was touched by the amendments: M1 = Reg (EU) 2024/1781 (ESPR), M2 = Reg (EU) 2025/1561, which moved Art 48 due diligence to 18 August 2027 only. Art 13(6) and 77(1) dates stand.
- The claim's warning about conflation is well-founded: its own stated source, rev-log.com, says "By February 2027, batteries will require a QR code linking to a battery passport" — which is wrong for a portable cell.

WHY I STILL REFUTE (imprecise in ways that matter for a parts order):

1. UNDERSTATES THE QR PAYLOAD. "Linking to battery information" is vague. Art 13(6)(b) specifies exactly what a non-passport battery's QR must reach: the Art 13(1)-(5) label information, the declaration of conformity (Art 18), the report referred to in Art 52(3), and waste-battery prevention/management information under Art 74(1)(a)-(f) — "complete, up-to-date and accurate." That is a durable hosted public resource with a defined content set, not a datasheet link. (Wrinkle: the Art 52(3) due-diligence report element is now unavailable at 18 Feb 2027, since Reg 2025/1561 pushed due diligence to 18 Aug 2027.)

2. TREATS 18 FEB 2027 AS THE OPERATIVE DATE, MISSING OBLIGATIONS ALREADY LIVE. Art 13(4) separate-collection symbol has applied since 18 AUGUST 2025 — already in force as of today, with hard geometry: at least 3% of the largest side, max 5x5 cm; at least 1.5% of surface area for cylindrical cells; and if the symbol would come out smaller than 0.47 x 0.47 cm, a symbol of at least 1 x 1 cm goes on the packaging instead. Art 13(5) requires Cd or Pb marking above 0.002%/0.004%. Art 13(1)-(3) label content applies from 18 August 2026 "or 18 months after the date of entry into force of the implementing act referred to in paragraph 10, whichever is the latest" — a floating date the claim does not mention. A spec anchored only on Feb 2027 omits marking duties that bind now.

3. USES THE WRONG SCOPE TEST. "A small portable cell" is not the statutory gate. Art 3(9) 'portable battery' requires sealed and 5 kg or less and not designed specifically for industrial use; Art 3(13) makes ANY battery over 5 kg that is not EV/LMT/SLI an industrial battery. The passport gate is capacity greater than 2 kWh (for industrial), or being LMT or EV. Art 1(3) confirms the Regulation reaches batteries "incorporated into or added to products," and Art 1(4) treats cells placed on the market for end use as batteries in their own right. So the spec should record the actual test result, not the informal "small portable cell" characterisation.

Also unaddressed and worth a line in the spec: Art 13(7) requires the QR to be "printed or engraved visibly, legibly and indelibly on the battery," and only where that is not possible or not warranted on account of nature and size may it go on the packaging AND the accompanying documents — both, not either. And the obligation attaches to the battery placed on the market, so whether it is discharged by the cell supplier or by you depends on whether you buy already-compliant EU-market cells or import cells and place them on the market yourself. That determines whether this is a purchasing spec line or your own compliance build.

Note also that amendment proposals 52025PC0258, 52025PC0501, 52025PC0504, 52025PC0981 and 52025PC0982 are pending against this Regulation; none are adopted law, but the Feb 2027 dates are not immune to further omnibus simplification.

corrected.original: Article 11 removability and replaceability applies from 18 February 2027 and is the provision that decides sealed-versus-replaceable for you.
corrected.corrected:
Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 applies from 18 February 2027 (Art 96(2)(a)). It is the BASELINE provision on end-user battery replaceability, not the sole one: Art 11(1), fourth subparagraph, makes it "without prejudice to" stricter EU law on electrical and electronic equipment (per guidance C/2025/214 §2.2, Ecodesign Reg (EU) 2023/1670 already imposes stricter rules, incl. 7-year spares, on phones and tablets).

Framing correction: "sealed vs replaceable" is a false dichotomy. Under Art 3(9) a "portable battery" IS by definition sealed — a battery that is sealed, weighs 5 kg or less, is not designed specifically for industrial use, and is neither an electric vehicle, LMT, nor SLI battery. Article 11 governs whether the end user can remove and swap the pack, not whether the cell is sealed.

BASELINE RULE (Art 11(1)): whoever places the product on the market must ensure the battery is readily removable and replaceable by the end user at any time during the product's lifetime. Applies to entire batteries, not individual cells. "Readily removable" = removable with commercially available tools, without requiring specialised tools (unless provided free of charge with the product), proprietary tools, thermal energy, or solvents. "Readily replaceable" (Art 11(6)) = substitutable by another compatible battery without affecting functioning, performance or safety. Guidance C/2025/214 adds that removal/replacement should avoid damaging the battery or the device, and maps "commercially available tools" onto EN 45554:2020e categories (basic tools/no tools + commercially available tools). Instructions and safety information must accompany the product and be permanently available on a public website.

SOFTWARE (Art 11(8)): software must not be used to impede replacement with a compatible battery or key components. Guidance C/2025/214 names "parts-pairing" as a specific example.

SPARES (Art 11(7)): available as spare parts of the equipment they power for a minimum of five years after the last unit of the equipment MODEL is placed on the market, at a reasonable AND non-discriminatory price for independent professionals and end users. Non-reusable fasteners must also be available as spares. Guidance: this does not apply to products placed on the market before 18 February 2027.

DEROGATIONS (omitted from the original claim — these decide the design):
- Art 11(2), partial (professional-only replacement permitted): (a) appliances specifically designed to operate primarily in an environment regularly subject to splashing water, water streams or water immersion AND intended to be washable or rinseable — only where required to ensure safety of user and appliance; (b) professional medical imaging/radiotherapy devices and IVD medical devices. Guidance applies five cumulative tests to (a): "specifically", "primarily", "washable/rinseable", documented evidence that user replacement would compromise safety, and documented evidence that redesign is impossible. An IP rating alone does not establish these (note: the OJ text's sentence "the IP rating alone is considered as sufficient" appears to be a typo contradicting Recital 39 and the surrounding text — do not rely on it).
- Art 11(3), full disapplication: where continuity of power supply is necessary AND a permanent connection is required to ensure safety of user and appliance; OR, for products whose MAIN function is collecting and supplying data, for data-integrity reasons. Guidance examples: professional weather stations, lab instruments, CMOS/volatile-memory backup cells, tolling on-board equipment, payment terminals. Expressly NOT available where data collection is a secondary feature, or where the device has non-volatile memory so no integrity loss arises.
- Art 11(5): LMT batteries need only be removable and replaceable by an independent professional, not the end user.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR SOURCING: Article 11 does not by itself prohibit a sealed cell, and it does not unconditionally require user-replaceability. It requires user-replaceability from 18 Feb 2027 UNLESS an Art 11(2) or 11(3) derogation applies and is evidenced in the product documentation at the time of placing on the market. For a device whose main function is collecting and supplying data, the Art 11(3) route must be assessed explicitly but will likely fail if the device uses non-volatile memory. Specify parts on the assumption that the baseline user-replaceability rule applies unless and until a derogation is documented.
corrected.why:
Verified against the official text of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 and Commission Notice C/2025/214, both retrieved from the EU Publications Office CELLAR repository (EUR-Lex itself was behind an AWS WAF bot challenge, which I did not attempt to bypass).

WHAT CHECKS OUT:
- Date is correct. Art 96(2)(a) states verbatim: "Article 11 shall apply from 18 February 2027." Guidance C/2025/214 repeats this.
- Commercially available tools / specialised tools free of charge / proprietary tools disqualifying — correct, Art 11(1) second subparagraph, verbatim.
- Software provision — correct, Art 11(8). And "parts-pairing" IS explicitly named in guidance C/2025/214 as "An example of software that impedes replacement," so that gloss is properly supported.
- Five-year spares — correct, Art 11(7).
- "without damaging the battery or device" — not in the Article text (the legal tests are "commercially available tools" for removability and "without affecting the functioning, the performance or the safety" for replaceability), but the phrasing does appear in guidance C/2025/214 §2, so it is defensible as the Commission's reading rather than as statutory language.
- The C/2025/214 citation is genuine: "Commission guidelines to facilitate the harmonised application of provisions on the removability and replaceability of portable batteries and LMT batteries in Regulation (EU) 2023/1542", OJ C, 10.1.2025.

WHY IT IS STILL REFUTED — the claim is stated far more confidently than the sources support, and the omissions are exactly the ones that decide a hardware design:

1. DEROGATIONS ARE ENTIRELY OMITTED. The claim presents Art 11(1) as absolute. It is not. Art 11(2) permits professional-only replacement for wet-environment appliances and certain medical devices; Art 11(3) fully disapplies the obligation where continuity of power supply plus a permanent connection is required for safety, or for data-integrity in products whose main function is collecting and supplying data. Guidance C/2025/214 devotes two of its five substantive sections to these. Even the claim's own stated source (prodlaw.eu) describes both derogations — so the claim is less accurate than the page it cites.

2. THE DATA-INTEGRITY DEROGATION IS DIRECTLY LIVE FOR THIS DEVICE AND WAS NOT MENTIONED. A friend-finder that collects and supplies location data as its main function is precisely the fact pattern Art 11(3) addresses. The guidance narrows it hard (excludes devices where data collection is secondary, and devices with non-volatile memory, since no integrity risk arises), so it will most likely NOT be available — but an engineer ordering parts must evaluate it, not be told the rule is unconditional.

3. "THE PROVISION THAT DECIDES SEALED-VERSUS-REPLACEABLE" IS WRONG TWICE OVER. (a) Art 11(1) fourth subparagraph makes Article 11 expressly "without prejudice to" stricter EU law on electrical and electronic equipment; guidance §2.2 confirms Ecodesign Reg (EU) 2023/1670 already goes further for phones/tablets (7-year spares vs 5). Article 11 is a floor, not the sole determinant. (b) More fundamentally, "sealed versus replaceable" is a category error: Art 3(9) defines a portable battery AS a sealed battery. Sealing the cell is not what Article 11 regulates — user-removability of the pack is. A sealed cell is definitionally compliant.

4. DEFINITION IS INCOMPLETE. Art 3(9) requires the battery also be "neither an electric vehicle battery, an LMT battery, nor an SLI battery" — omitted. Related: Art 11(5) requires LMT batteries to be replaceable only by an independent professional, not the end user, so "Article 11 = end-user removability" is a conflation.

5. SPARES WORDING IMPRECISE AND ONE MATERIAL CARVE-OUT MISSED. It is "reasonable and non-discriminatory" price, for independent professionals AND end users, measured from the last unit of the equipment MODEL. Guidance adds that the obligation does not apply to products placed on the market before 18 Feb 2027, and that non-reusable fasteners must also be stocked as spares.

6. TRAP TO FLAG: the wet-environment derogation is not an IP-rating shortcut. Guidance sets five cumulative tests (specifically / primarily / washable-rinseable / safety actually compromised / redesign impossible). Note the OJ text contains an apparent typo — "As such, the IP rating alone is considered as sufficient to demonstrate the compliance" — which contradicts the immediately preceding sentences and Recital 39; the plain intent is "not sufficient". An engineer should not rely on that sentence as printed.

Under the instruction to treat substantially-right-but-imprecise as refuted, this fails: the date and core mechanics are sound, but the unconditional framing and the missing derogations could drive a wrong sourcing decision in either direction.

corrected.original: The Article 11 derogations are narrow and a venue safety appliance probably does not qualify — do not design a sealed unit on the assumption you are exempt.
corrected.corrected:
SCOPE AND TIMING FIRST. Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 applies from 18 February 2027 (Art. 96). It bites only on products incorporating a "portable battery" — Art. 3: sealed, 5 kg or less, not designed specifically for industrial use, and not an EV, LMT or SLI battery. Settle that classification before any derogation analysis: a pack over 5 kg, or one designed specifically for industrial use, is outside Art. 11(1) entirely.

ART. 11(2) (professional-only replacement) is a closed list, extendable only by delegated act under Art. 11(4). It currently covers exactly: (a) appliances specifically designed to operate primarily in environments regularly subject to splashing water, water streams or immersion AND intended to be washable or rinseable — and only where the derogation is required to ensure safety of the user and the appliance; and (b) professional medical imaging and radiotherapy devices (MDR 2017/745) and in vitro diagnostic medical devices (IVDR 2017/746). It does NOT include smoke alarms. No Art. 11(4) delegated act has been adopted; the only amendments to 2023/1542 to date are 2024/1781 (Art. 77) and 2025/1561 (Art. 48).

ART. 11(3) is a full derogation from Art. 11(1) and is criteria-based, not a closed list. The test is conjunctive: continuity of power supply must be necessary AND a permanent connection between the product and the battery must be required — either to ensure the safety of the user and the appliance, or, for products whose main function is to collect and supply data, for data-integrity reasons. Note the permanent-connection element: you must be able to show a permanent connection is required, not merely that a long-lived cell is convenient.

FOR A VENUE SAFETY APPLIANCE the Art. 11(3) safety limb is a mainstream reading, not an aggressive one. Commission Notice C/2025/214 (10 January 2025) gives as the paradigm "life-saving, life-sustaining devices, and safety-critical devices", and expressly accepts smoke alarms, CO detectors and gas alarms designed for at least 10 years of uninterrupted operation with a battery matched to that service life. The guidance states its examples are non-exhaustive and illustrative; it is also non-binding, as only the CJEU binds.

DESIGN CONDITIONS TO SPEC AGAINST if relying on Art. 11(3): a design life of at least 10 years with a service-life-matched cell, and documented technical justification that a permanent battery connection is required for safety. Caveat for this product: the guidance's smoke-alarm reasoning is framed around residential products and rides on the CPR harmonised standard EN 14604, which itself requires a user-replaceable internal power source unless operating life is 10 years or more. A commercial venue appliance may instead sit under fire-detection product law (EN 54 series). Check whether a sector-specific harmonised standard imposes its own replaceability rule — Art. 11(1) is expressly without prejudice to stricter EU rules, and the guidance says that where a harmonised standard sets replaceability requirements, those apply instead.

OBLIGATIONS THAT SURVIVE ANY DEROGATION: Arts. 11(2) and 11(3) displace only paragraph 1. Art. 11(7) still requires batteries to be available as spare parts to independent professionals and end-users for at least 5 years after the last unit of the model is placed on the market, at a reasonable and non-discriminatory price; Art. 11(8) still prohibits software that impedes replacement with a compatible battery. Budget a serviceable cell and a spares channel even in a sealed design.

Have a regulatory lawyer confirm the Art. 11(3) rationale in writing before freezing the enclosure — but do not assume the exemption is unavailable.
corrected.why:
Checked against the authentic OJ text of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, the full amendment history via the Publications Office SPARQL endpoint, and Commission Notice C/2025/214 itself (fetched in full). Five defects, three of them load-bearing for a parts order.

1. SMOKE ALARMS ARE IN THE WRONG PARAGRAPH. The claim puts "10-year smoke alarms" in the Art. 11(2) closed list. The verbatim Art. 11(2) list contains exactly two items: (a) appliances designed to operate primarily in splashing-water/water-stream/immersion environments AND intended to be washable or rinseable; (b) professional medical imaging and radiotherapy devices plus IVD medical devices. No smoke alarms, and no "IVD devices for performance study" (that phrase is from IVDR 2017/746, not from Art. 11(2)). I confirmed Art. 11(2) is unamended: the only two acts amending 2023/1542 are 2024/1781 (ESPR, which amends Art. 77 only) and 2025/1561 (which amends Art. 48 only). No Art. 11(4) delegated act exists. The Commission guidance in fact discusses 10-year smoke alarms under Art. 11(3), i.e. as a FULL derogation, not professional-only replacement. The claim both misplaces the item and understates its effect.

2. THE ART. 11(3) TEST IS MISSTATED, IN THE PERMISSIVE DIRECTION. The claim renders it as "continuity of power supply is necessary for safety or data integrity." The actual test is conjunctive and has a third element the claim drops entirely: continuity of power supply must be necessary AND a permanent connection between the product and the battery must be required — either to ensure the safety of the user and the appliance, or, only for products that collect and supply data as their main function, for data-integrity reasons. The permanent-connection element is the design-necessity gate and the hardest to satisfy; omitting it from a hardware spec is the single most consequential error here.

3. THE APPLICABILITY JUDGEMENT IS CONTRADICTED BY THE CLAIM'S OWN CITED SOURCE. The claim calls the Art. 11(3) route "aggressive" and says the Commission "treats these as tightly drawn." C/2025/214 says the opposite in two ways. It names life-saving, life-sustaining and safety-critical devices as the paradigm for the Art. 11(3) safety limb, and works through smoke alarms, CO detectors and gas alarms as qualifying where designed for at least 10 years of uninterrupted operation with a battery of matching service life. And it states its examples are non-exhaustive and illustrative. Art. 11(2) is a closed list; Art. 11(3) is criteria-based with open examples. The claim collapses that structural distinction and thereby mischaracterises the guidance.

4. TWO THRESHOLD OMISSIONS THAT CHANGE THE PARTS DECISION. Article 96 provides that Article 11 applies from 18 February 2027 — the claim presents the duty as already live. And Art. 11(1) bites only on products incorporating a "portable battery," defined in Art. 3 as sealed, 5 kg or less, not designed specifically for industrial use, and not EV/LMT/SLI. A wall-mounted venue appliance with a >5 kg or industrial-use pack is outside Art. 11 altogether, with no derogation analysis needed. The claim instructs the engineer to abandon a sealed design without ever raising the classification question that logically precedes it.

5. WHAT SURVIVES ANY DEROGATION IS UNSTATED. Arts. 11(2) and 11(3) derogate only from paragraph 1. Art. 11(7) (spare batteries available to professionals and end-users for at least 5 years after the last unit of the model is placed on the market, at a reasonable non-discriminatory price) and Art. 11(8) (no software impediment to replacement) apply regardless. A sealed unit still owes a spares channel — a real BOM and logistics cost the claim never flags.

The claim's cautious instinct (get counsel; do not assume exemption) is sound, but the stated grounds are wrong, the statutory test is misquoted, and the risk is pointed in the wrong direction. corrected.original: A user-replaceable cell does NOT materially reduce the core compliance burden — it shifts the burden rather than removing it.
corrected.corrected:
A user-replaceable cell does not remove the core compliance burden — it redistributes it, and whether it reduces net testing depends on cell architecture, not on replaceability alone.

Unchanged by the replaceable-vs-sealed choice per se: IEC 62368-1 Annex M evaluation, UN 38.3 transport testing, WEEE registration, battery EPR registration, CE marking, and Battery Regulation labelling.

Caveat on "unchanged": this holds only if cell architecture is held constant. If the sealed option is a custom multi-cell or pouch pack, you own pack-level IEC 62133-2 and pack-level UN 38.3. If the replaceable option is a standard off-the-shelf cell (18650 / AA / coin), you inherit the cell manufacturer's 62133-2 certificate and UN 38.3 test summary. In that common pairing, replaceable genuinely does reduce your own test scope.

Replaceable removes the Art. 11 problem but adds:
- A spare-parts supply obligation running a minimum of five years from the date the LAST unit of the model is placed on the market (not from launch), at a reasonable and non-discriminatory price. A three-year production run implies roughly eight years of spares liability.
- A tooling constraint that is LESS restrictive than "tool-free": Art. 11 permits removal using commercially available tools. Specialised tools are permitted only if supplied free of charge with the product. Proprietary tools, thermal energy, and solvents are prohibited. A screwed battery hatch opened with a standard Phillips or Torx driver is compliant — do not over-constrain the mechanical design to latches or captive tools.
- New IEC 62368-1 work on the user-accessible compartment: contact protection, reverse-insertion, wrong-cell-type safeguards, and enclosure integrity after user access. Annex M was heavily revised in IEC 62368-1:2023 Ed. 4; if the cell is a button or coin cell, the Ed. 4 button-cell-cover requirements plus GPSR child-safety expectations are a hard, non-trivial addition.
- A standalone spares channel, which is its own compliance surface: spare cells shipped alone are UN 3480, not UN 3481 — forbidden as cargo on passenger aircraft and limited to 30% state of charge by air under PI 965 — and a spare placed on the market on its own carries its own Battery Regulation labelling, conformity, and EPR reporting.

Sealed avoids the above but is non-compliant for the EU market from 18 February 2027 unless the product falls within an Art. 11(2) derogation. Those derogations are self-executing category exemptions, not a waiver you apply for: devices designed to operate in an environment regularly subject to splashing water, water streams, or immersion and intended to be washable or rinseable; and professional medical imaging, radiotherapy, and in vitro diagnostic devices.

Net: replaceable remains the lower-risk path. Sell it on Art. 11 compliance and field-serviceability. Claim a testing reduction only if the replaceable design uses a pre-certified standard cell and the sealed alternative would have required a custom pack — otherwise the burden shifts rather than shrinks.

Status: engineering/regulatory synthesis of Reg. (EU) 2023/1542 Art. 11 (as read with Commission Notice OJ C/2025/214), IEC 62368-1:2023 Annex M, IEC 62133-2, and IATA/ICAO PI 965/966/967. Confirm the button-cell and compartment specifics against the actual Ed. 4 Annex M text with your test house before releasing tooling.
corrected.why:
The overall thesis (replaceable shifts rather than removes burden; sell it on Art. 11 compliance, not on reduced testing) is defensible. But three specifics are wrong or overstated in ways that would mislead an engineer ordering parts, and one omission understates the burden replaceability adds.

1. "Tool-free-or-free-tool constraint" is FACTUALLY WRONG and is the most consequential error, because it is a mechanical design constraint. Art. 11 and the Commission Notice (OJ C/2025/214) define readily removable as removable "with the use of commercially available tools, without requiring the use of specialised tools, unless provided free of charge with the product" — plus no proprietary tools, no thermal energy, no solvents. A screwed-down battery door opened with a common Phillips or Torx driver is compliant. The claim's phrasing would wrongly push the design toward latches, slides, or a bundled free tool and would wrongly reject a perfectly compliant screwed hatch. Confirmed verbatim in the Commission Notice snippet and in JRC stakeholder material (susproc.jrc.ec.europa.eu, Battery RR stakeholder decks, June and Oct 2023).

2. "Five-year spare-parts supply obligation" understates duration. The clock runs from placing the LAST unit of the model on the market, not from launch, and carries a "reasonable and non-discriminatory price" condition. A three-year production run therefore implies roughly eight years of spares liability. Verified via prodlaw.eu summary of Art. 11: spares available "at a reasonable price ... for at least five years after the last unit is placed on the market."

3. "IEC 62133-2 cell certification" and "UN 38.3 transport testing" listed as unchanged is true only if cell/pack architecture is held constant — which is not what the real decision looks like. IEC 62133-2 covers cells AND batteries. The sealed option in practice is usually a custom pouch or multi-cell pack, which lands pack-level 62133-2 and pack-level UN 38.3 on you. A user-replaceable standard cell (18650, AA, coin) lets you inherit the cell maker's existing 62133-2 certificate and UN 38.3 test summary. So the choice CAN materially reduce your own testing scope. The claim states the invariance more confidently than it holds.

4. OMISSION that strengthens the thesis: selling spare cells through a spares channel moves them from UN 3481 (contained in / packed with equipment) to UN 3480 (batteries shipped alone) — forbidden as cargo on passenger aircraft, and limited to 30% state of charge by air under PI 965. Confirmed via IATA Lithium Battery Guidance and 2026 IATA update summaries. That is a genuine NEW compliance and logistics burden the claim's list misses. Likewise, a spare battery placed on the market standalone is itself a product with its own Battery Regulation labelling, its own conformity/CE obligations, its own UN 38.3 test summary, and its own EPR reporting line — so "CE marking / labelling unchanged" is too strong.

5. "Absent a derogation" reads like an available waiver route. Art. 11(2) derogations are self-executing category exemptions (devices designed to operate in an environment regularly subject to splashing/water streams/immersion and intended to be washable or rinseable; professional medical imaging, radiotherapy, and IVD devices). There is no application process; you either fall in the category or you do not. Also, Art. 11 governs portable AND LMT batteries, and for some cases replacement by an independent professional is contemplated rather than the end user.

CONFIRMED as stated: the 18 February 2027 application date for Art. 11 (two independent sources), the "commercially available tools" standard, the existence of the spare-parts obligation, and the direction of the 62368-1 point — Annex M was heavily revised in IEC 62368-1:2023 Ed. 4 and does add specific requirements for button-cell covers (element.com change summary), so a user-accessible compartment genuinely does add safety-evaluation work, especially for coin cells where GPSR and the Ed. 4 button-cell provisions bite hard.

Verdict: substantially right thesis, materially imprecise in the details an engineer would build against. Refuted per the "substantially right but imprecise" rule.

Sources: [Commission Notice OJ C/2025/214](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/C/2025/214/oj/eng), [prodlaw.eu Art. 11 explainer](https://prodlaw.eu/2025/02/eu-battery-regulation-removability-and-replaceability-requirements-explained/), [JRC Battery RR stakeholder material](https://susproc.jrc.ec.europa.eu/product-bureau/sites/default/files/2023-11/Battery%20RR%20-%20stakeholder-%2030October23.pdf), [Element guide to IEC 62368-1](https://www.element.com/resources/articles/a-complete-guide-to-iec-62368-1), [UL Li-ion in consumer tech / Annex M](https://www.ul.com/resources/evaluation-li-ion-batteries-consumer-tech-products), [IATA Lithium Battery Guidance](https://www.iata.org/contentassets/05e6d8742b0047259bf3a700bc9d42b9/lithium-battery-guidance-document.pdf), [PI 965 state-of-charge](https://dginspector.com/blog/lithium-battery-state-of-charge-pi965).

corrected.original: Both WEEE and battery EPR registration are required, and the real cost is per-member-state registration across the EU, not the UK fee.
corrected.corrected:
Both WEEE and battery EPR registration are required, and the recurring cost is dominated by per-member-state EU registration rather than the UK registration itself — but only to the extent you are the entity first placing product on the market in each member state.

UK: Producers placing under 5 tonnes of EEE per year register directly with the environmental regulator as small producers via the WEEE online service (weee.service.gov.uk), rather than joining a producer compliance scheme; gov.uk does not publish a fee for this route, so confirm the current regulator charge before budgeting (the commonly cited ~GBP 30/year is unverified against the regulator's own pages). Batteries are a SEPARATE regime with a SEPARATE and lower threshold: producers placing more than 1 tonne of portable batteries per year must join a Battery Compliance Scheme. For a battery-powered product, 1 tonne of portable batteries — not the 5t EEE figure — is the threshold that governs, and crossing it is a step-change in cost, not a fee adjustment. Battery weight is reported separately from EEE weight.

EU: WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU Art. 16 (Registration, information and reporting) — NOT Art. 17, which is Authorised representative — requires registration in each member state where you place product. EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 Art. 56(1) requires registration per member state; Art. 56(3) is the separate requirement to appoint an authorised representative where you are not established in that member state.

Whether six EU markets means six registrations depends on your route to market: selling direct-to-consumer or as your own importer, yes — six registrations, six fee sets, six reporting cycles. Selling to an in-country distributor who acts as importer shifts the producer obligation to them, and this routing choice is the main lever available to a small hardware company.

Budget figures of EUR 500-2,000 per market per year via a consolidator are an unvalidated engineering estimate and must be replaced with an actual consolidator quote before use as a planning number.

Note also that packaging EPR is a third per-member-state regime that a boxed hardware product almost always triggers, and should be budgeted alongside WEEE and batteries.
corrected.why:
Core thrust is correct (both WEEE and battery EPR apply; recurring per-member-state EU registration dominates the UK fee), but the claim fails on four checkable points, and the instruction is to refute if substantially right but imprecise.

1. WRONG ARTICLE CITATIONS. Verified via legislation.gov.uk's copy of Directive 2012/19/EU: Article 16 is "Registration, information and reporting"; Article 17 is "Authorised representative". The claim cites Art. 17 for the registration duty — swapped. Same error for batteries: the claim's OWN stated source (circularcompliance.com) states Art. 56(3) is the authorised-representative obligation for producers not established in the MS; the registration duty is 56(1). The claim attributes registration to 56(3).

2. UK SENTENCE IS SELF-CONTRADICTORY AND THE FEE IS UNSOURCED. The claim says small producers register directly with the regulator "rather than joining a full producer compliance scheme", then prices it at "around GBP 30/year via a scheme". Both cannot hold. The cited gov.uk EEE page confirms the <5t direct-registration route via the WEEE online service but states no fee whatsoever; the GBP 30 figure does not appear in the stated source and could not be substantiated from regulator pages.

3. MISSING OPERATIVE THRESHOLD. The claim gives only the 5t EEE threshold. gov.uk batteries guidance states producers placing more than 1 tonne of portable batteries per year must join a Battery Compliance Scheme. For a battery-powered device that is the governing number, and crossing it is a step-change in cost, not a fee adjustment. Omitting it invites the exact under-budgeting the claim warns about.

4. OVERSTATED CONDITIONALITY. "Six EU markets can mean six registrations" is presented as unconditional. The obligation attaches to whoever first places product on the market in that member state. Direct/online sales or acting as own importer, yes; selling to an in-country distributor who imports shifts the producer obligation to them. That is the principal cost-avoidance lever and the claim does not qualify it.

5. The EUR 500-2,000/market/year figure is honestly flagged as an engineering estimate (correct disclosure) but must not be carried as a planning number without a consolidator quote. EUR-Lex was unreachable (empty responses); article headings were confirmed via legislation.gov.uk instead. WebSearch budget was exhausted, so the GBP 30 figure is unverified rather than affirmatively disproven — under the default-to-refuted rule it cannot be asserted.

Additional omission worth flagging: packaging EPR is a third per-member-state regime a boxed hardware product almost always triggers; a claim about under-budgeted recurring compliance cost that omits it still understates the total.

corrected.original: The EU authorised-representative requirement for EPR is currently in flux and may be relaxed for small enterprises, but the underlying registration duty will remain.
corrected.corrected:
As a UK-established company you are a third-country producer, and an EPR authorised representative IS required — not "likely." Treat this as firm and budget for it now.

Scope (the cost driver): the AR obligation is per-waste-stream AND per-Member-State. PPWR, WEEE and the Batteries Regulation each handle it differently, and each Member State of sale requires its own appointment. For a battery-containing device in packaging sold across several Member States this is a matrix of appointments, not a single one. Under the Batteries Regulation the duty (cited as Art. 56(3)) expressly covers producers established "in another EU Member State or third country." Under PPWR a NEW EU-level authorised representative for packaging is required for non-EU producers IN ADDITION to existing national representatives — so for a UK entity the AR burden is increasing, not relaxing.

Distinct obligations, do not collapse into one line item: (1) appointment of the AR; (2) entry in each national producer register — a public-authority act, typically executed by the AR; (3) membership of a PRO / compliance scheme; (4) periodic reporting of quantities placed on the market; (5) fees. These are separate and separately costed.

On the claimed reform: a Commission proposal to suspend the EPR-representative obligation, European Parliament draft reports of May 2026 limiting it to micro and small enterprises, and a decision scheduled for 1 October 2026 are NOT stated by either cited source, and could not be confirmed against EUR-Lex or the EP Legislative Observatory (both unreachable in this check). Do not carry those dates into the specification on this evidence. Critically, any such relaxation is by its own terms scoped to EU-ESTABLISHED companies and would not reach a UK entity. Existing registrations remain valid; reporting and fees continue.

Action for the spec: plan and cost AR appointment per stream per target Member State plus the EU-level packaging AR, with lead time ahead of first placing on the market. Do not defer on the expectation of relief. Confirm current status with a compliance advisor or the national register of each target Member State before ordering, and record the date of that confirmation.
corrected.why:
VERIFICATION METHOD: WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted (200/200), so I verified by fetching the two stated sources directly and attempted five separate primary-source fetches (EUR-Lex CELEX 32023R1542 in three URL forms, EUR-Lex CELEX 52025PC0501, the EP Legislative Observatory, and the Commission simplification page). EUR-Lex returned blank bodies (JS-rendered/blocked) and the Observatory 404'd. So the primary legislative record could NOT be independently checked. That alone forces refuted=true under the default rule — but the stated sources also affirmatively fail to support the claim.

FINDING 1 — THE LOAD-BEARING ASSERTIONS ARE ABSENT FROM BOTH CITED SOURCES. Every specific legislative-process fact in the DETAIL was checked against both URLs. Neither https://www.complir.io/resources/guides/extended-producer-responsibility-eu-guide nor https://circularcompliance.com/eu-battery-regulation-authorised-representative/ mentions: any proposed suspension of the AR obligation; any Omnibus proposal; any European Parliament draft reports; any micro/small-enterprise carve-out; or any decision date of 1 October 2026. The claim attributes to these two sources content they do not contain. The "in flux," "May 2026 draft reports," and "1 October 2026" specifics are, as sourced, unsupported. I am NOT asserting the Commission proposal does not exist (I could not reach EUR-Lex); I am asserting it is unsubstantiated as presented, and that a spec must not carry a precise date like 1 October 2026 on citations that do not mention it.

FINDING 2 — THE "IN FLUX" FRAMING IS CONTRADICTED BY RECENCY. The complir.io guide is dated 21 April 2026 — three months before the spec date of 2026-07-20, and well after the claimed Commission proposal. It describes the AR requirement as operative current law with no mention of any pending relaxation. A current source silent on a supposed live suspension is evidence against the framing, not neutral.

FINDING 3 — DIRECTION-OF-TRAVEL ERROR (the material one for a hardware spec). The claim implies relaxation. For a UK entity the burden is INCREASING. complir.io, verbatim: "A new EU-level Authorised Representative for packaging is required for non-EU producers, in addition to existing national representatives." The claim's "may be relaxed" framing invites an engineer to defer AR budget/lead-time. That is backwards.

FINDING 4 — HEDGE IN THE WRONG DIRECTION. "would likely still need an AR regardless" understates certainty. Both sources make it unconditional. complir.io: "Non-EU companies placing products on the EU market generally need to appoint an Authorised Representative for EPR in each Member State where they sell." circularcompliance on the Battery Regulation: producers "established in another EU Member State or third country" must appoint an AR. The claimed relaxation is scoped to EU-established companies by the claim's own text, so it cannot reach a UK entity. "Likely" should be "does."

FINDING 5 — CONFLATION OF TWO DISTINCT OBLIGATIONS. "registration with national PROs" merges (a) entry in national producer registers, a public-authority act typically executed by the AR, with (b) membership of a PRO/compliance scheme, a separate contractual obligation. circularcompliance lists AR duties as "Registering the producer in national battery registers" — a register, not a PRO. complir.io treats registration and PRO involvement as distinct elements. These are two separate cost and effort lines and must not be collapsed in a spec.

FINDING 6 — SCOPE UNDERSTATED, WITH A COST MULTIPLIER. The claim treats "an AR" as a single item. complir.io: "The exact rules differ by stream (PPWR, WEEE, and the Batteries Regulation each handle this differently) and by Member State." The obligation is per-waste-stream AND per-Member-State, plus the new EU-level packaging AR. For a device with a battery, packaging, and electronics sold into multiple Member States, that is a matrix of appointments, not one. Also a minor citation point: circularcompliance locates the Battery Regulation AR duty at Article 56(3), so any article reference in the spec should be checked rather than assumed.

NET: substantially right only on its least emphasised sentence (UK entity needs an AR); wrong in emphasis, unsourced on every specific date and legislative detail, imprecise on registration vs PRO, and understated on scope.

corrected.original: Battery Regulation due diligence obligations were postponed to 18 August 2027 and in any case only apply above a €40m turnover threshold — not a concern for a small company.
corrected.corrected: Regulation (EU) 2025/1561 (Omnibus IV) postponed the Battery Regulation's supply-chain due diligence obligations from 18 August 2025 to 18 August 2027, and the Commission's guidelines deadline to 26 July 2026 (first public due diligence report ~18 August 2028). A turnover-based exemption from those due diligence obligations exists in Article 47(4) of Reg (EU) 2023/1542 — reportedly EUR 40m net turnover, but VERIFY THIS FIGURE AGAINST THE OJ TEXT, as neither cited source states it. A pending proposal (COM(2025) 501) would raise that exemption to EUR 150m net turnover, but it is not yet adopted and is not binding; do not plan against it. Three caveats before discounting anything: (a) the exemption is tested on the net turnover of the economic operator placing the battery on the Union market — for a non-EU designer that is the EU importer, not you — on a group-consolidated basis, and re-tested each financial year; (b) the exemption covers ONLY the Chapter VII responsible-sourcing due diligence for cobalt, natural graphite, lithium and nickel; (c) it exempts nothing else in the Battery Regulation. The provisions that actually bind a hardware design and parts order have no turnover exemption and are NOT delayed: Article 11 end-user removability and replaceability of portable batteries (18 February 2027 — rules out glued-in or soldered cells in consumer devices), Annex I substance restrictions (Hg/Cd/Pb), CE marking and conformity assessment, labelling/marking (18 August 2026) and QR code (18 February 2027), and EPR producer registration and take-back. The battery passport (Article 77, 18 February 2027) was explicitly untouched by 2025/1561 and covers LMT, industrial >2 kWh and EV batteries; portable consumer batteries are excluded from it. Correct planning position: the due diligence workstream alone may be deferred to 2027 and may be exempt subject to the turnover test — the rest of the Battery Regulation must stay in the spec.
corrected.why: The two delay dates are correct and confirmed by the claim's own source (infodpp.eu): Reg (EU) 2025/1561 moved due diligence application from 18 Aug 2025 to 18 Aug 2027 and the Commission guidelines deadline to 26 July 2026. But the claim is refuted on three counts. (1) The EUR40m threshold is unsupported by either cited source. The infodpp page discusses only a EUR150m threshold and explicitly as a PROPOSAL under COM(2025) 501, not adopted law, warning that "until the final text is adopted and published in the Official Journal, none of these items are binding" and that companies in current scope "should not plan compliance on the assumption that COM(2025) 501 will land unchanged." EUR40m is likely the real existing Art. 47(4) figure (the source's phrasing "extend the Article 47 exemption to operators below EUR150 million" implies a lower existing one), but it is stated far more confidently than the sources support. (2) Fatal for a hardware spec: the Art. 47 exemption covers ONLY the Chapter VII responsible-sourcing due diligence. It does not exempt anything else in Reg (EU) 2023/1542. The obligations that actually constrain a parts order carry no turnover exemption at all: Art. 11 end-user removability/replaceability of portable batteries (18 Feb 2027, a hard physical design constraint), Annex I substance restrictions, CE marking and conformity assessment, labelling/marking and QR code, and EPR producer registration/take-back. The battery passport (Art. 77, 18 Feb 2027) is confirmed by the sources as untouched by 2025/1561. So "not a concern for a small company / discount this from your plan" would lead an engineer to wrongly discount the Battery Regulation as a whole. (3) The threshold is a net-turnover test on the economic operator PLACING the battery on the Union market (for a non-EU designer, that is the EU importer, not the designer), assessed on a group-consolidated basis and re-tested each financial year — not a simple "are we small" test. Access limitation: EUR-Lex (CELEX 32023R1542 and the 2025/1561 OJ text) and the Consilium press release both served AWS WAF bot-detection challenges, which I did not bypass, and the session WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200), so Art. 47(4) primary text remains unverified and should be checked against the OJ before this enters a spec.

corrected.original: No UK building regulation or fire regulation prohibits or specifically restricts a small lithium cell permanently installed in an occupied public venue — there is no threshold to clear.
corrected.corrected:
No UK regulation names lithium cells and prohibits them outright in occupied public venues, and Approved Document B is silent on lithium batteries in fixed equipment. That is not the same as "no threshold to clear" — the applicable regime is goal-setting rather than prescriptive, and it still imposes enforceable duties:

FIRE. Under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005, the venue's responsible person must hold a suitable and sufficient fire risk assessment (art. 9(1)) and must review it on any significant change to the premises or technical measures (art. 9(3)) — installing a permanent cell is such a change. Art. 2's "dangerous substance" definition reaches substances that create risk through their physico-chemical properties, potentially engaging art. 12. Breach placing occupants at risk of death or serious injury is a criminal offence under art. 32(1)(a) (fine and/or up to 2 years). Practical effect: the installation must be accepted into the venue's FRA, and the responsible person carries the liability.

BUILDING CONTROL. There is no automatic gate, but there is a conditional one. Building Regulations 2010 reg. 3 makes an alteration "material" — hence notifiable building work — if it would at any stage leave the building more unsatisfactory against a relevant requirement, and reg. 3(3) lists paragraphs B1, B3, B4 and B5 among those requirements. ADB's silence is not permission: ADB is guidance under s.7 Building Act 1984, and compliance is assessed against the functional B1–B5 requirements themselves.

WORKPLACE. DSEAR 2002 may apply, since cells in thermal runaway vent flammable gas.

PRECEDENT. BS 5839-1 and BS 5266-1 standby batteries are NOT usable as precedent here, because (as acknowledged) those systems conventionally use VRLA, NiCd or NiMH. They are precedent for non-lithium chemistries only.

PRODUCT AND TRANSPORT THRESHOLDS THAT DO BIND PROCUREMENT: UN 38.3 test summary (mandatory before the cells can be shipped); BS EN IEC 62133-2; UKCA marking under the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016; and the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017 if the device incorporates a radio. Note also that the Product Regulation and Metrology Act 2025 (c. 20) confers broad powers to make new product regulations, with lithium-ion batteries an active policy target — confirm the position at time of design freeze.

ACTION: specify UN 38.3, IEC 62133-2 and UKCA conformity as procurement gates, and treat sign-off by the venue's responsible person (via FRA review) as a delivery precondition. A competent fire engineer should confirm the B1/B3 position for the specific installation. Do not record this as "unregulated".
corrected.why:
REFUTED — substantially right on the narrow point, materially wrong on the conclusion, and wrong at a confidence level unsafe for a hardware spec.

WHAT SURVIVES: I found no UK regulation that names lithium cells and prohibits them in occupied public venues. Approved Document B appears silent on lithium batteries in fixed equipment.

WHAT FAILS:

1) "No fire regulation restricts" — the RRO 2005 is a fire regulation and it does bite, just not chemistry-specifically. Art. 9(1) requires a "suitable and sufficient" fire risk assessment; Art. 9(3) mandates review on "significant change" to the premises or to technical/organisational measures — permanently installing a cell is squarely that. Art. 2 defines "dangerous substance" to include any substance that "because of its physico-chemical or chemical properties and the way it is used or is present in or on premises creates a risk", engaging Art. 12 (eliminate/reduce risk SFAIRP, substitute, control). Art. 32(1)(a): breach of arts. 8–22B placing relevant persons at risk of death or serious injury is a criminal offence — fine and/or up to 2 years. There IS a threshold: the FRA must remain suitable and sufficient with the cell installed. It is a duty with criminal liability, not a permit — but "no threshold to clear" is false.

2) "No building-control approval gate" — stated unconditionally and wrong as stated. Building Regs 2010 reg. 3(1) includes "material alteration" in "building work"; reg. 3(2) makes an alteration material if it would at any stage result in the building not complying with, or being MORE UNSATISFACTORY in relation to, a "relevant requirement". Reg. 3(3) verbatim lists: Part A, paragraph B1 (means of warning and escape), B3 (internal fire spread—structure), B4 (external fire spread), B5 (access for fire service), Part M, Part T. Fire-safety paragraphs are relevant requirements. So the gate exists, conditional on whether the install worsens B1/B3 — which is exactly the question the claim assumes away.

3) ADB silence is treated as permission — a category error. ADB is statutory guidance under s.7 Building Act 1984, not the requirement. Compliance is judged against the functional Schedule 1 requirements B1–B5. "ADB doesn't mention lithium" is evidentially inert.

4) DSEAR 2002 unsurveyed. It applies in workplaces (a public venue is one) to substances creating fire/explosion risk by physico-chemical properties; cells in thermal runaway vent flammable electrolyte vapour and hydrogen. Arguable for a small cell, but a blanket "no regulation" claim must address it and does not.

5) The precedent argument is self-defeating. The claim concedes BS 5839-1/BS 5266-1 systems conventionally use VRLA, NiCd or NiMH, "not lithium-ion". If chemistry is the distinction, those standards are precedent for non-lithium standby batteries and provide zero support for lithium. Citing them as "well established precedent" while conceding the chemistry differs is a non-sequitur.

6) The thresholds that actually bind an engineer ordering parts are omitted entirely: UN 38.3 (UN Manual of Tests and Criteria) — mandatory for transport, you cannot lawfully ship cells without it; BS EN IEC 62133-2 (secondary lithium cell safety); UKCA under the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016; and the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017 if the device has a radio, which a mesh device does. For a spec an engineer orders against, "no threshold to clear" is the most dangerous possible framing.

7) Sourcing defect: the stated source concedes "absence of a prohibition is inherently hard to source positively; I found no regulation imposing one" — an argument from ignorance — yet the claim text renders it as the flat assertion "there is no threshold to clear". The hedge was dropped between evidence and conclusion.

VERIFICATION LIMITS (declared): WebSearch budget was exhausted at session start, so I worked from primary legislation via direct fetch. I could NOT verify (a) whether secondary regulations on lithium-ion batteries have been made under the Product Regulation and Metrology Act 2025 (2025 c. 20), which grants broad Secretary of State powers to make product regulations and is an active policy target — the regulatory picture may be moving; (b) whether BS 5839-1:2017, BS EN 54-4 or BS EN 50171 positively restrict battery chemistry, as these are paywalled. The claim's own cited standards therefore remain unchecked on the specific point it rests on.

Sources: [RRO 2005 art. 2](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1541/article/2), [art. 9](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1541/article/9), [art. 12](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1541/article/12), [art. 32](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1541/article/32); [Building Regulations 2010 reg. 3](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2010/2214/regulation/3/made); [HSE DSEAR](https://www.hse.gov.uk/fireandexplosion/dsear.htm); [Approved Document B](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/fire-safety-approved-document-b); [Product Regulation and Metrology Act 2025](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2025/20/contents).

corrected.original: The legal duty sits with the venue, not with you — but that makes it a commercial gate on your sales cycle rather than a compliance cost you can ignore.
corrected.corrected:
Two separate regimes apply, and only one of them sits with the venue.

**The venue's duty (fire safety law).** In England and Wales, the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 requires the venue's "responsible person" to make a suitable and sufficient fire risk assessment of the risks to "relevant persons" (anyone lawfully on the premises, plus anyone in the immediate vicinity at risk from a fire there), to keep it under review, and — since 1 October 2023, following the Building Safety Act 2022 s.156 — to record it in full regardless of headcount. Nightclubs and places of public entertainment are covered by general application, not by being named: Article 6 operates by listing exclusions, and non-domestic entertainment premises are not among them. Scotland (Fire (Scotland) Act 2005 Part 3; Fire Safety (Scotland) Regulations 2006) and Northern Ireland (Fire and Rescue Services (NI) Order 2006; Fire Safety Regulations (NI) 2010) impose parallel but separate duties — the RRO extends to England and Wales only.

**Our duty (product law) — this one is ours and cannot be delegated to the venue.** Placing the device on the market engages UK GPSR, the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017, the EMC Regulations 2016, and batteries placing-on-market obligations. For parts selection specifically: the lithium cell must have a UN 38.3 test summary and BS EN IEC 62133-2 certification, and the pack must have a protection circuit consistent with the cell datasheet limits. Order against certified cells only; an uncertified cell fails our own compliance irrespective of any venue's assessment.

**Where the two meet.** Do not assume we stay outside the RRO. Article 5(3) extends the responsible person's duties to anyone with control of the premises "to any extent," and Article 5(4) deems a party with a contractual obligation for "the maintenance or repair of any premises, including anything in or on premises" or for "the safety of any premises" to be exactly that. Any install-and-maintain contract, SLA, battery-swap service, or maintenance-bearing warranty therefore gives us direct RRO duties to the extent of that obligation. Legal review of the service contract is required before the first venue installation.

**Commercial consequence.** Because the venue must record its FRA, our device becomes a documented line item in it. Expect venues — or, frequently, their insurers and licensing conditions — to require a fire-safety data pack before permitting installation: cell certificates (UN 38.3, IEC 62133-2), pack protection design, charging regime, and mounting/isolation guidance. Treat this as a sales-cycle gate to be pre-empted with a standing compliance dossier, not as a cost we can ignore.
corrected.why:
Directionally right, but wrong in the two ways that matter for a document an engineer orders parts against.

**1. "You have no direct RRO duty as a manufacturer" — false under the supplier's own likely business model.** Article 5(3) imposes the responsible person's Article 8–22B duties on "every person... who has, to any extent, control of those premises so far as the requirements relate to matters within his control." Article 5(4) then deems you such a person: "Where a person has, by virtue of any contract or tenancy, an obligation of any extent in relation to (a) the maintenance or repair of any premises, **including anything in or on premises**; or (b) the safety of any premises, that person is to be treated... as being a person who has control of the premises to the extent that his obligation so extends." A venue-installed device sold with a service contract, SLA, battery-swap arrangement, or maintenance-bearing warranty pulls the supplier directly into the RRO. "No direct duty" holds only for a pure over-the-counter sale with zero maintenance obligation — which is not how installed hardware is sold.

**2. Wrong statute for "your" duty — the real manufacturer obligations are omitted.** The headline "the legal duty sits with the venue, not with you" invites an engineer to conclude there is no compliance constraint on part selection. There is. The manufacturer's direct, non-delegable duties come from product law, not fire law: UK GPSR, the Radio Equipment Regulations 2017 (a mesh device has a radio), the EMC Regulations 2016, batteries placing-on-market regs, and — the parts-ordering constraint proper — UN 38.3 transport test summary and BS EN IEC 62133-2 cell certification for the lithium cell itself. A cell ordered without those is non-compliant regardless of what any venue's FRA says.

**3. "Nightclubs and places of public entertainment are explicitly within the Order's scope" — not explicit.** Article 6 works by exclusion (domestic premises, ships, offshore, mines, vehicles, agricultural land); the Order applies to "any premises" by general application. Neither the legislation nor the cited London Fire Brigade page names nightclubs. Substantively covered, yes — "explicitly" is wrong.

**4. Territorial extent overstated.** Article 1(4): "This Order extends to England and Wales only." A UK festival product also meets Scottish venues (Fire (Scotland) Act 2005 Part 3 + Fire Safety (Scotland) Regulations 2006) and Northern Irish venues (Fire and Rescue Services (NI) Order 2006 + Fire Safety Regulations (NI) 2010). The claim cites an England-only source (LFB) to support a UK-framed proposition.

**5. "will refuse installation" — unsupported certainty.** Neither cited source mentions lithium devices or installation refusal. Plausible directionally (LFB has campaigned heavily on lithium-ion fires) but the gate in practice is at least as often the venue's insurer or licensing conditions as the FRA itself. Should be "may".

**One point that helps the claim and is missing:** since 1 October 2023 (Building Safety Act 2022 s.156 amending Article 9(7)), *all* responsible persons must record the FRA in full, regardless of employee count. The written record your device has to survive now always exists — which strengthens the commercial-gate argument the claim is making.

Minor: "anyone who might visit" is loose for the statutory "relevant persons" — anyone lawfully on the premises, plus anyone in the immediate vicinity at risk from a fire on the premises.

corrected.original: Venue insurers demonstrably do care about lithium-ion, and insurer sensitivity is rising sharply — expect this to surface in procurement.
corrected.corrected:
Insurer attention to lithium-ion is real and rising, but the evidence does not yet support a specific procurement requirement for small-battery hardware.

VERIFIED: QBE's FOI analysis of UK fire services recorded 1,760 lithium-ion battery fires in 2025 — 4.8 per day — up 147% from ~1.94/day in 2022 (QBE rounds this baseline to "two a day"; note 2 → 4.8 re-derives as +140%, so use QBE's unrounded basis). 23% occurred in commercial premises, ~46% in homes, 31% outdoors. Published May 2026. AXA ("Fire Risk Guidance: Lithium-ion Rechargeable Batteries", current — cites BS 63100:2024), Aviva (Loss Prevention Standards on general considerations, and storage and transit) and Allianz (Allianz Commercial "Emerging Risk: Lithium-ion batteries") all publish lithium-ion guidance to commercial policyholders. RISCAuthority — a research scheme administered by the Fire Protection Association and funded by a group of UK insurers — publishes RC59 "Recommendations for fire safety when charging electric vehicles", plus RC61 (secondary batteries), RE1 (BESS) and RE2 (lithium-ion use and storage).

CORRECTIONS: The britsafe.org article does not contain the QBE figures or the 15% statistic — cite QBE's May 2026 release directly. The 15% figure comes from a self-selecting poll of fire-safety webinar attendees run by IFSEC Insider and Firechief Global, gathered autumn 2023 and reported 2024 (n > 500) — not a 2024 survey of 500 UK organisations, and not strong evidence.

SCOPE CAVEAT (load-bearing for a hardware spec): this guidance corpus addresses EV charging, battery energy storage systems, and bulk battery storage and transit. None of it imposes requirements on small portable or wearable lithium-ion devices, and none of the located material is venue- or event-specific. A low assessment rate in workplace FRAs evidences a gap in current practice, not active insurer pressure — no source shows insurers pushing lithium-ion into assessments.

BASE RATE: ~405 commercial-premises lithium-ion fires per year across roughly 2 million UK non-domestic premises is on the order of 1 in 5,000 premises annually. The trend is steep; the absolute per-venue exposure is low.

PROCUREMENT POSITION: treat insurer interest as a plausible near-term risk to monitor and a reason to hold cell certification evidence (e.g. IEC 62133 / UN 38.3) on file — not as a confirmed requirement to design or order parts against. Confirm actual requirements with the specific venue's insurer before they drive component selection.
corrected.why:
The numbers mostly check out; the sourcing and the inferences do not. Substantially right in direction, but defective in ways that matter for a hardware spec.

WHAT I CONFIRMED
- QBE figures: verified. QBE's FOI analysis of UK fire services found 1,760 lithium-ion fires in 2025. Re-derived: 1760/365 = 4.82/day, matching "4.8 per day". Published ~11 May 2026, and 1,760 is a full-calendar-year 2025 count, so the figure is current and not a partial-year annualisation.
- "147% in three years": QBE's own figure, internally consistent. Note 2 → 4.8 is +140%, not +147%; the 147% implies an unrounded 2022 baseline of ~1.94/day (~709 fires). QBE rounds this to "two a day". The claim reproduces QBE correctly, but anyone re-deriving from the rounded "2 a day" will get 140% and think there is an error.
- "Almost a quarter in commercial premises": verified at 23% (breakdown ~46% homes, 31% outdoors, 23% commercial).
- AXA guidance: verified by direct extraction of the cited PDF — "Fire Risk Guidance: Lithium-ion Rechargeable Batteries", AXA Insurance UK plc. It cites BS 63100:2024, so it is current, not stale.
- Aviva guidance: the cited URL 403s to automated fetches, but the document is real — "Lithium-ion Batteries – General Considerations", one of several Aviva Loss Prevention Standards.
- Allianz guidance: verified, multiple documents including Allianz Commercial's "Emerging Risk: Lithium-ion batteries".
- RC59: verified as "Recommendations for fire safety when charging electric vehicles". The claim's parenthetical is correct.

DEFECTS
1. Broken source attribution. The stated britsafe.org source contains NONE of the figures attributed to that cluster — no 4.8/day, no 147%, no commercial-premises share, no 15%/500 survey. I fetched it and confirmed. The real sources are QBE's May 2026 FOI release and, separately, IFSEC Insider + Firechief Global. An engineer chasing the citation would find nothing.

2. The 15% statistic is misdescribed. It is not "500 UK organisations surveyed in 2024". It is a poll of self-selecting attendees at fire-safety webinars run by IFSEC Insider and Firechief Global, gathered autumn 2023 and reported in 2024, n = "over 500". Self-selection cuts both ways and the collection year is off by one. It is weak evidence dressed as survey data.

3. Unsupported causal inference — the worst defect. "Only 15% have assessed it, which means the topic is actively being pushed by insurers into assessments that currently omit it" does not follow. A low assessment rate evidences a GAP, not insurer pressure. Nothing in any source shows insurers driving lithium-ion into fire risk assessments. The statistic is being run backwards to manufacture the conclusion.

4. "Venue insurers" is not evidenced. Every verified document is general commercial property or motor guidance from AXA, Aviva, Allianz. I found nothing venue-specific or event-specific. The claim generalises commercial-property insurer behaviour to venue insurers without support.

5. Scope mismatch — most decision-relevant for a parts order. The entire insurer guidance corpus targets EV charging (RC59), battery energy storage systems (RE1), secondary batteries (RC61), and bulk storage/transit (Aviva LPS). Note that AXA's own reference list cites RC61, RE1 and RE2 — not RC59. None of this sets requirements for small portable or wearable lithium-ion devices. Inferring procurement constraints on small-battery hardware from a corpus about EVs, BESS and warehouse storage is a category leap.

6. Base rate omitted. 23% of 1,760 = ~405 commercial-premises fires per year across the whole UK commercial building stock (~2m non-domestic premises), roughly 1 in 5,000 premises annually. The trend is real and steep; the absolute per-venue probability is small. A spec that cites the growth rate without the base rate will over-engineer.

7. Minor: RISCAuthority is not "a group of UK insurers". It is an annually funded research scheme administered by the FPA and supported by a significant group of UK insurers.

VERDICT: the insurer-attention premise is real and well-sourced; the procurement conclusion is an unsupported extrapolation, and one of three cited sources does not contain what is attributed to it.

corrected.original: Best practice, not law: ship a one-page fire-safety statement with the product so the venue can drop it straight into their fire risk assessment.
corrected.corrected:
Ship a one-page fire-safety statement with the product so the venue can drop it straight into their fire risk assessment. Note that this is not purely optional: as a supplier you already owe safe-use information under HSWA 1974 s.6(1)(c) (articles for use at work) and GPSR 2005 reg 7(1) (non-obvious hazards), and the UN 38.3 test summary must be made available under Manual of Tests and Criteria 38.3.5. The one-pager is the cheapest vehicle for duties that exist anyway, and it happens to remove the largest non-technical obstacle to venue sales.

Contents: cell chemistry and format; watt-hour rating; the UN 38.3 Test Summary (38.3.5 — there is no such thing as a UN 38.3 certificate; obtain the summary and report from the cell maker) and the IEC 62133-2 CB Test Certificate and report number; protection circuit description (over-charge, over-discharge, over-current, thermal cut-off); enclosure fire-rating, citing both the fire-enclosure requirement for secondary lithium batteries in IEC 62368-1 Annex M.4 and the material flammability class from clause 6.4.8 / Annex S per IEC 60695-11-10/-11-20 — verify clause numbers against the edition in force; operating temperature limits; and end-of-life removal instructions (also owed under WEEE, and user-facing removal instructions become mandatory for portable batteries under EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 Art. 11 from Feb 2027).

Cost caveat: naming specific certificates on a shipped document locks the BOM to that exact cell. Any second-source cell change invalidates the sheet, so gate cell substitution behind a document update.
corrected.why:
The recommendation (ship a one-page fire-safety statement) is sound and I am not disputing it. But three specific assertions are wrong or imprecise, and this text is going into a spec an engineer will order parts against, so they matter.

1. "No regulation requires this" / "Best practice, not law" is unsupportable as stated. I confirmed two live statutory duties that this document substantially discharges:

- Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 s.6(1)(c) (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1974/37/section/6): a supplier of an article for use at work must "take such steps as are necessary to secure that persons supplied ... are provided with adequate information about the use for which the article is designed or has been tested and about any conditions necessary to ensure that it will be safe and without risks to health". s.6(1)(d) adds a duty to issue revised information on discovery of a serious risk. A device sold to a festival or venue is an article for use at work; this duty applies to the seller, not the venue.
- General Product Safety Regulations 2005 reg 7(1) (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1803/regulation/7/made): producers must give consumers information to "assess the risks inherent in a product throughout the normal or reasonably foreseeable period of its use" and "take precautions against those risks" — expressly where hazards are not obvious without adequate notice. A lithium cell sealed inside an enclosure is the textbook non-obvious hazard. (EU-market equivalent: Regulation (EU) 2023/988, applicable since 13 Dec 2024, which also requires accompanying safety information and an internal risk analysis; I could not fetch EUR-Lex to quote it, so I rely on the two UK instruments above, which I did verify.)

Two further content items in the list are also compelled rather than voluntary: the UN 38.3 test summary is required to be made available by manufacturers and distributors under Manual of Tests and Criteria 38.3.5 (mandatory since 1 Jan 2020, carried into ADR/IMDG/IATA DGR/49 CFR); and end-of-life battery removal information is already owed to treatment operators under WEEE, with EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 Art. 11 adding user-facing removal/replacement instructions for portable batteries from Feb 2027. I could not fetch UNECE or EUR-Lex to quote these (403 / empty body) and my web-search budget was exhausted, so I flag them as requiring the engineer's confirmation rather than asserting them as verified.

The practical consequence of the error: framing the one-pager as pure commercial upside invites it to be cut under schedule pressure, when in fact omitting it leaves a s.6(1)(c) gap. The correct framing is that the duty exists regardless and the one-pager is the cheapest way to discharge it.

2. "UN 38.3 ... certificate references" is a category error that will cause a real procurement failure. UN 38.3 is a transport test protocol; it issues no certificate. There is a Test Report and a mandatory Test Summary (38.3.5). An engineer who writes "UN 38.3 certificate" into a purchase spec will be sent a supplier-authored letter of conformity that is not the required document. IEC 62133-2 does yield a certificate — a CB Test Certificate plus report under the IECEE CB Scheme — so the two should not be bracketed under one word.

3. "Enclosure fire-rating basis under 62368-1 M.4.3" conflates two separate requirements. Annex M.4 covers additional safeguards for equipment containing a secondary lithium battery, and M.4.3 addresses whether a fire enclosure is required (with conditional exemptions). It does not itself set a flammability rating. The material classification actually cited on a datasheet (V-0/V-1/5VA/5VB, per IEC 60695-11-10/-11-20) comes from the fire-enclosure material requirements in clause 6.4.8 and Annex S. Citing M.4.3 alone gives the engineer nothing to specify a plastic against. I could not fetch the standard text to confirm M.4.3's exact title and exemption conditions, and Annex M was revised by amendment after the 2018 edition, so the clause number must be checked against the edition actually in force before it is printed.

4. Unflagged cost. "Costs almost nothing" is true for drafting but false for maintenance. A shipped sheet naming specific UN 38.3 and IEC 62133-2 documents is a representation that binds the product to one cell from one manufacturer. Second-sourcing the cell — routine in this market, and often done by a contract manufacturer without notice — invalidates the sheet and creates a misrepresentation on a safety document. That imposes a real BOM change-control obligation that belongs in the spec.

corrected.original: Choosing LiFePO4 over Li-ion NMC, or eliminating the cell entirely, is the highest-leverage risk reduction available and is a commercial rather than legal decision.
corrected.corrected:
Cell chemistry and cell elimination are both worth costing, but neither is a free win and the ranking below is unverified.

CHEMISTRY (LFP vs NMC). LFP's olivine cathode binds oxygen in covalent P-O bonds and does not readily release lattice oxygen at cell-relevant temperatures; reported cathode decomposition is in the ~500-600 C region versus roughly 200-300 C for layered NMC, and thermal runaway onset is correspondingly higher. This is a threshold difference, not an absence — LFP cells still undergo thermal runaway under overcharge, crush, or external heating, and LFP vent gas remains flammable (notably hydrogen-rich, a deflagration consideration in sealed enclosures). Do not state that LFP "does not release oxygen."

INSURANCE. Whether underwriters or fire risk assessors price LFP differently is UNVERIFIED. No insurer document differentiating by cathode chemistry has been sourced, and questionnaires are typically chemistry-agnostic, addressing lithium batteries generically alongside charging practice, storage quantity, and location. Treat any premium or acceptance benefit as a hypothesis to test with a broker before it influences the design, and never as a marketing claim.

REGULATORY (the solid part). LFP is a lithium-ion chemistry. UN 38.3, IEC 62133-2, IEC 62368-1 Annex M and Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 contain no cathode-chemistry carve-out and apply unchanged. Chemistry choice buys zero regulatory relief. One nuance: transport paperwork keys off watt-hour thresholds, so a lower-energy LFP pack may fall under different packing instructions even though the standards themselves apply identically.

ENGINEERING COST OF THE SWAP (must be visible before ordering). Nominal 3.2 V vs 3.6-3.7 V changes cell count, converter topology and fuel-gauge configuration. Gravimetric energy ~95-172 Wh/kg vs 200-300+ Wh/kg — roughly a 2x penalty, worse volumetrically. Poor charge acceptance below 0 C. Small-format availability is thin: LFP is dominated by cylindrical (14500/18650/26650) and large prismatic formats, with far fewer small-pouch options. For a compact device, confirm a specific sourceable part number and its datasheet before committing to the chemistry.

ELIMINATING THE CELL. Removing all batteries does remove UN 38.3, IEC 62133-2, Annex M and the Battery Regulation. It is not burden-free: mains-only substitutes LVD and 62368-1 mains-side requirements, reinforced isolation, creepage/clearance, EMC on the mains port, external-PSU ecodesign obligations, and country-specific PSU approvals. Note Annex M covers batteries generally, not only lithium, so a retained RTC coin cell keeps it in scope (with added ingestion requirements for lithium coin cells). A true electrostatic supercapacitor should fall outside the Battery Regulation, but confirm this for lithium-ion or hybrid capacitors rather than assuming, and note 62368-1 stored-energy and capacitor-discharge requirements still apply. Worth costing seriously as a net trade, not as an elimination.

ACTIONS BEFORE THIS GOES IN THE SPEC: (a) obtain a broker's written position on whether chemistry affects acceptance or premium; (b) identify a real, in-stock LFP part in the required format with a datasheet, or record that none exists; (c) cost the mains-only compliance layer against the battery layer rather than assuming it is smaller; (d) drop the "highest-leverage" ranking unless a comparison against cell supplier quality, protection-circuit design and mechanical abuse protection is actually performed.
corrected.why:
VERIFICATION LIMITS: WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before I could run searches; EUR-Lex returned empty bodies and iec.ch returned 403. I directly verified only the chemistry direction (Wikipedia, LFP article). The regulatory analysis below rests on my own knowledge of the instruments, not on freshly fetched primary text, and should be confirmed against the OJ text and the standards themselves before an engineer orders against it.

WHAT SURVIVES: The core regulatory-equivalence point is correct and is the most valuable sentence in the claim.
