UN 38.3, IEC 62133-2, IEC 62368-1 Annex M and Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 contain no cathode-chemistry carve-out. LFP is a lithium-ion chemistry and is treated identically. This correctly punctures the common vendor misconception that "LFP isn't really a lithium battery" for compliance purposes, and it belongs in the spec.

WHAT IS REFUTED OR OVERSTATED:

1. "does not release oxygen during decomposition" — absolute, and false as written. The olivine lattice binds oxygen in covalent P-O bonds and does not readily release it at cell-relevant temperatures; the verified source says layered oxides "release oxygen upon heating" whereas LFP has "higher decomposition temperatures." That is a threshold difference (LFP cathode decomposition is generally reported in the 500-600 C region vs roughly 200-300 C for NMC), not an absence. The same source explicitly notes LFP cells "can still catch fire under extreme conditions." A spec must not state a categorical negative here.

2. "which is the specific mechanism insurers and fire risk assessors object to" — this is the load-bearing sentence and it is unsourced. It asserts a causal fact about third-party underwriting behaviour. The author's own source note concedes no insurer document was found. In practice insurer and fire-assessor questionnaires I am aware of address lithium batteries generically, plus charging practice, storage quantity, and location — they rarely differentiate by cathode chemistry at all. Stated as written, this invites the engineer to assume a procurement advantage that has not been shown to exist.

3. "highest-leverage risk reduction available" — unsupportable as a ranking. No comparison was performed. For a small device, field incident rate is dominated by cell supplier quality and counterfeit risk, charge/protection circuit design, mechanical abuse protection, and end-user charging discipline. Chemistry is one lever among several, plausibly significant, but "highest-leverage" is an assertion with nothing behind it.

4. "commercial rather than legal decision" — the regulatory half is right, but "commercial" badly understates the engineering consequences, which is the specific failure mode for a document someone orders parts against. LFP nominal cell voltage is ~3.2 V vs ~3.6-3.7 V for NMC, which changes cell count, buck/boost topology and fuel-gauge configuration. Gravimetric energy is roughly 95-172 Wh/kg (verified) vs 200-300+ Wh/kg for NMC — close to a 2x penalty, worse volumetrically. LFP has poor charge acceptance below 0 C. Most critically for procurement: small-format LFP availability is thin, dominated by cylindrical (14500/18650/26650) and large prismatic cells, with far fewer small-pouch options than NMC/LCO. For a wearable or handheld this can be a blocking constraint, not a price negotiation.

5. "removes ... the entire Battery Regulation layer at a stroke" — directionally right, misleading in magnitude. Mains-only substitutes a different and arguably heavier layer: LVD and the mains-side requirements of 62368-1, reinforced isolation, creepage/clearance, EMC on the mains port, and for an external PSU the EU ecodesign regulation for external power supplies plus country-specific plug/PSU approvals. Also note Annex M of 62368-1 covers batteries generally, not only lithium — any retained backup cell such as an RTC coin cell keeps Annex M in scope, and lithium coin cells bring the ingestion requirements specifically. Supercapacitor ride-through should fall outside the Battery Regulation (electrostatic, not electrochemical, storage) but lithium-ion / hybrid capacitors are a grey area to confirm rather than assume, and 62368-1 still imposes stored-energy and capacitor-discharge requirements.

6. Precision point on "apply identically": true of the standards, but the transport paperwork is watt-hour-threshold-based, so a lower-energy LFP pack can land on a different side of the packing-instruction thresholds. The standards apply identically; the resulting shipping documentation may not.

corrected.original: A coin cell for RTC backup is not a free pass — the 4th edition of IEC 62368-1 added specific button/coin cell requirements.
corrected.corrected:
A coin cell for RTC backup is not a free pass, but the governing requirements are not primarily IEC 62368-1 clause 4.8.

IEC 62368-1:2023 (Ed. 4, published May 2023) heavily revised Annex M (batteries and protection circuits) and tightened — rather than first introduced — button/coin cell provisions, notably more precisely defining requirements for button cell covers. Coin-cell content already existed in EN IEC 62368-1:2020/A11:2020. The "clause 4.8" reference is unverified and contradicted by the available source, which locates this content in Annex M; confirm against the purchased standard before citing a clause number.

Ed. 4 is not yet the operative standard: the harmonized European standard remains EN IEC 62368-1:2020+A11:2020, with Ed. 4 not expected to be mandatory until roughly 2026-2027.

For a product sold in the US, the binding coin-cell requirement is not 62368-1 at all: it is the CPSC rule under Reese's Law (16 CFR Part 1263, incorporating ANSI/UL 4200A), which mandates child-resistant battery compartments, specific warning label content, and packaging requirements independently of any 62368-1 certification. Australia's ACCC mandatory button battery standards (effective 22 June 2022) preceded the US measures, so the driver is international, not solely US.

Scope matters for design: child-resistant compartment and packaging obligations attach primarily to accessible or user-replaceable cells and to cells sold separately. A non-replaceable coin cell soldered to the board inside a sealed enclosure sits in a materially different and lighter position than one behind a user-openable door — confirm the applicable scope for your specific mounting before budgeting compliance effort.

For transport, a lithium coin cell is subject to UN 38.3, but that testing is the cell manufacturer's obligation — the practical task is obtaining the supplier's UN 38.3 test summary. Lithium button cells installed in equipment, including on circuit boards, are excepted from the dangerous goods regulations under ICAO/IATA/ADR provisions.

Under EU Regulation 2023/1542, a coin cell is a portable battery. The design-binding provision is Article 11 removability/replaceability; RTC backup cells will typically qualify for the derogation where permanent connection is required for data integrity or continuity of supply, but that justification must be documented.
corrected.why:
Substantially right in thrust (a coin cell is not exempt from safety/battery regimes) but imprecise in ways that would misdirect an engineer, and the clause reference is contradicted by the stated source.

VERIFIED against the stated Element source: IEC 62368-1:2023 is Edition 4, published May 2023; Annex M (batteries and protection circuits) was "heavily revised"; "the requirements for button cell covers have been precisely defined."

REFUTATIONS:
1. Wrong location. The stated source places button-cell content in ANNEX M, not clause 4.8. The claim hedges on the clause number, but the source affirmatively points elsewhere rather than merely being silent.
2. "Added" overstates novelty. "Heavily revised" / "precisely defined" is refinement language; coin-cell provisions predate Ed. 4 (EN IEC 62368-1:2020/A11:2020 carried European button-cell content). Ed. 4 tightened rather than introduced.
3. Causal attribution unsupported and likely wrong on primacy. Australia's ACCC mandatory button battery standards took effect 22 June 2022, preceding Reese's Law (Aug 2022) and the CPSC rule (2023). The source says nothing about US drivers.
4. Most consequential omission: in the US the binding instrument is NOT IEC 62368-1. It is the CPSC rule under Reese's Law (16 CFR Part 1263, incorporating ANSI/UL 4200A), a standalone mandatory consumer product safety rule enforceable independently of 62368-1 certification. Framing coin-cell exposure as a 62368-1 matter sends the engineer to the wrong document.
5. Ed. 4 is not yet operative. Per the same source, Ed. 4 likely not mandatory until 2026-2027; harmonized EN remains EN IEC 62368-1:2020+A11:2020. Citing Ed. 4 as today's governing requirement is premature for a spec.
6. Scope caveat omitted. Child-resistant compartment and packaging requirements hinge on the cell being replaceable/accessible. A soldered RTC cell in a sealed enclosure is treated very differently from one behind a user-openable door; packaging requirements apply to cells sold separately, not board-mounted cells. The claim implies all three obligations apply universally.
7. UN 38.3 directionally right but burden misstated. Lithium button cells installed in equipment (including circuit boards) are excepted from dangerous goods regulations under ICAO/IATA/ADR provisions. UN 38.3 testing is the cell manufacturer's obligation; the device maker's task is obtaining the supplier's test summary, not testing.
8. EU Battery Regulation nuance: the design-binding provision for an RTC cell is Article 11 removability/replaceability, for which RTC backup cells typically qualify for the derogation (permanent connection needed for data integrity/continuity of supply) — but only if documented. Carbon-footprint and due-diligence obligations largely do not reach portable button cells.

SOURCE LIMITATIONS: Web search budget was exhausted at session start. IEC webstore (404), CPSC (403), Federal Register and eCFR (redirect-blocked), TUV SUD (403), Nemko/Intertek/InCompliance (404/empty) were all inaccessible. Only the stated Element source could be fetched. Clause numbering, the CPSC rule text, and Annex M subclause structure remain unverified against primary sources.

corrected.original: Realistic all-in first-product compliance cost for a small company: roughly £20,000–45,000, with EMC/radio testing — not the battery work — as the largest single line.
corrected.corrected:
Compliance cost, EU + UK only, unquoted planning envelope — NOT anchored to any published price list. The two previously cited sources do not support these figures: en.gdestl.com/529.html contains no prices at all, and ecocomply.ai quotes wireless/RED testing at $1,500–$3,000+ (~£1,200–£2,400), well below the figures below. Treat everything here as an internal engineering estimate requiring three written lab quotes before it enters a budget.

The total depends on one parts decision — pre-certified radio module vs. discrete radio:

CASE A — pre-certified/modular-approved radio module (recommended, and assumed by the current BOM direction): approx. £15,000–39,000
  EN 62368-1 safety evaluation incl. Annex M: £4,000–10,000
  Host EMC + limited RED radiated-spurious retest: £3,000–8,000
  UN 38.3, at PACK level, per configuration: £1,500–5,000
  RED cybersecurity, EN 18031 assessment: £3,000–8,000
  Technical file + DoC preparation (outsourced): £2,000–5,000
  UK WEEE/battery registration + first-year EU EPR: £800–2,500
  Largest single line here is SAFETY or CYBERSECURITY — not radio.

CASE B — discrete/open radio implementation: approx. £19,000–50,000, with full EMC + RED radio testing at £8,000–20,000 as the largest single line. Only in this case is the original claim's headline true.

Add to either case:
  Retest contingency, 20–40% of the EMC/radio line — the line most likely to fail first pass. Not optional for a first product.
  EU Authorised Representative / GPSR EU Responsible Person: recurring, ~€500–2,000/yr, excluded above.
  EU EPR registrations: €500–2,000 per market per year, recurring.
  FCC/ISED if selling into US/Canada: ~£3,000–8,000, excluded above.
  EU Battery Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 obligations: scope and cost not yet assessed — the "battery work is not the big line" conclusion is not established until it is.

Note on EN 18031: the harmonised standards were cited in the OJEU with restrictions, so presumption of conformity may not cover all clauses. If a Notified Body is drawn in, budget a further £4,000–12,000 and confirm current OJ citation status before relying on self-declaration.

Note on UN 38.3: buying cells with existing IEC 62133-2 CB certificates and UN 38.3 test summaries avoids roughly £5,000–15,000 of CELL-level qualification, but does not remove the pack-level UN 38.3 requirement for a newly assembled battery — that line stays in the budget.
corrected.why:
REFUTED on four independent grounds.

1. ARITHMETIC — the breakdown does not sum to the stated total. Adding the DETAIL's own line items (€ converted at ~0.86):
   Low: 4,000 + 8,000 + 1,500 + 3,000 + 300 + 430 + 2,000 = £19,230
   High: 10,000 + 20,000 + 5,000 + 8,000 + 500 + 1,720 + 5,000 = £50,220
   The breakdown yields ~£19,000–50,000, not the claimed "£20,000–45,000". The top end is understated by ~£5,200 (≈11%). A stated total that is not the sum of its own parts is a budgeting defect, not a rounding one.

2. SOURCES DO NOT SUPPORT THE FIGURES — and one contradicts them.
   - https://en.gdestl.com/529.html contains NO cost figures whatsoever. It is a marketing article by a Chinese lab (Guangdong ESTL, Dongguan) listing fee CATEGORIES ("Product Certification Fee", "Laboratory Testing Fee") with no prices, and directing readers to request a quotation. It cannot anchor anything.
   - https://ecocomply.ai/blog/what-does-ce-marking-cost-for-your-product gives, verbatim, "Wireless products (RED): $1,500–$3,000+", and for multi-radio devices "$2,000–$4,000 in testing alone". That is roughly £1,200–£3,200 — five to eight times BELOW the claim's £8,000–20,000 for the same line. The claim cites as support a source that contradicts its dominant cost item by nearly an order of magnitude.
   - The claim also misparaphrases its anchor: it reports a "£1,000–£10,000+ range". The source's figures are USD, and its non-Notified-Body electronics bands run $400–$3,000+ (~£300–£2,400). Neither the currency nor the magnitude survives checking.

3. THE "LARGEST LINE" ASSERTION IS CONDITIONAL ON AN UNSTATED DESIGN CHOICE. Whether EMC/radio dominates depends entirely on whether the product uses a pre-certified radio module or a discrete/open radio implementation — and for a spec an engineer orders parts against, that IS a parts decision. With a modular-approved BLE module (the standard choice for a small company's first product), RED Art. 3(2) spectrum conformity is largely inherited from the module and the host needs only host EMC plus limited radiated-spurious retest, collapsing that line to ~£3,000–8,000. In that case EMC/radio is NOT the largest line — EN 62368-1 safety or the EN 18031 cyber assessment is. The claim states the dominance unconditionally.

4. NO RETEST CONTINGENCY, DESPITE THE CLAIM'S OWN WARNING. The DETAIL states EMC/radio is "the one most likely to require redesign-and-retest", then builds a total that assumes first-pass success on exactly that line. A first-product EMC failure is common; retest typically adds 20–40% of the original test fee plus schedule. The envelope is self-acknowledgedly optimistic at its top end.

ADDITIONAL SCOPE GAPS (not fatal alone, but they make "all-in" wrong as a word): FCC/ISED excluded entirely (any US/Canada sale adds roughly £3,000–8,000); EU Authorised Representative / GPSR EU Responsible Person is recurring and omitted; EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 conformity obligations are omitted, which undercuts the "not the battery work" framing; and EN 18031-1/-2/-3 were cited in the OJEU with restrictions, so presumption of conformity does not extend to certain clauses — where a Notified Body is drawn in, the source's own "$5,000–$15,000+" NB fee band applies and can rival the radio line. (I flag the EN 18031 restriction point as a risk rather than a costed item — my web-search budget was exhausted and I could not re-verify the current OJ citation status independently.)

VERDICT: directionally plausible as an order-of-magnitude planning envelope, but the total contradicts its own breakdown, the sources are one empty and one contradicting, and the headline "largest line" conclusion flips depending on a design decision the spec has not fixed. Not usable as stated for a document parts are ordered against.

corrected.original: Realistic calendar time is 4–9 months from design freeze to shippable, and the dominant risk is failure-and-retest cycles rather than queue time.
corrected.corrected:
For a first battery-powered wireless product, budget 9–15 months from design freeze to shippable. Plan 12 months; hold contingency to 15. Certification occupies only ~3–5 months of that and runs largely in parallel with tooling and pilot builds — it is not the schedule.

Certification durations (largely PARALLEL, not additive):
- Lab booking lead time: 2–6 weeks. A failed sample costs a requeue, not just a retest.
- EN/IEC 62368-1: 4–6 weeks end to end (per the cited lab; not 4–8). For a <75 V DC battery device this enters via RED Art 3(1)(a) — the LVD does not apply below 50 V AC / 75 V DC.
- RED radio + EMC (EN 300 328, EN 301 489-1/-17): 4–8 weeks. This is the actual EMC gate and was missing from the original.
- RED cybersecurity, Art 3(3)(d)(e)(f) / Delegated Reg (EU) 2022/30, EN 18031-1/-2/-3: mandatory since 1 Aug 2025. 3–8 weeks plus substantial documentation. The most common first-product surprise in 2026.
- UN 38.3: 3–6 weeks. The 7-day observation belongs to T.7 (overcharge), not to 62133-2.
- IEC 62133-2: 4–8 weeks. Specifying a cell that already holds a certificate largely removes this.
- FCC / ISED equipment authorization (North America): 3–6 weeks. A pre-certified radio module removes most of this.
- EPR / WEEE / battery / packaging registration: 4–12 weeks per market. Start BEFORE design freeze — these gate market entry, not testing.

Dominant schedule risk is tooling and DFM iteration plus long-lead component procurement, NOT certification retest. Tooling T1 is 4–8 weeks with 2–3 respins normal; add pilot builds, mass production, and 4–6 weeks sea freight. A first EMC failure adds a bounded 4–8 weeks; a tooling respin or mis-specified long-lead part is unbounded and sits on the critical path. Carry the 4–8 week EMC reserve anyway, but treat "first-pass EMC failure is the norm" as an unverified rule of thumb — the commonly cited ~50% figure comes from test-lab marketing, not a published study.

SOURCING WARNING: do not cite the gdestl.com pages as evidence in a spec. en.gdestl.com/815.html contains no duration figures at all and does not support "5–7 weeks for IEC 62133-2"; en.gdestl.com/529.html says 4–6 weeks, not 4–8. Both are vendor marketing pages advertising their own services, not measured throughput data.
corrected.why:
REFUTED on four independent grounds — sourcing, scope, arithmetic, and omitted mandatory gates.

1. CITATION FAILURE (hardest finding). I fetched both stated sources.
- https://en.gdestl.com/815.html is cited for "5–7 weeks for IEC 62133-2". The page contains NO duration or lead-time information whatsoever — it covers test requirements, procedures, and the application process only. The attributed figure does not exist in the source.
- https://en.gdestl.com/529.html is cited for "4–8 weeks typical for 62368-1". The page actually states 4–6 weeks for a standard product. The claim widened the band and kept the citation.
- Both are marketing pages for Guangdong ESTL's own certification services (sales copy, service hotline, self-promotion of qualifications) — vendor lead-time advertising, not measured throughput. Exactly the "marketing figures presented as measured" failure mode. The "2–4 weeks testing" figure has no source at all.

2. SCOPE CONFLATION. The headline measures "design freeze to shippable"; the component list is 100% certification. Absent entirely: tooling (T1 typically 4–8 weeks, 2–3 respins normal), EVT/DVT/PVT builds, long-lead component procurement, pilot production, mass production, and sea freight (4–6 weeks). For a first hardware product these routinely dominate and are precisely what an engineer orders parts against. A schedule handed to a parts-ordering engineer that omits tooling and procurement lead time is not fit for purpose.

3. ARITHMETIC. "4–9 months" is reachable only under assumptions the claim itself contradicts. Serial sum: min 2+4+3+4 = 13 wk (3.0 mo); max 6+8+6+8 = 28 wk (6.4 mo); with one EMC failure, 17–36 wk (3.9–8.3 mo). That requires everything serial AND an EMC failure always occurring. But the claim states EPR runs in parallel, and in practice UN 38.3 and IEC 62133-2 run concurrently at one battery lab and in parallel with system EMC/safety. Realistically parallelized the certification path is ~10–20 weeks (2.5–4.5 months). The 4–9 month figure lands in a plausible range for the wrong reasons. Separately, "4–9 months" followed by "plan 6, contingency 9" is internally inconsistent — the 4-month floor never informs a decision and in a spec invites someone to quote 4 months externally.

4. OMITTED MANDATORY GATES for a wireless battery product in 2026. The claim names 62368-1 as the safety gate but never names the radio/EMC gate its own risk thesis depends on: RED Art 3(1)(b)/3(2), EN 300 328 and EN 301 489-1/-17. It also omits RED Art 3(3)(d)(e)(f) cybersecurity under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 — the EC RED page confirms 2022/30 activates those articles for connected/wearable equipment; deferred by (EU) 2023/2444 and in force since 1 Aug 2025, with EN 18031-1/-2/-3 cited with restrictions. That is the single most common first-product schedule surprise as of 2026. Also omitted: FCC/ISED authorization, GPSR EU Responsible Person, and EU Battery Regulation 2023/1542 CE-marking of portable batteries, which is closing the claim's "if you must do it" hedge on 62133-2.

5. SCOPE ERROR ON 62368-1. For a battery device below 50 V AC / 75 V DC the LVD does not apply; 62368-1 enters via RED Art 3(1)(a). It is not the standalone mandatory gate the framing implies, and most of the standard is trivially satisfied at 3.7 V.

6. UNSUPPORTED "DOMINANT RISK" JUDGEMENT. "First-pass EMC failure is the norm rather than the exception" is asserted as fact; the widely repeated ~50% figure traces to test-lab marketing, not a published study, and I could not verify it (WebSearch budget was exhausted — itself grounds not to state it as fact in a spec). More importantly the ranking is probably backwards: an EMC retest is BOUNDED at 4–8 weeks, whereas a tooling respin or mis-specified long-lead part is unbounded and sits on the critical path. Queue time is also understated — a 6-week lab slot lost to a failed sample means requeuing, not merely retesting.

Also minor: the 7-day post-abuse observation is canonically UN 38.3 T.7 (overcharge), not a distinguishing feature of IEC 62133-2, and days of observation inside a test do not justify the multi-week band attributed to it.

The claim is directionally sane about carrying EMC contingency but is not orderable-against as written.

Sources checked: https://en.gdestl.com/529.html , https://en.gdestl.com/815.html , https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/electrical-and-electronic-engineering-industries-eei/radio-equipment-directive-red_en

corrected.original: Sequencing matters more than total cost: three decisions should be locked before any lab is booked.
corrected.corrected:
Sequencing is worth managing, but the three items listed are not the right three and two of them are stated wrongly. Corrected version:

Freeze these before booking lab time, in this order of cost impact:

1. Radio implementation: pre-certified module vs. bare chip + custom antenna. This, not the power input, decides whether you pay for full EN 300 328 / FCC Part 15.247 / RSS-247 radio conformance. Changing it after test entry is the one item that reliably means retesting from scratch.

2. Power architecture: mains-wired vs. external DC adapter. Note this does NOT determine whether a safety regime applies. As radio equipment under RED 2014/53/EU the product is outside LVD scope regardless, but RED Art. 3(1)(a) imposes the LVD safety objectives with no voltage limit, so an EN IEC 62368-1 safety assessment is required at 5 V. What the choice changes is the size of that assessment (isolation, creepage/clearance, mains-transient and abnormal-operation clauses) and whether the adapter's CE is yours or the adapter vendor's.

3. Battery presence and removability. Reg. (EU) 2023/1542 already applies (general application 18 Feb 2024; CE marking and conformity assessment for batteries from 18 Aug 2024; labelling from 18 Aug 2026) — battery obligations are live now, not deferred to 2027. Art. 11 (user-removable and replaceable portable batteries, spares availability, instructions) applies from 18 Feb 2027 and is a design and aftermarket obligation rather than a test-lab one. Sealed is not automatically non-compliant: Art. 11(2) provides derogations, but relying on one requires documented justification, so decide and document early.

4. Cell sourcing: require an existing IEC 62133-2 CB certificate and a UN 38.3 test summary as a purchasing condition. This avoids roughly $5–15k of cell-level testing. It does not eliminate pack-level work — expect pack-level IEC 62133-2 evaluation and pack-level UN 38.3 (T.1–T.5, T.7 for rechargeable) unless the assembled-battery provisions of the UN Manual apply, plus the battery clauses of EN IEC 62368-1 at product level. Budget for pack testing separately.

5. Also freeze before test entry: enclosure and PCB layout, target market list, and intended-use questions (child appeal triggers the Toy Safety Directive; body-worn triggers RF-exposure assessment per EN IEC 62311).

On changes after test entry: most trigger partial or delta retesting, not a second full bill. The exceptions that genuinely reset the clock are antenna, PCB layout, and enclosure changes.

Provenance: this is an engineering estimate, not legal advice. Confirm the 18 Feb 2027 Art. 11 date against Reg. (EU) 2023/1542 Art. 79 and confirm pack-level transport-test obligations against the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria s.38.3 before issuing the spec.
corrected.why:
Substantially right in spirit (freeze power architecture and battery sourcing before test entry) but wrong or overstated on every specific it asserts. Six defects, ordered by how much money an engineer could lose acting on it.

(1) The LVD premise is wrong for this product class. Loc8 is a BLE/mesh radio product. Radio equipment in RED (2014/53/EU) scope is carved out of the Low Voltage Directive; RED Art. 3(1)(a) imposes the LVD *safety objectives* "with no voltage limit applying." So LVD does not apply either way, and electrical-safety assessment to EN IEC 62368-1 is required at 5 V just as at 230 V. Wikipedia's RED article confirms EN IEC 62368-1 is the harmonised standard cited against Art. 3(1)(a) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Equipment_Directive). Mains-vs-DC changes the *scope and cost* of the safety file (isolation, creepage/clearance, mains transient and abnormal-operation clauses, and whether you own the adapter's CE) — it does not switch a regime on or off. Even for a hypothetical non-radio variant, a sub-75 VDC device outside LVD is still covered by GPSR (Reg. (EU) 2023/988). An engineer reading "DC-fed means LVD doesn't apply" may skip budgeting safety testing entirely. That is the expensive error in this claim.

(2) Art. 11 is not the binary "replaceable vs sealed." Art. 11(2) contains express derogations — the Commission's own batteries page states that "Article 11(2) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 ... establishes derogations from the removability and replaceability requirements" (https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/waste-and-recycling/batteries-and-accumulators_en). Sealed can be lawful where justified (e.g. devices designed to operate primarily in wet conditions). Separately, Art. 11 is a design + aftermarket obligation (removable with commonly available tools, spare parts availability, instructions) — it involves essentially no lab testing, so it does not belong in a "lock before booking a lab" list on the logic given.

(3) The Feb 2027 date is correct for Art. 11 but is used to date the wrong thing. The claim says battery presence determines "the whole Battery Regulation layer" "from Feb 2027." Reg. (EU) 2023/1542 entered into force 17 Aug 2023 and has applied generally since 18 Feb 2024, with CE marking / conformity assessment obligations for batteries from 18 Aug 2024 and labelling obligations from 18 Aug 2026. A battery-bearing product shipping in 2026 is already in scope now. 18 Feb 2027 is only the removability date.

(4) The cell-certificate saving is optimistic. A cell-level IEC 62133-2 CB certificate does not cover the assembled pack: pack-level IEC 62133-2 evaluation (protection circuitry, pack construction) and pack-level UN 38.3 (T.1–T.5, plus T.7 for rechargeable batteries) are generally still required, subject only to the UN Manual's conditional assembled-battery provisions. The end product is additionally assessed against the battery clauses of EN IEC 62368-1. So the cell certificate avoids roughly $5–15k of cell testing, not "five figures of testing" outright — presenting it as total avoidance is exactly the optimistic assumption a parts budget should not inherit.

(5) "Paying for the testing twice" is overstated. Labs routinely quote delta/partial retests. Removing a mains input narrows scope rather than doubling it; a same-chemistry cell swap inside a qualified family often triggers a subset of retests. The genuine full-retest risk sits with radiated emissions and radio conformance, driven by antenna, PCB and enclosure — none of the three listed decisions.

(6) The list is not the right three. For a wireless product the highest-leverage pre-lab decision is pre-certified radio module vs. bare chip plus custom antenna: that alone decides whether you pay for full EN 300 328 / FCC Part 15.247 / RSS-247 radio testing, which dominates the mains-vs-DC question. Also missing: enclosure/PCB design freeze, target market list, and intended-user questions (child appeal → Toy Safety Directive; body-worn → RF exposure per EN IEC 62311).

Finally, "sequencing matters more than total cost" is unfalsifiable framing with no derivation, and the stated source is self-referential ("synthesis of the regulatory findings above"). That is not adequate provenance for a document an engineer orders parts against. Verification was limited: EUR-Lex would not render through WebFetch and the WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted, so the 18 Feb 2027 Art. 11 date and the UN 38.3 pack-level provisions were not confirmed against primary text and should be re-checked against Reg. (EU) 2023/1542 Art. 79 and the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria s.38.3 before the spec is issued.

corrected.original: In a total mains failure, only guard phones survive intrinsically; every other element of the chain dies unless separately backed.
corrected.corrected:
In a total mains failure, the battery-carrying elements survive and every mains-fed element dies; what is lost is the venue's network infrastructure, not Loc8 connectivity.

SURVIVES INTRINSICALLY: guard phones (own batteries; 3–5 h realistic under continuous BLE scan/advertise, less in screen-on relay mode — not open-ended).

DIES IMMEDIATELY: the PoE switch, venue LAN switching and distribution, venue Wi-Fi APs where they are PoE-fed from that switch (site-survey item, not an assumption), and any ISP router/ONT on venue mains.

CONDITIONAL — GATEWAY: Tier A (USB PSU) and Tier B (PoE+ HAT) die as specified in the BOM, but Tier B's §3 USB-C service/alt-power port accepts a USB-C power bank with no BOM change. Tier C's UPS battery HAT sustains the box for roughly 3–5 h — 2× 18650 = 19–26 Wh raw, ~16–23 Wh after boost losses, against a 4.5–6 W CM4 load with dual BLE radios and antenna. Budget ~$35–45, not $25: the HAT ships without cells (confirmed for Geekworm X728 and Waveshare UPS HAT), and cells are a consumable.

CONDITIONAL — UPLINK: not automatically lost. A USB-A LTE dongle (§2 add-on, §3 port, §7 pitch) runs off the gateway's own rail, and cell sites hold ~4–8 h of battery with most macro sites carrying generators for 24–72 h. There is no FCC backup-power mandate — the 8-hour rule was struck down in 2008 — so treat carrier backup as likely, not guaranteed, and expect degradation in a wide-area event.

CONDITIONAL — CONSOLE: a laptop running the Tauri Command app survives 2–6 h on its battery; a control-room desktop dies instantly. Specify the laptop if power-cut operation is a requirement.

NET RESULT: with Tier C plus an LTE dongle plus a laptop console, the mesh, the site database, the console link (over the gateway's own Wi-Fi per §6 Layer 0, bypassing the dead venue LAN) and the HQ uplink all survive for a bounded window of roughly 3–5 hours, set by the gateway's UPS HAT. The chain degrades to a radio-only topology rather than going dark. With Tier A or Tier B as specified, the gateway drops and the system falls back to phone-mesh plus the documented phone-bridges-to-laptop console path (§8).
corrected.why:
Substantially right in spirit (mains failure guts venue-owned infrastructure; the BLE mesh is the resilient layer) but the bucketing is wrong in ways that would cause an engineer to order the wrong parts. Five defects, in order of severity:

1. "The internet uplink dies immediately" is contradicted by the claim's own stated source. §2 add-ons specify "LTE dongle + SIM (~$25 + data): the box brings its own internet"; §3 lists "1× USB-A (LTE dongle...)"; §7 states the pitch explicitly — "a venue with *no working infrastructure at all* still appears live at HQ." An LTE dongle draws from the gateway's own rail, so on a battery-backed gateway the uplink survives with it. On the far end, cell sites carry independent backup: the FCC's 8-hour mandate was struck down in 2008 and formally abandoned, so there is no federal requirement, but macro-site practice is ~4–8 h of battery with most sites carrying permanent generators good for 24–72 h. The uplink therefore belongs in the CONDITIONAL bucket, not "dies immediately." This is the load-bearing error: an engineer reading the claim would skip the LTE dongle on the grounds that the uplink is doomed regardless, deleting the one part that preserves it.

2. "The network does not survive" is the wrong conclusion because it conflates the *venue's* network with *Loc8's* network. The gateway has onboard Wi-Fi — §2 Tier B: "BLE 5 + Wi-Fi onboard"; Tier A is "Wi-Fi only"; §6 Layer 0: "the box's Wi-Fi (when used) is WPA2/3". A battery-backed gateway can host its own AP for a battery-powered laptop console with zero venue LAN, zero PoE switch. The document names this as the designed fallback (§1: "the control room can run off a laptop in a car park"; §8: "no gateway → any guard phone bridges to a laptop console exactly as today"). What dies is venue-owned distribution, not connectivity.

3. Tier C "survives" is unbounded and needs a runtime figure. Re-deriving: a 2× 18650 UPS HAT is 5200 mAh nominal (Waveshare's default program assumes 2× 2600 mAh) up to ~7000 mAh with 3500 mAh cells → 19.2–25.9 Wh raw at 3.7 V; after boost-converter loss (~85–90%) ≈ 16–23 Wh delivered at 5 V. A CM4 idles at 2.7–3.5 W, and Tier C adds dual BLE radios (concurrent scan + advertise) plus an external antenna, plus the LTE dongle if fitted → realistically 4.5–6 W. Runtime ≈ 16–23 Wh ÷ ~5 W ≈ **3–5 hours**, i.e. comparable to or shorter than the guard phones it is supposed to outlast, not "survives" full stop.

4. The ~$25 Tier C UPS line is a bare board — cells are extra. Confirmed for both candidate parts: Geekworm X728 ("the batteries are not included in the packing list") and Waveshare UPS HAT ("2x 2600mAh 18650 batteries (NOT included)"). Two quality 18650s add ~$10–16, so realistic backup cost is ~$35–45, and the cells are a consumable with a service life the BOM does not acknowledge.

5. Tier B is not unconditionally dead. §3 — the same section the claim cites for the PoE port — also lists "1× USB-C (service/alt power)". A USB-C power bank backs Tier B with no BOM change, which matters because Tier B is named "the pilot workhorse."

Minor: "only guard phones survive intrinsically" leans on "intrinsically" to stay true, but phone runtime under continuous BLE scan/advertise — and especially under a screen-on relay mode — lands in the same 3–5 h band, so "hours of runtime" should not be read as an order-of-magnitude advantage over a UPS-backed Tier C.

Sources: [Geekworm X728](https://geekworm.com/products/x728), [Waveshare UPS HAT wiki](https://www.waveshare.com/wiki/UPS_HAT), [FCC 15-98 backup power proceeding](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/FCC-15-98A1.pdf), [Cell Tower Attorney — backup power rule history](http://www.celltowerattorney.com/backup-power-rule.html), [Pi Dramble power benchmarks](https://pidramble.com/wiki/benchmarks/power-consumption), [RasPi.TV Pi 4 power measurements](https://raspi.tv/2019/how-much-power-does-the-pi4b-use-power-measurements)

corrected.original: With only the Gateway battery-backed, peer-to-peer field operations continue fully intact and unaffected.
corrected.corrected:
With only the Gateway battery-backed, the PEER-VISIBLE subset of field operations continues: team map position frames, hold-to-fire SOS as an alert to nearby phones, and quick-reply statuses (codes 20–23) as peer-visible chips. These ride 25-byte BLE frames phone-to-phone and do not require the LAN.

Every control-room-mediated function is LOST in this state, because Loc8 Command has no BLE radio and reaches the mesh only via BridgedTransport over a WebSocket on the LAN:
- Dispatch with bearing is console-originated (IncidentDetail.tsx:203) — cannot be issued.
- Muster cannot be CALLED (MusterBoard.tsx:32; OperationsOverview.tsx:99). MUSTER SAFE confirmations can be transmitted but the headcount board that consumes them is a Command view, so nobody sees them.
- Duress is decoded ONLY by Command by explicit design — peer Guard phones deliberately never render it (guardStatus.ts:26; liveBridge.ts:41). A duress raised in this state reaches no one.
- SOS and statuses still reach peers, but not the control room.

Configuration caveats an order must resolve:
- The UPS battery HAT (~$25) is Tier C ONLY. The Tier B BOM has no battery, so this scenario cannot occur on a Tier B install. §1's "on PoE, battery-backed" contradicts §2's tiering and must be corrected.
- The Gateway is PoE-powered. In a mains blackout the PoE switch also dies, so even Tier C loses its Ethernet link and all consoles. Specify the UPS-HAT/PoE-HAT power arbitration and expected battery runtime under BLE-scan load.
- BOM correction: the stock Raspberry Pi 4 Model B has NO u.FL connector (requires board rework or a pre-modified third-party board). Only the CM4 provides it, and it requires dtparam=ant2 to enable. Specify CM4 + Raspberry Pi's own certified antenna kit; a generic $8 u.FL→SMA antenna voids modular FCC/CE certification and obliges the end-product manufacturer to fund its own testing.
- loc8-meshd is unbuilt (§4 "critical-path engineering project"; §8 item 1, still at spike stage). Gateway relay performance is a design intent, not a measured result. Do not state range or dead-spot improvement without bench data — BLE link budget is bidirectional and limited by the body-blocked phone side, and a high-mounted gain omni has a null cone directly below it.
corrected.why:
REFUTED on four independent grounds. Verified against the cited files plus the actual source.

1) THREE OF THE SIX NAMED FEATURES ORIGINATE IN COMMAND, ON THE LAN.
The claim asserts dispatch, muster and duress "ride BLE frames between phones and never touch the LAN." The code says otherwise:
- Dispatch: /Users/augustusedem/Loc8/.claude/worktrees/recursing-montalcini-d59018/apps/command/src/dashboards/IncidentDetail.tsx:203 — `onClick={() => store.dispatch(dispatchText, ...)}` behind a "Send dispatch" button. The ops brief §03 confirms the semantics: "Supervisor sends a named person to a named place." Dispatch is console-originated, never phone-originated. No console, no dispatch.
- Muster call: apps/command/src/dashboards/MusterBoard.tsx:32 ("Call muster / evacuation") and OperationsOverview.tsx:99 (`store.callMuster()`). A muster cannot be *called* without Command.
- Muster confirmations: MUSTER SAFE frames can be transmitted peer-to-peer, but the headcount board that gives them purpose is a Command view (MusterBoard.tsx), and the brief's own value statement is "the console shows a headcount that fills in as people confirm, and names the ones who have not." Frames sent into a void.

2) DURESS IS THE STRONGEST COUNTEREXAMPLE — IT IS CONSOLE-ONLY BY DESIGN.
packages/engine/src/core/guardStatus.ts:26 — "Silent duress — deliberately NOT in GUARD_STATUS (never rendered as a chip, never labelled on the sending device)... only the control room decodes its meaning." apps/command/src/services/liveBridge.ts:41 — "only the console decodes its meaning, and it NEVER replies." apps/guard/src/ui/MeshBadge.tsx:22 — "0 = broadcast; Command decodes."
Peer Guard phones are deliberately built NOT to surface duress. So a duress raised during a blackout with only the Gateway powered reaches literally no human. Citing duress as evidence that the layer is "unaffected" inverts the actual design.

Also relevant: Command has no BLE radio at all. The brief describes BridgedTransport as existing "so a laptop console can join a mesh it has no radio for" (packages/engine/src/transport/BridgedTransport.ts:3, WebSocket). Every control-room function is LAN-dependent by construction.

3) TIER B HAS NO BATTERY — THE CLAIM'S OWN CITED SECTION CONTRADICTS IT.
The claim cites §2 Tier B. In §2, the UPS battery HAT (~$25) appears ONLY under Tier C. Tier B ships PoE + microSD + antenna and nothing else. The doc is internally inconsistent: §1's table asserts "on PoE, battery-backed" as a general property. An engineer ordering the Tier B BOM against this spec gets zero battery backup and the scenario cannot occur at all. Additionally, the Gateway is PoE-powered — in a mains blackout the PoE switch/injector dies, so even a Tier C UPS HAT keeps the Pi alive while the Ethernet link and every console drop out. The doc never specifies the UPS-HAT/PoE-HAT power arbitration, which is an orderable-parts gap.

4) THE ANTENNA LINE IS NOT BUILDABLE AS WRITTEN, AND THE REGULATORY POSITION IS OVERSTATED.
§2 Tier B lists "Raspberry Pi 4 (2GB) or CM4 on carrier" with "External BLE antenna (u.FL → SMA) $8". The stock Raspberry Pi 4 Model B has NO u.FL connector — the trace to the pad is not populated (it needs an 0201 0-ohm resistor added, the PCB-antenna trace cut, and caps removed), which is a hand-rework/third-party-modified-board path, not a purchase. Only the CM4 ships the u.FL socket. The "or" makes an unbuildable BOM.
Worse for a spec: Raspberry Pi's modular certification covers their own antenna kit, not an antenna specification. Per the CM4 documentation and RPi forum guidance, substituting a different antenna requires the end-product manufacturer to redo FCC/CE testing. A generic "$8 u.FL→SMA" part therefore voids modular certification and imposes an unbudgeted compliance cost. The CM4 external antenna also requires an explicit software enable (dtparam=ant2), not plug-and-play.

5) loc8-meshd DOES NOT EXIST YET.
The claim's present tense ("The Gateway continues as loc8-meshd") describes unbuilt software. §4 calls it "the critical-path engineering project"; §8 lists it as item 1: "Spike on a bench Pi against two phones." The ops brief adds that Guard and Command "currently render mostly seeded demo data." Nothing has been measured.

6) "LIKELY THE SINGLE BEST RELAY" IS UNMEASURED AND PHYSICALLY OPTIMISTIC.
BLE link budget is bidirectional. Gateway-side antenna gain does not fix the limiting side — a phone at 0 to +8 dBm in a pocket, body-blocked. 2.4 GHz is strongly absorbed by human bodies, so a dense crowd degrades the phone→gateway leg regardless of gateway gain. A high-mounted gain omni also has a squashed pattern with a null cone directly beneath it, which is the opposite of what "high placement bridges dead spots" implies. No measured range figure appears anywhere in the doc.

WHAT ACTUALLY SURVIVES: team map (peer position frames), hold-to-fire SOS as a peer-visible alert, and statuses 20-23 as peer-visible chips. That is roughly half of what the claim asserts, and the control-room half of every one of those is gone.

corrected.original: The Gateway on battery becomes a silent recorder: it hears and stores everything but can show it to nobody, because loc8-relayd has no surviving transport to any console.
corrected.corrected:
On a venue power cut the control room does not go blind, and loc8-relayd is not peerless by architecture — but neither outcome is currently specified, and the battery the claim presumes is not in the default build.

Three transports survive a dead switch. (a) The gateway's own Wi-Fi: the Pi 4/CM4 CYW43455 supports AP mode (and concurrent AP+STA on one band), so consoles can associate directly to the battery-backed box — only Ethernet dies with the switch. (b) The laptop-hotspot + gateway-phone bridge, preserved by this same document at §1 and §8 ("both paths stay tested") and demonstrated in tools/mesh-bridge/README.md step 4 with venue wifi and cell killed. (c) The BLE mesh itself, which Command joins through any bridged gateway phone.

The features named as casualties are console-side computations, not gateway services: the coverage heatmap (apps/command/src/dashboards/CoverageHeatmap.tsx, src/domain/coverage.ts), muster/incident state (src/store/commandStore.ts) and the nearest-responder haversine (packages/engine/src/core/geoMath.ts, re-exported via apps/command/src/engine.ts) all run inside Command on 25-byte frames, and console-initiated dispatch is explicitly bidirectional over the bridge. They require frames, not loc8-relayd.

What is genuinely true and should be fixed in the spec: §5 step 4 specifies only "Consoles attach over the LAN (mTLS)", and blackout console connectivity is nowhere written down — Wi-Fi AP failover must be specified, not assumed, and a mains-powered control-room desktop dies on its own power regardless. Before an engineer orders parts, also note: the UPS HAT is Tier C only (~$25, no capacity, Wh or runtime given), Tier B "the pilot workhorse" has no battery, ~$25 UPS HATs often ship without 18650 cells, quoted 8-12h runtimes are bare-idle and will fall with BLE scan+advertise plus a Wi-Fi AP running, and the current PoE+ HAT PCB will not accept a stacked HAT without a special extra-tall push-fit header kit.
corrected.why:
The claim's central assertion — that loc8-relayd has "no surviving transport to any console" and the control room therefore goes blind — is contradicted by the source document itself, by the repo's code, and by the hardware.

(1) TRANSPORT IS NOT ZERO. The gateway's compute is specified in §2 as "Raspberry Pi 4 (2GB) or CM4 — BLE 5 + Wi-Fi onboard", and §6 Layer 0 refers to "the box's Wi-Fi (when used)". The CYW43455 radio supports AP mode and even concurrent AP+STA (same band only). A dead switch kills the Ethernet link, not the box's own radio. On battery the gateway can still serve consoles over Wi-Fi. The claim states a physical impossibility where the truth is an unwritten configuration.

(2) THE SAME DOCUMENT PRESERVES A SECOND PATH. §1 line 26: "The laptop/hotspot chain remains as a fallback mode". §8 line 169-170: "no gateway → any guard phone bridges to a laptop console exactly as today; both paths stay tested." The claim cites §4 and §5 while ignoring the two clauses in the same file that defeat it.

(3) THE BLACKOUT SCENARIO IS ALREADY THE TESTED DEMO. tools/mesh-bridge/README.md step 4: "kill the venue wifi/cell. Positions keep flowing, an SOS raised on a phone with no connectivity lands on the console via the gateway, dispatch orders typed in Command arrive on phones as dispatch takeovers, and status replies ('En route') come back." That is exactly the feature set the claim says is lost, demonstrated with venue infrastructure dead.

(4) THE NAMED CASUALTIES ARE CLIENT-SIDE, NOT GATEWAY SERVICES. CoverageHeatmap.tsx, domain/coverage.ts and store/commandStore.ts run inside Command; the haversine is packages/engine/src/core/geoMath.ts, re-exported by apps/command/src/engine.ts with the comment "getHaversineDistance → real nearest-responder distances and zone coverage". Command connects via BridgedTransport to ANY relay URL (?bridge=ws://host:8787, services/liveBridge.ts), and CommsStatus.tsx labels the live link "BRIDGE — gateway phone · real frames". These functions need frames, not loc8-relayd. Dispatch is explicitly bidirectional: Command "emits and ingests the SAME 25-byte mesh frames Guard speaks... so dispatch/status flow both ways".

WHAT IS RIGHT: §5 step 4 does say only "Consoles attach over the LAN (mTLS)", and the doc nowhere specifies blackout console connectivity — a real gap that must be written down rather than assumed. A mains-powered control-room desktop does die, but from its own power, not from relayd.

The claim also inherits an unexamined premise: the UPS HAT is Tier C only (~$25, no capacity/Wh/runtime stated); Tier B, called "the pilot workhorse", has no battery at all. Such HATs frequently ship without 18650 cells, ~8-12h figures are bare-idle (BLE scan+advertise plus a Wi-Fi AP will cut that materially), and the current PoE+ HAT PCB no longer accepts stacking 4-pin headers, so PoE+ and UPS HATs will not physically stack without a special extra-tall push-fit header kit. "The Gateway on battery" is not the default build.

corrected.original: The record-keeping value of a battery-backed Gateway is the strongest single justification, because Command's own audit log is not a durable substitute.
corrected.corrected:
Record-keeping is one legitimate argument for site-side persistence, but it does not carry a procurement decision as stated, and the battery framing is wrong for the tier most installs will order.

What the sources support: Command's audit log is bounded at 2,000 entries with older entries dropped, not archived (ops brief §04; AUDIT_MAX=2000 in apps/command/src/store/commandStore.ts:126). That is a RETENTION and tamper-evidence gap, not a durability-under-power-loss gap — the log persists to localStorage and survives reboot intact. Moving site state into a gateway with SQLite fixes retention and enables the hash chain; it does not rescue a log from a blackout, because a blackout was never going to destroy it.

Corrections an engineer must have before ordering:
- Battery backup is a TIER C line item only (UPS HAT ~$25, within the $180-240 ruggedized build). Tier B ($95-120) ships with a PoE+ HAT and NO battery. If battery-backed record-keeping is the justification, the spec must order Tier C, or add a UPS HAT to the Tier B BOM as an explicit line.
- A gateway UPS HAT alone does not keep the site recording. Both tiers draw power and network from PoE, so a mains outage kills the venue switch, the consoles, and all Ethernet-side ingest. Continuous recording through an outage additionally requires a UPS on the network switch (and on any console expected to keep generating operator entries). That switch UPS is currently unspecified and must be added or the claim dropped.
- No battery runtime figure exists in any source. Do not state a duration ("40 minutes" appears nowhere; the only 40 in the docs is the "last synced 00:40" sync-staleness string in gateway spec §7). Bench-measure the chosen HAT against the actual Tier C load (Pi + PoE HAT + dual BLE radios) and cite the measurement.
- The hash-chained audit log is unimplemented — zero hashing exists in the codebase, and the brief's own status table marks it open. The gateway is "fully specified and entirely unbuilt. No unit exists." Both must be written in the future tense.

Suggested honest form: "Moving site state into the Gateway gives the venue an unbounded, tamper-evident record that Command's 2,000-entry local log cannot provide. Adding a UPS — on the Gateway (Tier C, or a ~$25 HAT added to Tier B) and on the network switch — extends that recording through a mains outage for a duration to be established by bench test. Both the Gateway and the hash chain are specified and unbuilt."
corrected.why:
Verified against primary sources. The verbatim quote and its §04 attribution check out (docs/brochure/loc8-ops-brief.html:554), and AUDIT_MAX=2000 with drop-oldest is real in apps/command/src/store/commandStore.ts:126. Everything built on top of that is unsupportable for a hardware spec.

(1) BATTERY IS A TIER C PART, NOT A GATEWAY PROPERTY. gateway spec §2 places the UPS battery HAT (~$25) exclusively in Tier C ($180-240). Tier B — the doc's own "pilot workhorse" at $95-120 — lists a PoE+ HAT and no battery. Tier A has none. "Battery-backed Gateway" describes a SKU costing roughly 2x the tier an engineer would default to. The spec's own §1 prose ("screwed to a wall, on PoE, battery-backed") contradicts the BOM printed directly below it.

(2) POE DEFEATS THE BATTERY IN THE CLAIMED SCENARIO. §3 specs 1x RJ45 PoE-in as primary power and network. In a mains blackout the venue Ethernet switch is unpowered unless separately UPS'd, which no document specs. A UPS HAT keeps the Pi's SQLite alive but the LAN dies with it: Command consoles (the source of operator audit entries) and anything arriving over Ethernet stop. Only the BLE-side ingest survives on gateway battery alone. Conflates "the box stays up" with "the site keeps recording."

(3) THE HASH CHAIN DOES NOT EXIST. A repo-wide search for hash-chain/prevHash/createHash/sha256 returns zero implementation. The ops brief's own status table (line 713) marks "hash-chained tamper-evident log" with an OPEN pill: "No operator SSO yet." The claim writes an unbuilt feature in the present tense ("continues writing ... the hash-chained audit log").

(4) THE GATEWAY DOES NOT EXIST. Brief line 571: "fully specified and entirely unbuilt ... No unit exists. Treat costs as estimates to be re-quoted at order time." §8 puts persistence consolidation at step 2, behind the loc8-meshd BLE port. Present-tense "loc8-sited on battery continues writing" describes nothing that has run.

(5) THE BLACKOUT PREMISE IS WRONG. loadAudit/persistAudit write to localStorage key 'loc8.command.audit.v1' — non-volatile disk. Power loss does not erase it; the log is intact on reboot. The claim's "if the console machine dies in a blackout, that bounded log is the only other copy" implies loss that does not occur. The actual deficiency the brief names is RETENTION (2,000-entry drop-oldest) and tamper-evidence — a records problem, not a power problem. The claim fuses two independent failure modes into one argument.

(6) "40 MINUTES" HAS NO SOURCE. No battery runtime figure exists in any document for the ~$25 UPS HAT. The only "40" in the corpus is "last synced 00:40" in gateway spec §7 — a sync-staleness display string, unrelated to endurance. Nothing has been bench-measured; Tier C adds dual BLE radios, raising draw further. Presenting an endurance window without a measured figure is exactly the marketing-as-measured failure a spec must avoid.

(7) "STRONGEST SINGLE JUSTIFICATION" IS A RANKING NO SOURCE MAKES. §1 lists six reasons for a box; §8 names loc8-meshd as the critical path; the spec's own stated rationale for the Tier C battery is "the gateway rides out a venue power cut" — comms continuity, not record-keeping. §7 frames off-site sync as the manager question. Additionally, loc8-syncd store-and-forward means the gateway is not the only other copy whenever an uplink has existed.

corrected.original: Both of the system's safety watchdogs fail during a blackout, and moving them onto the Gateway is the highest-value design change the battery unlocks.
corrected.corrected:
One of the two limitations is blackout-relevant, and relocating it is a real but second-order gain that the battery does not by itself unlock.

Of the two gaps in ops brief §04, only the console's man-down watchdog (MAN_DOWN_AFTER_SEC = 15 min, apps/command/src/store/commandStore.ts) is console-bound: runWatchdog raises an incident in local store state and never transmits. The lone-worker check-in timer runs on the guard's battery-powered phone and, on expiry, already broadcasts an overdue message plus a full SOS onto the mesh (apps/guard/app/lone.tsx). It survives a blackout fine; its actual defect is that it dies when the app is backgrounded, which mains power has nothing to do with. That defect is fixed on-device with a scheduled local notification — no gateway, no battery, no hardware.

Relocating the man-down watchdog into loc8-sited is therefore a one-watchdog change, and three conditions gate it. (a) loc8-sited does not exist in the repo, and loc8-meshd — the Linux BLE port the box needs to transmit anything — is the doc's own acknowledged critical path. (b) Delivery is unreliable in the target scenario: per the project's spike brief, backgrounded iPhones sit in Apple's overflow area, invisible to Android scanners, with ~10 s of execution per BLE wake; the standing Screen-On Relay design explicitly does not promise background mesh, so a gateway-raised alert reaches screens that are on, not the pocketed phone of a guard who is actually down. (c) The UPS battery HAT (~$25) is a Tier C ($180–240) line item; Tier B, the stated pilot workhorse at $95–120, is PoE-only and loses power with the venue switch. Do not order Tier B expecting blackout survival.

Net: the battery plus a ported mesh daemon would let the box keep raising and broadcasting man-down alerts with no console — a genuine duty-of-care improvement, but contingent on unbuilt software, degraded by a known iOS background-BLE limit, and requiring the Tier C build.
corrected.why:
The two quotes are verbatim from docs/brochure/loc8-ops-brief.html line 549, and MAN_DOWN_AFTER_SEC = 15 * 60 in apps/command/src/store/commandStore.ts confirms the 15-minute figure. Everything built on top of those quotes fails.

1. FALSE PREMISE — watchdog #1 does not fail in a blackout. The lone-worker check-in timer runs on the guard's phone (apps/guard/app/lone.tsx), which is battery-powered. Its documented failure mode is app backgrounding, which is orthogonal to mains power. The ops brief never links it to a blackout; the claim imports that framing.

2. WATCHDOG #1 ALREADY DOES WHAT THE FIX PROPOSES. On expiry lone.tsx calls getMeshService().sendCrewMessage(opsMsg.loneOverdue(badge, plusCode)) then raiseSosNow(), which broadcasts a first-class 'sos' packet, a rally pin and a text alert via getTransport().broadcast(). It is already console-independent and already on the mesh. Moving it to the Gateway fixes nothing and would break it — the box cannot know a guard failed to press "I'M OK" on a screen it cannot render. Only watchdog #2 (runWatchdog, which contains no transmit call and only mutates local store state) is console-bound.

3. THE FIX DEPENDS ON THE CAPABILITY WHOSE ABSENCE IS GAP #1. "Raise the alert onto the BLE mesh where guard phones will see it" requires backgrounded phones to receive BLE. The repo's own spike brief (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-07-v2-mesh-spike-brief.md, risks #2/#3, sourced to Apple's Core Bluetooth background guide) records that a backgrounded iPhone's advert lands in Apple's proprietary overflow area — invisible to Android scanners and to iOS centrals not explicitly scanning that UUID — and that iOS background execution is ~10 s per BLE wake with coalesced discoveries. The standing mitigation is Screen-On Relay, which explicitly declines to promise background mesh. So the alert lands least reliably in the pocket-phone scenario it exists for.

4. "HIGHEST-VALUE" IS UNSUPPORTED. Gap #1 is fixable on-device with a scheduled local notification — no gateway, no battery, no mesh, no hardware spend. A battery cannot be what unlocks a fix that needs no battery.

5. THE BATTERY IS NOT STANDARD — ORDERING RISK. docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md §2 places the UPS battery HAT (~$25) in Tier C only ($180–240). Tier B, explicitly "the pilot workhorse" at $95–120, has a PoE+ HAT and no battery. An engineer ordering Tier B against this spec gets zero blackout survival. PoE also means power arrives from the venue switch, so a Tier B box dies with the switch; a Tier C box on battery keeps its BLE radio but loses its LAN and consoles unless the switch is separately on a UPS.

6. THE TARGET DAEMONS DO NOT EXIST. loc8-sited appears nowhere in the repo. loc8-meshd — without which the gateway cannot emit a frame at all — is described in the same doc as "the critical-path engineering project." The battery cannot keep alive a function with no radio and no state daemon.

7. MINOR OVERSTATEMENT. "The console dies" — the gateway doc describes the console as a laptop, which has its own battery. And runWatchdog only fires for staff with s.location and a prior lastPingSec, so it never covered devices the console had not already seen.

corrected.original: Yes, the Gateway should behave differently on battery — load-shedding roughly doubles usable runtime, which is the difference between covering an evacuation and covering the recovery too.
corrected.corrected:
Yes, the Gateway should behave differently on battery — but justify it as graceful degradation, not as a runtime multiplier. Load-shedding buys roughly **1.2-1.4×**, not 2×.

Re-derivation on measured figures: a Pi 4B idles at **2.7 W** (540 mA, nothing on USB) and reaches 6.4 W only under `stress --cpu 4`. A BLE scan/advertise/relay workload with SQLite writes runs ~**2.9-3.5 W**, not 4-5 W — the 4-5 W figure is a near-peak number presented as a duty-cycle average. The shed floor is bounded below by the ~2.7 W idle draw, so ~**2.4-2.9 W** is achievable, not 2.0-2.5 W. Against ~15 Wh usable from a 2× 18650 HAT (19.2 Wh raw, after DoD and boost losses), that is **~4.7 h unshed → ~5.8 h shed: about one extra hour.** Worth having; not the difference between an evacuation and a recovery.

The "ratio is robust even if absolutes aren't" reasoning is inverted and should be struck. Battery energy is the easy multiplication; the **ratio** is the fragile quantity, because both power figures sit on a large non-sheddable static floor (SoC leakage, LPDDR4 self-refresh, PMIC and boost-converter quiescent). Shedding acts only on the small variable component above it. The Pi 4B's *entire* idle-to-full-load span is 2.37×, so 2× from policy alone would require ~84% of that span while the gateway keeps working. On Tier C's actual compute the ceiling is worse: a CM4 measures 3.55 W idle / 5.2 W stress — a 1.46× total range.

Drop these levers from the spec as immaterial or illusory: LED dimming (~0.01 W), suppressed non-critical writes (tens of mW), powersave governor (~0 on an already-idle Pi), and "Ethernet PHY down" (on a PoE install the mains cut kills the switch, so the PHY auto-enters energy-detect regardless of policy). **LTE batching is the only materially large lever** — but note that disabling USB to save ~100 mA also disables Ethernet and the LTE dongle on a Pi 4, since both sit behind the VL805.

Three BOM corrections before ordering:
- **The described configuration is not in §2.** The Pi 4 is Tier B (PoE+, no UPS); the ~$25 UPS HAT is Tier C, where compute is CM4/CM5. Either re-scope this to a Pi 4 + UPS Tier B variant, or re-derive against CM4/CM5 — and account for Tier C's dual BLE radios, a constant load that cannot be shed because it is the core function.
- **Form factor.** Waveshare UPS HAT B/D/E mate via pogo pins to a Pi 3B+/4B/5 board outline; vendors list no CM4/CM5 support. Confirm the carrier exposes compatible pads, or budget a different power path for Tier C.
- **Prices.** "~$25" is board-only — cells are NOT included; add ~$10-20 plus Li-ion shipping constraints. Pi 4 2GB is now $45 after early-2026 DRAM price rises, so §2's "$35-45" and the "~$100 Tier B BOM" need re-quoting.

Treat every figure here as a sizing estimate pending a **measured discharge curve on the actual HAT, cells, and carrier at the real duty cycle** — including converter efficiency at the shed operating point, which is *lower* than at the unshed point and therefore erodes the ratio further.

The policy is still worth building, on different grounds: clean shutdown and SQLite integrity through brownout, prioritizing the local mesh over the cloud uplink as charge falls, and signaling on-battery state to HQ. Those justify it on their own. A ~1-hour runtime extension is a real but secondary benefit.
corrected.why:
The conclusion (build the policy) survives; the magnitude, the central reasoning, and the hardware pairing do not.

**1. The unshed figure conflates peak with average.** Measured Pi 4B: idle 2.7 W (540 mA), full 4-core `stress --cpu 4` 6.4 W, nothing on USB (pidramble/Geerling); raspi.tv independently measures 575 mA = 2.85 W idle. The claim's "4-5 W with BLE active" sits 55-80% of the way from idle to all-four-cores-pegged. A gateway doing BLE scan/advertise/relay/dedup plus SQLite writes is nowhere near that; the BLE radio itself is ~10-30 mW. Realistic unshed for this workload is ~2.9-3.5 W.

**2. The shed figure is below the measured floor.** 2.0-2.5 W is at or under the Pi 4B's bare idle of 2.7 W with nothing plugged in. The listed levers don't get there: powersave governor saves ~0 on an idle-dominated load (the Pi 4 is already at 600 MHz when idle — the "up to 30%" figure applies to light *tasks*, not idle floors); LED dimming saves ~2 mA = **0.01 W**, three orders of magnitude below relevance, yet is listed as a lever; suppressed microSD writes are tens of mW. "Ethernet PHY down" is not a policy saving at all — on a PoE install the mains cut kills the switch, so the link partner is gone and the PHY drops to energy-detect automatically whether or not the policy exists. LTE batching is the one genuinely material lever, but it only pays if a modem is fitted, and on Pi 4 the USB-disable trick that would save ~100 mA also kills Ethernet (shared VL805) and the LTE dongle you're trying to keep. Realistic shed: ~2.4-2.9 W.

**3. The meta-claim is backwards, and this is the load-bearing error.** "Absolute figures are uncertain but the ratio is robust" inverts the actual uncertainty structure. Battery energy is the *easy* part — a multiplication over known chemistry. The **ratio is the fragile part**, because both power figures sit atop a large non-sheddable static floor: SoC leakage, LPDDR4 self-refresh, PMIC quiescent, plus the UPS HAT's own boost-converter and fuel-gauge quiescent draw. Shedding acts only on the small variable component above that floor. The Pi 4B's entire dynamic range is 6.4/2.7 = **2.37×** — so a 2× shed ratio demands ~84% of the full span between four-cores-pegged and total idle, obtained while the gateway *keeps doing its job*. Not achievable.

**4. Boost-converter efficiency is assumed in the direction that flatters the conclusion.** A single "usable energy after losses" constant is applied to both scenarios, but converter efficiency falls at light load: a 5V/5A (25 W) rated HAT delivering 2.5 W runs at ~10% of rated load, where efficiency sags from ~90% toward ~78-85%. The shed case is penalized relative to unshed, compressing the ratio further. Peukert works slightly the other way but is negligible at ~0.1C.

**5. Battery energy, re-derived.** The ~$25 Waveshare-class UPS HAT is 2× 18650 in **series**, cells **NOT included** at that price. 2 × 2600 mAh × 3.7 V = **19.2 Wh** raw; after ~92% DoD and ~85% boost, **~15 Wh usable**. Caution: the widely-repeated "5200 mAh × 8.4 V = 43.7 Wh" multiplies parallel-summed capacity by series voltage and **overstates energy by 2.27×** — do not order against it. At the claim's own inputs, 15/4.5 = 3.3 h vs 15/2.25 = 6.7 h, so its stated 1.5-4 h / 3-8 h brackets are internally consistent; the arithmetic is sound, the inputs fail. At realistic inputs: **4.7 h → 5.8 h, a 1.23× gain of about one hour.**

**6. The configuration described does not exist in §2.** The Pi 4 is **Tier B**, powered by a PoE+ HAT with **no UPS**. The ~$25 UPS HAT is **Tier C only**, where compute is **CM4/CM5, not a Pi 4**. Three consequences: (a) a CM4 on the official IO board measures 3.55 W idle / 5.2 W stress (Tom's Hardware) — a total dynamic range of only **1.46×**, making 2× even less reachable on the tier that actually has the battery, and CM5 is higher still; (b) Tier C adds **dual BLE radios** for concurrent scan+advertise — constant load, and precisely the thing that cannot be shed because it is the core function; (c) **mechanical risk** — the Waveshare UPS HAT B/D/E mate via pogo pins onto the underside pads of a Pi 3B+/4B/5 board outline, and vendor listings state Pi 3B+/4B/5 compatibility with no CM4/CM5 mention. A CM4/CM5 carrier won't present those pads, so the engineer could order a HAT that cannot mount to Tier C compute.

**7. Stale prices.** Pi 4 2GB is now **$45** after early-2026 DRAM-driven price rises (a 3GB Pi 4 launched at $83.75), pinning §2's "$35-45" at its ceiling and putting the "~$100 Tier B BOM" out of date. The "~$25" UPS HAT is board-only; add ~$10-20 for cells plus Li-ion shipping constraints.

Sources: [pidramble power benchmarks](https://www.pidramble.com/wiki/benchmarks/power-consumption.html), [RasPi.TV Pi 4B measurements](https://raspi.tv/2019/how-much-power-does-the-pi4b-use-power-measurements), [Waveshare UPS HAT (B)](https://www.waveshare.com/ups-hat-b.htm), [Waveshare UPS HAT (E)](https://www.waveshare.com/ups-hat-e.htm), [Tom's Hardware CM4S review](https://www.tomshardware.com/raspberry-pi/raspberry-pi-compute-module-4s-review), [Raspberry Pi memory-driven price rises](https://www.raspberrypi.com/news/a-new-3gb-raspberry-pi-4-for-83-75-and-more-memory-driven-price-increases/), [core-electronics power-saving guide](https://core-electronics.com.au/guides/disable-features-raspberry-pi/)

corrected.original: Load-shedding tier 1 — must never stop: mesh receive/relay at full duty cycle, critical-class persistence, the status lens, and the shutdown supervisor.
corrected.corrected:
Load-shedding tier 1 — functions that must never stop (applies to Tier C, or Tier B with the UPS HAT option; Tier A/B as specced have no reserve and this tier does not exist for them).

SCOPE AND BUDGET. Tier 1 is a bounded promise, not an indefinite one. Reference figures for the ~$25 Tier C UPS HAT: 2× 18650 (5200 mAh, 19.2 Wh raw, ~17.3 Wh usable to cutoff) against a ~3.2 W rail load through an 85–90% boost converter gives ~4.7 h; ~5.3 h at bare idle, ~3.6 h with the LTE dongle transmitting; a single-cell HAT gives ~2.4–3.5 h. Specify the required hold time before selecting the pack. Note that the dominant load is the application processor (~2.7–2.85 W measured, Pi 4 2GB headless), not the radio — the radio is tens of mW. Any serious reserve extension comes from SoC governor, USB and PHY management, not from the radio.

1. Mesh receive/relay — loc8-meshd. The mesh function never stops. Its parameters may adapt: tier 1 guarantees a receive-latency budget (specify: advertisement caught within N ms at 95th percentile), not a fixed duty cycle. Note that "full scan AND advertise duty cycle" is not achievable on a single BLE radio; if simultaneity is required, the Tier C dual-radio option is mandatory, not optional, and must appear in the tier-1 BOM.

2. Critical-class persistence — loc8-sited. SOS, duress, muster and incident entries continue at full rate. Audit entries continue for security-relevant events; routine config/access audit may batch. Persistence is only credible with a hold-up reserve (item 4).

3. Status lens. Stays lit, changes meaning, and stays AMBER. Per IEC 60073, amber/yellow denotes an abnormal condition requiring monitoring or intervention; red denotes emergency/danger requiring immediate action. ON BATTERY is amber. Do not introduce red — it collides with the existing §3 assignment (red = fault) and dilutes red across the fleet. Distinguish ON BATTERY from the existing "amber pulse = uplink down" by waveform, not colour: propose a slow amber breath (rise-fall) for ON BATTERY versus the existing sharp amber pulse for uplink-down, with breath rate increasing as reserve drains. Rate is the primary channel because it survives red-green colour vision deficiency (~1 in 12 men), for whom red and amber are confusable and red appears dimmer. Do NOT dim to minimum: the lens draws ~2 mW dimmed, 0.05% of pack draw, so dimming saves nothing measurable while defeating legibility; hold normal or one step below normal brightness. If the BOM's addressable LED ring is used, budget ~60 mW of driver quiescent draw even when dark. Do not claim external-to-building visibility — the specified matte near-black wall/DIN and ceiling-tile mountings are usually enclosed; the lens serves someone at the box, not a passer-by.

4. Watchdog and safe-shutdown supervisor, with a reserved energy floor. Reserve an explicit hold-up budget (specify: stop-work threshold at a fixed SoC/minutes remaining) so the supervisor can flush the SQLite WAL, close the hash chain, fsync and unmount cleanly. Without a floor, tier-1 loads run the pack to cutoff and the legal record is lost to a dirty unmount — the exact risk the spec acknowledges by offering "no SD to corrupt" only at Tier C. The hardware watchdog does NOT simply "stay by definition": the supervisor must extend or disarm it on entering orderly shutdown, or undervoltage brownout produces reset loops and repeated dirty mounts.

5. Instrumentation prerequisite. Encoding remaining reserve in the breath rate requires a runtime estimate the current BOM cannot supply. INA219-based HATs derive remaining capacity from bus voltage and current via a formula requiring per-pack calibration, and Li-ion's flat 80–20% plateau makes that estimate least reliable where it matters most. Add a coulomb-counting fuel gauge (MAX17043, BQ27441 or equivalent) to the tier-1 BOM, or restate the lens as a two-state indication (ON BATTERY / RESERVE LOW at the stop-work threshold) rather than a continuous runtime readout.

Source: extends the light grammar in gateway spec §3 ("green breathing / amber pulse / red / white chase"); colour assignment per IEC 60073; runtime and power figures re-derived from published Pi 4 measurements and $25-class UPS HAT capacities, to be re-measured on the actual build before release.
corrected.why:
I read the cited source (/Users/augustusedem/Loc8/.claude/worktrees/recursing-montalcini-d59018/docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md) and re-derived the power budget. The tier-1 *set* is defensible in intent, but the claim is refuted on six independent grounds — three of which would cause an engineer to order the wrong parts.

1. SELF-CONTRADICTION WITH THE CITED SPEC — "full scan and advertise duty cycle" is not orderable at Tier B. The same document's Tier C line reads "dual BLE radios (concurrent scan + advertise)". That concession exists precisely because a single BLE radio (Tier A/B use the Pi's on-board CYW43455) time-shares scan and advertise; BlueZ cannot run both at 100%. So the claim mandates a behaviour the reference hardware in §3 ("Tier B reference") cannot perform. Either tier 1 requires the second radio in the BOM, or "full duty cycle" must be restated as a latency/interval budget.

2. THE POWER ARGUMENT DEFENDS THE WRONG LOAD. On the specified platform the radio is a rounding error, not the battery's consumer. A Pi 4 (2GB) headless idles at ~2.7–2.85 W measured; BLE scan on the shared combo chip adds on the order of tens of mW. The rhetorical line — "throttling the radio to save power would be saving power by disabling the exact reason the battery exists" — argues against a straw man, while the spec is silent on the ~90% that actually drains the pack: the application processor, its clocks, USB, and (on battery, with PoE dead) the LTE dongle that becomes the only uplink. A load-shedding tier list that never names the SoC is not a power budget.

3. NO RUNTIME NUMBER, AND THE REAL ONE IS SHORT. §2 specifies a "UPS battery HAT (~$25)" at Tier C. At that price that is 1–2× 18650. Re-derived: 2×2600 mAh = 19.2 Wh raw, ~17.3 Wh usable to cutoff; at 3.2 W rail load through an 85–90% boost converter that is ~4.7 h (~5.3 h at bare idle, ~3.6 h with LTE transmitting). A single-cell HAT gives ~2.4–3.5 h. Tier 1 is therefore a 2.5–5 hour promise, not an indefinite one, and the claim states no figure at all. Anyone ordering against "must never stop" will size nothing.

4. THE LIGHT PROPOSAL VIOLATES THE GRAMMAR IT CLAIMS TO EXTEND, AND A SAFETY STANDARD. §3 already assigns red = fault and amber pulse = mesh live/uplink down. An amber/red alternating breath collides with both: a responder at the door cannot separate "on battery" from "fault" or from "uplink down". Worse, IEC 60073 assigns red to emergency/danger requiring immediate action and yellow/amber to abnormal condition requiring monitoring or intervention. "On battery" is textbook amber. Putting red in the ON BATTERY code both mis-signals urgency and erodes red's meaning fleet-wide on a life-safety product. Separately, red and amber sit on the same protan/deutan confusion line — for the ~1 in 12 men with red-green CVD the alternation carries zero information (and protanopes see red as markedly dimmer), so the colour channel is decorative and only the breath rate survives.

5. "COST IS MILLIWATTS" IS TRUE AND IRRELEVANT, AND THE DIMMING IS SELF-DEFEATING. A dimmed indicator LED at ~2 mW is 0.05% of a 3.7 W pack draw. If the cost is genuinely negligible, there is no power justification for "dimmed to minimum brightness" — and dimming directly destroys the stated function ("a person walking past a dark building knows the box is on reserve"). That function is largely fictional anyway for the specified mounting: §3 describes a matte near-black wall/DIN unit with an optional ceiling-tile bracket and a single small lens, i.e. normally inside a comms cupboard or above a ceiling. Note also the BOM offers a "Status LED ring", and a 12-pixel addressable ring has ~60 mW of driver quiescent draw even dark — 30× the claimed figure, still small but not what was stated.

6. THE RESERVE-REMAINING ENCODING EXCEEDS WHAT THE BOM CAN MEASURE, AND THE WATCHDOG CLAIM IS WRONG. Breath rate encoding "roughly how long it has" requires a runtime estimate. $25-class HATs (e.g. Waveshare UPS HAT (B)) derive remaining capacity from an INA219 bus-voltage/current reading via a formula that Waveshare's own documentation says must be recalibrated per pack and defaults to an assumed 5200 mAh — that is not a coulomb-counted, temperature- and age-compensated fuel gauge. Li-ion's discharge plateau is flat from roughly 80% to 20% SoC, so the estimate is least trustworthy exactly in the region an operator would act on. If the spec wants runtime signalling it must add a real gauge (e.g. MAX17043/BQ27441) to the BOM. And "the watchdog... stays by definition" is wrong as written: a hardware watchdog left armed through an undervoltage brownout produces reset loops and repeated dirty mounts of the volume holding the hash-chained audit log — the opposite of tier 1's purpose. The supervisor must take ownership of the watchdog when it begins an orderly stop. Relatedly, tier 1 lists the shutdown supervisor but reserves no hold-up energy for it; if tier-1 loads run to cutoff there is no margin to flush the SQLite WAL, close the hash chain and unmount. The spec concedes SD corruption is real by advertising "no SD to corrupt" only at Tier C, so on Tier B this is the exact failure mode that loses the legal record tier 1 exists to protect.
