Sources: [Raspberry Pi power consumption measurements](https://raspberry.tips/en/raspberrypi-tutorials/raspberry-pi-power-consumption-update-2026-all-models-compared), [RasPi.TV Pi 4B power measurements](https://raspi.tv/2019/how-much-power-does-the-pi4b-use-power-measurements), [IEC 60073 beacon colour meanings](https://www.hazeng.com/news/beacons-what-is-the-meaning-of-each-colour-lens-iec-60073), [Waveshare UPS HAT (B) wiki](https://www.waveshare.com/wiki/UPS_HAT_(B)), [DFRobot ONPOWER UPS HAT runtime](https://wiki.dfrobot.com/ONPOWER_UPS_HAT_for_Raspberry_Pi_SKU_DFR0677).

corrected.original: Load-shedding tier 2 — degrade: position-frame persistence collapses to a last-known-position table, and sync sends one urgent event then goes quiet.
corrected.corrected:
SHED-2 (rename: "tier 2" collides with build Tiers A/B/C in §2) — degrade: position-frame persistence collapses to a last-known-position table plus a coarse 30-60 s appended track; loc8-syncd emits one high-priority SITE ON BATTERY event immediately, then batches all further traffic to bursts no more frequent than 1 per 15 min, retaining a low-rate heartbeat so HQ can distinguish "quiet" from "dead".

JUSTIFICATION (corrected). This is a card-wear and write-integrity measure, not a meaningful power measure. Measured microSD write current is ~20-25 mA @ 3.3 V (~70-80 mW) and stays elevated ~250 ms after each write, so a few commits/second pin the card near-continuously at ~70 mW. Against a Tier C on-battery load of ~4 W (Pi 4/CM4 idle alone measures ~2.85 W), removing it is ~2% of budget — roughly 5 minutes on a ~4.5 h UPS-HAT runtime. State the wear benefit; do not claim a power benefit alongside it.

TIER MISMATCH — resolve before ordering. The wear rationale applies to Tier B (industrial microSD), which has no battery in the BOM. The battery rationale applies to Tier C, which specifies soldered eMMC, where endurance is not the binding constraint. Either add a UPS option to Tier B or drop the wear rationale from the on-battery ladder.

LTE. Application-layer silence does not reduce modem power: a Cat-4 USB dongle stays enumerated and RRC-attached (~0.3-0.6 W) regardless of send rate, and PSM/eDRX are LTE-M/NB-IoT features it will generally not expose. The real saving (~10-15% of budget, ~30-40 min) requires cutting the dongle's power — and on Pi 4B USB port power is ganged all-or-nothing and needs VL805 firmware >= 00137ad. Spec that explicitly, or spec an M.2/mPCIe modem on a switchable rail. Specify burst cadence numerically: each burst pays RRC setup plus a ~10 s tail at ~1 W (~3 mWh), so 10 bursts/hour adds ~28 mW.

PEAK vs AVERAGE. LTE transmit peaks (1.5-2.7 A class on module datasheets) size the regulator, battery C-rate and bulk capacitance; they do not set runtime. By energy on battery: SoC ~75-85% >> LTE attached-idle > BLE radios > storage. If runtime is the goal, SHED-2 must also cut CPU wakeups, apply a low-power governor, and disable unused PHYs — it currently does not touch the dominant term.

"EST. RUNTIME X" — add the part or downgrade the message. The ~$25 UPS HAT reports terminal voltage at best; Li-ion plateau estimation is ±30-50%. Add a fuel gauge (MAX17048/BQ27441 class, ~$1-3) or an INA219/INA226 shunt monitor to the Tier C BOM and recompute the estimate per shed tier. Until then send state-of-charge proxy and instantaneous load, or coarse buckets ("> 2 h" / "< 30 min"), not a confident runtime figure.

FORENSICS — do not assert "low value". §6 specifies a hash-chained, tamper-evident audit log. If position frames are in that chain, in-place row updates break append-only verification; if they are not, §4/§6 must say so explicitly. Retain the coarse 30-60 s appended track rather than discarding history, and make any discard an explicit, logged, customer-visible policy — the position track is often the contractual proof-of-presence deliverable, and a venue power cut is a high-incident window.

BLE. Hedge retained and correct; expected size is order 50-100 mW per continuously scanning radio (~2-3% of budget), so measurement will likely show it is not worth the mesh cost.
corrected.why:
Directionally sound engineering (last-known-position table, coarse sampling, batched sync, hedging the BLE question) but the justification contains a power error of ~2 orders of magnitude, a tier mismatch, a peak/average conflation, an unbudgeted part, and a conflict with the spec's own §6.

1) POWER CLAIM WRONG BY ~2 ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE. "Cuts SD/eMMC write volume dramatically, which helps power and card-wear simultaneously" presents two benefits as co-equal. Measured microSD write current is ~20-25 mA @ 3.3 V (~70-80 mW), and the card stays elevated ~250 ms after each write (goughlui.com, Arduino/NXP forum measurements). At N guards x several frames/min (~2-3 commits/s) the post-write tails overlap, so the card is pinned near ~70 mW continuously — that is the honest upper bound on the saving, and it comes from the post-write tail, not data volume. Against a Tier C on-battery load of ~4 W (Pi 4 idle measured 2.85 W / 575 mA per RasPi.TV and Pi Dramble; plus dual BLE ~0.12 W, LTE attached ~0.3-0.6 W, boost-converter losses), that is ~2% of budget: on ~18 Wh usable from a 2x18650 UPS HAT, 4.44 h -> 4.53 h, about 5 minutes. The wear benefit is real and multi-year; the power benefit is noise. Bundling them misleads.

2) THE TWO RATIONALES APPLY TO DIFFERENT BOXES. §2 Tier B specifies "Industrial microSD 32GB" — wear argument strong — but Tier B has no battery in the BOM (PoE only); the UPS battery HAT appears only in Tier C. §2 Tier C specifies "CM4/CM5 with soldered eMMC (no SD to corrupt)", where endurance is not the binding constraint. So the battery rationale lives on the eMMC box and the wear rationale lives on the SD box. No single configuration gets both.

3) "GOES QUIET" != MODEM POWER REDUCTION. Application-layer silence does not power down a Cat-4 USB dongle; it remains enumerated and RRC-attached (~0.3-0.6 W). PSM/eDRX are LTE-M/NB-IoT features a Cat-4 dongle generally will not expose (Nordic Developer Academy). The material ~10-15% saving requires cutting the dongle's power rail — and per §3 the LTE dongle sits on USB-A of a Pi 4B, where uhubctl documents the ports as ganged (all-or-nothing) and requiring VL805 firmware >= 00137ad. That is a hardware-topology decision that belongs in the spec, not a daemon behavior.

4) PEAK/AVERAGE CONFLATION. "An LTE modem's transmit peaks are likely the largest single draw in the box" — module datasheets do show large peaks (Quectel EC25 Mini PCIe cites input peak up to 2.7 A in 2G TX), but peaks size the regulator, battery C-rate and bulk capacitance; they do not dominate energy, which is what sets runtime. By energy the ranking is SoC (~75-85%) >> LTE attached-idle > BLE radios > storage. Tier 2 as written does not touch the dominant term at all.

5) "INFREQUENT BURSTS" IS UNSPECIFIED AND CAN BACKFIRE. Each burst after RRC_IDLE pays connection setup plus a ~10 s tail at ~1 W (~3 mWh) versus ~50 mW idle (AT&T Video Optimizer). Ten bursts/hour adds ~28 mW average. Without a stated cadence the guidance is unfalsifiable.

6) "EST. RUNTIME X" IS NOT ORDERABLE AGAINST THE BOM. The ~$25 UPS HAT in §2 Tier C reports terminal voltage at best; Li-ion runtime estimation on the flat discharge plateau is ±30-50%. Sending a confident runtime figure as "the single message HQ most needs" requires a fuel gauge (MAX17048/BQ27441 class, ~$1-3) or an INA219/INA226 shunt monitor — not currently in the BOM. The estimate also changes the moment a shed tier engages, so it must be recomputed per tier.

7) "FORENSIC VALUE IS LOW" CONFLICTS WITH §6. §4 (loc8-sited) and §6 Layer 3 specify a hash-chained, tamper-evident audit log "exportable as the after-action record". If position frames are inside that chain, "update one row in place" breaks append-only verification and leaves a provable gap; if they are outside it, the spec must say so. Independently, in a guarding contract the position track is often the proof-of-presence deliverable, and a venue power cut is a high-incident window — so this is a business judgment presented as an engineering fact, and it is the shakiest premise in the claim.

8) NAMING COLLISION. "tier 2" and "Tier C" appear in the same claim, where A/B/C are §2 build tiers. An engineer ordering parts against this cannot tell which axis is meant.

9) MINOR: shedding position-frame persistence does not reduce mesh/radio load — the frames still arrive over BLE. Only storage cost changes.

Correctly hedged: "dropping to a single BLE radio should be evaluated by measurement, not assumed." Expected size is order 50-100 mW per continuously scanning radio (~2-3% of budget), i.e. likely not worth the mesh cost.

Sources: [RasPi.TV Pi4B power measurements](https://raspi.tv/2019/how-much-power-does-the-pi4b-use-power-measurements), [Pi Dramble power benchmarks](https://pidramble.com/wiki/benchmarks/power-consumption), [Gough's Tech Zone microSD power experiment](https://goughlui.com/2021/02/27/experiment-microsd-card-power-consumption-spi-performance/), [Arduino forum SD write current](https://forum.arduino.cc/t/power-consumption-to-write-to-sd-card/129434), [uhubctl README (Pi 4B ganged ports, VL805 firmware)](https://github.com/mvp/uhubctl/blob/master/README.md), [Quectel EC25 Mini PCIe spec](https://quectel.com/content/uploads/2024/03/Quectel_EC25_Series_Mini_PCIe_LTE_Standard_Specification_V2.4-1.pdf), [AT&T Video Optimizer LTE vs 3G energy / RRC tail](https://developer.att.com/video-optimizer/docs/best-practices/comparing-lte-and-3g-energy-consumption), [Nordic Developer Academy power saving (PSM/eDRX)](https://academy.nordicsemi.com/courses/cellular-iot-fundamentals/lessons/lesson-1-cellular-fundamentals/topic/lesson-1-power-saving-techniques/), [SQLite forum: running a DB from SD card](https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/59f2c378eb). Spec read at /Users/augustusedem/Loc8/.claude/worktrees/recursing-montalcini-d59018/docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md

corrected.original: Load-shedding tier 3 — stop entirely: the OTA updater must be a hard interlock, not a policy, plus provisiond, the Ethernet PHY, remote reads, and all database housekeeping.
corrected.corrected:
Load-shedding tier 3 — stop entirely.

A/B image updater — hard interlock gated on a mains-present hardware signal, covering the USB-stick update path (§4) as well as OTA. Correct the rationale: a battery death mid-write does not leave a dangerous "corrupt boot slot." Writing the inactive slot is the failure mode A/B is designed to absorb — a partial image fails signature/hash verification and is discarded while the active slot still boots. The genuine hazards are (a) the slot-switch metadata commit and the first unconfirmed boot, where automatic rollback itself needs enough charge to complete a second reboot, and (b) the reboot dropping loc8-meshd and loc8-relayd mid-incident. Refuse to start on battery; if mains drops mid-update, stop writing and leave the active slot untouched rather than attempting a slot switch on a dying battery.

loc8-provisiond — shed the gateway claiming/adoption path ONLY. Keep cert issuance and the per-shift key path running. §4 assigns provisiond both claiming and "cert issuance for enrolling devices"; §5.3 makes clock-in the moment a guard's device cert and per-shift key are issued; §6 Layer 2 derives frame encryption from that enrollment. A guard arriving on shift during a blackout who cannot enroll has no key, cannot join the mesh, and is invisible for the entire outage — that fails the tier-3 test outright, and the cost of keeping it is a few signatures on an otherwise idle daemon. mDNS beacon follows whichever interface is live.

Wired NIC/PHY — shed, but book it as a tens-of-mW item, not a headline saving. "A few hundred mW" is the delta for a PHY with a live link (~30 mA / ~150 mW at 5 V). With the venue switch dead the PHY has already auto-entered energy-detect, which powers down TX and most of RX unaided; explicit power-down buys only tens of mW more. Note also that `ip link set eth0 down` disables the SoC-side MAC and leaves the Pi 4's BCM54213PE in auto-GREEN, so it does not deliver the claimed saving. Do NOT credit link-detect as the "mains is back" signal: energy-detect is what makes link-detect work, so a hard PHY power-down destroys that signal. On this PoE-powered box (§3, "1x RJ45 (PoE in)") the mains-back signal is PoE voltage returning on the same cable, detected by the PD controller — a power-rail event, independent of PHY state. Use that.

HQ-initiated remote reads — shed. State explicitly that loc8-syncd's outbound heartbeat continues at reduced cadence, because §7 promises the cloud "shows staleness honestly"; HQ must be able to tell "site dark but alive" from "box dead."

Database housekeeping (SQLite VACUUM, log rotation, metrics, index rebuilds) — shed, for the right reasons. Plain VACUUM is not uniquely unsafe to interrupt: per the SQLite docs the "incomplete and corrupt" warning applies to the output file of VACUUM INTO, while plain VACUUM overwrites the original under a rollback journal or WAL "just as it would be for any other database transaction," so power loss rolls back to the pre-VACUUM state. Suspend it because (1) it needs up to 2x the database size in free space, (2) it is a large sustained write to a Tier B microSD whose controller is the actual power-loss corruption vector for all writes, and (3) — decisively — it holds a write lock that blocks incident and audit-log writes, violating the "preserve the record of what happened" half of the test.

Before anyone orders parts: the spec carries no power budget, no battery capacity, and no runtime target (§3 covers dimensions, mounting, ports and industrial design only), so both the "few hundred mW" and the "next 90 minutes" horizon must be sourced or derived first. Tier 3 also adds a BOM requirement the spec does not yet carry: a named UPS HAT that exposes mains-present and state-of-charge over I2C or GPIO, since a hard interlock needs a signal to gate on and §2 specifies only "UPS battery HAT (~$25)". Confirm that HAT can physically coexist with the PoE+ HAT before ordering.
corrected.why:
The citations exist and are quoted accurately (§4 has the "watchdog + A/B updater | ... signed OTA images with rollback" row and the loc8-provisiond mDNS row). But the claim is substantially right in its conclusions and wrong in its reasons, which matters because the reasons are what an engineer sizes parts against.

1. A/B updater rationale is backwards. The claim's stated danger — "a battery death mid-write can leave a corrupt boot slot" — is precisely the failure mode A/B partitioning exists to absorb. The image is written to the INACTIVE slot; a partial write fails verification and is discarded, and the active slot still boots. Sources confirm the write is verified before the bootloader is pointed at the new slot. The genuine bricking window is the slot-switch marker/metadata commit and the first unconfirmed boot (industry sources: power-loss recovery "does not, on its own, guarantee that the small markers and metadata controlling the switch are written atomically... That gap is where bricking still happens"). Interlock = right call, wrong hazard. The claim also says "OTA updater," but §4 also ships "USB-stick updates for offline sites" — same hazard, and the interlock wording excludes it.

2. provisiond is over-shed, and it fails the claim's OWN test. §4 gives provisiond both "claiming" AND "cert issuance for enrolling devices"; §5.3 makes clock-in the moment a guard's device cert and per-shift key are issued; §6 Layer 2 derives frame encryption from that enrollment via HKDF. A guard arriving on shift during a 90-minute blackout who cannot enroll gets no cert and no per-shift key, so cannot decrypt or join the mesh at all — invisible for the whole outage. That directly fails "does this help a guard in the next 90 minutes?" Only the gateway adoption/claiming path should be shed; cert issuance costs a handful of signatures on an otherwise idle daemon.

3. The PHY item has wrong arithmetic AND a self-cancelling mechanism. "A few hundred mW" is the delta for a PHY with a LIVE link (~30 mA idle increase with cable connected, ~150 mW at 5 V; disabling an already-idle PHY via register saves a further ~15-20 mA). In the tier-3 scenario the venue switch is dead, so the PHY has ALREADY auto-entered energy-detect, which powers down TX and most of RX on its own — the marginal saving is tens of mW, not hundreds. This is exactly the peak-vs-average conflation to look for. Worse, the two rationales are mutually exclusive: energy-detect is what provides link-detect on repower, so a hard PHY power-down destroys the "mains is back" signal it is credited with providing. And on a Pi 4, `ip link set eth0 down` disables the MAC inside the SoC while leaving the BCM54213PE in auto-GREEN — it does not deliver the claimed saving. Separately, §3 specifies "1x RJ45 (PoE in)": the box is PoE-powered, so the real mains-back signal is PoE voltage returning on that same cable, detected by the PD controller as a power-rail event independent of PHY state.

4. The VACUUM rationale is wrong. Per sqlite.org/lang_vacuum.html the "interrupted by an unplanned shutdown or power loss... might be incomplete and corrupt" warning applies to the OUTPUT FILE of VACUUM INTO, not to the original under plain VACUUM. Plain VACUUM overwrites the original using "a rollback journal or write-ahead log WAL file... just as it would be for any other database transaction" — power loss rolls back to the pre-VACUUM state. So VACUUM is not "precisely what must not be interrupted." The real reasons (needs up to 2x DB size free space; large sustained write to a Tier B microSD whose controller is the actual power-loss corruption vector for all writes; and it holds a write lock blocking incident/audit writes) are stronger and the claim misses the lock argument entirely — which is the one that violates the "preserve the record" half of its own test.

5. Both numbers are unsourced against the cited sections. §3 is dimensions/mounting/ports/industrial-design and says nothing about power; the spec contains no power budget, no battery capacity, and no runtime target anywhere in its 170 lines. "A few hundred mW" and "the next 90 minutes" are presented as if grounded in §3/§4 and are not.

6. Parts-order gap: a "hard interlock, not a policy" needs a hardware mains-present signal to gate on. §2 specifies only "UPS battery HAT (~$25)" with no part number and no interface, so nothing in the BOM guarantees the interlock is implementable.

Remote-read shedding is defensible and I did not refute it, though it needs an explicit carve-out for the outbound syncd heartbeat or §7's "shows staleness honestly" promise breaks.

corrected.original: The guard-phone bridge is the zero-work answer for reaching a console when the LAN is dead, and it is already built and tested.
corrected.corrected:
The guard-phone bridge is a real fallback path for reaching a console without a Gateway, but it is neither zero-work nor fully tested, and it does not by itself survive a dead LAN.

What exists: BridgedTransport (packages/engine/src/transport/BridgedTransport.ts) implements gateway mode, console mode, frame mirroring of the engine's 25-byte packets, and a 3s reconnect, with six unit tests covering mirroring, broadcast fan-out, malformed-frame rejection and closed-socket behaviour against a fake socket.

What the claim overstates:
1. Test status. The cited ops brief §03 row carries a third column the claim omits — "Verified with simulated transport, not real BLE" (status: partial). The same document states the bridge has been verified in software only, not over real Bluetooth between physical handsets, and lists this among the top two items still on the engineering plan. Reconnect specifically has no coverage: every test passes reconnectMs: 0, which disables it. No test exercises a real WebSocket, the relay, or the app-side wiring.
2. "Zero-work" / "LAN is dead". The bridge is a WebSocket over IP and cannot cross a dead LAN; it needs a substitute network. Standing it up requires a hand-started relay (node tools/mesh-bridge/index.mjs, :8787), the gateway phone joined to the laptop's hotspot, and the console opened with ?bridge=ws://<host>:8787.
3. "Any guard phone". The bridge URL comes from EXPO_PUBLIC_BRIDGE_URL, which Expo inlines at bundle time and which cannot change at runtime without a rebuild. A production Guard build without it has no bridge capability at all; the documented procedure requires a dev machine running Metro and the relay IP known before bundling.

Correctly stated in the original and worth keeping: this path restores live mesh operations to the console but not the Gateway's stored site state — no incident timeline, muster history or audit log from the box's SQLite. The console falls back to its own bounded local log, capped at 2,000 entries (AUDIT_MAX, apps/command/src/store/commandStore.ts:126).

BOM impact: budget a laptop capable of running Node and serving a Wi-Fi hotspot, or a battery-powered travel router/AP, plus a fixed relay IP address. Do not cost this fallback as requiring no additional parts.
corrected.why:
Refuted on two of three assertions, most damningly by the claim's own cited source.

(1) "Already built and tested" is contradicted by the ops brief row the claim quotes. docs/brochure/loc8-ops-brief.html:487 has THREE columns; the claim reproduces the first two and drops the third: "Verified with simulated transport, not real BLE", with status pill class "part" (partial), not done. Line 494 of the same document states the live bridge "has been verified in software with a simulated transport bridged end to end — not with real Bluetooth between physical handsets," and names this one of "the top two items on the engineering plan" and "the difference between a working prototype and a shippable product." Selectively quoting columns 1-2 while deleting the caveat column materially misrepresents the source.

(2) "Zero-work answer when the LAN is dead" inverts the real requirement. BridgedTransport is a WebSocket over IP (packages/engine/src/transport/BridgedTransport.ts:110-122) — it cannot span a dead LAN, it requires a substitute IP network. The project's own runbook (tools/mesh-bridge/README.md:10-22) requires: a relay process started by hand (node tools/mesh-bridge/index.mjs on :8787), the gateway phone joined to "the laptop's hotspot", and the console opened with ?bridge=ws://<host>:8787. The LAN-dead demo works only because a replacement network is stood up first.

(3) "Any guard phone" is false for shipped app binaries. packages/engine/src/services/appServices.ts:42-43 selects the bridge from process.env.EXPO_PUBLIC_BRIDGE_URL. Expo's documentation (docs.expo.dev/guides/environment-variables) confirms EXPO_PUBLIC_* values are inlined into the bundle at build time and cannot be changed at runtime without rebuilding. A production Guard build without that variable falls through to `inner` — a plain mesh node with no bridge capability whatsoever. Electing an arbitrary guard's phone as gateway in the field requires `npx expo start` on a dev machine and knowing the laptop's IP before bundling — an IP not knowable until on-site unless pinned.

(4) "Reconnect" is implemented (scheduleReconnect, 3000ms default) but has zero test coverage: all six tests in packages/engine/src/transport/__tests__/bridgedTransport.test.ts construct via a helper passing reconnectMs: 0, which disables reconnection outright (`if (!this.started || delay <= 0 || this.reconnectTimer) return`). No test exercises a real WebSocket, the relay, appServices transport selection, or liveBridge.ts. The spec's "both paths stay tested" is an aspiration in a forward-looking engineering plan, not a property of the current suite.

Accurate parts, which should be preserved: the gateway spec §8 quote is verbatim (docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md:169-170, inside "§8 Engineering plan"); AUDIT_MAX = 2000 is confirmed at apps/command/src/store/commandStore.ts:126; and the stated limitation about live frames vs. the Gateway's stored SQLite site state is honest and correct.

Hardware-spec consequence: the fallback is not parts-free and must not be costed as zero. It requires a laptop able to run Node and serve a Wi-Fi hotspot (or a battery-powered travel router/AP) plus a fixed, known relay IP so a pre-built Guard binary's baked-in URL resolves on site.

corrected.original: USB-C gadget mode should be shipped before a soft-AP: it restores the full console including the site database, costs almost no power, adds no broadcast surface, and the port already exists in the spec.
corrected.corrected:
USB-C gadget mode is a cheap, radio-free service path that — unlike the phone bridge — reaches loc8-sited directly, so it recovers the muster board, incident timeline and audit log. Its idle power cost is negligible. It is NOT free in the current spec, and the following must be settled before parts are ordered:

1. The USB-C port must be redesignated data-only. Per Raspberry Pi's OTG white paper (RP-009276-WP, Rel. 1, 1 Oct 2025), the Pi 4/Pi 5 USB-C supports peripheral mode only when not powering the board; the documented procedure powers the board via the GPIO header and leaves USB-C free. Section 3 must change from "1x USB-C (service/alt power)" to "1x USB-C (service data / OTG)", and the alt-power role must move to the GPIO header or a separate input.

2. Confirm D+/D- are routed. Existence of a power connector is not evidence of a data path. On a CM4 carrier, USB_OTG must be deliberately routed to the panel USB-C (the reference CM4 IO Board routes it to micro-USB); this is a pre-fabrication layout decision.

3. On CM4 only, gadget mode is exclusive with the USB-A port. The CM4 has one USB 2.0 controller; enabling device mode disables the host port carrying the LTE dongle and the offline update stick. Either accept that trade (and document that gadget mode and LTE uplink cannot be used together), add a PCIe USB host controller, or restrict gadget mode to the Pi 4 variant, whose separate VL805 controller has no such conflict.

4. Scope the recovery claim to Tier C. Tier B is PoE-only with no battery, so in a venue power cut the box is off and gadget mode is unreachable; the Pi 4B is not a PD sink and cannot be run from a laptop port. "Survives power cuts" requires the Tier C UPS HAT.

5. Use the CDC-NCM gadget function, not g_ether/RNDIS. RNDIS has not been inbox on Windows since Windows 10; Windows 11 ships UsbNcm.sys, and macOS supports NCM/ECM natively. Budget for host-compatibility testing — Raspberry Pi's own guidance is that "not all host systems handle Raspberry Pi 4's OTG mode reliably."

6. State the security position precisely: gadget mode adds no RF surface, but it does present a network interface to anyone with physical access to a wall-mounted box. It must enforce the same section 6 Layer 1 mTLS as the LAN path.

Sequencing: gadget mode serves one tethered laptop and requires physical presence and a stocked cable; soft-AP uses wireless already in the BOM, serves several devices at range, and is already covered by the WPA2/3 commitment in section 6 Layer 0. Treat gadget mode as the guaranteed single-operator recovery path and soft-AP as the multi-user one; the ordering between them is a product judgement, not something section 3 Ports establishes.
corrected.why:
Directionally reasonable but three of its four supporting assertions are wrong or unsupportable as written, and the marquee scenario is the case where it fails.

(1) PORT CONFLICT. Raspberry Pi's official OTG white paper (Rel. 1, 1 Oct 2025): "Raspberry Pi 4's USB-C power/OTG port supports peripheral mode WHEN IT IS NOT BEING USED TO POWER THE BOARD," and its procedure opens "Power your Raspberry Pi through the GPIO header (5V and GND), leaving the USB-C free." The spec (docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md:70) labels the port "1x USB-C (service/alt power)". Those two roles are mutually exclusive on one connector. The claim cites the port's existence as support while the port's stated function is the thing that blocks it.

(2) CM4 IS NOT INTERCHANGEABLE WITH PI 4 HERE. The claim says "Pi 4 and CM4 support USB device mode" as if equivalent. Pi 4 has a separate VL805 host controller so gadget mode is free. CM4 has ONE USB 2.0 controller: white paper says CM4's USB_OTG "is routed to the Compute Module 4 IO Board's micro-USB connector" (not USB-C), and host+device are exclusive ("they are both using the same usb controller, so there is no way to get both at the same time"). The same section 3 the claim cites also lists "1x USB-A (LTE dongle / offline update stick)" — so on the CM4 variant, enabling gadget mode kills the LTE uplink and the offline update stick. Tier B says "Pi 4 (2GB) OR CM4 on carrier," so the capability is not uniform across the BOM an engineer would order.

(3) BLACKOUT SCENARIO IS BACKWARDS. Tier B is PoE-only; the UPS battery HAT (~$25) is a Tier C line item. In a power cut the PoE switch is dead, so the box is dead and gadget mode is moot. A laptop cannot power it out of that: the Pi 4B is not a USB-PD sink, so it takes the host port's default advertisement, against a bare-board draw already above the USB 2.0 500 mA budget before the PoE HAT, LTE dongle and antenna. The scenario is only coherent at Tier C.

(4) "RESTORES THE FULL CONSOLE" IS OVERSTATED. Raspberry Pi's own hedge: "Not all host systems handle Raspberry Pi 4's OTG mode reliably. Ethernet and serial work best." Host-side: RNDIS has not shipped inbox since Windows 10; Windows 11 ships UsbNcm.sys for CDC-NCM, but the g_ether module the white paper demonstrates is not NCM. Driverless enumeration on an arbitrary supervisor's Windows laptop requires deliberately selecting the NCM function via configfs — not automatic.

(5) "NO BROADCAST SURFACE" IS TRUE ONLY OF RF. It converts a radio surface into a physical-access surface on a wall-mounted box in a public venue, presenting an L2/L3 link plus DHCP to whoever holds the connector. Defensible only if section 6 Layer 1 mTLS is enforced on usb0 identically to the LAN path — which must be stated, not assumed.

(6) THE PRIORITY ARGUMENT IS UNSUPPORTED BY THE REST. Soft-AP uses the onboard wireless already in the BOM, reaches multiple devices at range with no cable and no physical presence, and section 6 already commits it to WPA2/3. Gadget mode serves exactly one laptop, requires physical presence and a cable stocked on site. "Ship before soft-AP" is an opinion, not something section 3 establishes.

WHAT SURVIVES: gadget mode genuinely reaches loc8-sited directly (unlike the phone bridge), so it does recover the muster board, incident timeline and audit log; and its idle power cost is genuinely negligible. Those two parts hold.

corrected.original: A Gateway soft-AP is the right long-term answer but is currently a security hole, because the two layers that would make it safe are both unimplemented.
corrected.corrected:
A Gateway soft-AP is a plausible long-term fallback, but it is not described in any current spec and must not be ordered against as if it were. Corrected security status, per docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md §6 and ops brief §06: FOUR of five layers are unbuilt, not two. Layer 0 (network, WPA2/3) is marked "Specified" — the same status as Layer 1 (mTLS relay auth); Layer 2 (AEAD payload encryption) is "Zero lines written"; Layer 3 (operator identity) is "No operator SSO yet". Only the privacy invariant (no attendee identity store) is "True today".

Consequently the perimeter is NOT a built control that a soft-AP would be "leaning on." Today's actual perimeter is the operator laptop's hotspot (loc8-gateway.md:6; tools/mesh-bridge/README.md step 2) — an OS-provided WPA2 PSK on hardware that is not in the BOM — not the specified Gateway Layer 0, which lives on a box that does not exist yet.

The exposure is worse than "a new attack surface": tools/mesh-bridge/index.mjs listens on 0.0.0.0:8787 over plaintext ws:// with no authentication, no TLS and no origin check (the 25-byte length filter at line 28 is framing, not auth), and line 30 fans every frame out verbatim. Any client that reaches the socket therefore gets unauthenticated WRITE access — it can inject spoofed muster-safe or SOS frames — which compounds with the §06 finding that Command auto-registers unrecognised devices as on_duty_staff.

Strike the PSK claim entirely: no source describes Wi-Fi PSK derivation at claim time. The claim flow (loc8-gateway.md §5 step 2) is mDNS discovery, site naming, device-identity minting and an org key for subsequent claims; the per-shift key (step 3) is issued via HKDF at enrollment, not at claim, and is a payload key, not a Wi-Fi credential.

For the hardware spec specifically: any blackout-mode operation presumes the UPS battery HAT (~$25), a Tier C-only line item. Tier A and Tier B carry no battery, so blackout soft-AP is impossible on the pilot workhorse tier unless PoE is supplied from a UPS-backed switch — budget one or the other explicitly. Note also that §3 specifies no display and no buttons beyond a recessed factory-reset pin, so there is no on-box mechanism to surface a Wi-Fi credential to an operator; any soft-AP provisioning path needs a separate design.

The SSID-naming concern is reasonable operational hygiene but is speculative rather than source-backed, and should be labelled as a recommendation, not a finding.
corrected.why:
The verbatim quotes all verify: mesh-bridge/index.mjs:19 is exactly `new WebSocketServer({ port: PORT, host: '0.0.0.0' })` with no auth, no TLS (ws:// not wss://), no origin check — the only input constraint is the 25-byte binary length filter at line 28, which is framing, not authentication. Ops brief §03 line 488 says "Zero lines written"; §03's risk call-out line 494 says "plaintext on air and plaintext on the relay socket"; §06 line 711 marks Relay auth (mTLS) as "Specified". Section numbers §03 and §06 map correctly. But the claim is materially imprecise in five ways, three of which would mislead an engineer.

(1) "The two layers that would make it safe are both unimplemented" undercounts. The §06 table marks Network as "Specified" — the identical pill to Relay auth. Layer 3 (operator identity) is "No operator SSO yet". Four of five rows are unbuilt; only privacy invariants is "True today". So it is at minimum Layers 0, 1 and 2, not two layers.

(2) The claim's central argument — "the perimeter is today genuinely load-bearing" — presumes Layer 0 is a functioning control. Per the brief's own table it is not built. It also conflates two different perimeters: loc8-gateway.md:6 describes the current arrangement as "operator's laptop as hotspot + server + database + security perimeter," and tools/mesh-bridge/README.md step 2 confirms the phone joins "the laptop's hotspot." Today's perimeter is a laptop hotspot PSK on hardware not in the BOM. Gateway Layer 0 is WPA2/3 on a box that does not exist yet.

(3) The soft-AP appears nowhere in either cited source. Grep for soft-AP/hotspot/blackout returns nothing in loc8-gateway.md §6 and nothing in the ops brief. §03's risk call-out is headed "Say this plainly to any technical diligence" and concerns plaintext frames plus BLE never having been compiled or run on hardware. It says nothing about raising an SSID. The claim cites §03 as if it supported a soft-AP risk analysis.

(4) The PSK secondary concern is fabricated. No source describes Wi-Fi PSK derivation at claim time. loc8-gateway.md:101-108 step 2 is mDNS discovery, site naming, device-identity minting, org key for further claims; step 3 issues device certificates and the per-shift key via HKDF from enrollment. There is no Wi-Fi PSK in the lifecycle at all. This is invented detail presented as source-backed, and an engineer would design against a requirement that does not exist.

(5) It omits the only parts-ordering consequence in the entire claim. Blackout operation requires the UPS battery HAT (~$25), which is a Tier C-only line item (loc8-gateway.md:48-52). Tier A and Tier B have no battery, so the soft-AP-during-blackout scenario is physically impossible on the pilot workhorse tier unless PoE is fed from a UPS-backed switch. Separately, §3 specifies "No display, no buttons except a recessed factory-reset pin," so there is no mechanism on the box to surface a PSK to an operator.

(6) It also understates the actual risk. Line 30 forwards frames verbatim to every peer, so an unauthenticated client gets write access, not merely eavesdropping — it can inject spoofed muster-safe or SOS frames. This compounds with the §06 call-out that Command auto-registers unrecognised devices as on_duty_staff. That is a sharper and more actionable finding than "a new attack surface."

corrected.original: If a soft-AP is adopted, it must be on-demand and quadruple-gated, never automatic on mains loss.
corrected.corrected:
Soft-AP is an on-demand break-glass path, never an unconditional auto-raise. Justify it on attack-surface and misuse grounds, NOT on power — on Tier B/C hardware the energy argument does not hold.

POWER (corrected). Prior drafts claimed AP beaconing conflicts with load-shedding. That is ESP32-class reasoning and does not transfer: Tier B/C is a Pi 4 / CM4 running Linux at ~3-4 W. hostapd adds ~+0.2-0.5 W (~5-15%). A 20-min window costs ~0.1 Wh — under 1% of the ~21 Wh usable UPS HAT pack, versus ~0.02 Wh for a graceful shutdown. The cost driver is the always-on receive chain (AP mode cannot use station power save), not beaconing (~1% TX duty). Gate the AP for security and radio-conflict reasons; do not claim it threatens the shutdown reserve.

TRIGGERS. Two paths, stated honestly:
(a) Physical (SINGLE-gated by design — physical presence is the control). Use a dedicated second pinhole or a reed/magnet switch (Tier C already carries a tamper switch). Do NOT overload the factory-reset pin: it wipes the site SQLite and audit log, and a nested long-press gesture will be misfired by a stressed installer in the dark. If a shared pin is unavoidable, require a distinct NON-NESTED gesture (double-tap vs. hold) with unambiguous LED feedback.
(b) Delayed-automatic, permitted but not called "never automatic": after mains loss AND grace period >= 15 min elapsed AND zero authenticated console sessions for >= 10 min AND remaining reserve >= 6 Wh measured (not "40%"). Specify Wh, not percent: 40% of an 8 Wh pack and of a 25 Wh pack differ 3x, and cheap UPS HATs report voltage-derived SoC with 5-10% error on the flat part of the Li-ion curve. Note that the no-console condition is near-tautological when the LAN is down — it is a sanity check, not a real gate.

TIME-BOX. 20 min per activation, renewable ONLY from an authenticated session on the AP itself, hard cap 3 renewals (60 min) per outage. Unbounded renewal bounds nothing.

RADIO (new, blocking). CYW43455 does concurrent AP+STA only on the SAME band and SAME channel, ~5 clients max. Constrain soft-AP to 2.4 GHz (5 GHz master operation drags in DFS/radar obligations under FCC U-NII and EN 301 893, and CYW43455 5 GHz AP support is restricted). Consequence: on sites with a 5 GHz Wi-Fi uplink, raising the AP drops or force-migrates that uplink during the outage. Either accept and document that regression, or budget a second radio — noting §3 currently commits USB-A to the LTE dongle and USB-C to service/alt power, leaving no free port.

CRYPTO. WPA3-SAE with Hash-to-Element (H2E) ONLY — the legacy hunting-and-pecking derivation is the Dragonblood timing side-channel. PMF/802.11w required. WPA2/WPA3 transition mode explicitly DISABLED (it reopens the downgrade path). Per-device PSK = HKDF(org_key, device_id), org key never leaving an HSM, PSK independently rotatable so org-key compromise is not retroactively fatal. mTLS on loc8-relayd remains mandatory behind the AP — the AP is a transport, never an auth boundary. NOTE: §6 Layer 0 currently permits "WPA2/3" and must be amended to WPA3-SAE-only for the soft-AP interface; it cannot be cited as support for this requirement as written.

PSK DELIVERY (new, BOM impact). The PSK is unreadable through the network that is down. If soft-AP ships, the 0.9" OLED moves from optional to REQUIRED on any SKU carrying the feature (§3's "no display" must be revised), or the PSK is label-printed at claim time by the installer. Cloud-portal escrow alone fails in a true outage.

SHIPPING ORDER. phone-bridge (built) -> USB-C gadget mode -> soft-AP, the last gated behind mTLS and AEAD landing. PREREQUISITE, unverified: USB peripheral mode is SKU-dependent (Pi 4 yes via dwc2; Pi 5 USB-C is reported power-only; CM4 needs the carrier to route OTG). Confirm for the exact Tier C module before this ordering is used to defer soft-AP.
corrected.why:
The policy instinct is sound, but the claim is refuted on four independent grounds — one of them a category error about which silicon this box runs on.

1) WRONG SoC CLASS — the power premise collapses. The claim's engine is "running an AP with continuous beaconing is one of the more expensive things the SoC's wifi can do... direct conflict with the load-shedding policy." That is microcontroller reasoning (on an ESP32 the radio IS the load: SoftAP ~100-150 mA vs. modem-sleep 3-20 mA, and esp_wifi_set_ps works only in station mode, so the radio never sleeps — a 5-20x swing). But /docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md §2 specifies Raspberry Pi 4 (2GB) or CM4 (Tier B) and CM4/CM5 (Tier C), running a full Linux appliance image (§4). On a Pi-class board drawing ~3-4 W at idle-with-BLE-scanning, hostapd adds roughly +0.2 to +0.5 W — a ~5-15% adder, not a first-order term. Arithmetic against the spec'd ~$25 UPS HAT (2x 18650 ≈ 25 Wh raw, ~21 Wh usable after boost; cheaper single-cell HATs ~8-11 Wh): a 20-minute AP window costs ~0.1 Wh, i.e. ~0.5% of a 21 Wh pack or ~1% of a 10 Wh pack. A graceful Pi shutdown (~15 s at 3.5 W) needs ~0.02 Wh. So the window is ~5x the shutdown reserve but under 1% of the pack — it cannot "silently drain the reserve" as stated. What drains the reserve is the Pi being awake at all (2.4-6 h to empty regardless of the AP). Also the mechanism is misattributed: beacon TX is ~1% duty cycle; the cost is the mandatory always-on receive chain, since AP mode cannot use station power save. Conclusion: soft-AP is a legitimate thing to gate, but NOT on load-shedding grounds — that justification is quantitatively wrong by an order of magnitude on the actual hardware.

2) "QUADRUPLE-GATED" IS A MISCOUNT, and "NEVER AUTOMATIC ON MAINS LOSS" CONTRADICTS ITS OWN DETAIL. The structure is (physical trigger) OR (three ANDed conditions). On the physical path exactly ONE gate applies — a pinhole press raises the AP, full stop. On the auto path, "grace period elapsed" is a delay, not a gate; "zero console connections for N minutes" is near-tautological in the exact failure it addresses (LAN/uplink down implies no consoles attached), leaving battery threshold as the single substantive gate. The 20-min box is a limiter, not a gate. Separately, the headline says "never automatic on mains loss" while the detail specifies an automatic path whose entry condition is precisely a post-mains-loss state. Self-contradictory as written. N is also left unspecified, which is not shippable in a spec.

3) SINGLE-RADIO AP+STA CONFLICT — omitted, and it is a functional regression. The CYW43455 (Pi 3B+/4/5, CM4) can do concurrent AP+STA but only on the SAME band and SAME channel, and is limited to roughly 5 associated clients (firmware RAM). §4 lists loc8-syncd doing store-and-forward over "Ethernet/Wi-Fi/LTE". On any Wi-Fi-uplink site, raising the soft-AP forces the AP onto the uplink's channel or drops the uplink — degrading sync during the exact outage the AP exists to service. If the AP is constrained to 2.4 GHz (advisable, since 5 GHz master operation drags in DFS/radar obligations under FCC U-NII and EN 301 893, and CYW43455 5 GHz AP is notoriously restricted), then a 5 GHz uplink and the soft-AP are mutually exclusive. This belongs in the spec because the mitigation is a BOM line: a second radio. §3 already commits both USB ports (USB-A to the LTE dongle, USB-C to service/alt power), so there is no free port for a USB Wi-Fi dongle. Must be resolved before parts are ordered.

4) THE PSK HAS NO DELIVERY PATH — and this is also a BOM consequence. "Per-site PSK derived from the org key at claim (never a printed default)" is good practice but unimplementable as specified: claiming happens via Loc8 Command over the LAN (§5.2), so the PSK is only visible through the network that is down. §3 states "No display, no buttons except a recessed factory-reset pin"; the 0.9" OLED is an optional BOM line (§2 Tier B). If soft-AP ships, the OLED must move from optional to REQUIRED (or the PSK must be escrowed in the cloud org portal, which fails in a true outage, or label-printed at claim). Also, deriving every site PSK from one org key means org-key compromise retroactively yields every site's AP credential — use HKDF(org_key, device_id) with the org key never leaving an HSM, and make the PSK independently rotatable.

5) SOURCE OVERREACH. §6 Layer 0 reads "the box's Wi-Fi (when used) is WPA2/3" — it PERMITS WPA2. Citing it as support for a WPA3-SAE mandate is a misuse; the claim is stricter than its own source, so §6 must be amended rather than cited. "WPA3-SAE" is also underspecified: it must say SAE with Hash-to-Element (H2E) only — the original hunting-and-pecking derivation is the Dragonblood (2019) timing side-channel, fixed in WPA3 Release 2 — PMF/802.11w required (mandatory in SAE-only, optional in transition mode), and WPA2/WPA3 transition mode explicitly DISABLED, since transition mode reopens the downgrade path the mandate exists to close.

6) FORESEEABLE-MISUSE HAZARD on the trigger. §3 makes the factory-reset pin the only control. Overloading a destructive control (wipes the site SQLite, incidents, hash-chained audit log) with a recovery gesture, to be performed by a stressed installer in the dark during an outage, is a bad control assignment — "hold a bit longer" wipes the site.

7) "RENEWABLE" DEFEATS THE TIME-BOX. An unbounded renewal count means the 20-minute box bounds nothing. Needs a hard per-outage cap and authenticated renewal.

8) SHIPPING ORDER assumes an unverified capability. Putting USB-C gadget mode ahead of soft-AP is defensible (host-powered, physically-present-only), but peripheral mode is SKU-dependent: Pi 4 supports it via dwc2 on the USB-C port; Pi 5's USB-C is widely documented as power-only; CM4 requires the carrier to route the OTG port. Tier C is spec'd as "CM4/CM5". I could not re-verify Pi 5/CM5 peripheral-mode support before the search budget ran out — flagging it as a hard prerequisite to confirm per SKU, not as a settled fact.

Sources consulted: [ESP-IDF Wi-Fi low-power guide](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/api-guides/low-power-mode/low-power-mode-wifi.html), [ESP32 sleep modes / power consumption](https://lastminuteengineers.com/esp32-sleep-modes-power-consumption/), [ESP32 forum: power save is station-mode only](https://esp32.com/viewtopic.php?t=2026), [Infineon: CYW43455 concurrent STA+AP](https://community.infineon.com/t5/Wi-Fi-Combo/Looking-for-details-regarding-CYW43455-concurrent-Station-and-AP-operation/td-p/122651), [raspberrypi/linux #3010: AP client limit](https://github.com/raspberrypi/linux/issues/3010), [AP+STA on Raspberry Pi](https://nrlewis.dev/blog/rpi-hotspot/), [WPA3/SAE/PMF explained](https://svenvg.com/posts/wifi-explained-wpa3-sae-and-pmf/), [Microsoft: WPA3 SoftAP driver requirements](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/netcx/wificx-wpa3-softap), [Cisco WPA3 deployment guide](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/wireless/controller/9800/technical-reference/wpa3-dg.html). Local: /Users/augustusedem/Loc8/.claude/worktrees/recursing-montalcini-d59018/docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md §2 (lines 37-52), §3 (lines 65-78), §4 (lines 88-97), §5 (lines 99-118), §6 (lines 120-133).

corrected.original: Battery-state sensing is a purchasing requirement that must be written into the BOM — a UPS HAT that only supplies power without reporting to the OS makes the entire shutdown design impossible.
corrected.corrected:
The Tier C BOM line "UPS battery HAT (~$25)" is underspecified and underpriced, and should be rewritten — but not for the reason stated, and the market risk is much smaller than claimed.

Corrected line: "UPS battery HAT with I2C battery monitoring (INA219-class voltage/current, or a MAX17040-family fuel gauge); dedicated power-fail GPIO preferred. Batteries often sold separately. ~$30-55 incl. cells. MUST be verified against the chosen CM4/CM5 carrier board — most UPS HATs are 40-pin-header Pi parts and are not specified for Compute Modules. Check stack compatibility with the PoE+ HAT."

Corrections to the underlying reasoning:

1. No shutdown design currently exists in loc8-gateway.md to be made "impossible." The doc's only stated requirement is power-cut ride-through, which a pass-through UPS meets. Graceful-shutdown-on-low-battery is a sensible feature to ADD (it belongs in the §4 daemon table alongside the watchdog, and in the §8 engineering plan), and adding it is the actual justification for the interface requirement. State it as "we intend to add battery-aware shutdown, so procure accordingly," not as a broken existing dependency.

2. I2C battery monitoring is the norm, not the exception, on branded Pi UPS HATs. Waveshare's whole line (original/B/C/D/E) has it; Geekworm X728/X1200 add a fuel gauge plus an AC-power-loss GPIO. The requirement is worth writing down as a purchasing filter against no-name boards, but it does not represent a likely procurement failure.

3. A mains-present GPIO is a nice-to-have, not a hard requirement. Signed INA219 current directly distinguishes charging from discharging; ~1 s poll latency is immaterial for a UPS with minutes-to-hours of runtime. Specify it as "preferred," not mandatory.

4. Do not name MAX17048 specifically — real boards use MAX17040-family or INA219. Specify the capability (state-of-charge or voltage/current over I2C), not a part number.

5. The two higher-severity BOM risks are the ones to lead with: (a) CM4/CM5 in Tier C is not a 40-pin-header Pi, so HAT fit is carrier-board-dependent and unverified; (b) ~$25 is stale — the cheapest branded I2C-monitored board with a cell included is $29.95 and it is the Pi Zero variant, while Pi4/CM-class boards typically exclude cells (+$8-20). Budget ~$30-55. Also flag the unaddressed PoE+ HAT / UPS HAT stacking conflict inherited from Tier B.
corrected.why:
The claim is directionally right that the BOM line should carry an interface requirement, but it is refuted on its central factual premise and on three supporting points.

(1) PREMISE FAILURE — the design it claims to protect does not exist. I read the full source (/Users/augustusedem/Loc8/.claude/worktrees/recursing-montalcini-d59018/docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md) and grepped the repo for shutdown/threshold/battery/power-loss logic. There is none. The gateway doc mentions UPS exactly once (lines 50-51); the §4 systemd daemon table (loc8-meshd, relayd, sited, syncd, provisiond, watchdog/updater) contains no power-management service. The only stated requirement is that the gateway "rides out a venue power cut" — pure ride-through, which a dumb pass-through UPS satisfies. So "makes the entire shutdown design impossible" asserts a dependency of a design that has not been written. Battery-state sensing is a proposed new feature, not an unmet requirement of an existing one.

(2) MARKET CLAIM IS BACKWARDS. "Many cheap UPS HATs in the ~$25 bracket are dumb pass-throughs that expose neither" contradicts the evidence. Waveshare's entire UPS HAT line — original, B, C, D, E — ships I2C voltage/current or fuel-gauge monitoring per their own wiki/product pages. Geekworm X728/X1200 ship a Maxim fuel gauge over I2C AND an explicit AC-power-loss GPIO (GPIO26 on current X728 revisions, relocated from GPIO13 to avoid an I2S conflict). I2C battery monitoring is the market norm on branded Pi UPS HATs, not a trap to be dodged. The residual risk is real but confined to unbranded/no-name boards, so the correct remedy is a sourcing note, not the alarm level the claim uses.

(3) MAINS-PRESENT GPIO OVERSTATED. The claim demands a GPIO "so the OS learns the moment power drops rather than inferring it." INA219 reports signed current; charge-vs-discharge is a direct measurement, not an inference. At 1 Hz polling, detection latency is ~1 s against a UPS sized for minutes-to-hours of Pi runtime — operationally irrelevant. An interrupt-driven GPIO is preferable, not a hard purchasing gate.

(4) NAMED PART IS ARBITRARY. MAX17048 is not what these boards actually use — Geekworm uses MAX17040-family, Waveshare predominantly INA219. Specifying MAX17048 risks over-constraining the order.

(5) MISSES THE TWO BIGGER ORDERING HAZARDS. (a) Form factor: Tier C specifies CM4/CM5, which is not a 40-pin-header Pi. Geekworm's compatibility list reads "All RPi that use a 40-pin header" and does not cover Compute Modules; fit depends entirely on the carrier board. A HAT that physically cannot mount is a harder failure than a missing sensor. (b) Stale price: ~$25 is optimistic. The nearest branded part with I2C monitoring and a cell included is $29.95 (PiShop, Waveshare UPS HAT (C)) — and that is the Pi Zero variant. Pi 4/CM-class boards (Waveshare UPS HAT D/E, Geekworm X728) mostly exclude cells; 18650/21700 cells add roughly $8-20, putting a realistic all-in Tier C line at ~$35-55. (c) Tier C inherits the Tier B PoE+ HAT; stacking a PoE HAT and a UPS HAT contends for the same 40-pin header and stack height, unaddressed in the doc.

Per the instruction to mark substantially-right-but-imprecise claims as refuted, refuted=true with a corrected version supplied.

corrected.original: Proposed battery thresholds: shed at mains-loss, checkpoint at 50%, mesh-broadcast the warning at 25%, begin shutdown at 15%, complete by 10%.
corrected.corrected:
The staged-response STRUCTURE is sound; the numbers, the physics rationale, and the "zero new protocol" claim are not. Corrected version:

TRIGGERS (state-of-charge percentages are placeholders until calibrated; the governing triggers must be pack voltage under known load, or coulomb count, derived FROM the measured discharge curve — not SoC percentages, which are the least trustworthy quantity in the 80–20% band):

- At mains loss: enter BATTERY state; apply load-shedding; emit high-priority 'on battery' event; change the lens; block OTA. Drop the Ethernet PHY ONLY if link is already down — do not unconditionally sever the console/sync path to save a few hundred mW. ALSO: perform the WAL checkpoint (TRUNCATE) + fsync HERE, not at 50%. It costs seconds and a negligible fraction of a Wh, and this is the only placement that satisfies the stated goal of a recovery point independent of the shutdown succeeding. Optionally re-checkpoint at 50%.
- At ~50% of usable reserve: push a status event. Report remaining runtime as a RANGE with an explicit confidence caveat, not a point estimate — this is the flat-plateau region where voltage-derived SoC can be off by 20–30% of capacity.
- WARNING STAGE: pick ONE trigger, not two contradictory ones. Either ~25% of reserve OR ~20 min estimated — on a 90 min reserve these agree at ~22 min. Do NOT pair "25%" with "~15 min"; those differ by 1.5x, and as an OR the 15-min arm fires at ~17%, leaving under 2 minutes before shutdown begins and collapsing the warning stage entirely.
- At ~15%: begin controlled shutdown.
- At ~10%: shutdown complete. Justification corrected: not "SoC estimates are unreliable at the knee" (voltage discriminates BETTER at the knee, where dV/dSoC is steep) but that remaining runtime margin collapses there, load sag can trip cutoff early, and an aged or cold cell reaches cutoff sooner than a rated one.

SHUTDOWN BUDGET: specify in SECONDS, measured against the actual shutdown sequence with margin, then convert to a voltage/coulomb trigger. Do not derive it from a 5-percentage-point band in the region the spec itself calls untrustworthy.

BEFORE PARTS CAN BE ORDERED, the spec must state: pack capacity (Wh) and cell count; measured post-load-shed draw (W) with converter efficiency; measured discharge curve at the specified pack and load; low-temperature and end-of-life capacity derating for the intended enclosure environment. Note that ~90 min total reserve (implied by "50% = 45 min") back-solves to ~7.5 W — roughly an UNSHED Pi 4 — which contradicts the claim that shedding already occurred. Reconcile this before quoting the UPS HAT. docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md §2 currently specifies only "UPS battery HAT (~$25)" with no capacity, so no runtime figure in this spec is currently traceable to hardware.

MESH BROADCAST — corrected scope: byte 19 exists (packetCodec.ts:70 encode, :108 decode, PACKET_SIZE=25), so no new FRAME FORMAT is needed. But this is not "zero new protocol." Byte 19 is present only on non-fragment packet types; for 'text'/'profile' fragments, bytes 9–24 carry fragment payload and decode returns a hardcoded batteryPct: 0 (packetCodec.ts:92). Any client rule of the form "battery < 25 means the recorder is going down" MUST gate on packet type, or every text/profile fragment from every peer will read as 0% and false-alarm. Additionally, byte 19 carries a bare 0–100 integer with no "shutting down" semantic, so the interpretation, the type gate, and the operator-facing UI are new work on every phone and console. Budget that work explicitly, and consider whether an explicit status bit is cheaper than an agreed threshold convention replicated across every client.
corrected.why:
VERIFIED TRUE: byte 19 is a battery field. packetCodec.ts:70 encodes `v.setUint8(19, clamp(batteryPct))`, :108 decodes it, PACKET_SIZE=25 (line 5). The citation checks out.

Five substantive defects, in severity order.

1. ARITHMETIC CONTRADICTION (hard refutation). "50%, est. 45 min" anchors total reserve at ~90 min. Linearly: 25% = 22.5 min, 15% = 13.5 min, 10% = 9 min. The spec offers "~25% (or ~15 min estimated)" as equivalent triggers — they are not. 15 min corresponds to ~16.7%, a 1.5x disagreement. Because it is an OR, the 15-min trigger fires at ~17%, only ~2 points above the 15% shutdown trigger. The mesh-warning stage, intended to give peers ~22 min of notice, collapses to under 2 minutes of it. The second trigger destroys the stage it belongs to.

2. THE PHYSICS RATIONALE IS INVERTED. The 10% floor is justified by "SoC estimates under load are unreliable at the knee." Voltage-based SoC is least reliable in the 80–20% flat plateau, where ~400 mV spans ~60% of capacity and a 50 mV ADC error maps to 20–30% SoC error; at the knee dV/dSoC is steep, so voltage discriminates better there, not worse. Two consequences: the stated reason is backwards, and the spec's most precise-sounding output ("50%, est. 45 min") is emitted at the point of MAXIMUM SoC uncertainty. The real reason for a 10% floor is collapsing time margin, load sag, and cutoff risk — not estimator error.

3. NOT ORDERABLE AS A HARDWARE SPEC. All thresholds are percentages of an unspecified pack: no capacity (Wh), no post-shed load budget (W), no temperature derating, no end-of-life derating. The single absolute back-solves badly: 90 min total against a typical 2x18650 UPS HAT (~21.6 Wh raw, ~18 Wh after converter loss) implies ~7.5 W continuous — roughly an UNSHED Pi 4, contradicting the spec's own claim that load-shedding already happened at mains loss. Either the 45 min was measured pre-shed and mislabeled, or the pack is single-cell, or it is a guess. docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md §2 specifies only "UPS battery HAT (~$25)" with no capacity. An engineer cannot order against this.

4. THE 50% CHECKPOINT DEFEATS ITS OWN STATED GOAL. The rationale is "a clean recovery point not dependent on the shutdown going well" — which argues for checkpointing at mains loss, not after half the reserve is spent. A WAL checkpoint (TRUNCATE) + fsync costs seconds and a negligible fraction of a Wh. Deferring to 50% leaves the entire 100%-to-50% window with no clean recovery point, and that window contains exactly the sudden-death modes (cell fault, connector, HAT converter failure) the checkpoint exists to survive.

5. "ZERO NEW PROTOCOL" IS OVERSTATED AND THE REUSE HAS A LIVE TRAP. Byte 19 exists only on non-fragment types. For 'text'/'profile', bytes 9–24 are overlaid by fragment payload (encode :44–55) and decode HARDCODES `batteryPct: 0` (line 92). A peer applying "battery < 25 means the recorder is going down" to every received frame reads 0% from every text/profile fragment of every peer and false-alarms continuously. Correct reuse requires gating on packet type. Further, byte 19 is a bare 0–100 uint8 with no "shutting down" semantics — every phone and console must independently implement that interpretation. This is zero new FRAME FORMAT, not zero new protocol; the semantics, type gate, and UI are new work on every client.

MINOR: "drop the Ethernet PHY" is near-null in the dominant failure mode and harmful in the minority one. The gateway is PoE-powered (§2), so mains loss means the injector is dead and the link is already down — no PHY load to shed. If the switch is on its own UPS, dropping the PHY severs the console link and sync uplink precisely when you want to report the outage, to save a few hundred mW against a multi-watt budget. Make it conditional on link state.

Source for the SoC-plateau physics: https://zbotic.in/how-to-read-battery-state-of-charge-voltage-vs-actual-capacity/ and https://doi.org/10.3390/wevj17020083. Cold-temperature derating could not be independently verified (session web-search budget exhausted), so it is flagged as a required measurement rather than asserted numerically.

corrected.original: Structural mitigations matter more than thresholds — read-only root, a split database, and no boot-loop on flapping mains.
corrected.corrected:
Structural mitigations matter more than thresholds — read-only root, a split database, and no boot-loop on flapping mains. But the storage media, not the pragma, is the load-bearing choice, and a hash chain does not self-report loss.

READ-ONLY ROOT. Mount the OS image read-only in normal operation, pairing with the A/B image updater in §4. Writable set is one persistent partition (/var/lib/loc8) plus tmpfs overlays for /run, /tmp, /var/log, and the systemd/network state that a running system requires (machine-id, resolv.conf, DHCP leases, SSH host keys). "Only /var/lib/loc8" will not boot as stated.

MEDIA (hardware line item, not firmware). Specify industrial pSLC microSD or managed eMMC with vendor-documented power-loss protection. synchronous=FULL issues a cache-flush command that consumer SD cards may not honor, so the pragma alone buys no durability on a consumer part. Budget hold-up energy sufficient to complete a clean unmount after mains loss.

SPLIT DATABASE. Split into a low-volume audit/incident/muster DB (WAL, synchronous=FULL) and a high-volume position DB (WAL, synchronous=NORMAL). The benefit is tunable durability and reduced write amplification on the high-value data — NOT corruption isolation: both files share one FTL, and FTL metadata damage from the high-volume writer takes the whole card. Physical isolation of the audit DB requires a separate device.

AUDIT LOG INTEGRITY. Per SQLite, synchronous=FULL in WAL mode is ACID and does not lose committed transactions on power loss; this is the reason to use it. Do NOT rely on the chain "simply ending" as a loss signal — tail truncation is the known undetectable failure mode of a plain hash chain (Ma & Tsudik 2008), and a truncated chain verifies clean. Add an external anchor: periodically export the signed chain head plus entry count off-box (uplink, operator handset at muster, or a monotonic counter in separate storage) so a missing tail is detectable by comparison against the last anchor.

MAINS FLAPPING. Primary mitigation is that the SoC never power-cycles with mains at all: the battery rides through breaker resets, with a low-voltage cutoff with hysteresis triggering a clean shutdown only on genuine depletion. The boot hold-off applies solely after a depletion shutdown — require mains-present GPIO stable 60–120s before boot. Charging must be autonomous PMIC hardware that runs with the SoC powered off; otherwise a battery-percentage boot gate deadlocks (won't boot until charged, won't charge until booted). Because this device backs muster during evacuation, provide a documented physical override (long-press force-boot) that bypasses the hold-off and boots degraded/read-only, so the gateway is never unavailable during the incident it exists to record.
corrected.why:
Direction is right but three of four supporting arguments are wrong, overstated, or contain a hardware deadlock.

(1) FACTUALLY INVERTED — the hash-chain rationale. The claim says losing the tail "is at least detectable (the chain simply ends) rather than silently wrong." Tail truncation is the canonical UNDETECTABLE failure of a plain hash chain. Ma & Tsudik (eprint.iacr.org/2008/185): hash chain schemes do not defend against truncation attacks, deletion of a contiguous subset of tail-end entries. A truncated chain is internally self-consistent and verifies clean; from the file alone you cannot distinguish "lost N entries to power loss" from "nothing was written after entry N." Detection requires an external anchor the device does not control (exported chain head, remote replica, RFC 3161 TSA). The muster/incident DB is therefore silently wrong in exactly the manner the claim says it cannot be.

(2) INTERNALLY INCOHERENT. "Losing the tail is acceptable because detectable" is the argument for synchronous=NORMAL. The spec sets the audit DB to FULL. Per SQLite docs, FULL in WAL mode is ACID and specifically does NOT lose committed transactions on power loss; NORMAL is the mode that "might roll back following a power loss." The justification argues against the configuration it justifies.

(3) OVERSTATED ISOLATION. Two SQLite files on one card share one filesystem, one block layer, one FTL. The high-volume position DB at NORMAL carries most write traffic and therefore most of the power-loss exposure window; FTL metadata damage takes the whole card including the FULL database. The split buys tunable durability, not corruption isolation, but the headline sells it as corruption mitigation.

(4) fsync != durable on consumer flash. synchronous=FULL issues a cache-flush a consumer microSD may not honor. Without specifying industrial/pSLC or eMMC with power-loss protection plus hold-up energy for clean shutdown, an engineer orders a consumer card believing FULL bought durability it did not. This is a hardware line item missing from a hardware spec.

(5) DEADLOCK + SAFETY HAZARD in the boot rule. "Battery recovered above ~30% before booting" deadlocks if charge control is under application-processor software: won't boot until charged, won't charge until booted. Charging must be autonomous PMIC hardware independent of the SoC. Separately, this is a muster system; refusing to boot through a long charge window during the incident muster exists for is an availability failure needing a documented physical override. Most fundamentally, a battery-backed device should ride through flapping mains and never power-cycle; the hold-off only applies after full depletion shutdown. As written it implies the SoC cycles with mains, contradicting the presence of a battery.

(6) Minor: "only /var/lib/loc8 writable" is under-specified for systemd Linux, which needs writable /run, /tmp, /var/log, machine-id, resolv.conf, DHCP leases, SSH host keys — normally tmpfs overlays plus one persistent partition.

Surviving: read-only root + A/B updater is genuinely the highest-value mitigation, and "structure over thresholds" is sound framing.

corrected.original: Battery-only-in-Tier-C is wrong as drawn, but the fix is to split the battery into two products, not to move the Tier C HAT down.
corrected.corrected:
The structural insight is right — the tier table conflates "survive a power cut without corrupting yourself" with "keep running the site for hours," and only the second is legitimately premium — but the numbers and the ranking are wrong. Corrected version for the spec:

(1) Order of priority. The cheapest fix for power-cut corruption is not hardware. Ship read-only root (overlayfs), a small journaled data partition, and SQLite in WAL with synchronous=FULL on the industrial SD already in the Tier B BOM. That is ~$0 added BOM and removes most of the failure mode. This — not the capacitor — is the highest-value change. Holdup is the second-order belt-and-braces on top of it, and neither works without the power-fail-detect and clean-shutdown service (the same Q3/Q5 dependency the battery has).

(2) Specify holdup in energy, not seconds. Requirement: deliver ≥60 J to the 5 V rail after mains/PoE loss, sufficient for ≥10 s at the tier's worst-case shutdown load (Tier A ~1.5 W, Tier B ~4 W, Tier C ~6 W with radios up), with a power-fail interrupt asserted ≥50 ms before the rail leaves regulation. 10–15 s covers detect + checkpoint + fsync + remount-ro + halt with margin; 60–90 s is ~8x the requirement and is what breaks the budget.

(3) Sizing and cost, honestly. At 10–15 s: two 2.7 V / 20–25 F cells in series charged to ~5.0 V (derated), boosted down to ~1.8 V dropout, sized ~1.4x for the −30% end-of-life capacitance criterion, plus a supercap backup controller with balancing, inrush limiting and ORing. Budget $8–15 in parts for Tiers A/B, $12–20 for Tier C's higher load — plus one-time NRE for the board, layout and EMC retest inside the metal enclosure, which the off-the-shelf $25 UPS HAT does not carry. The original claim's own 60–90 s target sizes to two ~100–120 F cans and a $18–35 added BOM; do not quote $8–15 against that duration.

(4) Lifetime claims. Do not write "no lifecycle burden / decade-plus." EDLC life halves per 10 °C of internal temperature rise and doubles per 0.1 V of derating; a sealed fanless wall box runs 15–25 °C above ambient. Specify instead: charge to ≤85% of rated cell voltage, place the bank away from the PoE converter and SoC, rate the enclosure's internal ambient, and add a monthly self-test that measures actual holdup energy and reports degradation over the mesh. Expect 5–10 years at a controlled internal ambient, less in a hot riser. The advantage over Li-ion that does survive scrutiny is failure mode (graceful capacitance fade, no thermal runaway) and no UL1642/IEC62133 cell qualification — not immortality.

(5) Regulatory wording. UN 38.3 applies to all transport modes, not air alone; air adds ICAO/IATA packing instructions and state-of-charge limits, and a single small cell installed in equipment ships under UN 3481 / PI 967 Section II (marking and training, not prohibition). Supercapacitors are not exempt by nature: EDLCs above 0.3 Wh are UN 3499 Class 9 (asymmetric types UN 3508), with special-provision exceptions for small/installed/short-circuit-protected units. A 10–15 s bank stores well under 0.3 Wh and should fall outside scope, but state this as "verify against the DGR edition in force at order time," not as settled.

(6) Tier split. Non-optional capacitive holdup, sized per (2), in every tier including A — but note that Tier C's soldered eMMC already gives it the best corruption resistance, so the urgency is greatest in Tiers A and B, which is the opposite of how the table is drawn today. The full UPS battery HAT stays a paid Tier C / Tier B+ option, and its spec must state that it keeps the gateway alive but not the PoE switch: without a UPS in the comms cabinet the box rides the outage with BLE mesh only, no LAN and no consoles.
corrected.why:
Directionally right, quantitatively wrong, and wrong in its priority ranking. Checked against the actual spec at /Users/augustusedem/Loc8/.claude/worktrees/recursing-montalcini-d59018/docs/hardware/loc8-gateway.md §2 and re-derived the energy budget. Note: WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted (200/200), so distributor pricing could not be independently verified — under the "default to refuted if unsubstantiated" rule, the $8–15 figure is an unsourced estimate presented as a costed BOM line.

1) MISSING UNIT — the spec as written cannot be ordered against. "60–90 seconds of holdup" is not a specification; holdup is energy (J or Wh), not time. Time is only meaningful with a stated load current at a stated rail. Nothing in the claim says whether the 90 s is against a Pi Zero 2 W at 0.9 W (Tier A) or a CM5 with dual BLE radios and an LTE dongle (Tier C) — a ~6x spread in the part you would buy.

2) THE ARITHMETIC DOES NOT CLOSE AT $8–15. Re-derived, using the tiers in the spec. Tier B is a Pi 4 (2GB) + PoE+ HAT; Pi 4 idle is ~2.7–3.5 W at the 5 V rail and a power-fail shutdown is not idle (flush, fsync, unmount, radios still up), so 4 W average is the honest design point, with peaks higher. Also note that when PoE drops, the HAT's 48V→5V converter is dead, so the holdup circuit must carry the entire 5 V load through a boost stage — an ideal-diode-only design on the 5 V rail extracts almost nothing (½C(5.0²−4.75²) ≈ 1.2 J per farad).
  • 90 s × 4 W = 360 J at the load; at ~85% average boost efficiency from a decaying rail, ~424 J must come out of the cap.
  • Two 2.7 V cells in series, charged to 5.0 V (already voltage-derated for life), converter dropout 1.8 V: usable = ½C(5.0²−1.8²) = 10.9 J per farad of stack. → 39 F stack → 78 F per cell.
  • EDLC end-of-life is conventionally −30% capacitance / 2x ESR, so the design value is 78/0.7 ≈ 110 F per cell. Cold-ambient ESR rise eats more headroom.
  So the claim's own 60–90 s target lands on two 2.7 V / ~100–120 F cans (each a snap-in can roughly AA-to-C sized), plus a supercap charger/backup controller with cell balancing (LTC3350 / LTC3128 / MAX38888 / TPS61094 class, $3–8 even in volume), inrush limiting for a 39 F bank that looks like a dead short at cold start, ORing, a power-fail comparator into a GPIO, plus PCB area, assembly and test. That is realistically $18–35 added BOM at pilot volume, not $8–15 — and it is a custom board with NRE (schematic, layout, respin, EMC retest inside the Tier C metal enclosure, firmware), whereas the $25 Tier C UPS HAT it is being compared against is an off-the-shelf module with zero NRE. The $8–15 vs $25 comparison is a category error: raw cell cost versus finished-module price. The only shipping supercap UPS for a Pi that advertises exactly this window — Juice4halt, "60 seconds backup time including a safe shutdown" — is a finished product retailing well above the $25 Li-ion HAT, which is the market's answer to whether 60 s of supercap holdup is the cheap option.
  Where $8–15 IS correct is at ~10–15 s: 12 s × 5 W worst case = 60 J / 0.85 = 71 J → 6.5 F stack → ~13 F/cell → ~19 F/cell after EOL derate → two 20–25 F cells (~$1–3 total) plus a small backup-controller IC. The claim's dollar figure and its duration figure are internally inconsistent by roughly 6–8x.

3) THE 60–90 s REQUIREMENT IS ITSELF ~10x OVERBUILT, and cost/volume/inrush scale linearly with it. The stated job — detect loss, checkpoint, flush, remount read-only, power down — is a WAL checkpoint and fsync of a small SQLite site DB plus a halt. On eMMC that is seconds, not a minute and a half. Industrial holdup designs budget 2–10 s for exactly this. Specifying 90 s makes the part ~8x larger than the function requires and is what pushes it out of the price window the claim says it fits into.

4) "NO THERMAL/LIFECYCLE BURDEN, DECADE-PLUS SERVICE LIFE" IS OVERSTATED. KEMET/Yageo's own life model: EDLC life doubles for each 10 °C of temperature reduction and each 0.1 V of voltage derating — which means it halves per 10 °C hotter. Typical EDLC endurance ratings are 1,000–2,000 h at 65–70 °C at rated voltage; extrapolating 1,000 h @ 65 °C to 25 °C gives ~16,000 h ≈ 1.8 years at rated voltage. Ten-plus years is reachable only by combining voltage derating with a genuinely cool internal ambient. This box is sealed, fanless, wall-mounted, with a PoE converter and a CPU inside, often in a plant room or above a ceiling tile — i.e. the exact thermal environment the claim invokes to argue against Li-ion. The supercap inherits a version of the same periodic-replacement burden. It is still much better than Li-ion (degradation is graceful — capacitance fade shortens holdup rather than venting), but "no lifecycle burden" is not supportable and must be replaced by explicit derating, placement and self-test requirements. "Near-unlimited cycles" is true (500k–1M) and irrelevant: holdup events are rare; calendar/thermal life is the binding constraint.

5) THE REGULATORY CLAIMS ARE STATED MORE CONFIDENTLY THAN THE SOURCES SUPPORT, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. UN 38.3 is not an "air-freight rule" — it is a transport-test requirement in the UN Model Regulations adopted across air, sea and road/rail; air adds the ICAO/IATA packing instructions and state-of-charge limits on top. And a single small Li-ion cell installed in equipment ships under UN 3481 / PI 967 Section II, which is a marking-and-training obligation, not the freight catastrophe the steelman implies. Conversely, supercapacitors are not regulation-free: EDLCs above 0.3 Wh energy storage capacity are UN 3499 Class 9 (asymmetric/Li-ion capacitors UN 3508), subject to special provisions that except small, installed, or short-circuit-protected units. The 90 s bank derived above stores ~0.19 Wh at full charge — probably under the threshold, but "probably" is the honest word, it must be checked against the current DGR edition, and a Tier B+ "hours" bank would clear it comfortably. Neither the exemption nor the burden should be asserted in a spec without a citation to the edition in force.

6) "SINGLE HIGHEST-VALUE CHANGE TO THE BOM" IS LIKELY FALSE. The sharpest version of the structural argument is one the claim under-uses: Tier C is the only tier with soldered eMMC ("no SD to corrupt"), so as drawn, the tier with the best storage resilience also gets the battery, while Tiers A and B — the SD-card tiers actually vulnerable to power-loss corruption — get nothing. But the cheapest fix for that is not a capacitor. Read-only root via overlayfs, a small journaled data partition, SQLite in WAL with synchronous=FULL, and the industrial SD already budgeted at $10 in Tier B eliminate most power-cut corruption for ~$0 of added BOM. Holdup is the correct second-order belt-and-braces, not the top line. Two further checks on the claim's own logic: (a) its argument that a battery without the Q3/Q5 software is "a promise you fail" applies verbatim to the supercap — without power-fail detection and a clean shutdown path, a cap is a part that does nothing; (b) on a PoE box the switch dies in the same outage, so Tier C's "keep running for hours" keeps a gateway alive with no LAN and no consoles unless the comms cabinet is also backed. The BLE mesh still works so it isn't fatal, but the premium tier's value proposition depends on an assumption the spec never states, and in many venues a rack UPS on the switch already delivers it at zero BOM.
