Sources consulted: [Juice4halt supercapacitor UPS for Raspberry Pi](https://www.juice4halt.com/) (60 s backup including safe shutdown; supercap, −40 to +85 °C, no maintenance); [KEMET/Yageo supercapacitor life expectancy](https://yageogroup.com/en/us/technical-resources/supercapacitor-life-expectancy.html) (life doubles per 10 °C reduction or 0.1 V derating; EOL by capacitance loss / ESR rise). Distributor pricing and IATA DGR text could not be retrieved (search budget exhausted / sites blocked fetch), so those figures are flagged rather than relied on.

corrected.original: Both documents make an unqualified 'survives power cuts' claim directly above a tier table where only the top tier does — an accuracy defect that will be falsified in front of a customer.
corrected.corrected:
Substantially right that an unqualified power-cut claim needs fixing, but wrong on tier attribution, wrong on adjacency, misattributed on precedent, and the recommended fix is itself unsafe. Corrected version:

DEFECT: Both documents assert power-cut survival as an unconditional Gateway property, twice each and never qualified — loc8-gateway.md line 10 ("survives power cuts") and line 20 (§1 table: "Screwed to a wall, on PoE, battery-backed"); loc8-ops-brief.html line 567 (lede, verbatim) and line 575 (same table row in prose). Only Tier C specifies a UPS battery HAT. The §1/line-575 table row is the stronger instance, since it states the property as a bare Gateway characteristic; the ledes are separated from the tier tables by a full section (md) and by prose plus a figure (brief), so "directly above" is inaccurate and the fix must be document-wide rather than a re-ordering.

CORRECT TIER PICTURE — the axis is self-contained survival, not tier rank:
- Tier A: no power-cut provision.
- Tier B: PoE+ powered, so it continues through a power cut whenever the PoE switch is on a UPS — common where a rack already feeds cameras and access control. No on-board battery; survival is inherited from site infrastructure, not bought with the unit.
- Tier C: the only tier that survives independent of the venue. But even here the UPS HAT backs only the appliance. The PoE switch, the LAN and the control-room console are unbacked, so through a real power cut a Tier C site degrades to a BLE mesh node plus local SQLite — mesh and audit logging continue; console-over-mTLS and uplink do not, unless switch and console are separately backed. The headline "control-room backbone that survives power cuts" is therefore overstated at every tier, Tier C included.

DO NOT ADOPT the proposed wording "every tier can truthfully claim survives power cuts, meaning comes back healthy." Tiers A and B boot from microSD, and both documents sell Tier C on "soldered eMMC (no SD to corrupt)" — the docs already concede that unexpected power loss risks corruption on the lower tiers. Tier B's "Industrial microSD" mitigates but does not eliminate this; Tier A has no such qualifier. Clean-restart survival for A/B requires an explicit engineering commitment (read-only root, power-loss-safe filesystem, or eMMC), not a copy change.

SUGGESTED HONEST FRAMING: lede — "works with zero internet, and rides out power cuts when specified with the UPS option." §1 table row — "Screwed to a wall, on PoE; battery-backed at Tier C or from a UPS-backed switch." Add a per-tier power-resilience row stating what continues and what stops.

ALSO FIX, same table, higher order-impact: loc8-gateway.md line 37 headlines Tier B at "$95-120" while its own six line items sum to $93-113 (35+20+10+8+15+5 to 45+20+10+8+25+5). The brief already carries the corrected $93-113 silently, so the md is stale. Unflagged arithmetic error in the table parts get ordered from.

OPEN, UNVERIFIED: the "~$25 UPS battery HAT" carries no hold-up time and no load figure. Cheap Pi-class UPS HATs are often sized for graceful shutdown rather than sustained runtime, and a CM4/CM5 with dual BLE radios draws more than a bare Pi. Specify a required hold-up time before ordering. I could not verify specific products — this session's web search budget was exhausted (200/200), so this point rests on document-internal evidence and general engineering practice only.

SOURCING NOTE: the brief flags three arithmetic errors in the STRATEGY DOCUMENTS' TAM table (§08 line 780) and a contradiction in the repo's CHANGELOG.md lines 10 vs 87 (§01 line 267, §09 line 807) — not, as claimed, in its own TAM table or its own CHANGELOG. The repo-wide honesty precedent holds; the citation does not.
corrected.why:

Only Tier C carries a UPS battery HAT (md line 50, brief line 654). So a real defect exists. But the claim is imprecise on four points and its remedy is wrong, so per instructions: refuted=true with correction.

(1) "DIRECTLY ABOVE A TIER TABLE" IS FALSE IN BOTH DOCS. In the md the pitch is lines 9-11 and the tier BOM is §2 line 31 — the whole of §1 intervenes. In the brief the lede is line 567 and the Build tiers table is ~line 650 — a Status callout, two paragraphs and a full-width SVG figure intervene, roughly 80 lines. This is a document-wide consistency defect, not a juxtaposition defect. The §1/line-575 "battery-backed" table row is the stronger instance and should carry the argument.

(2) "ONLY THE TOP TIER DOES" IS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. It understates Tier B: Tier B is PoE+ powered (md line 42), so its power originates at the network switch. Where the comms rack is UPS-backed — routine practice where a PoE switch already feeds cameras and access control — a Tier B gateway rides through a power cut with no battery HAT. The true distinction is SELF-CONTAINED power-cut survival independent of site infrastructure, not tier rank. This also plausibly explains the §1 wording: "on PoE, battery-backed" likely means PoE-fed from a battery-backed rack, a coupled claim rather than a per-unit one. It simultaneously overstates Tier C: a UPS HAT keeps the Pi alive but does nothing for the PoE switch, the LAN, or the control-room console. Per md §5 step 4 and the brief's own topology figure, Command attaches over mTLS LAN — so through a genuine venue power cut even Tier C degrades to a mesh node plus local SQLite. The BLE mesh and audit logging survive; the "control-room backbone" does not, unless switch and console are separately backed. The headline is therefore overstated at EVERY tier, including C.

(3) THE PROPOSED FIX WOULD ITSELF BE AN ACCURACY DEFECT — the most serious problem, given an engineer orders parts against this. The claim recommends that "every tier can then truthfully claim 'survives power cuts' meaning comes back healthy." Tiers A and B boot from microSD. Both documents sell Tier C precisely on "soldered eMMC (no SD to corrupt)" (md line 49, brief line 654) — i.e. the docs themselves concede that unexpected power loss risks filesystem corruption on the lower tiers. Tier B specifies "Industrial microSD," which mitigates but does not eliminate this; Tier A specifies a plain 32GB microSD with no such qualifier. The brief does not flag errors in "its own" TAM table or "its own" CHANGELOG. §08 line 780 attributes three arithmetic errors to "our own strategy documents" (a separate TAM table); the contradiction is in the repo's CHANGELOG.md lines 10 vs 87, flagged at §01 line 267 and §09 line 807. corrected.original: The blackout case is where the product's core positioning is most sharply true, which is the strategic argument for treating it as first-class rather than a tier upsell.
corrected.corrected:
Blackout is a strong secondary case, not the sharpest expression of the positioning, and battery backup should be made first-class for a narrower and more defensible reason.

Per §08, the defensible claim is network-independent live location: Loc8 is the only phone-based live team map with SOS that needs no special hardware and keeps working when the network is congested, jammed or dead. §08 explicitly cautions that Motorola MOTOTRBO radios do ship GPS and guard-tour platforms do offer live GPS, so "radio carries voice but no position" must not be used as a premise. The positioning is sharpest in the RF-denied cases §01 actually names — jammed or overloaded cell site, basement, tunnel, ship, crush, evacuation — where cellular and satellite paths both fail, the mesh works, and the Gateway is still on mains power and needs no additional part. A mains blackout is the one scenario that leaves battery-powered handhelds and satellite-backed lone-worker devices comparatively intact while handing Loc8 a new hardware dependency, so it is the weaker, not the stronger, case.

The Gateway is also not the only Loc8 component affected. Per gateway spec §5 and §6, consoles attach over the venue LAN via mTLS; a total mains failure takes down the PoE switch, the LAN and any desktop console. Battery-backing the Gateway alone preserves the site database, the BLE mesh role and the HQ uplink, but not the on-site console — so the backup scope must be stated explicitly (Gateway only, or Gateway plus a console path such as gateway Wi-Fi AP mode to a laptop or phone).

Nor is it the only mechanism by which HQ learns of an outage: §7 already surfaces staleness ("last synced 00:40") and §1/§8 preserve any guard phone as a spare gateway bridging to a laptop console. The accurate statement is that a battery-backed Gateway plus LTE is what lets HQ receive a positive mains-lost event and an uninterrupted feed, rather than inferring an outage from silence — and only if the serving cell survives the outage, which an in-building DAS or small cell will not.

Ordering consequences that must be fixed before parts are bought:
- Tier B's BOM sums to $93-113, not the "$95-120" in the §2 header. Correct the header.
- Tier B is described as "battery-backed" in §1 and in the brief's §06 lede, but carries no battery line item; battery appears only in Tier C. Either add it to Tier B or remove the claim.
- A ~$25 single-18650 UPS HAT yields ~12.6 Wh nameplate and ~10 Wh usable at 5 V. That is ~2.8 h for Pi 4 + BLE, ~1.8 h once the USB LTE modem shares the rail, and ~1.5 h for Tier C's dual-BLE configuration. It is a graceful-shutdown budget, not "rides out a venue power cut." Specify a hold-up target: a 6-hour event-length hold with LTE needs ~39 Wh of cells (~3x 18650), 8 hours ~52 Wh, which changes the price, the enclosure and the lithium-shipping posture.
- The LTE dongle sharing USB-A does co-terminate with the Gateway, but it cuts shared runtime by roughly 35% and its transmit peaks exceed its average; size the pack against peak-inclusive average draw, not idle.
- Making battery and LTE standard puts Tier B at ~$143-163, which invalidates the "~$100 BOM -> sell at $299-399" line in §2; restate the economics.
- Remove the §2 line "a venue with no wifi and jammed cell still appears live on HQ's dashboard" — a jammed cell also jams the LTE dongle.
- Do not assert that the phone mesh is "completely unaffected." §08 marks real BLE mesh between physical phones as Open and the native module as never built on hardware, and §09 lists full-shift battery drain as an unrun gate.
corrected.why:
The claim's conclusion (make battery backup first-class rather than a Tier C upsell) is defensible, but nearly every load-bearing premise is wrong, unsupported, or contradicted by the cited sources.

1. MISATTRIBUTED SOURCE. The claim cites §08 "The framing sentence" in support, but §08 exists specifically to retract the premise the claim uses. §08 states: "Be careful with the competitive claim. Motorola MOTOTRBO radios DO ship GPS, and guard-tour platforms DO offer live GPS." The claim's detail restates the retracted cover/§01 line ("radio still carries voice but no position"). §08's defensible formulation is network-independent live location — "congested, jammed or dead" NETWORK — which is about comms failure, not mains failure.

2. "THE GATEWAY IS THE ONLY LOC8 COMPONENT THAT FAILS" IS FALSE per the gateway spec. §5 step 4 and §6 Layer 1 put consoles on the venue LAN over mTLS. In a total mains failure the PoE switch, the LAN, and any desktop Command console are also dead. Battery-backing only the Gateway yields a box that keeps feeding HQ while the on-site control room has no console — an argument for a different backup scope than the one claimed.

3. "ONLY MECHANISM BY WHICH HQ EVER LEARNS" IS FALSE. Gateway spec §7 already gives HQ a staleness signal ("last synced 00:40"); §1 and §8 both preserve "every guard phone remains a spare gateway" with the laptop-console fallback, so a guard phone on its own cellular data is a second path. The narrower true statement is that a battery-backed box is what lets HQ receive a positive "mains lost" event and a continuous feed, rather than inferring an outage from silence.

4. THE STRATEGIC PREMISE IS INVERTED. §01's named archetypes are a crush, an evacuation, a jammed or overloaded cell site, a basement, a tunnel, a ship. Mains blackout is not among them; "archetypal instance" is the claim's own extrapolation. A blackout is in fact where the phone-mesh edge is comparatively WEAKEST: battery-powered handhelds and satellite-based lone-worker devices (which §01 itself acknowledges — "cellular or satellite") are largely unaffected, while Loc8 acquires a NEW hardware dependency. Positioning is sharpest in the RF-denied cases (jammed/congested cell, basement, tunnel, ship) where every cellular and satellite path fails, the mesh works, and the Gateway is still on mains needing no new part.

5. "PHONE MESH IS COMPLETELY UNAFFECTED" IS STATED AS FACT BUT IS UNPROVEN in the same document. §08's status table marks "Real BLE mesh between physical phones" as Open (repo contradicts itself) and "Native module compiled and run" as "Never built on hardware." §09 lists "battery drain over a full shift" as an unrun gate. Presenting this as an operating property in a parts-ordering document is exactly the marketing-as-measured failure mode.

6. ARITHMETIC/HARDWARE ERRORS THAT AFFECT THE ORDER.
- Gateway spec §2 header says Tier B is "$95–120"; its own table sums to $93–113 (35+20+10+8+15+5 / 45+20+10+8+25+5). The ops brief ledger has $93–113. The spec contradicts itself.
- The $25 UPS HAT does not deliver an event-length hold-up. A $25-class Pi UPS HAT is a single 18650: 3.4 Ah x 3.7 V = 12.6 Wh nameplate, ~10 Wh usable at 5 V after boost efficiency (~88%) and depth-of-discharge (~90%). Pi 4 + BLE ~3.5 W = 2.8 h; with the USB LTE modem ~5.5 W = 1.8 h; Tier C dual-BLE + LTE ~6.5 W = 1.5 h. A 6-hour hold-up with LTE needs ~39 Wh (~3x 18650); 8 hours ~52 Wh. So the currently specified part is a graceful-shutdown budget, not "rides out a venue power cut."
- "Powered from the Gateway's USB-A, so it survives exactly as long as the Gateway does" is trivially true as co-termination but misleading as a runtime statement: putting the modem on the same rail cuts shared runtime roughly 35%. Peak TX current on a USB LTE modem also exceeds its average, which the "exactly as long" framing elides.
- Tier B already asserts a battery it does not budget: §1's table and brief §06 say "battery-backed" and the spec's one-sentence summary says "survives power cuts," yet battery appears only in Tier C's BOM ($180–240). An engineer ordering Tier B against this spec receives no battery.
- Cost consequence unabsorbed: battery ($25) + LTE ($25) on Tier B gives ~$143–163, breaking §2's "~$100 BOM at Tier B -> sell at $299–399" economics; sizing the battery for real event-length runtime pushes it further.

7. UPLINK ASSUMED, NOT ESTABLISHED. The claim assumes the LTE dongle reaches HQ during the blackout. In an area-wide outage the serving macro cell may be on limited battery, and in-building DAS/small cells serving a venue are mains-powered and die with the venue. Gateway spec §2's own LTE pitch is self-contradictory ("no wifi and jammed cell still appears live" — a jammed cell jams the dongle). I could not externally verify carrier backup-power obligations this session (web search budget exhausted), so any resiliency claim should be stated as conditional rather than assured.

8. TWO INCUMBENT FAILURE MODES LIKELY MISSTATED (not externally verified this session): RTLS beacon tags are typically coin-cell BLE devices that survive a blackout — it is the anchors/readers and server that fail; and guard-tour capture is normally offline-buffered on the handheld against passive NFC/RFID tags, so it keeps recording — §01's actual criticism is that it "only looks backwards," not that it is power-dependent.

Verdict: the recommendation survives; the argument offered for it does not. It should be rewritten around continuity of the site record and a stated hold-up target, not around a claim of unique positioning that the brief's own §08 disclaims.
